case_summary.text: Excise & Custom : Merely because Chartered Accountant's certificate does not give details of costing etc., will not turn it into a bad certificate when it is clearly stated by Chartered Accountant that assessee had not passed on burden to clients; it is valid for proving that there is no unjust enrichment
TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee was providing business support service to its AE, company engaged in providing technical inspection and certification services could not be accepted as comparable

INCOME TAX/CHARTERED ACCOUNTANT ACT : Where respondent-Chartered Accountant had assisted various companies in availing credit facilities of huge amounts from various banks by issuing false certificates, in view of fact that respondent was naturally aware that issuing such certificates was a fraud on banks as such public and financial institutions rely upon certificates of professionals as part of its due diligence, respondent was thus reprimanded in accordance with section 21(6)(b)

TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee had reimbursed expenses to its AE and in certificate given by AE had given details of services provided by AEs and also reimbursement expenses incurred by assessee and paid to AE, Assessing Officer was not justified in making TP adjustment

TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee had claimed deduction for payments made by its AEs contending same to be reimbursement of out of pocket expenses incurred by AEs on behalf of assessee, since auditors in audit report had certified financial statements to be true after carrying out verification on test check basis and TPO had not pointed out any discrepancy in supporting documents furnished by assessee, no adjustment would be permitted

INCOME TAX/CHARTERED ACCOUNTANT ACT : Where respondent-Chartered Accountant had assisted various companies in availing credit facilities of huge amounts from various banks by issuing false documents certifying valuation of work undertaken and completed by accused companies and he was naturally aware that issuing such certificates in absence of proper valuation was a fraud on banks as such public and financial institutions rely upon certificates of professionals as part of its due diligence,

INTERNATIONAL TAXATION : Where assessee, a UK based company, provided services to its Indian AE pertaining to human resources, finance, legal and compliance and conducting of internal audit assurance work and received certain sum with respect to said services, since services provided by assessee were merely for enabling and assisting Indian AE in making correct decisions on certain aspects and did not result in transfer of technical knowledge,

TRANSFER PRICING : No transfer pricing addition should be made in relation to reimbursement of out-of-pocket expenses to AE, where auditors in audit report had certified financial statements to be true and correct after carrying out verification on test check basis and TPO had not pointed out any defect/discrepancy in bills/supporting documents furnished by assessee which constituted 78 per cent of out of pocket expenses reimbursed by assessee to its AE

INTERNATIONAL TAXATION : Where assessee, a UK based company, received certain sum for providing services to its Indian AE pertaining to human resources, finance, legal and compliance and conducting of internal audit assurance work, since said services were merely for enabling and assisting Indian AE in making correct decisions on certain aspects and did not result in transfer of technical knowledge, know-how, skill etc., 'make available' condition provided under article 13(4)(c) remained non-compliant and, thus, receipts would not fall within definition of FTS as provided under article 13(4) of India - UK DTAA
ITAT affirms sanctity of CA certificate; denies to impose penalty for TDS default relying upon such certificate
Auditor's certificate can't be a substitute for TP study to benchmark international transaction
ITAT affirms sanctity of CA certificate; no disallowance for TDS default relying upon such certificate

TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee had entered into an agreement with its AE for rendering advisory services, and Tribunal found, on basis of documentary evidence on record that there was no considerable difference between services actually rendered by AE and those specified in agreement, such factual findings could not be attacked on ground of perversity

TRANSFER PRICING : Where marketing support services costs, duly certified by Independent Accountant, had been allocated to assessee and same had been absorbed by making payment to AEs for services rendered by AEs, then action of lower authorities in determining ALP of such services at Rs. Nil is unwarranted

INTERNATIONAL TAXATION/TRANSFER PRICING : Where a sum was claimed to be paid by assessee for internal audit services received from its Associated Enterprise and assessee-company submitted that it did not have any internal audit department and, hence, internal audit services were required to be availed in order to have an internal audit system commensurate with its size and nature of business and even benefits received from such internal audit services were explained by assessee, authorities below were not justified in making addition on ground that no tangible benefit was derived by assessee
ST : Certificate issued by Chartered Accountant is alone a valid piece of evidence without corroboration

EXCISE/ST/VAT : Certificates issued by qualified professionals like Cost Accountants, Chartered Accountants, Chartered Engineers should not be brushed aside merely because corroborative evidence not produced

TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee company was engaged in export of customers electronic data to its AEs, a comparable company, earning revenue from operation which mainly included activities of certification, recertification, safety audit, HSE management system for offshore and onshore oil and gas facilities, third-party inspection of equipment and installation in hydrocarbon and other sectors, could not be accepted as valid comparable

No TP additions for reimbursement of exp. to AE if auditors verified financial statements on a test check basis: ITAT
TPO can’t ignore certificates issued by third-party vendors of AE confirming price charged from assessee: ITAT

TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee-company had imported raw materials from third party vendors under an agreed arrangement claiming that said transaction was at arm's length price by demonstrating that rate charged by assessee-company was lower than market price by providing certificate obtained from third party vendors but TPO rejected said certificates as same were signed by vendors which were also AEs of assessee, since certificates issued by third party vendors whereby, they confirmed that price they had charged to assessee-company was lower than original price, could not be ignored by holding that these certificates were issued by AEs, matter required remission to Assessing Officer/TPO to examine benchmarking analysis furnished by assessee

TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee was providing engineering and technical assistance services in field of fertilizer, petro-chemical, refinery and oil & gas industries etc., a company whose activities were confined to recertification, safety audit and HSE management systems for offshore and onshore oil & gas facilities and it also undertook third party inspection of equipments and installations in hydrocarbon and other quality sensitive sectors of industry, being dissimilar to assessee's profile, could not be accepted as comparable

The same will have to be benchmarked to an external comparable for determining Arm's Length Price. Auditor's certificate cant be substitute for Transfer Pricing study (TP Study) even though such certificate as basis for

TPO can’t question service provided to AE; his jurisdiction is limited only to benchmark transaction u/s 92C: ITAT

TRANSFER PRICING : Under TP Regulations what TPO has to determine is whether services which has been provided by AEs were at ALP and analysis of nature of services and benefits arising to assessee on availing such services was beyond scope of transfer pricing provision
TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee was rendering project support services to AE, a company engaged in providing custom/excise and service tax related services, was not acceptable as comparable

ST : CA certificate certifying that assessee had not received any service tax from service recipient and such fact had been verified and confirmed by department, burden of unjust enrichment stood discharged and assessee was eligible for refund

INCOME TAX/CHARTERED ACCOUNTANTS ACT : Where Council of ICAI found Chartered Accountant guilty of professional misconduct for having issued two Utilisation Certificates without verification and later, it was found that said certificates were forged and recommended to High Court that his name be removed from Register of Members for a period of one year, since proceedings against respondent had remained pending for about 19 years and there was no history of any other complaint or allegation of

TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee paid information technology consultancy charges to its AE and TPO determined ALP of said payment at nil holding that no such services were rendered by AE, since there was an agreement entered into by AE for provision for these services and bills raised on assessee by AE demonstrated rendering of IT services,

TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee was availing specialized services which were provided by AEs from common pool and evidences in this regard had been filed by assessee, there was no merit in order of Assessing Officer in questioning availment of services and benefit derived by assessee

TRANSFER PRICING : When Assessing Officer makes reference to TPO for determining ALP of international transaction of services availed by assessee from its AE, job of TPO is to consider actual transaction of rendition of service and find out its ALP, however, TPO has no jurisdiction to examine whether service was needed or is duplicate in nature or stewardship or shareholder service because such an exercise falls in exclusive domain of Assessing Officer

IT/ILT : Where assessee had already placed on record, details of employees rendering IS services and complete details of tickets raised during year which lend credence to fact that services, were in fact, availed by assessee and quantum of external cost as well as internal cost were certified by external auditor, TPO was not justified in making T.P. adjustment on ground that assessee failed to submit substantial evidence to substantiate its claim of internal cost
ITAT remanded matter back to TPO to examine rendition of services by AE to assessee

IT/ILT: In case of assessee rendering marketing support services to AE, a company engaged in procurement related advisory services and financial audit for projects in India and abroad, could not be accepted as comparable

TRANSFER PRICING: Where assessee availed certain intra-group services from its AE and Commissioner (Appeals) computed ALP of such services being 30 per cent of value, since incurring of expenditure by assessee was not in dispute and only reason given by Revenue authorities was that assessee did not need such services as same were duplicative and that assessee did not file sufficient details to establish that it received some benefit, order of Commissioner (Appeals) was to be set aside and AO/TPO
ITAT remanded matter to verify genuineness of certificate issued u/s 195(3) to grant relief to assessee

TRANSFER PRICING : Authority of TPO is to conduct a transfer pricing analysis to determine ALP and not to determine whether there is a service or not from which assessee benefits as that aspect of exercise is left to Assessing Officer therefore, TPO restoring matter to file of Assessing Officer to find out as to whether any service is rendered by AE to assessee and from which assessee has drawn any benefit from it is not correct

TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee claimed that services rendered to its AE were in nature of engineering design services, but TPO had characterized services rendered by assessee to AE as ITES/BPO services, without assigning any reasons as to how services rendered by assessee were coming within ambit of ITES, issue needed to be restored to file of TPO for de novo consideration and to decide issue of characterization of services rendered by assessee to its AE

TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee paid FTS and MCC to its foreign AEs for availing certain services and TPO determined ALP of said payments at Nil on view that assessee did not furnish any evidence to substantiate its claim of receipt of services, matter was to be restored to AO/TPO in view of Tribunal's order in assessee's own case for previous year wherein it was held that TPO should not dispute that services were rendered by AEs

TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee-company made payment towards professional services to its AE and TPO held that no benefit was derived by assessee-company from receipt of professional services and no services were received, since assessee had filed description of services received in several forms and also filed copies of descriptive evidence in respect of receipt of services, matter was to be remanded back

IT/ILT: Authority of TPO is limited to conducting transfer pricing analysis for determining ALP of an international transaction and not to decide if such services exist or benefits did accrue to assessee

TRANSFER PRICING: Where TPO held that assessee failed to prove nature of services rendered by AE and treating entire payments made to AE as an adjustment added it to income of assessee, in view of evidence already available on record and additional evidence now filed before Tribunal to prove type of services rendered by AE, matter was to be remanded back to TPO for adjudication afresh

TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee paid information technology consultancy charges to its AE and TPO determined ALP of said payment at nil holding that no such services were rendered by AE, since there was an agreement entered into by AE for provision for these services and bills raised on assessee by AE demonstrated rendering of IT services, impugned adjustment made by TPO was to be deleted

TRANSFER PRICING : Where selected companies was engaged in providing medical chemistry services whereas assessee is providing only clinical support services to its AE proper examination of nature of services provided by selected companies in a broad manner is required in order to ascertain as to whether same can be considered as a comparable case

INCOME TAX/CHARTERED ACCOUNTANTS ACT : Mere omission to mention that net worth certificate is issued on basis of provisional balance sheet does not attract any misconduct or otherwise as such omission is technical in nature

Chartered Accountants Act : High Court rightly set aside findings of fact recorded by disciplinary committee as well as Council finding respondent guilty of professional misconduct for issuing certificates for consumption of raw materials showing value of imported raw material as CIF value to units as there was no material on record to establish that units had paid an amount more than what was mentioned in CIF value or purchase vouchers

TRANSFER PRICING: Where assessee provided engineering services to its AE but TPO re-characterized same as 'ITES' and made certain transfer pricing adjustment, following decision of Tribunal in previous year, issue was to be restored to file of TPO/AO to decide same afresh

TRANSFER PRICING : When documentary evidences submitted by assessee and claim of assessee that services provided in earlier Assessment years were akin to services provided in impugned Assessment year in which assessee was characterized as routine ITeS provider have not been examined either by TPO or by DRP while re-characterizing assessee as high-end ITeS/KPO service provider, then assessee should be accepted as low-end ITeS provider

HEADNOTE: Section 65 (83) of the Finance Act, 1994 - Chartered accountant’s services - Assessee was a practising chartered accountant - Revenue levied service tax on certification service provided by assessee holding that it was an auditing service and, therefore, not entitled to exemption in terms of Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated 16-10-1998 - Whether since certification follows transfer pricing audit, certification in question would clearly fall under ‘Audit/certification services’ - Held, yes - Whether, since verification of books of account precedes issue of certificate and such verification would fall within scope of ‘Accounting and auditing’, it could not be said that assessee was not rendering auditing service liable to tax and, therefore, impugned order was to be upheld - Held, yes [Para 3] Circulars & Notifications : Notification No. 59/89-ST, dated 16-10-1998

FACT: The assessee was a practising chartered accountant. The revenue levied tax on certification service holding that it was an auditing service and, therefore, not entitled to exemption in terms of Notification No. 59/89-ST, dated 16-10-1998.

On appeal :

HELD: The certification relating to computation of income from international transactions is in accordance with the provisions of section 92E of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and rule 10E of Income-tax Rules. [Para 2]

The certification follows transfer pricing audit. Therefore, the certification in question would clearly fall under ‘Audit/certification services’ even as per the clarification, dated 7-10-1998, issued by the Ministry of Finance. The verification of the books of account precedes issue of a certificate and such verification will fall within the scope of ‘Accounting & auditing’ function. Therefore, it could not be said that what the assessee was rendering was not ‘auditing service’ liable to service tax. Accordingly, the impugned order was to be upheld and the appeal was to be rejected. [Para 3]

S. Ramachandran for the Appellant. Ms. Indira Sisupal for the Respondent.

[Para 22]

Further the Supreme Court in T.D. Venkata Rao (supra) has accepted the fact that Chartered Accountants by the reason of their training have special aptitude in the matter of audit. The act of maintaining accounts is neither pleading, practice nor acting. For the reasons already discussed, the challenge to the Constitutional validity of the Legislation under articles 14 and 19 at the instance of the Bar Council will also have to be rejected. [Para 23] The Petitioners have not disputed that in the matter of enacting the law pertaining to recovery of sales tax, the same clearly fall within entry 54 of the State List. If in the process of making legislation, the legislature in its wisdom provides for the procedure in the manner in which tax has to be levied, maintenance of books, procedure for checking correctness or verification of books, it cannot be said that the same amounts to ancillary legislation or procedure not falling within the competence of the State Legislature under Entry 54. The Act requires that the dealer has to maintain books and the books have to be audited and required to be certified by a Chartered Accountant. That will not result in the legislation falling outside the competence of the State Legislature. The Legislation in pith and substance is relatable to imposition of sales tax which is within the competence of the State Legislature. The Courts examine and ascertain the pith and substance on scrutiny of the true character of the enactment. [Para 24]

It also cannot be said that in such a case audit by a Chartered Accountant would amount to outsourcing the statutory power to the third party. The Legislature can always delegate its powers as long as such delegation does not amount to abdication of its essential legislative functions. In the instant case, there is no abdication of the essential legislative functions. All that the section requires is that the accountant has to audit the accounts and to issue certificate that the dealer has maintained the books as required to be maintained under the Act and rules. The dealer has to file his accounts audited with the certificate. This neither amounts to abdication nor excessive delegation. Such an exercise also does not amount to conferring on the accountant a power to determine the correct tax liability of the dealer. The power to accept returns is of the Authorities under the Act. Even after the certificate is issued, that the dealer has maintained books, it is always open to the Commissioner under section 20 to ascertain whether the return is correct and complete or order an audit under section 22 to get the accounts audited by the officers of the department. A certificate, therefore, is not determinative but to enable the department to consider that the person having knowledge of audit and subject to the disciplinary control of its parent body has certified that the accounts are properly maintained. This is to aid the officers in discharging their statutory duties. This challenge, therefore, has to be rejected. [Para 25]

Further, it is for the dealer to decide whose services he seeks to obtain for appearance before the Sales Tax Authorities or for getting the accounts audited. Under section 82, there are a class of persons from whom a dealer can obtain services for being represented before the authorities under the Act. Under section 61, he is bound to select one of the class of accountants also. This is for a category of dealers whose turnover is more than 40 lakhs. The amount of fee which has to be paid is the amount to be decided between the dealer and that person, whom he selects from amongst the accountants that are available. This cannot be said to amount of compulsory levy amounting to tax. That being the case, the challenge under article 265 must also fail.

Similarly, the question of article 301 being attracted, does not arise. The challenge on that count also has to be rejected as the right claimed by the petitioners or their members or by the dealer is that Advocate and Sales Tax Practitioner cannot carry out audit in terms of section 61 in the State of Maharashtra. The enactment is pursuant to the power of the State Legislature to make law within its competence. This does not attract article 301. [Para 27]

Further, it is for the dealer to decide whose services he seeks to obtain for appearance before the Sales Tax Authorities or for getting the accounts audited. Under section 82, there are a class of persons from whom a dealer can obtain services for being represented before the authorities under the Act. Under section 61, he is bound to select one of the class of accountants also. This is for a category of dealers whose turnover is more than 40 lakhs. The amount of fee which has to be paid is the amount to be decided between the dealer and that person, whom he selects from amongst the accountants that are available. This cannot be said to amount of compulsory levy amounting to tax. That being the case, the challenge under article 265 must also fail.

Similarly, the question of article 301 being attracted, does not arise. The challenge on that count also has to be rejected as the right claimed by the petitioners or their members or by the dealer is that Advocate and Sales Tax Practitioner cannot carry out audit in terms of section 61 in the State of Maharashtra. The enactment is pursuant to the power of the State Legislature to make law within its competence. This does not attract article 301. [Para 27]

. The demand was barred by limitation.

Revenue's Arguments

There was no exemption during interregnum period, though services were exempt prior to July 2003 and from 20-11-2003 in view of exemptions, as consideration was received in convertible foreign exchange.

Circular dated 25-4-2003 clarifying that service tax is destination based consumption tax and it is not applicable on export of services was inapplicable in present case, as service was consumed/provided in India. The foreign-importer has placed orders for certain goods on the exporter in India. The assessee renders services by testing the samples in India. The certification after such testing is in India. The origin of the goods is in India. Hence, provision of services is India.

Issue Involved

Whether services were liable to service tax ?

HELD: Services were not liable to service tax :

Assessee is a testing agency. The contract of service was with the overseas purchaser of goods. Thus, the privity of contract of the assessee is with the buyers of the goods who are located or situated outside India. This is a contract based tax. The contract is of services. There is no contract in this case with the manufacturer of goods in India. Further, there is no contract and no privity between the assessee and the exporter of the goods who is stated to be based in India. In these circumstances, the exemption notification though required to be strictly construed, has to be construed in favour of the assessee. [Para 17]

Clients of the assessees are located abroad. The Tests Reports may have been prepared in India. The tests may have been conducted in India. However, the certificates have been forwarded to the clients of the assessee abroad. In such circumstances, assessee had exported the services by way of testing and analysis in India and transmitting the test report/analysis report to the foreign clients. The service was complete when the report was delivered to the foreign client. Since the delivery of the report to the foreign client was considered to be an essential part of the service that the demand of service tax was liable to be set aside. [Paras 18 & 19]

Assessee received payment in India in convertible foreign exchange and this payment is not repatriated by the assessee from or sent outside India. [Para 20]

Definition of Term Taxable service is inclusive. It also includes technical testing and analysis (see section 65 (106) (zzh)). By section 65(106), technical testing and analysis has also been defined. In such circumstances, when technical inspection and certification is also a service and goods in question have been inspected or tested, but the services were of the nature noted above, the payment was also made in terms aforesaid, then, the benefit of exemption/Circular was available. That was on the footing that the services rendered were exempt from whole of the liability to pay service tax. [Para 21]

Circular dated 25th April 2003 referred to Notifications dated 1st March 2003 and 9th April 1999. The 9th April 1999 is a notification of exemption. The April 2003 circular clarifies that service tax would be levied on all taxable services consumed or rendered in India, irrespective whether the payment thereof is received in foreign exchange or not. Since representations were received by the Board with regard to the withdrawal of the notification no.6 of 1999, exports of service would be affected as it would be costlier in the international market, that the board clarified that service consumed/provided in India in the manufacture of goods which are ultimately exported, no credit of service tax paid can be availed or reimbursed till April 2003 because intersectoral tax credit between service and goods are not allowed. It has been clarified that the question of taxability of secondary services which are used by primary service provider for the export of services. Hence, the services provided by the assessee were not taxable. This aspect once becomes more clear if one peruses the notification no.21/03ST, dated 20th November, 2003. [Para 22]

The services rendered in the present case are fully covered by the clarification given and even by the principle laid down in the decision of the Supreme Court of India in All India Federation of Tax Practitioners v. Union of India [2007] 10 STT 166. Service tax is a tax on each activity. When it comes to a service tax on professions, the services rendered are of advise and hence, the Supreme Court with regard to the nature of the tax concluded that it is rendered by a Chartered Accountant, for example when he advises his client or audits his account. Similarly, a cost accountant charges his client for advise as well as doing his work of costing. For each transaction or contract, Chartered Accountant/Cost Accountant renders professional based services. If the taxable event is the provision of services, then, the place where the services have been rendered is of significance. The services will be taxable only if they are provided within India. Service tax is a destination based consumption tax and therefore, it is not applicable on export of services. [Para 23]

HEADNOTE: †Section 44D of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with articles 12 and 7 of DTAA between India and Germany (Royalty/FTS) - Royalties in case of foreign companies - Assessment Years 1998-99 and 2000-01 - Assessee, a company incorporated at Germany, had a branch office in India - Indian branch was engaged in business of audit and procedure of norms for ISO 9000 certification - Assessee treated said income as its business income - However, Assessing Officer opined that said services came within purview of technical service under article 12 DTAA with Germany - Accordingly, by applying section 44D he assessed income at rate of 20 per cent of entire gross receipts - Whether services rendered by assessee were mostly in nature of audit work and, thus, services could not be termed as technical, managerial or consultancy services - Held, yes - Whether, entire nature of services and activities of assessee came within realm of 'professional services' and not within meaning of FTS as provided in article 12 and, thus, assessee's income could not be determined under section 44D but had to be computed as per provisions of sections 28 to 43 in view of article 7(1) - Held, yes [In favour of assessee]

FACT: The assessee, a company incorporated at Germany, had a branch in India. The Indian branch was engaged in the business of audit and procedure of norms for ISO 9000 certification. The services offered by Indian branch were ISO 9000 quality system certification where in quality system auditor of assessee company would visit the company opting for ISO certification, carry out a pre-assessment audit and then a certification audit and submit report to the assessee. After verification of report by the assessee, ISO 9000 certification was granted. The assessee treated its income as business income. The Assessing Officer opined that such services should be taxed as 'fees for technical services' under article 12 of Indo German DTAA. The assessee submitted that these services did not come under FTS within meaning of article 12 and, thus, it was business income which was to be computed in view of article 7(1) as business was carried out through PE. However, the Assessing Officer held that said services came within purview of FTS and, hence, provisions of section 44D had to be applied, and, accordingly, he assessed the income after applying tax rate of FTS; i.e., at rate 20 per cent of entire gross receipts. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the findings of Assessing Officer.

On appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: After examining the value of services and activities carried out by the assessee in the light of definition of terms 'royalty' and 'fees for technical service', it is found out that the assessee's case does not in any manner come within the meaning of 'royalties', as there is no right to use of any other items described therein. One is concerned with the meaning of term 'fees for technical services' as given in para 4 of Article 12. FTS has been defined as the payment of any amount in consideration of service for 'managerial' or 'technical' or 'consultancy' in nature, which is quite similar to definition given in Explanation 2 to section 9(1)(vii). Looking to the nature of services provided by the assessee as has been described above, it is simply evident that it is mostly in the nature of 'audit work' wherein the auditors of the assessee visit the sites of the client's and evaluate the clients' quality system as prescribed in International Standard for ISO 9001/2, ISO 14001, QS 9000 etc. Based on this audit work, a report is prepared which is sent to certification body the assessee company in Munich, Germany, which provides a certificate for a certain period, after reviewing the report and several stages of audit work which has been carried out for this purpose. Nowhere from such services, it can be inferred that the assessee has been providing technical, managerial or consultancy. Technical services require expertise in technology and providing the client such technical expertise. In this case no technology is transferred. 'Managerial services' is used in the context of running and management of the business of the client while here in this case, there is no management of client's business, but evaluation of standards as per international guidelines. Consultancy is to be understood as advisory services wherein necessary advice and consultation is given to its clients for the purpose of client's business. In an audit work there may be some incidence of advice at the time of evaluation but certainly it cannot be termed as pure consultancy services as in the audit work the auditor has to only evaluate the quality system and environmental system. [Para 10.2]

HEADNOTE: Section 21, read with section 22, of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 - Professional misconduct - On basis of report of Disciplinary Committee and after taking into consideration representations made, respondent was held guilty of gross negligence, for having signed and certified a statement of export of leather goods including those of other manufacturers, without verifying facts from relevant books/documents of company concerned - Whether, on facts, respondent had been rightly found to be guilty of gross negligence, and recommendation of reprimand was reasonable and had to be accepted - Held, yes

FACT: Company ‘S’ had furnished to the Joint CCI & E a statement of export of leather goods including those of other manufacturers for the years 1976-77 and 1977-78, duly certified by the respondent - Chartered Ac-countant, and on that basis, the Export House Certificate was issued. The respondent had certified that he had checked and verified the particulars of export from the books/documents of the company and found them to be correct. On demand by the Jt. CCI & E, the company replied that it had not purchased any finished leather/leather goods from any other party and denied having exported finished goods manufactured by other units. The Jt. CCI & E made a complaint to the Institute that the respondent had issued the certificate without verifying the books of account inasmuch as he did not have any contact with that company. The respondent, in his reply, asserted his certificate to be correct and complete, based on the documents produced by the concerned parties. He further submitted that he was retained by the consultants of the company to verify the export statements from the records produced by it and he certified the facts accordingly. The Disciplinary Committee held that the then existing export policy required that 20 per cent of the total exports goods should be manufactured by others to get Export House benefits and since the only dispute was that the figures were not correct, the respondent was guilty of professional misconduct under section 21, read with section 22, and under clauses 5, 6 and 7 of the Part I of the Second Schedule. The Council, after considering representations, found him grossly negligent and thus guilty under clause 7 of Part I of the Second Schedule. It accordingly recommended that the respondent be reprimanded.

On a reference under section 21(5) :

HELD: It would be necessary to take note of the examination of the respondent by the Disciplinary Committee. The respondent admitted not to have known the policy which was prevalent at the relevant point of time. Even there was an admission to the effect that he had not verified as to whether some of the units he had certified as cottage industries, were really so. To a pointed query made by the president as to for what purpose the certificate was issued, the respondent stated that they related to the purchase of raw skins, that the position of the parties had been indicted and the party who sought for the certificate had asked him to simply sign the statement and he was not aware of the policy. To another query made by the president as to why he had not put any date on the certificate, he could not give any reply except saying that he could not tell as to why he had not put the dates. He also stated that he had not indicated as to what goods were exported. Similarly in response to a particular query as to whether he checked the books of account, the reply was that he could not say what books were shown to him. Another interesting feature was that the respondent stated to have verified books of account written in English, when the company stated that its books of account were maintained in Tamil language. The respondent was asked as to how two different figures appeared in the copy submitted to the complainant and the one produced by the company. He gave an evasive and vague reply stating that he checked the parties only.

"Professional misconduct" has been defined in section 22. Intendment and object of the Act is to maintain standard of the profession at a high level, and, consequently, a code of conduct has been prescribed. Misconduct implies failure to act honestly and reasonable either according to the ordinary and normal standard, or according to the standard of a particular profession. Authenticity and sanctity is attached to certification done by a Chartered Accountant.

Hence, while holding that the above charges could not be included in the value of CHA services, the matter was to be remanded to the Commissioner to re-examine the issue after giving an opportunity to the assessee to produce the chartered accountant’s certificate in respect of the various deductions claimed by it including the reimbursement. The scope of the CHA as defined in the CHA Regulation, 2004, could not be ignored even in the matter pertaining to service tax as observed to the contrary by the Commissioner in the impugned order. The activity of CHA relates to entry or departure of conveyances or import or export of goods at any customs station. Therefore, activities of CHA are limited to customs station and they cannot extend beyond it. For example, in the instant case, the assessee collected air freight for export from the consignee. The said activity was related to freight charges collected for transportation service rendered by airline company. In other words, this freight forwarding could not be said to be an activity of CHA. In a similar manner, each charge ought to have been examined by the Commissioner. This had not been done. Moreover, the Commissioner had exactly confirmed the same amount in his first order-in-original which was set aside by the Bench. The demand of service tax on transportation under the category of CFA was not correct in the light of various case laws. There were various reimbursements of the taxable services relating to CHA in terms of the Board’s Circular F. No. B43/1/97-TRU, dated 6-6-1997. In such circumstances, the de novo order suffered from various defects. [Para 6]

As regards the demand under CFA services, the assessee had made a strong case for non-includibility of rental income, distribution charges, warehousing and transportation. Such charges were collected under separate contracts. They did not represent the charges for CFA services. The commission received by CFA was only subject to service tax. As regards the includibility or non-includibility of various charges, the findings had already been given. The matter was to be remanded to the Commissioner. [Para 6]

HEADNOTE: Section 65(35) of the Finance Act, 1994 - Custom house agent - Period 2000-04 - Whether activities relating to freight forwarding cannot be brought under category of services of ‘Customs house agents’ (CHA) - Held, yes - Whether activity of CHA relates only to entry or departure of conveyances or import or export of goods at any customs station and, therefore, activities of CHA are limited to customs station and they cannot extend beyond it; and where assessee collected air freight for export from consignee, activity being related to transportation service rendered by airline company, such freight forwarding could not be said to be a part of activities of CHA - Held, yes - Whether where, from nature of various charges collected by assessee, it was found that those were not includible in computation of service tax towards CHA services; however, Commissioner held that those charges were related to CHA services though he himself had repeatedly pointed out that assessee had not produced a chartered accountant’s certificate with regard to deductions claimed by it, matter was to be remanded to original authority for re-adjudication - Held, yes [Para 6]

Section 65(25) of the Finance Act, 1994 - Clearing and forwarding agent - Period 2000-04 - Whether a clearing and forwarding agent (CFA) receives commission only and that too against a service provided by it - Held, yes - Whether, where rental income, distribution charges, warehousing charges and transportation charges were collected by assessee under separate contracts, they would not represent charges for CFA services - Held, yes - Whether since Commissioner’s order suffered from various defects, matter was to be remanded for readjudication - Held, yes [Para 6] Circulars and Notifications : Board’s Circular F.No. B43/1/97-TRU, dated 6-6-1997

FACT: The assessee provided three distinct services, viz., freight forwarding, Customs House Agent (CHA) and Clearing and Forwarding Agent (CFA). The Commissioner proceeded against the assessee for short payment of service tax under the category of CHA and also in respect of services provided as CFA. The Tribunal remanded the matter for de novo decision. Subsequently, the Commissioner concluded that the amounts, viz., charge collect fees, break bulk fees, profit share from margin, unallocated income, currency adjustment factor, air/sea freight rebate, commission/brokerage, air freight incentive and expenses reimbursement billing were liable to be taxed under CHA services. Similarly, certain other charges such as rental income, distribution charges, warehousing charges and transportation charges had been held to be forming a part of the value of the CFA services rendered by the assessee. The assessee opposed the said order.

On appeal :

HELD: The activities relating to freight forwarding could not be brought under CHA. The assessee had clearly explained the nature of the charges collected such as charge collect fees, break bulk fees, profit share from margin, unallocated income, currency adjustment factor, air/sea freight rebate, commission/brokerage, air freight incentive, expenses reimbursement billing, etc. Such charges would not be includible in the computation of service tax towards CHA services. However, the Commissioner in the impugned order even while holding that those charges were related to CHA services, had also repeatedly pointed out that the assessee had not produced a chartered accountant’s certificate with regard to the various deductions claimed by it. Hence, while holding that the above charges could not be included in the value of CHA services, the matter was to be remanded to the Commissioner to re-examine the issue after giving an opportunity to the assessee to produce the chartered accountant’s certificate in respect of the various deductions claimed by it including the reimbursement.

raised by the assessee, the DRP issued direction holding that the Assessing Officer had considered all the arguments of the assessee. It was further held that there was no error in the order of the Assessing Officer in holding that the assessee's services satisfy the make available test and therefore, the decision of the Assessing Officer was justified. Consequently, final order was passed by the Assessing Officer taxing the sum received from customers in India as fees for technical services.

On appeal to Tribunal: HELD: There is no dispute between the parties that the sum so received is chargeable to tax according to the provisions of domestic tax laws. Therefore, only issue to be examined is whether the above sum can be taxed in India as per the articles of Indo-UK Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement. The claim of the assessee is that above sum is chargeable to tax as fees for technical services as per article 13(4)(c) of DTAA if the assessee makes available technical, knowledge, experience, skill etc to the Indian entities. The Assessing Officer has agreed that the services provided by the assessee are technical in nature. According to him as the assessee is also carrying analysis, testing and inspection, hence, it is providing the consultancy services also. He therefore, held that on close scrutiny of nature of services the service recipient get equipped to carry on that business model or service model on their own without reference to the service provider. Therefore, according to him such services fall within the ambit of making available technical knowledge under the tax treaty. The Dispute Resolution Panel also agreed with the order of the Assessing Officer and accordingly, sum received of Rs. 187.7 lakhs was considered as fees for technical services. Now coming to the nature of services rendered by the assessee to the various entities, the assessee has provided services to Hindalco Ltd. and the nature of services is umpire instruction based on which a certificate of Umpire Analysis was given. For the certification, different methods such as F25, G18, I18, i20 and I23 were employed. It also certified the state of material and element of such certification. The other service rendered to Hindalco Industries Ltd. is with respect to weighing, sampling the moisture determination services. After providing these services a certificate of inspection was also provided. The service provided to Grifith India also involved chemical analysis of different products and then providing a certificate thereof. The services of Indian Oil Corporation is inspection of the vessel on arrival. The services provided to Dell International is also with respect to data security audit and auditing. The services provided to Nirma was also with respect to the certificate of analysis of various parameters of spent pacol catalyst. The services provided to Vedanta Ltd. is also pertaining to chemical certification of material. Undoubtedly all the above services provided by the assessee are in the nature of technical analysis and unless the assessee is able to perform those services independently without the help of the service provider then only it can be said that services have been made available by the service provider to the service recipient. According to article 13 of Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement the fees for technical services can be chargeable to tax in India only such services are made available to the recipient of such services. However, the assessee has not at all made available any such services to the Indian entity but has merely provided the services in the ordinary course of its business. The revenue has not brought on any material to show that subsequently the recipient of those services have performed these services on their own without the help of the assessee or any other similar service provider. Inspection and survey of imported/exported cargo and certifying in relation to the quality and price, provision of such services does not make available technical knowledge, experience, skill, know-how or processes to the recipient of the service. Hence, the fees for technical services earned by the assessee is not chargeable to tax in India according to article 13(4)(c) of the DTAA as these services are not made available to the Indian parties. Accordingly, it is held that Rs. 187.72 lakhs received by the assessee is not chargeable to tax in India. [Para 6]

HEADNOTE: Section 73, read with section 86, of the Finance Act, 1994 - Recovery of service tax not levied or paid or short levied or short paid or erroneously refunded - Appellant, engaged in manufacture and sale of castings on specific rate of contract, paid service tax on account of services of goods transport operator - On basis of Chartered Accountant’s Certificate, said amount of service tax was refunded to it - However, Commissioner in exercise of its revisional power demanded back amount of refund sanctioned - It was case of appellant that it paid service tax which was not payable by it and said amount was not recovered from customers and so, doctrine of unjust enrichment did not arise in its case - It was found that said service tax amount had not vitiated contract price in any way - Commissioner in his order had not relied on any contradictory certificate of another professional - Whether certificate issued by a professional generally, should not be challenged without having contradictory certificate from another professional and in absence of such a contradictory certificate, it was to be held that appellant had a strong prima facie case in its favour for waiver of requirement of pre-deposit of service tax for hearing appeal - Held, yes

FACT: The appellant was sanctioned a refund by the adjudicating authority on basis of the factual situation prevailing and certificate given by the Chartered Accountant. However, the Commissioner reviewed the order of adjudicating authority and demanded the refund amount back on the ground that the certificate of the Chartered Accountant only stated that amount had been debited to expenses account in profit and loss statement. In appeal, the appellant contended that the amount had been paid as service tax which was not payable by the appellants and since they had not recovered the said amount from their customers. Therefore, the question of doctrine of unjust enrichment did not arise.

HELD: The Chartered Accountant’s Certificate was a detailed certificate which had been considered in depth by the adjudicating authority. The appellant was engaged in the manufacture and selling of casting on specific rate of contract. The amount of service tax paid by the appellant was on the goods transport operator. That had not vitiated the contract price in any way. Further, the certificate issued by the professional, generally should not be challenged without having contradictory certificate from another professional. The Commissioner in his order had not relied on any contradictory certificate of another professional. In the absence of which, it was to be held that the appellant had made out a prima facie case for waiver of pre-deposit of amount of service tax. [Para 5]

K.K. Banerjee for the Appellant. A. Hore for the Respondent.

covered under clause (ii) of Rule 3 of the Taxation of Services (Provided from Outside India and Received in India) Rules, 2006. As per clause (ii) of Rule 3 of the Taxation of Services (Provided from Outside India and Received in India) Rules, 2006 at the relevant time the service to be taxable under this category must be performed in India. Since no part of service was performed in India, it was not liable to tax. Technical inspection & certification services : Service received by the assessee can, alternatively, be classified under the category of 'technical inspection & certification services'. The word 'process' in definition of said service simply means the activities performed for the purpose of achieving the desired objectives. Therefore, under the said definition all types of examination or inspection will be covered. No particular form of certification has been stated. Therefore certification in any form will be covered under the definition. It may further be noted that the taxability of certification under this category is not restricted to advice, consultancy or technical assistance but includes any work done in connection with the inspection or examination of the items specified therein. Manufacture of the vessel is a complex and costly affair and service provider gives certification as regards to the standard of the developed model. In view of the above, service is to be classified under the category of 'Technical inspection and certification service'. Since the said service is covered under clause (ii) of Rule 3 of the Taxation of Services (Provided from Outside India and Received in India) Rules, 2006, the service to be taxable under this category must be performed in India. Since no part of it was performed in India, no service tax could be charged.

Limitation & Penalty : The audit was conducted and all details were supplied to Department in February and March, 2008. Since all the facts were to the knowledge of the department, issuance of notice on 31-3-2011 was barred by limitation as there was no suppression. Even otherwise, merely wrong claim of classification by itself does not amount to suppression or mis-declaration. Even mere non-declaration is not sufficient to invoke larger period but some positive act is required. Further, assessee was Government of India Undertaking under the Ministry of Defense, and it is inconceivable that they would try to evade tax. Further, payment under reverse charge would have neutral effect, as tax paid would be eligible as credit. The entire demand is barred by limitation. Similarly, penalty was not leviable.

Calculation incorrect : Value of services should be = Value of Purchase Contract (net of discount) - Cost of manufactured goods (net of discount).

Revenue's Arguments

Assessees claim for classification of the services received by them either in the category of Technical Testing & Analysis Services defined under Section 65(109) or under Technical Inspection & Certification Services defined at Section 65(108) could not be entertained as the assessee did not furnish any other evidence on record to justify that M/s. MARIN is a Technical Inspection & Certification/Technical Testing and Analysis Agency.

The service received by the assessee and rendered by M/s. MARIN requires specialized knowledge having to do with technical know-how/functioning of the machinery, i.e., the off shore patrol vessel and therefore these services would rightly be classifiable under Consulting Engineers Services.

Even though the assessee were aware that service tax is payable on the services received by them and had paid part of the amount during the time of audit, yet they deliberately did not pay the said amount and the balance till the detection of the offence of the evasion of Service Tax by the audit. This is tantamount to deliberate suppression/evasion on the part of the assessee.

Consequent to the act of suppression/evasion, penalty has to follow. This is not a case of technical or venial bridge as claimed by the assessee, as prior to detection by Audit, the assessee had not approached the department on their own to ascertain the Service-tax liability.

Issue Involved

Whether services in question were liable to service tax ?

HELD: The service received by the assessee is not covered under the category of 'Consulting Engineer'. The reports filed by M/s. Maritime Research Institute, Netherlands are Test results. It spells out Tests performed like Manoeuvring test programme, review of the tests, presentation and discussion of the test results, zig-zag test, combined turning circle and pull-out tests. Hence, it is only appropriate that the service merits classification under section 65(105)(zzh) - Technical Testing and Analysis. [Para 45]

For the applicability of section 66A, the taxable services must be received in India. The rules provide that only such services which are provided from outside India and received in India are taxable. The criteria for determining taxable service as to when taxable service is said to have been received in India are spelt out in Taxable Services (Provided from Outside India and Received in India) Rules, 2006 vide Notification No. 11/2006-S.T., dated 19-4-2006. [Para 43]

Similarly, a cost accountant charges his client for advise as well as doing his work of costing. For each transaction or contract, Chartered Accountant/Cost Accountant renders professional based services. If the taxable event is the provision of services, then, the place where the services have been rendered is of significance. The services will be taxable only if they are provided within India. Service tax is a destination based consumption tax and therefore, it is not applicable on export of services. [Para 23] Assessee rendered services, but they were consumed abroad. The clients of the assessees used the services of the assessee in inspection/test analysis of the goods which the clients located abroad intended to import from India. In other words, the clients abroad were desirous of confirming the fact as to whether the goods imported complied with requisite specifications and standards. Thus, client of the assessee located abroad engaged the services of the assessee for inspection and testing the goods. The goods were tested by the assessees in India. The goods were available or their samples were drawn for such testing and analysis in India. However, the report of such tests and analysis was sent abroad. The clients of the assessee were foreign clients, paid the assessee for such services rendered, in foreign convertible currency. It is in that sense that benefit of the services accrued to the foreign clients outside India. This is termed as 'export of service'. In these circumstances, if services were rendered to such foreign clients located abroad, then, the act can be termed as 'export of service'. Such an act does not invite a service tax liability. Once the Supreme Court has taken the view that service tax is a value added tax which in turn is destination based consumption tax in the sense that it taxes non-commercial activities and is not a charge on the business, but on the consumer, then, it is leviable only on services provided within the country. [Para 24]

Any larger or wider controversy and based on the submissions of assessee need not be decided in this case. Suffice it to hold that the view taken by the Tribunal does not raise any substantial question of law. [Para 26]

service tax will not be payable if a professional like a chartered accountant or a cost accountant has in reality not rendered any professional service to a customer. These aspects are distinct aspects and, therefore, an aspect which entirely depends upon the services offered by the professional, though may have a nexus with the profession, yet the service becomes a distinct aspect in itself and can be legitimately taxed by the Parliament under Entry 97 of List I, as had been done in the instant case. [Para 30] The petitioners also argued that the provisions of section 65(48) and section 67(r) and (s ) were confusing and arbitrary. The contention in short was that the services which the chartered accountants give is a bundle of service. It is akin to the services rendered by any professional, including a medical practitioner and a lawyer, and the relationship between a chartered accountant and his clients is like that of a lawyer and his client and it cannot be merely construed as a ‘service’ under the Finance Act 32 of 1990. The argument was that the Legislature had picked and chosen the chartered accountants or the cost accountants and left out the other professionals like doctors and lawyers. [Para 36]

That argument was obviously incorrect, because it is for the Legislature to select any particular service or any particular subject for taxing. The tests of the vice of discrimination in a taxing law are less rigorous. In examining the allegations of a hostile discriminatory treatment what is looked into is not its phraseology, but the real effect of its provisions. Therefore, there would be no question of finding any fault with the Legislature for picking up the chartered accountants or the cost accountants or the architects also for taxing their services. [Paras 37 & 38]

What is relevant is to consider the object of the Act and in selecting the class of professionals whether the legislature has acted unreasonably or has imposed unreasonable restrictions on the right of the assessee and or Income Tax Practitioners to carry on their occupation or profession. It must be noted that the Chartered Accountant cannot certify the correctness and completeness of the sales tax returns unless they audit the accounts of the dealer as maintained in the first part of section 61. After audit Chartered Accountant has to certify the various items in Part I of Form No. 704. These items are subject to audited Chartered Accountant’s observations and comments about the non-compliance, shortcomings, deficiencies, in the return filed by the dealer. There are various other requirements. Suffice it to say that it is a specialized job which can only be undertaken by the person professionally competent and trained to audit. Advocates are not qualified. The other sales tax practitioner and retired employees definitely not. [Para 19]

The settled law on the subject is that as long as the twin tests of reasonableness of the classification and nexus with the object are satisfied, wisdom of legislation cannot be substituted. The State Legislature is free to decide in its wisdom as to how best to safeguard the State revenue the different States may adopt different standards and policy of one legislature may not be adopted by another Legislature as the matter lies in the domain of policy making. Because some States have permitted Sales Tax Practitioners to carry on audit need not necessarily mean that as the Legislature of the State of Maharashtra has not so provided, that would be arbitrary or that the classification considering the nexus of the object is arbitrary. It is for the State Legislature to decide how to protect its revenue and this is more true with regard to economic legislation. [Para 20]

The Act was enacted pursuant to a decision to introduce VAT system in the country. An empowered committee of Finance Ministers was appointed. As noted by the Supreme Court there can be no denial of the fact that Chartered Accountants have the expertise in the matter of accounts. What section 61 requires is that the dealer must get the accounts audited and produce the report of such audit alongwith the certifications that may be prescribed. This certificate has nothing to do with the provisions of Section 22. Section 22 is a special Power conferred on the Commissioner for selection of dealers for audit. The entire object of the Act is maintenance of proper accounts by the dealers and certification of the accounts so that the books are in order and there is no fraud considering what is required by Form 704. Inspite of certificate issued by the Accountant, section 22 empowers the Commissioner to carry out special audit. It is not that on obtaining certificate under section 61 the authorities are precluded from going through the accounts. Under section 22, it can still order an audit and arrive at the conclusion that the accounts have not been properly maintained. The scheme of the Act requires the dealer to maintain accounts under section 63. These accounts have to be kept by every dealer liable to pay tax under the Act. There is no restriction as to who can write these accounts. Next is section 61 as now amended and the Explanation. This requires audit to be done and the certificate to be issued only by a Chartered Accountant and or Cost Accountant. Section 22 is a special power in the Commissioner to direct an audit even if an audit was earlier done and certified by a Chartered Accountant or a Cost Accountant. [Para 21]

As regards the challenge under article 19(1)(g ) it is clear that in the instant case considering section 82, the category of persons who are excluded from the ambit of Explanation of section 61 are not denied their right of appearance before the Authorities under the Act. In other words, they are not prohibited from carrying on their profession. In the matter of carrying out audit the State has chosen to confer that right only on a class of persons having expertise in the field. This cannot be said to be arbitrary or excessive in nature so as to go beyond the requirement of the interest of the general public. That would be yet another reason as to why the challenge under Article 19(1)(g) must fail. [Para 22]

Further the Supreme Court in T.D. Venkatrao (supra ) has accepted the fact that Chartered Accountants by the reason of their training have special aptitude in the matter of audit. The act of maintaining accounts is neither pleading, practice nor acting. For the reasons already discussed, the challenge to the Constitutional validity of the Legislation under articles 14 and 19 at the instance of the Bar Council will also have to be rejected. [Para 23]

Thus the word ‘audit’ has a specific connotation in the matter of examination, investigation and auditing of accounts, where detection of fraud is of primary importance. [Para 10]

The challenge in a nutshell is to the exclusion of Advocates and Sales Tax Practitioners from doing the work of audit under section 61. [Para 11] To consider the challenge under articles 14 and 19(1)(g) one may refer to section 44AB of the Income tax Act, 1961. This provision as in the instant case provides for audit of persons whose total sales or turnover or gross receipts exceed forty lakhs per year. This provision was challenged before the various High Courts. The Supreme Court in an appeal before it, has upheld the legality of the section. Once the Supreme Court in T.D. Venkata Rao v. Union of India AIR 1999 SC 2242 has upheld the legality of section 44AB of the Income-tax Act, 1961 where the same terminology was used and which was also a provision pertaining to audit, and considering the object of both the provisions which is prevention of evasion of tax dues, the challenge by the petitioners on the ground of infraction of articles 14 and 19 of the Constitution will have to be similarly rejected. There are practically no distinguishing features. The only distinction, if any, is that, whereas section 44AB of 1961 Act is for the purpose of ascertaining "total income", section 61 is for certification whether VAT has been correctly assessed, collected and paid. [Para 16]

The challenge based on article 14 is to be rejected on the following grounds :

(i)Chartered Accountants by reason of their training have special aptitude in the matter of audit. An Income Tax Practitioner does not have the same expertise as the Chartered Accountants in the matter of accounts. The argument, therefore, that the effect of such a provision will be to exclude all other categories of authorized representatives except the Chartered Accountants from carrying on their profession is liable to be rejected, as they constitute two distinct classes having a nexus with the object of the provisions, which is evasion of tax dues.

(ii)The contention that such a provision brings in an oppressive restriction is also liable to be rejected as auditing accounts is a specialized job. It may be true that some Income Tax Practitioners may also acquire that skill by sheer practice without passing the necessary examination. But that does not preclude Parliament from prescribing special qualification with reference to the auditing of accounts.

(iii)Legal Practitioners and Chartered Accountants are equal for the purpose of representation of assessee before Assessing Authority but they are not equals for the purpose of compulsory audit. The preferential treatment given to the Chartered Accountants for the purpose of compulsory audit does not militate against the rule of equality under article 14 of the Constitution. The terms "audit", "auditing" and the "functions of auditor" clearly bring about the difference between the Chartered Accountants and others. The object and purpose in providing compulsory audit is to facilitate the prevention of evasion of taxes, administrative convenience in quick and proper completion of assessments etc. In the light of this object, Chartered Accountants and others cannot be said to be similarly situate. The qualifications and eligibility to be enrolled as Income Tax Practitioners are entirely different from that of Chartered Accountants from the point of view of auditing.

HEADNOTE: Classification of services - Section 65(108) of the Finance Act, 1994 - Technical inspection and certification (OR) - Assessee dealing in LPG sent LPG through tank trucks to various LPG bottling plants of oil distribution companies - Whenever LPG tank truck required any repair or mandatory testing of safety valves, tank truck was cleaned and completely degassed - During this activity, water was filled in tank mounted on truck and discharged - Water was displaced by LPG vapors - For this activity, assessee collected cost of water and labour charges from truck owner - Adjudicating Authority held that said activities undertaken by assessee would fall under category of 'technical inspection and certification service' - Whether assessee though was performing certain activities in relation to maintenance and safety of tank trucks and was issuing a certificate to effect that tank trucks were purged/degassed, same could not be considered to be a service within scope of 'technical inspection and certification service' - Held, yes [Para 5] [In favour of assessee]GST/Service Tax: Where assessee dealing in LPG was performing certain activities in relation to maintenance and safety of tank trucks and was issuing a certificate to effect that tank trucks were purged/degassed, said activities could not be considered to be a service within scope of 'technical inspection and certification service'

FACT: The assessee dealing in LPG sent LPG through tank trucks to various LPG bottling plants of oil distribution companies.

Whenever LPG tank truck required any repair or mandatory testing of safety valves, the tank truck was cleaned and completely degassed. During this activity, water was filled in tank mounted on the truck and discharged. Water was displaced by LPG vapors. For this activity, the assessee collected cost of water and the labour charges from the truck owner.

The Adjudicating Authority held that the said activities undertaken by the assessee would fall under the category of 'technical inspection and certification service' and raised tax demand upon it.

The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the impugned order.

On second appeal:

HELD: The assessee though is performing certain activities in relation to maintenance and safety of the tank trucks and is issuing a certificate to the effect that the tank trucks are purged/degassed, same cannot be considered to be a service within scope of 'technical inspection and certification service'. It is to be understood that the assessee is not basically an agency involved with the testing and certification. In fact, it is abundantly clear that it is performing certain activities which make the tank truck fit to be filled with LPG for further transportation. This is to be construed only as an activity related to the safety and maintenance of the tank truck. The assessee has not fulfilled the conditions so as to impart the activity of purging and degassing tank truck as 'technical inspection and certification service'. [Para 5]

HEADNOTE: Section 65(108) of the Finance Act, 1994 - Technical inspection and certification service - Period 1-7-2003 to 31-3-2004 - Assessee was operating as licensed registrar under office of AQA, USA - It represented AQA for purpose of assisting clients in achievement of ISO 9000, ISO 14000 and QS 9000 certifications - It received Company Information Sheet (CIS) from prospective clients, reviewed CIS, prepared quotation and sent same to clients, provided information connected with quality management system certification, conducted audit/assessment of quality system at clients’ place with reference to ISO standard and after successful completion of assessment process, sent such assessment report to AQA - It charged audit fee for doing audit work from clients - Revenue treated said service of assessee as that of ‘Technical inspection and certification agency’ and demanded service tax - Whether word ‘process’ mentioned in definition of ‘Technical inspection and certification’ can relate only to physical and chemical processes and it cannot be transported to province of management relating to human beings - Held, yes - Whether therefore, activities carried out by assessee for certification of quality management system practised by clients, would not come within purview of ‘Technical inspection and certification service’ - Held, yes [Para 5.2] Words & Phrases : Word ‘process’ as occurring in section 65(108) of the Finance Act, 1994 Interpretation of statutes : Principles of Ejusdem Generis

FACT: The assessee was operating as licenced registrar under the office of AQA, USA. As per the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between the parties, the assessee was to represent AQA for the purpose of assisting clients in achievement of ISO 9000, ISO 14000 and QS 9000 certificates. It used to receive Company Information Sheet (CIS) from prospective clients, review the CIS, prepare quotation and send same to prospective clients, provide information connected with Quality Management System (QMS) certification, conduct audit/assessment of the quality system at client’s place with reference to ISO standard and after successful completion of the assessment process, send such assessment to AQA, which issues above certificates. For doing the audit work, the assessee charged certain fee as audit fee from the prospective customers. The revenue treated the service of the assessee as that of ‘technical inspection and certification agency’ and demanded service tax. The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the demand.

On appeal :

HELD: The assessee received certain consideration for the services rendered by it. Without going into the nitty-gritty, it could be safely concluded that the activities of the assessee were pre-requisites for any client in India to obtain ISO certification. However, the certification relates only to management system or management processes. The principles of ejusdem generis are clearly applicable in the interpretation of the word ‘process’ which is found in the definition of ‘technical inspection and certification service’. No doubt, the said word keeps company with the other words ‘goods or material or immovable property’. These inspections relate only to activities connected with matter. In other words, the ‘process’ mentioned in the definition can relate only to physical and chemical processes. It cannot be transported to the province of management relating to human beings. In other words, the activities carried out by the assessee for certification of quality management system practised by clients would not come within the purview of ‘Technical inspection and certification service’. Further, the assessee had carried out the audit of quality of various schools and organizations. Obviously, these processes would not relate to matter or immovable property. [Para 5.2]

The assessee had stated that on its, own it had approached the Department as early as on 18-8-2003 with regard to the taxability of its services. However, the show-cause notice, dated 7-1-2005, had invoked the longer period, which is invoked for only suppression of facts, mis-statement or fraud with an intent to evade tax. In the instant case, the ingredients for invocation of longer period were not present. Hence, invocation of the longer period was not sustainable. In view of the above, there was no merit in the impugned order and the same was to be set aside. [Para 5.3]
