HELD: In order to fall within exception of section 9(1)(vii )(b), the technical services, for which, the fees have been paid, ought to have been utilized by a resident in a business outside India or for the purposes of making or earning any income from any source outside India. [Para 16] The KEMA certification obtained by the assessee from 'C' for enabling exports of its products was unassailed. The sole stand of the department was that this service of testing and certification had been applied by the assessee for its manufacturing activity within India. However, neither the Assessing Officer, nor the Commissioner (Appeals) had been able to bring anything on record to buttress such a stand. Thus, the initial onus under section 9(1)(vii)( b) lay squarely on the assessee to prove that the exemption available thereunder was in fact available to it. The assessee had maintained throughout that the testing and certification services provided by 'C' were utilized only for its export activity and that the same were not utilized for its business activities of production in India. Thus, the assessee had discharged the onus, which lay on it under section 9(1)(vii)(b ). Therefore, the impugned payment made by the assessee to 'C' was not chargeable to tax in India. [Para 21]

Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) had erred in confirming the disallowance made by the Assessing Officer. [Para 30]

. The contention of Shri Mehta for revenue that the certificate of the Singapore revenue authorities is opposed to provisions of section 10 of the Singapore Income Tax Act also cannot be accepted. The Revenue does not question genuineness of the certificate. It cannot dispute the contention on the ground that the same are opposed to the statutory provision." [Para 13] ■

The Tribunal has referred to and relied upon the above findings of this Court in relation to applicability of Article 8 of the DTAA. However, the Tribunal has ventured to distinguish the decision of this Court on the question of the veracity of the certificate dated 09.01.2013 on the ground that the genuineness of the said certificate was not questioned by the Revenue before this Court and hence, the Tribunal has thought it fit to restore the matter to the Assessing Officer to verify the contents of the said certificate with a rider that in case the Assessing Officer is not able to obtain any specific material to rebut the contents of the certificate issued by the Singapore Tax Authority, then respectfully following the decision of this Court, relief was to be granted to the appellants. [Para 14]

■

When this Court has already considered the certificate dated 09.01.2013 and during the pendency of the appeal before the Tribunal for the year under consideration, the Revenue has not been able to bring any material on record or has challenged or doubted the certificate issued by the Singapore Tax Authority, as observed by the Tribunal in Para 20 of the impugned order, it has noted that the Departmental Representative has challenged the veracity of the certificate issued by the IRAS during the course of the appellate proceedings before the CIT (A) and thereafter, the Tribunal has referred to the territorial tax system of the Singapore Income Tax Act to hold that the certificate has not given any basis whatsoever as to how the assessee is deriving income from "business carried on in Singapore", when admittedly, the appellants-assessee have been operating in international waters. The Tribunal has also considered the fact that the certificate does not specify the factual basis on which the Singapore Tax Authority has concluded that the income from shipping business have been derived by the assessee from "business carried on in Singapore". Thus, in effect, the Tribunal has overreached the findings arrived at by this Court in case of M.T. Maersk Mikage v. DIT (International Taxation) (supra) in absence of any material brought on record by the Revenue before the Tribunal to show that the certificate issued by the IRAS is not reliable or cannot be considered for the income of ST Shipping to be taxed in Singapore on accrual basis. [Para 15]

■

It is also pertinent to note that from the documents placed in form of paper- book filed before the Tribunal, in fact, the ST Shipping has shown the income arising from the operations as per letter dated 09.10.2012 issued by the Deloitte and Touche LLP, Certified Public Accountants, Singapore stating that the ST Shipping has confirmed that the position adopted in the Year of Assessment 2010 to treat charter income derived by the overseas branches as Singapore sourced income and part of qualifying income under Approved International Shipping Enterprise Incentive remains unchanged in the Year of Assessment 2012. [Para 16]

■

The impugned order of the Tribunal is, therefore, contrary to the decision of this Court as the Tribunal could not have restored the matter back to the Assessing Officer only on mere suspicion and the doubts contrary to the findings arrived at by this Court regarding the same certificate dated 09.01.2013 issued by IRAS. The Tribunal ought not to have analysed the certificate in its order more particularly in Para 22 of the order in absence of any material on record. On perusal of Para 22 of the impugned order it is clear that the Tribunal has made the observation with regard to the language of the certificate more particularly, when this Court has accepted the part of the certificate which certified that the income earned by the ST Shipping from the operations carried out in ports at India was liable to be taxed at Singapore on accrual basis and as per Article 8 of DTAA, when the income accrues in Singapore and was taxed as such, the same would be exempt from tax in India. This Court has further clarified that reference to Article 24 of DTAA in the certificate is nothing but an opinion of the IRAS. [Para 17]

■

Hence, the Tribunal ought not to have further deliberated upon contents of the certificate which is already held to be applicable in the facts of the case in the absence of any other material on record to demonstrate that the veracity of the certificate issued by IRAS is doubtful and merely because the Tribunal is of the opinion that the language of the certificate is not conducive to the opinion of the Tribunal, the matter could not have been restored to the Assessing Officer in face of the observation made by this Court regarding the same certificate dated 09.01.2013 issued by the IRAS. [Para 18]

HEADNOTE: Section 22 of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 - Misconduct - Professional or other misconduct - Petitioner was a partner of a firm - It filed a complaint against respondent-chartered accountant before ICAI alleging various acts of misconduct - According to petitioner, respondent certified balance sheet of firm without carrying out audit and said balance sheet was accepted by Arbitrator while settling dispute between partners regarding settlement of accounts of firm - Council was of prima facie opinion that complaint filed by petitioner was frivolous and that respondent was not guilty of any professional or other misconduct - Whether since arbitrator who was an independent person had accepted balance sheet audited by respondent as correct, there was no reason to interfere with prima facie view of ICAI on complaint filed by petitioner - Held, yes [Para 13]Chartered Accountants Act : Where balance sheet audited by chartered accountant was accepted by arbitrator in arbitration proceedings, ICAI was right in forming prima facie opinion that chartered accountant was not guilty of any professional misconduct

FACT: The petitioner was one of the partners of a firm.

On retirement of the petitioner, dispute arose between the partners regarding the settlement of the accounts of the firm.

According to petitioner, another partner made changes in the accounts of the firm which were detrimental to the interest of petitioner.

According to petitioner, respondent No. 1 who was a chartered accountant certified the accounts of the firm without taking proper care.

According to the petitioner, during the arbitration proceedings filed by that partner against the petitioner and the other partners, the said partner submitted a purported audited accounts of the said firm.

During the pendency of the said arbitration proceedings, the petitioner filed a complaint against the respondent No. 1 before the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI) alleging various acts of misconduct and praying for disciplinary action.

During the pendency of the said complaint, the arbitrator made an award in which he accepted the figures as reflected in the balance sheet which was audited by the respondent No. 1 and was duly signed by the other two partners of the said firm.

Later, the petitioner was informed that Council was prima facie of the opinion that the respondent No. 1 was not guilty of any professional or other misconduct and, therefore, the papers relating to the case had been filed.

The petitioner was further informed that since the Council was of the opinion that the complaint filed by the petitioner was frivolous, deposit of Rs. 100 made by the petitioner had been forfeited.

The petitioner filed instant writ petition for quashing the order passed by the Council holding that the complaint filed by the petitioner against respondent No. 1 was frivolous.

Arguments of petitioner

The appointment of respondent No. 1 as an auditor was not by consent of the petitioner.

Respondent No. 1 had not carried out audit but had certified the purported balance-sheet.

He had mentioned the status of the firm as registered, though he was aware that the firm was not registered.

The procedure followed by the Institute was in violation of principles of natural justice.

Argument of Institute

The rejection of the complaint made by the petitioner could not be faulted with, once the balance sheet audited by respondent No. 1 was accepted as correct.

Issue involved

Whether ICAI was right in holding that respondent No. 1 was not guilty of any professional or other misconduct?

HELD: From the perusal of the arbitration award, it is clear that one of the partners had examined the witness to prove the contents of the balance sheet audited by respondent No. 1 which was signed by the other two partners.

The arbitrator had given a finding of fact that though repeated opportunities were given to the petitioner to cross-examine the witness examined by the one of the partners, no cross-examination was conducted by the petitioner and as a result thereof, the statement made by the said witness remained unchallenged. The arbitrator accepted the balance sheet of the firm based on the books of the account maintained in the regular course duly audited by respondent No. 1 and accepted the figures as reflected in the said balance-sheet. [Para 12]

Considering the fact that the dispute between the partners in respect of the accounts of the said firm was referred to the arbitrator who was an independent person and the said arbitrator looking to the entire evidence has accepted the balance sheet audited by respondent No. 1 as correct, there is no reason to interfere with the prima facie view of the Institute on the complaint filed by the petitioner.

HEADNOTE: Section 21 of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 - Disciplinary Directorate -  Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (Institute) received a complaint from complainant-Central Bank of India alleging that respondent-Chartered Accountant had assisted various companies in availing credit facilities of huge amounts from various banks by issuing false documents certifying valuation of work undertaken and completed by accused companies - Bank also alleged that respondent had also certified sales registers and list of supply bills of accused companies without verifying facts and figures to facilitate loans being sanctioned to said companies - Institute prima facie, found respondent guilty of professional misconduct and accordingly, referred case to Disciplinary Committee - Committee also held respondent guilty of misconduct - Accordingly, Institute decided to recommend to High Court that respondent be reprimanded - It appeared from report of committee that working papers of respondent revealed nothing of substance pertaining to basis of material on which certificates were issued by him - Certificates simply stated that they were issued on specific request of firm - On being asked to produce vouchers for purchase and machinery documents regarding statements of expenditure incurred by accused firms, invoices/vouchers for purchase of plant and machinery for civil work and land development etc, respondent was unable to produce any document - Committee also enquired from respondent as to how he had satisfied himself about existence and valuation of assets as mentioned in certificates issued by him, but apart from his working papers which also did not contain any basis for arriving at any satisfaction, respondent failed to establish any cogent justification for same - Respondent thus, failed to perform due diligence before issuing certificates - Further, respondent was completely aware that accused companies were seeking specific verification and certification to complete documentation required by bank to sanction credit facilities to them and, he was naturally aware that issuing such certificates in absence of proper valuation was a fraud on banks as such public and financial institutions rely upon certificates of professionals as part of its due diligence - Whether in these circumstances, respondent was reprimanded in accordance with section 21(6)(b) - Held, yes [Paras 8, 10 and 15]INCOME TAX/CHARTERED ACCOUNTANT ACT : Where respondent-Chartered Accountant had assisted various companies in availing credit facilities of huge amounts from various banks by issuing false certificates, in view of fact that respondent was naturally aware that issuing such certificates was a fraud on banks as such public and financial institutions rely upon certificates of professionals as part of its due diligence, respondent was thus reprimanded in accordance with section 21(6)(b)

Section 21 of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 - Disciplinary Directorate -  Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (Institute) received a complaint from complainant-Central Bank of India alleging that respondent-Chartered Accountant had assisted various companies in availing credit facilities of huge amounts from various banks by issuing false documents certifying valuation of work undertaken and completed by accused companies - Bank also alleged that respondent had also certified sales registers and list of supply bills of accused companies without verifying facts and figures to facilitate loans being sanctioned to said companies - Institute prima facie, found respondent guilty of professional misconduct and accordingly, referred case to Disciplinary Committee - Committee also held respondent guilty of misconduct - Accordingly, Institute decided to recommend to High Court that respondent be reprimanded - It appeared from report of committee that working papers of respondent revealed nothing of substance pertaining to basis of material on which certificates were issued by him - Certificates simply stated that they were issued on specific request of firm - On being asked to produce vouchers for purchase and machinery documents regarding statements of expenditure incurred by accused firms, invoices/vouchers for purchase of plant and machinery for civil work and land development etc, respondent was unable to produce any document - Committee also enquired from respondent as to how he had satisfied himself about existence and valuation of assets as mentioned in certificates issued by him, but apart from his working papers which also did not contain any basis for arriving at any satisfaction, respondent failed to establish any cogent justification for same - Respondent thus, failed to perform due diligence before issuing certificates - Further, respondent was completely aware that accused companies were seeking specific verification and certification to complete documentation required by bank to sanction credit facilities to them and, he was naturally aware that issuing such certificates in absence of proper valuation was a fraud on banks as such public and financial institutions rely upon certificates of professionals as part of its due diligence - HEADNOTE: Section 21, read with section 22 and clause (7) of Part I of Second Schedule to the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 - Professional misconduct - Respondent CA certified wrong FOB value of export in terms of Import and Export Policy - Whether failure of CA to exercise skill, care and caution while making wrong verification amounted to gross negligence - Held, yes - Whether having regard to fact that respondent had communicated said mistake to exporter involved but only failed to inform authorities concerned he was acting bona fide and, therefore, word of caution to be more careful would suffice instead of reprimanding him - Held, yes
Words & phrases - ‘negligent’ occurring in clause (7) of Part I of the Second Schedule to the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949

FACT: The respondent Chartered Accountant had certified an application of certain exporter in accordance with the requirements of Import and Export Policy certifying the FOB value of exports at Rs. 4,44,77,996. The figure was found to be wrong and on information in this regard being given to the Institute, the matter was referred to the Disciplinary Committee who found the respondent guilty of professional misconduct within the meaning of section 21, read with section 22, and clauses (6) and (7) of Second Schedule to the Act. When the matter came up before the Council, the benefit of doubt was given in respect of charge under clause (6) but in respect of the charge under clause (7) it was found that the respondent had not exercised due care and skill and, therefore, reprimand to him was recommended.

On reference under section 21(5) :

HELD: The respondent had not been found to have contravened clause (6), but clause (7). The latter clause relates to grossly negligent action in the conduct of professional duties. On the background facts, it had to be seen whether failure of the respondent to notice the mistake would constitute an act of negligence. It depends upon the fact whether the concerned person had applied his mind diligently to the job entrusted to him, and whether due care and caution, as is required to be adopted, was taken. The respondent took the stand that by mistake CIF value was typed out instead of FOB value. When a certificate is given, arithmetical accuracy has to be ensured. That is the minimum requirement to be done by a Chartered Accountant. The test is whether in addition to the failure to do the duty, there was failure to act honestly and reasonably. The word ‘negligence’ is associated in the provision with the word ‘misconduct’ and involves some element of moral culpability. Mere imprudence or want of judgment or grave error in judgment is not enough. Misconduct implies failure to act honestly and reasonably either according to the ordinary and natural standard or according to the standard of a particular profession. But error or mis-interpretation of law and specially one view or another over a debatable construction cannot be a ground for the allegation and finding of professional misconduct against a Chartered Accountant. Negligence is the omission to do something which a reasonable man, guided upon those considerations, which ordinarily regulate the conduct of human affairs, would do, or doing something which a prudent and reasonable man would not do. It is not absolute or intrinsic, but relative to some circumstances of time, place or persons, imposing a duty to take care. In dealing with the matters of professional propriety, one cannot ignore the fact that the profession of Chartered Accountant occupies the place of nobility, pride and honour and is a profession of trust. Expertise in the field of accounting and auditing is the hallmark of Chartered Accountant’s profession. When a Chartered Accountant signs certificates, the minimum that he is expected to do is to verify the accuracy of the figures certified. As part of his professional duty and responsibility, he is required to take reasonable steps to satisfy himself that the figures were correct. Elementary verification would have been sufficient to notice the mistake. Failure to carry-out such elementary verification amounts to gross negligence and carelessness. Skill, care and caution, which a reasonably competent and cautious auditor was expected to exercise, was not exercised. Lack of it had affected veracity of his competence. The intendment and object of the Act is to maintain the standard of the profession at a high level.

It was observed by the Apex Court in the context of an Advocates’ professional misconduct that an act which is done otherwise than with utmost good faith is unprofessional - Pandurang Dattatreya Khandekar v. Bar Council of Maharashtra AIR 1984 SC 110.

HEADNOTE: Section 21 of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 - Preferential or other misconduct - Assessee claimed deduction under section 80HHC - In order to claim said deduction, provisions of section 80HHC required that a certificate be filed in Form 10CCAC which was to be issued by chartered accountant certifying that export had in fact been made - Respondent, a chartered accountant, issued said certificate which was submitted before Assessing Officer - Assessee's claim was found to be false because export amount remained outstanding and was not realized though as per certificate given by respondent, amount had been realized - Whether, on facts, respondent was guilty of professional misconduct falling within meaning of clause (7) of Part-I of second schedule under section 22, read with section 21 and, thus, ends of justice would be subserved by removing name of respondent from register of members for a period of six months - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee had claimed deduction under section 80HHC. In order to claim this deduction, the provisions of section 80HHC required that a certificate be filed in Form 10CCAC which was to be issued by the chartered accountant certifying that the export had in fact been made. This certificate was given by the respondent as chartered accountant which was submitted before the Assessing Officer. The claim of the assessee was found to be false as against the alleged export the amount remained outstanding and was not realized. Though, as per the certificate given by the respondent, the amount had been realized. This would clearly show that certificate furnished by the respondent was wrong and bogus. An inquiry was held by the Council of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India on the allegations contained in a complaint submitted by the Commissioner. The Disciplinary Committee found that the allegations were substantiated and proved. After considering the report, the Council held the respondent guilty of professional misconduct falling within the meaning of clause (7) of Part-I of the second schedule under section 22, read with section 21 of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949. It accordingly recommended to this Court that the name of the respondent be removed from the register of members for a period of three years.

On reference :

HELD: The entire controversy was about the certificate issued by the respondent certifying that the exports were duly made and payments had been received by the assessee against those exports. It has been established on record that no such payment was received. The assessee had also accepted this fact when he was confronted with this aspect during the assessment proceedings whereby the claim of deduction under section 80HHC was rejected. Once it is established that no payment was received against the export, certificate issued by the respondent was false. It is a bogey raised by the respondent that he has verified all the documents and only then issued the certificate. One fails to understand what kinds of documents were shown by the assessee to the respondent on the basis of which the respondent felt satisfied. Thus, there was a clinching evidence to prove the charge. [Para 7]

In the instant case, on the one hand the respondent pleads his sickness, has otherwise unblemished practice of 21 years and that the incident is old which may provide some mitigating factors in his favour, on the other hand, the misconduct is of serious nature. Submitting a false/bogus certificate to the client to enable him to make false claim of deduction under the Income-tax Act, is a serious offence. The deduction to the tune of Rs. 18,32,985 was claimed on the strength of this certificate which would mean the tax saving of almost 6.5 lakhs. The attempt was thus to dupe the tax authorities and help the assessee to avoid the tax to that extent such a conduct has to be taken seriously. [Para 11]

After weighing the aforesaid factors on either side, it is opined that in the present case the respondent cannot be left off merely by giving him reprimand. Some penalty needs to be imposed so that it acts as deterrent and such professional misconduct is not committed. Weighing the circumstances, the ends of justice would be subserved by removing the name of the respondent from the Register of Members for a period of six months. [Para 12]

HEADNOTE: Section 21, read with section 22, of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 and regulation 11 of the Chartered Accountants Regulations, 1964 - Misconduct - Chartered Accountant certified accounts prepared by client as correct without verifying totals in profit and loss account resulting in excess deduction under the Agricultural Income-tax Act - Whether failure to carry out elementary verification amounted to gross negligence and carelessness affecting veracity of his competence and, therefore, respondent was guilty of 
 professional misconduct within meaning of section 21, read with section 22 and clause (7) of Part 1 of the Second Schedule to the Act and penalty of reprimand as recommended by Council was adequate and proper - Held, yes

FACT: The respondent was the Chartered Accountant who audited the accounts of an assessee and certified the same to be correct. Based on it, the Agricultural ITO allowed the entire claim of expenditure of Rs. 3,19,163.55 as shown in the expenditure side of the profit and loss account filed by him. However, on subsequent scrutiny it was found that the total amount on expenditure side of the profit and loss account was really Rs. 2,19,163 which resulted in penal consequence to the assessee. A complaint was made to the ICAI against the respondent which called for the statement of the auditor with respect to charge of professional misconduct under regulation 11(6). After going through the complaint and the written statement of the auditor, the President of the Council called for the copies of the profit and loss account, etc., under regulation 11(8) and after considering the documents the matter was referred by the counsel to the Disciplinary Committee which was of the view that the respondent was guilty of professional misconduct within the meaning of section 21, read with section 22 and clause (7) of Part I of the Second Schedule to the Act. The Council accepted the view of the Committee and recommended the penalty of reprimand.

HELD: The job of a Chartered Accountant is not to make a compilation. When a certificate is given, arithmetical accuracy has to be ensured. That is the minimum requirement to be done by a chartered accountant. The test is whether in addition to the failure to do the duty, there is failure to act honestly and reasonably. The word ‘negligence’ is associated in the provision with the word ‘misconduct’ and involves some element of moral culpability. Mere imprudence or want of judgment or grave error of judgment is not enough. Misconduct implies failure to act honestly and reasonably either according to the ordinary and natural standard or according to the standard of a particular profession. But error or misinterpretation of law and specially one view or another over a debatable construction cannot be a ground for the allegation and finding of professional misconduct against a chartered accountant. Negligence is the omission to do something which a reasonable man, guided by those considerations which ordinarily regulate the conduct of human affairs, would do. It is not absolute or intrinsic, but relative to some circumstances of time, place or persons, imposing a duty to take care. In dealing with matters of professional propriety, one cannot ignore the fact that the profession of chartered accountancy occupies the place of nobility, pride and honour and is a profession of trust. Expertise in the field of accounting and auditing is the hallmark of the chartered accountant’s profession. When a chartered accountant prepares a profit and loss account from the books of account and signs a certificate to that effect, the minimum that he is expected to do is to verify the accuracy of the figures in the profit and loss account with reference to the relevant books of account and he cannot escape the responsibility by pleading that he did not audit it and that verification of accounts was done by the staff. As part of his professional duty and responsibility, he is required to take reasonable steps to satisfy himself that the work is carried out in a proper, fair and efficient manner. The certificate is issued by him and the professional relationship is between him and the client. There could not be any escape by the respondent by taking the plea that an experienced accountant was verifying the totals. Elementary verification of totalling would have been sufficient to notice the mistake. Failure to carry out such elementary verification amounted to gross negligence and carelessness. Skill, care and caution, which a reasonably competent and cautious auditor is expected to exercise, was not done. The lack of it had affected the veracity of his competence. Delegation of duties does not necessarily absolve a principal from the liability arising out of gross negligence. The intendment and object of the Act is to maintain the standard of the profession at a high level.

HEADNOTE: Section  40(a)(i), read with section  143(1), of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Business disallowance -  Interest, etc., paid to a non-resident without deduction of tax at source (Scope of provision) - Assessment year 2020-21 - Assessee-company made payment to a foreign company towards certification fees for products which was necessary to sell products in USA and Canada market - Centralized Processing Centre (CPC) made disallowance under section 40(a)(i) for non-deduction of tax at source on said payment - Assessing Officer in scrutiny proceedings under section 143(3) accepted contentions of assessee and had not made any disallowance under section 40(a)(i) - However, while computing total taxable income Assessing Officer inadvertently took income computed under section 143(1) which inter alia included disallowance under section 40(a)(i) - Whether since issue had been examined in scrutiny proceedings and details in support of same were placed, impugned disallowance made by CPC deserved to be deleted - Held, yes [Paras 8 and 9] [In favour of assessee]INTERNATIONAL TAXATION/INCOME TAX : Where Assessing Officer accepted contentions of assessee that payment made to a foreign company towards certification fees for products was not chargeable to tax in India and had not made any disallowance under section 40(a)(i), however, while computing total taxable income Assessing Officer inadvertently took income computed under section 143(1) which inter alia included disallowance under section 40(a)(i), since issue had been examined in scrutiny proceedings, impugned disallowance made by CPC deserved to be deleted

Section  40(a)(i), read with section  143(1), of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Business disallowance -  Interest, etc., paid to a non-resident without deduction of tax at source (Scope of provision) - Assessment year 2020-21 - Assessee-company made payment to a foreign company towards certification fees for products which was necessary to sell products in USA and Canada market - Centralized Processing Centre (CPC) made disallowance under section 40(a)(i) for non-deduction of tax at source on said payment - Assessing Officer in scrutiny proceedings under section 143(3) accepted contentions of assessee and had not made any disallowance under section 40(a)(i) - However, while computing total taxable income Assessing Officer inadvertently took income computed under section 143(1) which inter alia included disallowance under section 40(a)(i) - Whether since issue had been examined in scrutiny proceedings and details in support of same were placed, impugned disallowance made by CPC deserved to be deleted - Held, yes [Paras 8 and 9] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee-company made payments to a foreign company towards certification fees for products which was necessary to sell the products in USA and Canada market. The return was processed under section 143(1)(a) wherein CPC made prima facie adjustments making disallowance under section 40(a)(i) for non-deduction of tax on the payment.

■

The assessee's case was selected for scrutiny and the same was carried out under section 143(3) read with section 144B and in the course of scrutiny proceedings one of the issue raised in the show cause notice by the Assessing Officer was regarding the alleged addition made under section 40(a)(i). The Assessing Officer accepted the contention of the assessee and it was further stated that no disallowance was required under section 40(a)(i).

■

However, while computing the total taxable income the Assessing Officer inadvertently took income computed under section 143(1)(a) which inter alia included the disallowance under section 40(a)(i).

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) dismissed the ground for statistical purposes.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: ■

following factors should be present in the transaction :

(a)

There should be a consideration for use or transfer of right to use;

(b)

The payment shall be towards grant or share for acquiring, inter alia, information concerning industrial, commercial or scientific experience, including gains derived from the alienation of any such right, property or information;

(c)

Such use or right to use such property or information shall be for the stipulated period in accordance with the terms of the contract. [Para 9] From the impugned order of the authorities, it emerged that GIA, by using its experience, does the work of diamond grading. In other words, parts in favour of the person seeking its specialized knowledge to the particular diamond in the form of grading certificate. It was on account of that activity that in the impugned order, it was set out that there was a transfer of commercial experience in the shape of diamond grading report. It is true that GIA may have the experience of grading. However, there is no imparting of its experience in favour of the client. What the client receives is the report where the GIA uses its commercial or technical knowledge to give a report to the client. Illustrative example would be a lawyer giving advise to his client; a doctor giving his medical opinion; a laboratory submitting blood analysis report and the like. These cannot be said to be imparting of information by the person who possesses such information. What such person does is to use of his experience and technical know-how for a consideration without parting with that information. Therefore, considering the definition of royalty under article 12, there was no parting or rendering of technical services either of managerial, technical or consultancy nature or industrial, commercial or scientific experience. Once the consideration/fees received did not fall within the expression 'royalty', the action of the respondents in refusing the certificate under section 195 was clearly without jurisdiction and, consequently, the impugned order was to be set aside with a further direction to the Deputy Director to issue the certificate as applied for by the assessee. [Para 11]

]

In the entirety of facts and circumstances of the case, the matter is to be set aside to the file of the Assessing officer for verification of declarations so filed by the assessee in Form 27C and examination of claim of the assessee under section 206C(1A) afresh in accordance with law. [Para 48]

Issue of alleged relief on basis of additional evidence without calling for remand report under Rule 46A and enquiry under section 250(4) The certificates in Form 27BA from the Chartered accountant and related declarations from the buyers were filed before the Assessing officer during the course of assessment proceedings and the same have been taken on record and examined by the Assessing officer. It was observed by the Assessing Officer that he has gone through the documentation so submitted by the assessee firm and on perusal thereof, he noticed that complete information in the Form/certificate have not been given by the accountant/party as required by the legislature and most of the columns are either not filled up as required or simply mentioned as per details/enclosure. Moreover, the accountant has signed the forms with conditional remarks "As certified by the buyer" whereas the forms should have been filled up and certified by the accountant itself on the basis of records. Further, some of the parties have not filed return on or before due dates prescribed under section 139. Further, on appeal, it is founed that these certificates in Form 27BA from the Chartered accountant and related declarations from the buyers have again been considered and examined by the Commissioner (Appeals) and the observations of the Assessing Officer regarding these certificates were not found tenable by the Commissioner (Appeals) and on basis his independent review and examination, the relief has been provided to the assessee firm as per his findings of his order. The Revenue has not pointed out what further evidence by way of additional evidence has been filed by the assessee during the appellate proceedings before the Commissioner (Appeals). Therefore, the ground so taken by the Revenue is to be dismissed. [Para 54]

The limited issue under consideration is whether at the time of submitting the certificates in Form 27BA as required under proviso to section 206C(6A), the assessee is required to deposit interest and give details of such interest deposit in such certificates. Firstly, on reading of provisions of proviso to section 206C(6A), it may be found that there is no requirement as such which has been specified in the statute. All it requires is that the accountant should certify as to whether the buyer has furnished his return of income, has taken into account such amount for computing income in such return of income and has paid taxes due on the income declared by him in such return of income or not. Further, on perusal of Form 27BA, it is found that besides such certification, it contains a statement whether the assessee has to specify whether it has paid any interest under section 206C(7) or not for non-collection or short collection of taxes. Thus, there is no mandatory requirement to pay any interest under section 206C(7) as part of certification in Form 27BA and where the assessee has already paid, he has to specify that he has paid and where he has not paid, he has to specify accordingly. It is only an information seeking requirement and not a requirement in absence thereof which will make the certification in Form 27BA invalid where there is substantial compliance as to the mandatory requirements of certification. In the result, the ground so taken by the Revenue is dismissed. [Para 58]

The Commissioner (Appeals) has clearly held and directed the Assessing Officer to allow the benefit to the assessee in light of Supreme Court decision in case of Hindustan Coca Cola Beverage (P.) Ltd. (supra) which he has discussed at length in the earlier part of the order and held that ratio of the said decision clearly applies in the instant case as there is no substantive difference in provisions relating to TDS and TCS. However, such direction was subject to verification by the Assessing Officer as to the filing of the return of income by the respective buyers and where it was found by the Assessing Officer that return of income has been filed, relief was directed to be allowed to the assessee and where such return of income has not been filed, no relief was directed to be allowed. Such direction by the Commissioner (Appeals) is well within his powers and jurisdiction under section 250(1) and doesn't result in setting aside the matter to the file of the Assessing Officer for making a fresh assessment and adjudication afresh. In the result, the ground of appeal so taken by the Revenue is dismissed. [Para 63]

The Revenue has challenged the findings of the Commissioner (Appeals) where he had held that there is no material difference in the provisions of tax deduction at source (TDS) under Chapter-XVIIB and tax collection at Source (TCS) under Chapter-XVIIBB of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and the facts and the judgment held in assessment proceedings under section 201(1)/201(1A) for default in the case of Hindustan Coca Cola Beverage (P.) Ltd. (supra) are squarely applicable in the case of the assessee for assessment proceedings under section 206C(6)/206C(7) for TCS defaults. [Para 64]

]

FACT: One MA opened a bank account in the name of some persons induding entity, BK in Indian Bank, and presented some import documents to the Branch Manager, requesting him to transfer foreign exchange to certain entities abroad. The Branch Manager sent said import documents to the Principal Commissioner of Customs for verification. The Principal Commissioner of Customs verified those import documents, including the documents of BK and found that most of them were forged ones immediately, the Principal Commissioner of Customs informed the Enforcement Directorate about this transaction. The Enforcement Directorate initiated investigation and found that BK was started in the name of one K, and, current accounts were opened in the name of BK in seven banks, but, in all the applications submitted to the bank, the photograph of K was not affixed. After completion of investigation against BK a complaint was filed under PMLA with allegation to the effect that these persons have opened fictitious bank accounts, submitted forged bills of entry, parked huge amounts in those bank accounts and had them transferred to various parties abroad through the bank, in order to make it a licit transaction for the alleged purpose of import.

During investigation, the Enforcement Directorate stumbled upon some Form 15CB that were issued by petitioner auditor. During interrogation, petitioner revealed facts that one of his clients KM had approached him for issuance of Form 15CB under rule 37-BB of the Income-tax Rules, 1962, and submitted documents in support of his request; accordingly, petitioner perused those documents and issued certificates to the effect that it is not necessary to issue Form 15CB in respect of overseas payment of imports. The five numbers of Form 15CB relating to BK were also uploaded in the website portal of Income-tax Department and were presented to the Branch Manager, State Bank of Travancore, for transferring a sum to various entities in Honk Kong. After completing this part of the investigation, the ED filed a supplementary complaint under PMLA by virtue of which, petitioner KM and AH were arrayed.

In instant petition, the petitioner-auditor had requested for quashing of prosecution.

HELD: As regards the requirements for submission of Form 15CB, it is found from the records that only the State Bank of Travancore had insisted upon the said certificates and not the other six banks through which, foreign remittances were made by KM and AH. The complaint and the accompanying background show that AH had operated the bank accounts and KM had facilitated the opening of the bank account and preparation of various documents by availing the services of various persons including petitioner - auditor, for the limited purpose of obtaining Form 15CB for transferring monies from State Bank of Travancore. A reading of the impugned complaint, shows that petitioner had issued five numbers of Form 15CB in favour of entity BK, which were handed over by him to his client KM for which, a sum of Rs. 1,000 per certificate was given to him as remuneration. [Para 10]

Even on a demurrer, on a perusal of Form 15CB, it is found that a CA is required to only examine the nature of the remittance and nothing more. The Chartered Accountant is not required to go into the genuineness or otherwise of the documents submitted by his clients. This could be compared with the legal opinion that are normally given by panel lawyers of banks, after scrutinizing title documents without going into their genuinity. A Panel Advocate, who has no means to go into the genuinity of title deeds and who gives an opinion based on such title deeds, cannot be prosecuted along with the principal offender. Applying the same anomaly, the prosecution of petitioner, in the facts and circumstances of the case at hand, cannot be sustained. [Para 11]

In the result, this Criminal Revision is allowed and the order passed on the file of XII Additional Special Court for CBI cases at Chennai, is set aside and the petitioner is discharged from the prosecution. [Para 12]

Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 12 of the DTAA between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties and fee for technical services) - Assessment year 2012-13 - Assessee was engaged in business of manufacturing of switch mode power supplies and other computer peripherals in its factory located in SEEPZ - Assessee's products were being mainly exported to US and European countries - Assessee availed certification services from non-residents in US for certifying its products to be sold in USA and Europe which was a precondition for selling products in those markets - Besides, assessee paid professional charges for compilation of documents in USA for satisfying transfer pricing requirements - In course of assessment, Assessing Officer treated said payment as 'fees for technical services' under Article 12(4) of DTAA between India and USA - It was undisputed that as per article 12(4) of DTAA between India and USA, fee was chargeable to tax in India if services rendered 'make available' any technical knowledge, experience, skill, know-how and a process or transfer of technical plans or designs - However, in instant case, certification agencies and professional firms had not made available such services to assessee - Whether in view of aforesaid, payment made for services rendered by non-resident entities was not taxable in India as 'fee for technical services' - Held, yes [Para 8][In favour of assessee]

Section 67 of the Finance Act, 1994 - Valuation of taxable services - Stay order - Assessee was rendering clearing and forwarding agent’s service - During relevant period, it received a consolidated sum of about Rs. 94 lakhs as service charges - Revenue raised demand of Rs. 5,43,618 - Assessee contested quantification of demand and submitted that it was liable to pay Rs. 94,272 as service tax - Its case was that out of Rs. 94 lakhs, about Rs. 78 lakhs was relatable to activities which were not covered by services of clearing and forwarding agent and in support of same, it produced a Chartered Accountant’s certificate - On other hand, revenue was of view that said certificate was not supported by relevant documentary evidence and, hence, assessee was liable to pay service tax as per demand notice - Whether issue in question was required to be gone into in detail at time of final hearing and, as such, assessee had not made out a prima facie case for total waiver of service tax demand and, accordingly, it was to be directed to deposit Rs. 2.5 lakhs and requirement to pre-deposit balance amount of duty and penalties was to be waived - Held, yes [Para 6] [Stay partly granted]

Section 65(108) of the Finance Act, 1994 - Technical inspection and certification service - Period 1-7-2003 to 31-3-2004 - Assessee was operating as licensed registrar under office of AQA, USA - It represented AQA for purpose of assisting clients in achievement of ISO 9000, ISO 14000 and QS 9000 certifications - It received Company Information Sheet (CIS) from prospective clients, reviewed CIS, prepared quotation and sent same to clients, provided information connected with quality management system certification, conducted audit/assessment of quality system at clients’ place with reference to ISO standard and after successful completion of assessment process, sent such assessment report to AQA - It charged audit fee for doing audit work from clients - Revenue treated said service of assessee as that of ‘Technical inspection and certification agency’ and demanded service tax - Whether word ‘process’ mentioned in definition of ‘Technical inspection and certification’ can relate only to physical and chemical processes and it cannot be transported to province of management relating to human beings - Held, yes - Whether therefore, activities carried out by assessee for certification of quality management system practised by clients, would not come within purview of ‘Technical inspection and certification service’ - Held, yes [Para 5.2] Words & Phrases : Word ‘process’ as occurring in section 65(108) of the Finance Act, 1994 Interpretation of statutes : Principles of Ejusdem Generis

Classification of services - Section 65(108) of the Finance Act, 1994 - Technical inspection and certification (OR) - Assessee dealing in LPG sent LPG through tank trucks to various LPG bottling plants of oil distribution companies - Whenever LPG tank truck required any repair or mandatory testing of safety valves, tank truck was cleaned and completely degassed - During this activity, water was filled in tank mounted on truck and discharged - Water was displaced by LPG vapors - For this activity, assessee collected cost of water and labour charges from truck owner - Adjudicating Authority held that said activities undertaken by assessee would fall under category of 'technical inspection and certification service' - Whether assessee though was performing certain activities in relation to maintenance and safety of tank trucks and was issuing a certificate to effect that tank trucks were purged/degassed, same could not be considered to be a service within scope of 'technical inspection and certification service' - Held, yes [Para 5] [In favour of assessee]GST/Service Tax: Where assessee dealing in LPG was performing certain activities in relation to maintenance and safety of tank trucks and was issuing a certificate to effect that tank trucks were purged/degassed, said activities could not be considered to be a service within scope of 'technical inspection and certification service'

Section 65(35) of the Finance Act, 1994 - Custom house agent - Period 2000-04 - Whether activities relating to freight forwarding cannot be brought under category of services of ‘Customs house agents’ (CHA) - Held, yes - Whether activity of CHA relates only to entry or departure of conveyances or import or export of goods at any customs station and, therefore, activities of CHA are limited to customs station and they cannot extend beyond it; and where assessee collected air freight for export from consignee, activity being related to transportation service rendered by airline company, such freight forwarding could not be said to be a part of activities of CHA - Held, yes - Whether where, from nature of various charges collected by assessee, it was found that those were not includible in computation of service tax towards CHA services; however, Commissioner held that those charges were related to CHA services though he himself had repeatedly pointed out that assessee had not produced a chartered accountant’s certificate with regard to deductions claimed by it, matter was to be remanded to original authority for re-adjudication - Held, yes [Para 6]

Section 9, read with sections 40(a)(i) and 195, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and article 12 of India-USA DTAA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalty/FTS - Certification charges) - Assessment years 2005-06 and 2008-09 - Revenue was of view that services rendered by said organization to assessee qualified as 'included services' as it involved making available technical know-how to assessee and, thus, same was taxable in terms of article 12(4) of DTAA with USA and TDS was to be deducted on same - It was noted that procedure which IFANCA followed for halal certification did not mention what technical know-how was made available to assessee - In fact entire procedure adopted by IFANCA ensured that proper sanitation and cleanliness procedures were followed by assessee while manufacturing its product and product was not contaminated so as to qualify as halal - Assessing Officer directed assessee to furnish details of transactions and method adopted for determining Arm's Length Price (ALP) - Assessee stated that it had applied Cost Plus Method (CPM) for determining ALP on basis of agreement entered into with AE.s and basis is adapted as per agreement was mark-up of 23.45 per cent on salary and rent expenses incurred by assessee - Assessing Officer directed assessee to explain as to why mark-up should not be applied to entire cost incurred since assessee was rendering exclusive services to AE.s - On reply, however, Assessing Officer opined that assessee did not file an explanation with regard to proposed mark-up adjustment - Considering available material, Assessing Officer held that assessee had not submitted any documentary evidence like transfer of shares, appointment of new directors to substantiate its claim and certificate of chartered accountant of foreign entity was without any authority - One of directors in company was existing director and shareholder in assessee company is on close of balance sheet date i.e. 31-3-2011 and audit report was filed almost after one and half year from date of entry of shareholders/directors of foreign entities and there was no reason as to why assessee had not disclosed such vital facts of time of filing audit report - Thus, Assessing Officer rejected claim of assessee and held that two entities were AE's of assessee and transactions entered by it with them were squarely covered under definition of IT within meaning of provisions of section 92 - As regards proposed adjustment and working of CPM, Assessing Officer held that assessee had not submitted any explanation as to why other than salary and rent had not been included in invoices raised and mark-up had been charged thereon and assessee was into service sectors and was providing software related services to AE's involving lead restrictive utilities and method followed by assessee was not in accordance with provisions of Act, and entire cost was required to be taken into consideration for applying mark-up under CPM - Since, assessee had failed to do so total amount of expenditure debited to profit  loss account had to be considered as qualifying amount for mark-up on invoices to be raised on AE's as per method applied by it, Assessing Officer made an upward adjustment to total income of assessee under section 92C(4) - On appeal, after considering submission of assessee and assessment order, FAA held that assessee had argued that Star and DTL were not its AE's and it had merely submitted a copy of certificate issued by chartered accountant of AE and certificate was not supported by any documentary evidence like transfer of shares hence, argument was not acceptable - Further FAA held that assessee had not filed an explanation with regard to mark-up rate of 23.45 per cent for expenses other than salary and rent and assessee had not produced any documentary evidence with regard to annual reports of other companies for verification and it had not filed any TP study report during assessment proceedings for appellate proceedings and it had not followed provisions of section 92, thus, assessee had not discharged its primary onus of benchmarking transaction and upheld order of Assessing Officer - Whether since assessee did not file any confirmation or certificate from auditors about incorrectness of audit report especially about existence of AE's therefore, order of FAA does not suffer from any legal infirmity - Held, yes - Whether since assessee had included only two of items of profit and loss account i.e. salary and rent, and had not included other charges for determining ALP then mark-up determined as 23.45 per cent needs further verification on part of Assessing Officer and if assessee had not incurred any expenditure for alleged three items same should not be considered for mark-up purposes - Held, yes [Para 5] [Partly in favour of assessee]

On appeal, after considering submission of assessee and assessment order, FAA held that assessee had argued that Star and DTL were not its AE's and it had merely submitted a copy of certificate issued by chartered accountant of AE and certificate was not supported by any documentary evidence like transfer of shares hence, argument was not acceptable - Whether since assessee did not file any confirmation or certificate from auditors about incorrectness of audit report especially about existence of AE's therefore, order of FAA does not suffer from any legal infirmity -
