Held, yes [Para 5] [Partly in favour of assessee]

Section 73 of the Finance Act, 1994 - Recovery of service tax not levied or paid or short-levied or short-paid or erroneously refunded - Assessee was registered under category of ‘Security Agency’ and had been paying service tax - However, department proceeded to work out short-levy of service tax in terms of returns filed by assessee with income-tax department - Assessee submitted that amount shown in income-tax return had not been received and same was still due - But as it did not produce chartered accountant’s certificate in support of its plea, Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed demand - However, before Tribunal, assessee produced chartered accountant’s certificate in support of its plea - It also pleaded issue of time bar, which had not been considered by adjudicating authority - Whether, on facts, order of Commissioner (Appeals) was to be set aside and matter was to be remanded to original authority for de novo consideration - Held, yes [Para 3]

Section 65 of the Finance Act, 1994 - Practising chartered accountants - Whether billing activity carried out by ordinary clerks who have not even completed SSLC is not part of chartered accountants’ activity - Held, yes

I. Section 9, read with sections 40(a)(i) and 195, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and article 12 of India-USA DTAA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalty/FTS - Certification charges) - Assessment years 2005-06 and 2008-09 - During year, assessee-company made payment to an organization, namely, IFANCA for obtaining certification of product exported by assessee to USA as 'halal' so as to enable said product access to Islamic market in USA - Revenue was of view that services rendered by said organization to assessee qualified as 'included services' as it involved making available technical know-how to assessee and, thus, same was taxable in terms of article 12(4) of DTAA with USA and TDS was to be deducted on same - It was noted that procedure which IFANCA followed for halal certification did not mention what technical know-how was made available to assessee - In fact entire procedure adopted by IFANCA ensured that proper sanitation and cleanliness procedures were followed by assessee while manufacturing its product and product was not contaminated so as to qualify as halal - Whether, on facts, such payment made by assessee for halal certification did not qualify as 'included services' in terms of article 12(4) of India-USA DTAA and, thus, no TDS was to be deducted on such payment - Held, yes - Whether accordingly, impugned disallowance of certificate charges paid by assessee under section 40(a)(i) for non-deduction of TDS was unwarranted - Held, yes [Paras 17 and 18] [In favour of assessee]  II. Section 40(a)(ia), read with section 148, of the Income-Tax Act, 1961 - Business disallowance - Interest, etc., paid to a resident without deduction of tax at source (Reassessment) - Assessment years 2005-06 and 2008-09 - Regular assessment in case of assessee was framed under section 143(3) - Thereafter, Assessing Officer issued a reopening notice on ground that assessee had not deducted TDS on legal and professional charges and carriage outward expenses paid by it - He further made disallowance on account of these payments - It was noted that Commissioner (Appeals) found that this issue pertaining to disallowance was not discussed during original assessment order and no opinion was formed on it, thus, reopening was to be upheld - Whether since assessee was unable to controvert findings of Commissioner (Appeals) that this issue was not discussed during original assessment, validity of reassessment framed under section 147 could not be challenged on account of change of opinion and impugned reopening was unjustified- Held, yes [Para 10] [In favour of revenue]

II. Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm's length price (Adjustments - Reimbursement of expenses) - Assessment year 2008-09 - Assessee had claimed deduction for payments made by assessee to its AEs contending same to be reimbursement of out of pocket expenses incurred by AEs on behalf of assessee - Since assessee could only furnish bills for part of amount, TPO determined ALP of balance out of pocket expenses to be 'Nil' and proposed transfer pricing adjustment - Whether since auditors in audit report had certified financial statements to be true after carrying out verification on test check basis and TPO had not pointed out any discrepancy in supporting documents furnished by assessee which constituted 78 per cent of expenses reimbursed by assessee to its AE, no adjustment on account of such expenses would be permitted - Held, yes [Para 18] [In favour of assessee]

Section 11B of the Central Excise Act, 1944 - Claim for refund of duty - Assessee, a receiver of services of goods transport agencies, discharged service tax liability - However, it having noticed that it had paid service tax in excess without claiming any abatement as per Notification No. 1/2006-ST, dated 1-3-2006, filed refund claim by furnishing Chartered Accountant’s certificate certifying that incidence of tax had not been passed on to customers -Revenue, however, rejected refund claim - Whether in view of Chartered Accountant’s certificate, assessee was entitled to refund - Held, yes [Para 7]
Section 65(83) of the Finance Act, 1994 - Practising Chartered accountants service

I. Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm's length price (Adjustments - Reimbursement of expenses) - Assessment year 2011-12 - Assessee-company had claimed deduction for payments made by it to its AEs contending same to be reimbursement of out of pocket expenses incurred by AEs on behalf of assessee and submitted third-party invoices for part of expenses - TPO proposed transfer pricing adjustment by taking ALP of out-of-pocket expenses as 'Nil' - Auditors in audit report had certified financial statements to be true and correct after carrying out verification on test check basis and TPO had not pointed out any defect/discrepancy in bills/supporting documents furnished by assessee which constituted 78 per cent of out of pocket expenses reimbursed by it to its AE - Whether TPO was not justified in making additions - Held, yes [Para 11] [In favour of assessee]TRANSFER PRICING : No transfer pricing addition should be made in relation to reimbursement of out-of-pocket expenses to AE, where auditors in audit report had certified financial statements to be true and correct after carrying out verification on test check basis and TPO had not pointed out any defect/discrepancy in bills/supporting documents furnished by assessee which constituted 78 per cent of out of pocket expenses reimbursed by assessee to its AE  TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee had made payment to it's AE claiming same to be reimbursement of software maintenance expenses incurred by AE in form of connectivity charges which were in addition to Software Maintenance Expenses and project closure report of AEs and monthly intra-group account statements showed that same were being reimbursed at cost, TPO was not justified in making addition for reimbursement of software maintenance expenses and IT connectivity charges

Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and article 13 of India-UK DTAA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties/Fees for technical services - Make available) - Assessment years 2018-19 and 2019-20 - Assessee, a UK based company, entered into intragroup agreement with its Indian AE and provided services pertaining to human resources, finance, legal and compliance and conducting of internal audit assurance work - Assessee received certain amount with respect to said services which was not offered to tax while filing return - Assessing Officer held that such receipts were for services in nature of FTS under article 13 and would be taxable in India - It was noted from service agreement that services rendered by assessee were in nature of advisory services and assessee's role was to assist AEs in making correct decision on aspects specifically referred to in agreement - Whether since such rendition of services did not result in transfer of technical knowledge, know-how, skill etc. to Indian AE, 'make available' condition provided under article 13(4)(c) remained non-compliant and thus, receipts would not fall within definition of FTS as provided under article 13(4) of India - UK DTAA - Held, yes [Para 12] [In favour of assessee]INTERNATIONAL TAXATION : Where assessee, a UK based company, received certain sum for providing services to its Indian AE pertaining to human resources, finance, legal and compliance and conducting of internal audit assurance work, since said services were merely for enabling and assisting Indian AE in making correct decisions on certain aspects and did not result in transfer of technical knowledge, know-how, skill etc., 'make available' condition provided under article 13(4)(c) remained non-compliant and, thus, receipts would not fall within definition of FTS as provided under article 13(4) of India - UK DTAA

Section 65 of the Finance Act, 1994 - Consulting Engineer - Period April 2000 to June 2003 - Assessee claimed that test inspection and certification done by it was not consulting engineer’s service and it was not taxable service prior to 1-7-2003 - However, agreement with some heavy industrial companies showed that assessee’s mechanical engineers had to inspect customers’ machines and to certify those as fit for use - In case, machinery required modification of design or other changes, engineers would render requisite advice - Whether prima facie nature of service rendered by assessees looked like consulting engineer’s service - Held, yes - Whether further since assessee could not show that copies of agreements together with relevant invoices had been produced before departmental authorities, assessee could not said to have been able to establish that there was no suppression on its part and plea of limitation could not be held genuine - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, stay on requirement of pre-deposit could not be granted - Held, yes [Paras 2 & 3]

Section 92CA, read with section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Reference to TPO (Section 37(1) v. section 92CA) - Whether jurisdiction of Assessing Officer under section 37 and TPO under section 92CA is distinct and, therefore, a referral made by Assessing Officer to TPO for limited purpose of determining ALP does not take away power of Assessing Officer to determine as to whether payment made by assessee to its AE for services rendered was basically an expenditure incurred for purpose of business so as to allow same under section 37(1) - Held, yes [In favour of revenue]IT/ILT : Jurisdiction of Assessing Officer under section 37(1) and TPO under section 92CA is distinct and, therefore, a referral made by Assessing Officer to TPO for limited purpose of determining ALP does not take away power of Assessing Officer to determine as to whether payment made by assessee to its AE for services rendered was basically an expenditure incurred for purpose of business so as to allow same under section 37(1)  IT/ILT : Authority of TPO is to conduct a transfer pricing analysis to determine ALP and not to determine whether there is a service or not from which assessee benefits; therefore, TPO cannot determine ALP of payments made by assessee to its AE at nil taking a view that assessee did not derive any benefit from services rendered by AE

Section 271B of the Income-tax Act
Where assessee had accepted that books of account were handed over to his auditor in July 1992 for tax audit and this fact had also been accepted by auditor, but subsequently audit reports signed by some other Chartered Accountants were filed along with income-tax returns on 29-11-1992, it could be taken as proved that books of account were not at all audited and in such a case of levy of penalty on assessee would be justified
C. Ramaswamy v. ITO [1999] 63 TTJ (Mad.) 647
Where the assessee had accepted that the books of account were handed over to his auditor in July 1992 for tax audit and this fact had also been accepted by the auditor, but subsequently the audit reports signed by some other Chartered Accountants were filed along with the income-tax returns on 29-12-1992, it could be taken as proved that books of account were not at all audited and in such a case of levy of penalty on the assessee was justified.

Section 9  of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 13 of the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement between India and United Kingdom (FTS) - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India - Assessment years 2010-11 and 2014-15 - Whether where assessee a UK based company rendered inspection and testing services to Indian customers in respect of imported/exported cargo and certifying in relation to quality and price, without making available any technical knowledge, experience, skill, know-how or processes to recipient of service so as to enable recipients to use those services independently, payment made for services in question could not be termed as 'fee for technical services' - Held, yes [Para 6][In favour of assessee]IT/ILT: Where inspection and testing services rendered by assessee a UK based company to Indian customers but no technical knowledge, etc. were made available so as to enable recipients to use those services independently, payments received could not be termed as 'fee for technical services'

Held, that when a chartered accountant prepares a profit and loss account from the books of account and signs a certificate to that effect, the minimum that he is expected to do is to verify the accuracy of the figures in the profit and loss account with reference to the relevant books of account. He cannot escape responsibility pleading that he did not audit it and that verification of accounts was done by the staff As part of his professional duty and responsibility, he was required to take reasonable steps to satisfy himself that the work was carried out in a proper, fair and efficient manner. Failure to carry out such elementary verification amounted to gross negligence and carelessness. Skill, care and caution, which a reasonably competent and cautious auditor was expected to exercise, was not done. The Council was justified in its conclusion that the respondent was guilty of professional misconduct within the meaning of section 21 read with section 22 and clause 7 of Part I of the Second Schedule to the Act. Penalty of reprimand, as recommended by the Council, was adequate and proper.

Section 65 (31) of the Finance Act, 1994 - Consulting engineer - Period prior to 1-7-2003 - Revenue on finding that assessee was providing technical inspection and certification service during relevant period, confirmed demand under category of ‘Consulting engineer’ - Commissioner (Appeals) held that prior to 1-7-2003 assessee was not held to be providing any technical inspection and certification service as same came under scope of service tax only with effect from 1-7-2003 - Whether there was no infirmity in impugned order of Commissioner (Appeals) - Held, yes [Para 4]

Section 92CA of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Reference to TPO (General principles) - Whether authority of TPO is to conduct a transfer pricing analysis to determine ALP and not to determine whether there is a service or not from which assessee benefits - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, TPO cannot determine ALP of payments made by assessee to its AE at nil taking a view that assessee did not derive any benefit from services rendered by AE - Held, yes [Para 34] [Matter remanded]

Section  92C,  read with section  92CA,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Transfer Pricing  -  Computation of Arm’s length price  (Adjustments - Segmentation) - Assessment year  2018-19  - Assessee, engaged in testing, inspection and certification (TIC) services to third-party customers in India and to AEs, also provided ITES support and shared services to AEs - For transfer pricing, it prepared segmental accounts showing AE margins of about 15% in ITES, shared services and certification segments, a 4% margin in non-AE certification services, an overall margin of about 6%, and ITES revenue of about Rs. 4.53 crores out of total revenue of about Rs. 124.81 crores (non-AE certification about Rs. 97.40 crores; AE certification about Rs. 15.09 crores; shared services about Rs. 7.79 crores) - In its TPSR, it benchmarked ITES transactions of about Rs. 4.5 crores under TNMM using OP/OC with a margin of 15% - On reference, TPO grouped TIC, shared services and ITES together as ITES, rejected assessee's segmental results stating that HR, finance, operations, legal and admin costs were not allocated to AEs, computed a consolidated margin of 4.44%, rejected TPSR and proposed a TP adjustment of about Rs. 26.18 crores - Whether since for earlier AYs TIC and ITES services were benchmarked separately, as TIC services and ITES services did not share same FAR, and TP Order did not explain why TIC and ITES services were being grouped together, combining TIC and ITES services for benchmarking was not justified - Held, yes [Para 24] [In favour of assessee]

Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Reference to TPO - Assessment year 2011-12 - Whether when Assessing Officer makes reference to TPO for determining ALP of international transaction of services availed by assessee from its AE, job of TPO is to consider actual transaction of rendition of service and find out its ALP, however, TPO has no jurisdiction to examine whether service was needed or is duplicate in nature or stewardship or shareholder service because such an exercise falls in exclusive domain of Assessing Officer, thus, if undertaken by TPO, it would thwart determination of ALP - Held, yes [Para 26] [In favour of assessee]

I. Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Comparables - Functional similarity - Business support services) - Assessment year 2010-11 - Assessee was engaged in provision of business support services to its AE - Whether a company engaged in provision of highly technical consultancy services in nature of project report preparation, technical and economic studies, feasibility studies, micro enterprise development, skill development, project management consulting, industrial cluster development, environmental management consulting, energy management consulting, market and social research and asset reconstruction management services would not be comparable to assessee - Held, yes [Paras 1.5 and 1.6] [In favour of assessee]TRANSFER PRICING : Company engaged in provision of highly technical consultancy services would not be comparable to company engaged in provision of business support services to its AE  TRANSFER PRICING : Company engaged in providing support services for execution of various projects and, thus, primarily engaged in back-office support services would be functionally similar to assessee engaged in provision of business support services to its AE  TRANSFER PRICING : Payroll processing support services are comparable to activities in nature of processing of accounting data for AEs  TRANSFER PRICING : Company engaged in provision of business support services to its AE would be comparable to company engaged in services of valuation of assets of third parties and assisting in their disposal by way of auction  TRANSFER PRICING : Company engaged in rendering services, namely, registrar and transfer agent activity, records management activity and payroll  trust fund activity, which had majority of income from registry and share transfer business would not be comparable to company engaged in provision of business support services to its AE

II. Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Comparables and adjustments - Professional services) - Assessment year 2008-09 - In transfer pricing proceedings, TPO took a view that ALP of professional fee paid by assessee was to be taken at nil as assessee failed to furnish evidence showing that services were actually rendered - Accordingly certain adjustment was made to assessee's ALP - In appellate proceedings, assessee brought on record an agreement entered into with AE in terms of which CEO of said AE himself provided consultancy/managerial service - Assessee also produced invoice raised by AE for said fee and tax paid thereon - Whether in view of above, impugned adjustment was to be set aside - Held, yes [Para 10][In favour of assessee]

Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Comparables, functional similarity - Consultancy service providers) - Assessment year 2014-15 - Whether where assessee was captive service provider rendering routine marketing support services to AE, a company engaged in providing consulting and liasioning services relating to foreign trade, customs, excise, GST etc., to independent clients/agencies could not be accepted as comparable - Held, yes [Para 6] [In favour of assessee]TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee was rendering marketing support services to AE, a company engaged in providing consulting and liasioning services relating to foreign trade, customs, excise, GST etc., could not be accepted as comparable

Limitation - Section 11-A - price approved by the Assistant Collector on the basis of Chartered Accountant's certificate given without verifying the books - suppression established proviso to section 11-A rightly invoked

Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Comparables and adjustments/Comparables - Illustrations) - Assessment year 2011-12 - Whether in case of assessee rendering marketing support services to AE, a company engaged in procurement related advisory services and financial audit for projects in India and abroad, could not be accepted as comparable - Held, yes [Para 30] [In favour of assessee]

IX. Section  92C , read with sections  92  and  92CA , of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section 165, read with sections 161 and 166 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 – Transfer Pricing - Computation of Arm’s length price (TP Adjustments -  Illustrations  - Support Services Fee) - Assessee paid its US AE for marketing, regulatory liaison and customer support services, reimbursed on cost plus 20 per cent basis, and benchmarked transactions under entity-level TNMM showing higher margins than comparables - TPO held entity-level TNMM inappropriate, proposed to treat AE as tested party, questioned necessity/benefit and documentation, and determined ALP of service charge/markup at Nil - CIT(A) recorded that assessee had substantial US exports and multiple ANDA filings, that services were actually rendered and costs were certified by an independent CPA, and that TPO had not brought comparables or disproved rendition; disallowance of mark-up was deleted - Whether ALP cannot be determined at Nil in absence of contrary evidence; services accepted and TNMM sustained; adjustment deleted - Held, yes [Paras 19.21 to 19.28] [In favour of assessee]

III Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Comparables, functional similarity - Consultancy service providers) - Assessment year 2011-12 - Whether where assessee was engaged in providing consultancy and advisory services including project construction and execution thereof in field of water management industry, a BPO company whose business products were payroll and employees trust fund administration and management, Registry and Transfer for shares, debentures and FD, category I registrar by SEBI, records management, transaction/ document processing for securitization, loans etc, could not be accepted as comparable - Held, yes [Para 36] [In favour of assessee]

VI. Section  92C  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Transfer Pricing  -  Computation of Arm’s length price  (Comparables - Factors to determine - Data in Public Domain) - Assessment year  2014-15  - Whether a company engaged in accounting, audit support, tax and consultancy services, being professional and consultancy-oriented in nature and lacking adequate public domain financial data, was functionally not comparable with assessee providing routine IT enabled services and, therefore, was to be excluded from final set of comparables - Held, yes [Para 64] [In favour of assessee]

facts.text:
The assessee was a practising chartered accountant. The revenue levied tax on certification service holding that it was an auditing service and, therefore, not entitled to exemption in terms of Notification No. 59/89-ST, dated 16-10-1998.

On appeal :

The assessee was operating as licenced registrar under the office of AQA, USA. As per the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between the parties, the assessee was to represent AQA for the purpose of assisting clients in achievement of ISO 9000, ISO 14000 and QS 9000 certificates. It used to receive Company Information Sheet (CIS) from prospective clients, review the CIS, prepare quotation and send same to prospective clients, provide information connected with Quality Management System (QMS) certification, conduct audit/assessment of the quality system at client’s place with reference to ISO standard and after successful completion of the assessment process, send such assessment to AQA, which issues above certificates. For doing the audit work, the assessee charged certain fee as audit fee from the prospective customers. The revenue treated the service of the assessee as that of ‘technical inspection and certification agency’ and demanded service tax. The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the demand.

On appeal :

The assessee company made payment to an organisation, namely, IFANCA for obtaining certification of product exported by it to USA as 'halal' so as to enable said product access to islamic market in USA. The Assessing Officer disallowed said payment towards certification fee for non-deduction of tax at source on same under section 40(a)(i).

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) went through the supervision procedure adopted by the IFANCA, and after going through the same he came to the conclusion that entire process of supervision and certification involved making available to the assessee specific methods to be adopted in the manufacturing process so as to ensure the products manufactured being halal, and therefore, it involved making available technical knowledge to the assessee so as to be treated as "included services" as per article 14(2) of the DTAA with USA for the purpose of holding taxes on the same.

On appeal :

The assessee dealing in LPG sent LPG through tank trucks to various LPG bottling plants of oil distribution companies.

Whenever LPG tank truck required any repair or mandatory testing of safety valves, the tank truck was cleaned and completely degassed. During this activity, water was filled in tank mounted on the truck and discharged. Water was displaced by LPG vapors. For this activity, the assessee collected cost of water and the labour charges from the truck owner.

The Adjudicating Authority held that the said activities undertaken by the assessee would fall under the category of 'technical inspection and certification service' and raised tax demand upon it.

The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the impugned order.

On second appeal:

The assessee, a company incorporated at Germany, had a branch in India. The Indian branch was engaged in the business of audit and procedure of norms for ISO 9000 certification. The services offered by Indian branch were ISO 9000 quality system certification where in quality system auditor of assessee company would visit the company opting for ISO certification, carry out a pre-assessment audit and then a certification audit and submit report to the assessee. After verification of report by the assessee, ISO 9000 certification was granted. The assessee treated its income as business income. The Assessing Officer opined that such services should be taxed as 'fees for technical services' under article 12 of Indo German DTAA. The assessee submitted that these services did not come under FTS within meaning of article 12 and, thus, it was business income which was to be computed in view of article 7(1) as business was carried out through PE. However, the Assessing Officer held that said services came within purview of FTS and, hence, provisions of section 44D had to be applied, and, accordingly, he assessed the income after applying tax rate of FTS; i.e., at rate 20 per cent of entire gross receipts. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the findings of Assessing Officer.

On appeal to the Tribunal:

The applicant, a tax resident of Hong Kong, belongs to X group of companies. The group entities are engaged in the business of inspection, verification, testing and certification (IVTC) services to various customers. The X trademark is owned by ABC (Parent Company), who had entered into a trademark license and Support Services Agreement (Support Services Agreement) with all its group entities, separately, including the applicant. The support service agreement is stated to bring uniform standards, procedures and policies described therein to IVTC services. It is stated that the inspection services are generally performed either at the load port or discharge port of a product or activity and are based on scientific and internationally accepted techniques and as per the clients' requirements. Verification services are used to evaluate whether the product services are system complaint with given regulation, specifications or condition. Testing services are used to determine the quality of the product or services as per the customer's requirements and are carried out in laboratories owned by respective X entities which are accredited to international bodies. Certification services refers to the confirmation of regulations, standards or contractual specifications of a product or organization or training. The applicant provided IVTC services to Indian Customers either directly or through X India. The applicant states that the IVTC Services are provided to the Indian Customer outside India if there is a direct arrangement between the customer and the applicant and the payment is made on the invoice raised by the applicant. But when the arrangement is not direct and is through the X India, then the invoice is raised either on X India or the Indian customer. Explaining it by an example, the applicant states that where a customer approaches X India to have its goods inspected in India and outside India, then X India sub-contracts the inspection to its applicant and the applicant raises invoice on X India for services provided by it and a consolidated invoice is raised on the customer. The applicant sought advance ruling on the question as to (i) whether the payments received/receivable the applicant in connection with transactions under taken/proposed to be undertaken in relation to the (a) inspection and verification services (b) testing/analysis services; and (c) certification services are chargeable to tax in India as 'fees for technical services' (FTS) under section 9(1)(vii)( b) and (ii ) whether payments received/receivable in connection with procurement of goods/services and reimbursement of other expenses proposed to be incurred for and on behalf of X India are chargeable to tax in India. The applicant also raised issue relation to withholding of taxes under section 195 and filing of return under section 139.

The respondent-Chartered Accountant had issued a tax audit certificate in favour of the assessee-concern under section 44AB of the Income-tax Act. The Commissioner of Income-tax, during the course of survey proceedings at the premises of the assessee, found certain discrepancy and recorded a statement of the respondent in which the respondent had accepted that he had issued a back-dated certificate showing the completion of audit of the assessee on behest of and to oblige his friend who was the tax consultant of the assessee. The Commissioner further averred that the respondent had prepared the tax audit report without examination and verification of the books of account. On complaint, the Disciplinary Committee of the petitioner-Council concluded that the respondent was guilty of both charges and was, thus, guilty of professional misconduct under sections 21 and 22. The petitioner-Council accepting the aforesaid conclusion recommended in terms of section 21(5) that the respondent be removed from the register of members for a period of six months.

On reference :

The assessee-firm was engaged in the business of import of rough diamond, cutting and polishing and sale thereof. It paid a certain sum to a Belgian company (HRD) towards grading and certification of diamonds.

The assessee contended that the service of certification was carried out by HRD entirely outside India, i.e., in Belgium and the gradation certificate/report given by HRD was only an analysis of the quality of each piece of diamond and it did not constitute transfer of any technology, commercial interest, skill or technical knowledge in favour of the assessee and, therefore, such services could not be regarded as 'technical services'.

The Assessing Officer noted that HRD was having a specialized knowledge in diamond grading and certification, which was technical in nature, and therefore, he held that the impugned payment fell in the category of 'fees paid for technical services' and the assessee was liable to deduct tax at source therefrom.

The Commissioner (Appeals) noted that in providing grading or certification services of diamonds to the assessee, HRD had not parted with any technical knowledge or made available any technical expertise to the assessee so as to classify the impugned payment to HRD as 'fees for technical services' in view of MFN clause in India-Belgium DTAA. Accordingly, he deleted the disallowance made by the Assessing Officer by invoking section 40(a)(i).

On appeal:

On second appeal :

Company ‘S’ had furnished to the Joint CCI & E a statement of export of leather goods including those of other manufacturers for the years 1976-77 and 1977-78, duly certified by the respondent - Chartered Ac-countant, and on that basis, the Export House Certificate was issued. The respondent had certified that he had checked and verified the particulars of export from the books/documents of the company and found them to be correct. On demand by the Jt. CCI & E, the company replied that it had not purchased any finished leather/leather goods from any other party and denied having exported finished goods manufactured by other units. The Jt. CCI & E made a complaint to the Institute that the respondent had issued the certificate without verifying the books of account inasmuch as he did not have any contact with that company. The respondent, in his reply, asserted his certificate to be correct and complete, based on the documents produced by the concerned parties. He further submitted that he was retained by the consultants of the company to verify the export statements from the records produced by it and he certified the facts accordingly. The Disciplinary Committee held that the then existing export policy required that 20 per cent of the total exports goods should be manufactured by others to get Export House benefits and since the only dispute was that the figures were not correct, the respondent was guilty of professional misconduct under section 21, read with section 22, and under clauses 5, 6 and 7 of the Part I of the Second Schedule. It accordingly recommended that the respondent be reprimanded.

In consideration of rendering of services, ‘L’ agreed to recover only the costs incurred by it for providing the above services to the assessee-company. According to the agreement, the cost recovery was based on the time spent in rendering of services to the assessee-company. The recovery did not include any profit mark up. The auditors report also certified that the amounts charged to the assessee-company did not include any profit mark up. An application was made under section 197(1) by ‘L’ for receiving the payments under the MSA without deduction of tax at source. A copy of the auditors report certifying that the payments under the MSA did not include any profit element was also enclosed along with the said application. The Assessing Officer, after considering the application issued certificate under section 197 to the assessee-company for making payments to ‘L’ without deduction of tax at source. The certificates issued under section 197 on various dates were neither revoked nor cancelled thereafter. Subsequently, notices were issued under section 201 by the Assessing Officer to show cause as to why the payer should not be treated as an assessee-in-default under section 201(1A) and also why interest should not be levied under section 201(1A). Detailed written submissions were made rebutting the Assessing Officer’s claim. Rejecting the submissions of the assessee-company, the Assessing Officer went ahead and passed the impugned orders, wherein it was held that the payments represented fees for technical services under the Act as well all the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement (Treaty) between India and Singapore and that the certificates issued were not in accordance with law. On appeal :

The respondent, a Chartered Accountant, was appointed as a Statutory Auditor of the company.

During the course of investigation, SEBI found that the respondent, as the statutory auditor of the company, had given a certificate dated 9-6-1995 certifying that the entire promoters contribution had been received by the company.

It was noticed by the SEBI that promoters contribution, only to the extent of Rs. 35 lakhs, was received by the company and not Rs. 225 lakhs as certified by the Auditor. The cheques issued against the balance amount had bounced. However, shares worth Rs. 225 lakhs were allotted to the promoters by the company.

SEBI concluded that the respondent/Auditors, without actually verifying the bank statements regarding realisation of the cheques, had given a false certificate regarding receipt of promoters contribution, in full, by Company. The respondent was held guilty of professional misconduct, and to have abetted the promoters in the fraudulent activity by issuing a false certificate, as he could have issued the certificate with the remark that subject to realisation of the Cheques deposited. Instead of doing so, the respondent had issued certificate as if the entire contribution of the promoters was received.

On receipt of the said letter from SEBI, the Institute addressed letter dated 28-07-2005 to the respondent alleging that the amount received towards contribution was only Rs. 35 lakhs, but the respondent had certified that Rs. 225 lakhs was received by the company towards promoters contribution, and the cheques issued against the balance amount had bounced. However, shares for Rs. 225 lakhs were allotted to the promoters by the company. The respondent was called upon to disclose the name(s) of the member (s), answerable to the charge of misconduct, as per Regulation 12(6) of the Chartered Accountants Regulations, 1988.

In response to the letter dated 28-07-2005 of the Institute, the respondent submitted his reply dated 05-08-2005 admitting that he, as the Proprietor of 'G' had issued the certificate dated 09-06-1995 stating that the promoters contribution of Rs. 225 lakhs was received as per the books of account maintained by the Company. The certificate was issued, after verifying the Share Application Account maintained in the General Ledger of the Company, the bank book showing receipt of the payments (in the form of cheques deposited) into State Bank of Mysore, and the bank deposit slip counterfoils duly bearing the bank acknowledgements of the cheques deposited. The certificate was issued, on the basis of the documentary evidence produced before him on the date of issue of the certificate, in the belief that the cheques deposited would not bounce, keeping in view the past track record of the promoters. The respondent, however, admitted that he should have issued the certificate with the remark subject to realisation of the cheques deposited, and stated that, while it was an omission on his part, it was not done with any mala fide intention, and he did not receive any financial benefit in this connection.

Being dissatisfied with the explanation submitted by the respondent, the Institute initiated disciplinary proceedings. The disciplinary committee framed charges and, after following the procedure prescribed under the Act and the Regulations, found the respondent guilty of misconduct under clause (7) of Part I of the Second Schedule read with sections 21 and 22.

Recommended that the Court impose the punishment of removal of his name from the Register of Members, for a period of 3 years, on the respondent.

The assessee was engaged in providing taxable service under the category of ‘Technical inspection and certification service’ and was also liable to pay service tax on goods transport service received by it. It availed benefit of abatement under Notification No. 32/2004-ST, dated 3-12-2004 with respect to goods transport service received. The revenue issued show-cause notice to the assessee denying benefit of said notification on ground that in view of relevant Boards’ circular in the consignment notes issued to the assessee by goods transport agencies, there was no declaration to the effect that no credit on input or capital goods used for providing services had been taken nor the benefit of Notification No. 12/2003-ST, dated 20-6-2003 was availed. However, the Commissioner taking into consideration the Chartered Accountant’s certificate to the effect that the transporters had neither availed CENVAT credit nor the benefit of Notification No. 12/2003-ST, dated 20-6-2003, dropped the demand against the assessee.

On appeals :

The assessee undertook to do job work on the materials sent by the Space Research Stations. The adjudicating authority levied service tax on it on the ground that it was rendering technical inspection and certification services. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the assessee was not rendering any technical inspection and certification service and, therefore, it was not liable to pay service tax.

On appeal :

Facts

Assessee was a Government of India Undertaking under the Ministry of Defence and was engaged in shipbuilding, ship repair and engineering for the Indian Navy & Coast Guard.

They placed a purchase Order on M/s. Maritime, Netherlands for the Model Testing of 90M OPV. The activities covered were preparation of ship model including all appendages as per the technical data and design provided by assessee and verification of the correctness of technical data.

The above referred service was to be received by assessee in Netherlands. No part of the service was performed by M/s. Maritime, Netherlands in India.

The Department demanded service tax under reverse charge relying on section 66A and classified under Consulting Engineer service and not under 'technical testing and analysis service' or 'technical inspection and certification service'.

Assessee's Arguments

Since the said service was wholly received in Netherlands they were not liable to service tax under the reverse mechanism.

Consulting Engineer : Service received was not covered under the category of 'consulting engineer'. The word 'technical assistance' is preceded by the words 'advice and consultancy', the term should be read ejusdem generic with the preceding word viz 'advice' and 'consultancy'. Both 'advice' and 'consultancy' does not involve any physical work. Hence, 'technical assistance' could not include any physical work such as repair/maintenance/servicing etc. Therefore, physical work such as development of the model could not be covered. Further, service provider Maritime Research Institute, Netherlands, was a non-profit institute and did not come within the definition of 'consulting engineer'.

Technical testing & analysis service : Service received by the assessee can be classified under the category of 'technical testing & analysis service'. No specified qualification has been prescribed for technical testing and analysis agency. Such agency may or may not be approved under any statutory provisions for rendering the said service. Service of 'Technical testing and analysis service' are covered under clause (ii) of Rule 3 of the Taxation of Services (Provided from Outside India and Received in India) Rules, 2006. As per clause (ii) of Rule 3 of the Taxation of Services (Provided from Outside India and Received in India) Rules, 2006 at the relevant time the service to be taxable under this category must be performed in India. Since no part of service was performed in India, it was not liable to tax.

Technical inspection & certification services : Service received by the assessee can, alternatively, be classified under the category of 'technical inspection & certification services'. The word 'process' in definition of said service simply means the activities performed for the purpose of achieving the desired objectives. Therefore, under the said definition all types of examination or inspection will be covered. No particular form of certification has been stated. Therefore certification in any form will be covered under the definition. It may further be noted that the taxability of certification under this category is not restricted to advice, consultancy or technical assistance but includes any work done in connection with the inspection or examination of the items specified therein. Manufacture of the vessel is a complex and costly affair and service provider gives certification as regards to the standard of the developed model. In view of the above, service is to be classified under the category of 'Technical inspection and certification service'. Since the said service is covered under clause (ii) of Rule 3 of the Taxation of Services (Provided from Outside India and Received in India) Rules, 2006, the service to be taxable under this category must be performed in India. Since no part of it was performed in India, no service tax could be charged.

Limitation & Penalty : The audit was conducted and all details were supplied to Department in February and March, 2008. Since all the facts were to the knowledge of the department, issuance of notice on 31-3-2011 was barred by limitation as there was no suppression. Even otherwise, merely wrong claim of classification by itself does not amount to suppression or mis-declaration. Even mere non-declaration is not sufficient to invoke larger period but some positive act is required. Further, assessee was Government of India Undertaking under the Ministry of Defense, and it is inconceivable that they would try to evade tax. Further, payment under reverse charge would have neutral effect, as tax paid would be eligible as credit. The entire demand is barred by limitation. Similarly, penalty was not leviable.

Calculation incorrect : Value of services should be = Value of Purchase Contract (net of discount) - Cost of manufactured goods (net of discount).

Revenue's Arguments

The assessee was engaged in providing services to promote, coordinate, guide, implement and maintain an accreditation system for laboratories, suitable for the country in accordance with the relevant national and international standard and guides and also to ensure that all measurements either during calibration or testing by accredited laboratories were related to appropriate national/international standards. It appeared to the department that these services were covered under 'Technical inspection and certification services' and were being provided to commercial and other laboratories on commercial terms without charging and paying service tax on the services rendered under section 65(105)( zzi). The Commissioner, accordingly, confirmed service tax demand on the assessee under category of 'Technical inspection and certification service', along with interest and penalty. In the instant application, the assessee contended that the Commissioner had wrongly invoked the extended period when no evidence was available to the effect that it had wilfully suppressed the facts by not filing the returns with intent to evade tax. The assessee further submitted that the show-cause notice which was answerable to the Commissioner had been issued by Additional Director General of Central Excise Intelligence. The Commissioner had failed to appreciate that law does not envisage that one authority would initiate the proceedings and other would pass the adjudication order.

The assessee, a UK based company, entered into intragroup services agreement with the Indian AE. According to the agreement assessee provided services pertaining to human resources, finance, legal and compliance and conducting of internal audit assurance work. The cost incurred for performing said services was allocated to the group companies on the basis of time spent, activity level or head count and cost incurred was cross charged to the group companies on cost plus 5 per cent basis. The assessee filed return of income for relevant assessment years.

The Assessing Officer opined that services provided by the assessee were in nature of technical or consultancy services. He, thus, held that receipts for said services would be in nature of FTS under article 13 of India-UK DTAA and brought receipts to tax at rate of 10 per cent.

The DRP upheld the order of the Assessing Officer.

On appeal to the Tribunal.

The assessee, engaged in the business of project and construction management, entered into an agreement with a Singapore Company, under which the Singapore Company was to provide certain services to the assessee in relation to day-to-day business operations consisting of administrative, legal finance and accounting matters. In consideration of rendering of services, the Singapore Company agreed to receive the costs incurred by it. The cost recovery, according to the agreement, was based on the time spent for rendering the services. The Chartered Accountant's report certified that the amounts charged to the assessee did not include any profit margin.

An application under section 197(1) was made by the Singapore Company for receiving the payments under the agreements without deduction of tax at source. The assessee was authorized to make payments to the Singapore Company without deduction of tax at source. Notices were issued to show-cause as to why the payer should not be regarded as an assessee-in-default under section 201(1). Detailed submissions were made in response to this notice. Rejecting the submissions of the assessee-company, the Assessing Officer passed orders under section 201 wherein it was held that the payment represented fees for technical services under section 9(1)(vii) as well as the DTAA between India and Singapore. It was held that the certificates issued permitting payments without deduction of tax at source were not in accordance with law.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the action of the Assessing Officer. On further appeal, the Tribunal allowed the appeal of the company. It was concluded that the assessee cannot be treated as an assessee-in-default under section 201(1) and no interest is leviable under section 201(1A).

On rectification petition :

The assessee, a charitable trust, was granted exemption from levy of tax under section 11 up to the assessment year 1983-84. For the assessment year 1984-85, however, the IAC denied exemption under section 11 on the ground that while the accounts of the assessee were audited by a firm of chartered accountants, namely, L, the certificate required under clause (b) of section 12A was given by another firm of chartered accountants, namely, K, which did not satisfy the requirements of section 12A(b). on appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the disallowance of exemption claimed and added that the assessee in obtaining the prescribed particulars from an accountant who had not audited the accounts failed to satisfy the requirements of section 12A.

On second appeal:

■

The assessee–company, incorporated in Singapore and engaged in the practice of law, provided legal services including advisory services in relation to mergers, acquisitions, restructuring, financing, taxation and allied matters to its client Barclays Bank Plc, U.K., in relation to client of Barclays bank (REC Ltd). The assessee filed a return declaring nil income. The invoice for these services was raised on Barclays, with payment arranged by REC Ltd., and the assessee asserted there was no contractual relationship with REC Ltd.

■

During reassessment, the AO proposed taxability under section 9(1), including section 9(1)(vii), and Article 12(4)(b) of the India–Singapore DTAA; the assessee contended the services were rendered from Singapore to Barclays and not taxable in India. The Assessing Officer held that technical knowledge, experience and skill were made available through the legal advice and treated the receipts as Fees for Technical Services; a draft order proposed an addition of about Rs. 1.01 crores.

■

The DRP, after considering the assessee’s submissions, upheld the AO’s action.

On the assessee’s appeal to the Tribunal.

Facts

The assessees had provided chartered accountant's services prior to 1-4-2012 and raised the bills therefor prior to that date, levying service tax at the rate of 10 per cent.

Up to 1-4-2012, Chartered Accountants services were governed by rule 7 of the Point of Taxation Rules, 2011 wherein point of taxation was determined based on date of receipt of payment.

With effect from 1-4-2012, rate of service tax was increased to 12 per cent and services of chartered accountants were excluded from Rule 7 ibid.

Circular No. 158/9/2012-ST dated 8-05-2012 and Circular No.154/5/2012-ST dated 28-03-2012 had provided that since, prior to 1-4-2012, services of Chartered Accountants were covered by rule 7 of the Point of Taxation Rules, 2011, hence, point of taxation of services provided prior to that date will continue to be governed by said Rule 7, as it stood before that date. Accordingly, in case of services provided and invoices raised before 1-4-2012, the point of taxation would be date of payment and if payment was received on or after 1-4-2012, revised rate of service tax viz. 12 per cent would apply.

The assessees argued that point of taxation, in their case, was determinable as per Rule 4 of the Point of Taxation Rules, 2011.

Therefore, the assessees challenged the said circulars as ultra vires the Constitution and the provisions of the Finance Act, 1994 and rules.

Issue Involved

Whether Circular was ultra vires the Act ?

The assessee, a public sector undertaking, was engaged in the business of refining of crude oil and marketing of petroleum products. During the previous year, the assessee had engaged one ‘P’ of Singapore for carrying out market study for updating its assessment of the out look for domestic refining capacity throughout India. The assessee applied for issue of no-objection certificate (NOC) for making the payment to ‘P’ based on the proposal agreed upon by the assessee. In the application for NOC, the assessee contended that the scope of services rendered by ‘P’ fell outside the ambit of article 12 of the DTAA between India and Singapore. The Assessing Officer passed an order under section 195 authorising the assessee to make the payment to ‘P’ after deduction of income-tax at source. The Assessing Officer treated the amount payable for the services rendered by ‘P’ as fees for technical service. The assessee, therefore, made the payment to ‘P’ after deducting tax at source and deposited the TDS with the department.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the impugned order. He held that the consultancy fees paid by the assessee to ‘P’ was chargeable to tax in India as per the provision of article 12.

On second appeal :

For the assessment year in question, the assessee claimed deduction under section 80-I in respect of a sheller as supported by the requisite certificate of the chartered accountants. The Assessing Officer found that the sheller was installed in the accounting year 1983-84 and the first year of the business was shown as 1985-86 and the assessee having already availed of deduction for eight years it was not eligible for deduction under section 80-I for the assessment year in question. The Assessing Officer, therefore, referred the matter to the assessee’s chartered accountant who apparently sent a letter stating that they were neither competent to certify nor had certified that the assessee was eligible for deduction under section 80-I. In view of the said submissions of the chartered accountants, the Assessing Officer disallowed the claim for deduction and also imposed penalty on the assessee under section 271(1)(c) for furnishing inaccurate particulars of the income. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) dismissed the same. On further appeal, the Tribunal accepted the assessee’s contention that it had claimed the deduction in a bona fide manner on the basis of the certificate issued by the chartered accountant and, therefore, cancelled the penalty.

On appeal :

■

During the year under consideration, the assessee incurred expenses towards customisation existing systems to comply with the GST regulations implemented in India. The assessee recharged the said costs to its Indian AE and the same was reimbursed.

■

The Assessing Officer treated the said customisation receipts as FTS. The DRP held that these receipts are not independent service and very much part of BSS, thereby, holding that these services being akin to / part of BSS fall within purview of make available and is taxable as FTS.

■

On appeal to Tribunal:

• The advisory services also involved special technical knowledge and hence, it was nothing but technical service.

The assessee— a management consultancy company focused on Human Resource Management services—filed its return under section 139(1) declaring income of about Rs. 2.56 crores for AY 2022-23. The case was selected for scrutiny under CASS due to large value of international transactions and low profitability risk parameters. The assessee entered into international transactions with AEs in Hong Kong and Japan; its entire revenue was from export of services to AEs. For benchmarking, it adopted TNMM as the most appropriate method and operated on a cost-plus model with about 5% markup as per the service agreement, supporting this with a FAR-based set of comparables.

■

A reference under section 92CA(1) was made. The TPO rejected the assessee’s comparables, selected a fresh set of comparables, noted the assessee’s OP/OC at about 3.51% as below the stipulated 5% markup under the agreement, held the assessee’s benchmarking unreliable, and proposed a TP adjustment of about Rs. 6.99 crores under section 92CA(3). Consequent draft assessment under section 143(3) read with section 144C(1) proposed to assess total income at about Rs. 9.56 crores.

■

On objections, the DRP confirmed the TPO’s action, treated the services under the broader head of management consultancy, accepted the TPO’s comparables, held that the service agreement primarily governed pricing and did not materially affect comparability, and rejected objections on export filter, turnover disparity and functional dissimilarity. The AO thereafter passed the final assessment under section 143(3) read with section 144C(13) in line with the DRP’s directions.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal.

An agreement was entered into between an Indian company and the assessee, a non-resident company, whereunder the assessee agreed to render technical assistance and consultancy services to the Indian company in erecting its plant and in putting it on stream. The agreement provided, inter alia, (i) that the assessee would train Indian personnel abroad, (ii) that during the construction of the plant, the assessee would render consultancy services relating to the problems of construction, etc., by deputing a group of designing experts to India, (iii) that the consultancy activity would consist of granting of expert technical advice, opinions, and/or recommendations in basic technical matters by the assessee's experts to the corresponding experts of the Indian company, and (iv) that the total fee for the consulting activities of the assessee for the designing works and for introducing production would be a specified amount worked out on the basis of man-months calculated in direct proportion to the number and duration of stay in India of the assessee's specialists. The assessee claimed that the consultancy fees paid by the Indian company to it was not on account of any activity carried on by it in India but on account of something done by it in the foreign territory itself and, therefore, the said amount was not taxable. The ITO rejected the assessee's claim and held that part of the total turnover of the Indian company should be treated as income arising on account of the assessee's activity in India. On appeal, the Tribunal held that the consultancy fees paid to the assessee must be held to have arisen on account of its activity carried on in India, but observed that what part of it should be attributed to the consultancy service in India and what part to its activity/if any, carried on in the foreign country would have to be determined. Accordingly, it remitted the matter to the ITO with a direction to recompute the profit attributable to the consultancy service in India in accordance with the law and on the basis of a certificate to be produced by the assessee from a qualified chartered accountant in the foreign country.

On reference :

The applicant is a tax resident of Australia. It provides accreditation to CABs (Conformity Assessment Bodies) in several countries including India. It accredits organizations which provide third party certification and/or inspection services. Its main function is to accredit, following the successful assessment, those bodies which are considered competent and impartial to provide an effective service in various spheres. The accreditation vouchsafes the independence of a CAB in performing the certification and such accreditation further assists the CAB in the fields of certification and inspection. Post accreditation, regular surveillance visits are carried out by the applicant’s auditors to ensure that CAB maintains and operates its procedures in accordance with the requirements of the accreditation criteria. In consideration of the accreditation work done by the applicant, it receives fees from CABs in the form of application fee, programme fee, certification fees and fee for conducting surveillance audit, witnessing audit and reassessment visits. On these facts, the applicant has sought advance ruling, inter alia, on the questions whether consideration received by it from an Indian CAB would fall within ambit of ‘royalties’ as defined under article 12 of the DTAA; and whether the visits of the personnel of the applicant for conducting the on-site assessment and witness audit constitutes/deems existence of applicant’s permanent establishment (‘PE’) in India in accordance with the provisions of article 5 of the DTAA.

The certification relating to computation of income from international transactions is in accordance with the provisions of section 92E of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and rule 10E of Income-tax Rules. [Para 2]

The certification follows transfer pricing audit. Therefore, the certification in question would clearly fall under ‘Audit/certification services’ even as per the clarification, dated 7-10-1998, issued by the Ministry of Finance. The verification of the books of account precedes issue of a certificate and such verification will fall within the scope of ‘Accounting & auditing’ function. Therefore, it could not be said that what the assessee was rendering was not ‘auditing service’ liable to service tax. Accordingly, the impugned order was to be upheld and the appeal was to be rejected. [Para 3]

S. Ramachandran for the Appellant. Ms. Indira Sisupal for the Respondent.

Management consultant’s service was a taxable service under section 65(48) during the relevant time and, therefore, the appellants were entitled to exemption under Notification No. 2/99-ST. As regards non-repatriation of foreign exchange, chartered accountant’s certificate had since been produced before the Tribunal, and since the same was not available before the adjudicating authority, the matter was to be remanded back to the adjudicating authority to look into the chartered accountant’s certificate and if nothing contrary was found the exemption should be extended to them. [Para 6(3)]

It could be noticed from the certificate of the chartered accountant that the chartered accountant before issuing certificate had verified the entire books of account and had come to a categorical conclusion that neither the assessee had passed on burden of service tax to the customers nor had it recovered the amount from the transporters. The certificate also categorically stated that the assessee had borne the incidence of service tax. The Commissioner (Appeals) after checking the records was satisfied with the evidences produced before him as regards the non-passing of the incidence of service tax by the assessee to its customers. The revenue in its appeal had not produced any contrary evidence to the said findings nor there was any challenge to the chartered accountants Certificate. [Para 2]

Accordingly, in the facts and circumstances of the case, the impugned order was correct and legal and did not require any interference. The appeal filed by the revenue was to be dismissed. [Para 3]

The Chartered Accountant’s Certificate was a detailed certificate which had been considered in depth by the adjudicating authority. The appellant was engaged in the manufacture and selling of casting on specific rate of contract. The amount of service tax paid by the appellant was on the goods transport operator. That had not vitiated the contract price in any way. Further, the certificate issued by the professional, generally should not be challenged without having contradictory certificate from another professional. The Commissioner in his order had not relied on any contradictory certificate of another professional. In the absence of which, it was to be held that the appellant had made out a prima facie case for waiver of pre-deposit of amount of service tax. [Para 5]

Entry 54. The Act requires that the dealer has to maintain books and the books have to be audited and required to be certified by a Chartered Accountant. That will not result in the legislation falling outside the competence of the State Legislature. The Legislation in pith and substance is relatable to imposition of sales tax which is within the competence of the State Legislature. The Courts examine and ascertain the pith and substance on scrutiny of the true character of the enactment. [Para 24] It also cannot be said that in such a case audit by a Chartered Accountant would amount to outsourcing the statutory power to the third party. The Legislature can always delegate its powers as long as such delegation does not amount to abdication of its essential legislative functions. In the instant case, there is no abdication of the essential legislative functions. All that the section requires is that the accountant has to audit the accounts and to issue certificate that the dealer has maintained the books as required to be maintained under the Act and rules. The dealer has to file his accounts audited with the certificate. This neither amounts to abdication nor excessive delegation. Such an exercise also does not amount to conferring on the accountant a power to determine the correct tax liability of the dealer. The power to accept returns is of the Authorities under the Act. Even after the certificate is issued, that the dealer has maintained books, it is always open to the Commissioner under section 20 to ascertain whether the return is correct and complete or order an audit under section 22 to get the accounts audited by the officers of the department. A certificate, therefore, is not determinative but to enable the department to consider that the person having knowledge of audit and subject to the disciplinary control of its parent body has certified that the accounts are properly maintained. This is to aid the officers in discharging their statutory duties. This challenge, therefore, has to be rejected. [Para 25]

Further, it is for the dealer to decide whose services he seeks to obtain for appearance before the Sales Tax Authorities or for getting the accounts audited. Under section 82, there are a class of persons from whom a dealer can obtain services for being represented before the authorities under the Act. Under section 61, he is bound to select one of the class of accountants also. This is for a category of dealers whose turnover is more than 40 lakhs. The amount of fee which has to be paid is the amount to be decided between the dealer and that person, whom he selects from amongst the accountants that are available. This cannot be said to amount of compulsory levy amounting to tax. That being the case, the challenge under article 265 must also fail.

Similarly, the question of article 301 being attracted, does not arise. The challenge on that count also has to be rejected as the right claimed by the petitioners or their members or by the dealer is that Advocate and Sales Tax Practitioner cannot carry out audit in terms of section 61 in the State of Maharashtra. The enactment is pursuant to the power of the State Legislature to make law within its competence. This does not attract article 301. [Para 27]

While deciding the issue Assessing Officer/FAA had not gone in the full details of expenditure incurred under the head credit analysis. Details of expenditure incurred on account of Head Office control, software implementation (including implementing any upgrade patches or mods etc. to software) and Head Office support activities have not been considered. Terms and conditions of agreement, if any, to carry out credit analysis job have not been discussed in the orders of the Assessing Officer and FAA. It is not clear whether as such details were called for or not and whether such pieces of information were provided or not by the assessee. In court opinion these are vital factors to decide the taxability of the amount in question. It is found that the certificate issued by the auditor had been issued for the information of and assistance to the Bank's management in connection with the review by 'local tax authorities'. It was 'not to be used' circulated quoted or otherwise referred to 'for any other purposes'. FAA has not inquired into the relevance of the said certificate as per the Indian tax laws. Assessee itself has disallowed an expenditure of Rs. 16.89 lacs incurred under the head for the year under consideration and similar expenditure in subsequent years has been allowed by the Assessing Officer what were the circumstances for such diverse course of action is not clear from the order of the Revenue Authorities. FAA has held that expenditure incurred by the assessee was not reimbursement, but the basis for arriving at this conclusion has not been mentioned. It is accepted principle of taxation that if any payment is only reimbursement it cannot be taxed-but if profit is embedded in it same has to be taxed. A clear finding based on facts has to be given as how a payment can be treated a sum embedded with profit and not a mere reimbursement payment. Considering the above, it was held that matter needs further verification. Therefore, in the interest of justice matter is restored back to the file of the FAA for fresh adjudication. He surrendered to afford a reasonable opportunity of hearing to the assessee. [Para 2.4]

Services were not liable to service tax :

Assessee is a testing agency. The contract of service was with the overseas purchaser of goods. Thus, the privity of contract of the assessee is with the buyers of the goods who are located or situated outside India. This is a contract based tax. The contract is of services. There is no contract in this case with the manufacturer of goods in India. Further, there is no contract and no privity between the assessee and the exporter of the goods who is stated to be based in India. In these circumstances, the exemption notification though required to be strictly construed, has to be construed in favour of the assessee. [Para 17]

Clients of the assessees are located abroad. The Tests Reports may have been prepared in India. The tests may have been conducted in India. However, the certificates have been forwarded to the clients of the assessee abroad. In such circumstances, assessee had exported the services by way of testing and analysis in India and transmitting the test report/analysis report to the foreign clients. The service was complete when the report was delivered to the foreign client. Since the delivery of the report to the foreign client was considered to be an essential part of the service that the demand of service tax was liable to be set aside. [Paras 18 & 19]

Assessee received payment in India in convertible foreign exchange and this payment is not repatriated by the assessee from or sent outside India. [Para 20]

Definition of Term Taxable service is inclusive. It also includes technical testing and analysis (see section 65 (106) (zzh)). By section 65(106), technical testing and analysis has also been defined. In such circumstances, when technical inspection and certification is also a service and goods in question have been inspected or tested, but the services were of the nature noted above, the payment was also made in terms aforesaid, then, the benefit of exemption/Circular was available. That was on the footing that the services rendered were exempt from whole of the liability to pay service tax. [Para 21]

Circular dated 25th April 2003 referred to Notifications dated 1st March 2003 and 9th April 1999. The 9th April 1999 is a notification of exemption. The April 2003 circular clarifies that service tax would be levied on all taxable services consumed or rendered in India, irrespective whether the payment thereof is received in foreign exchange or not. Since representations were received by the Board with regard to the withdrawal of the notification no.6 of 1999, exports of service would be affected as it would be costlier in the international market, that the board clarified that service consumed/provided in India in the manufacture of goods which are ultimately exported, no credit of service tax paid can be availed or reimbursed till April 2003 because intersectoral tax credit between service and goods are not allowed. It has been clarified that the question of taxability of secondary services which are used by primary service provider for the export of services. Hence, the services provided by the assessee were not taxable. This aspect once becomes more clear if one peruses the notification no.21/03ST, dated 20th November, 2003. [Para 22]
