The IVTC services specific to certification with reference to a factory assessment services extends to production capability, quality system, health and safety measures and is carried out as per ISO9001 standards. Findings on factory strengths/weaknesses and recommendations for improvements/development is also stated. [Para 8.3]

tax would not be payable if a professional like a chartered accountant or a cost accountant has in reality not rendered any professional services to a customer. These aspects are distinct aspects and, therefore, an aspect which entirely depends upon the services offered by the professional though may have a nexus with profession, yet the service becomes a distinct aspect in itself and can be legitimately taxed by the Parliament under Entry 97 of List I as had been done in the instant case. [Paras 25, 27] Therefore, the aspect of service is entirely a distinct aspect from the aspect of the profession though there can be some latent overlapping but there is no overlapping in law. The criticism against the judgments of the Gujarat High Court and Bombay High Court in Chartered Accountants' Association v. Union of India [2001] 252 ITR 53/ 115 Taxman 543 and All India Federation of Tax Practitioners v. Union of India [2002] 256 ITR 401 could not be upheld. [Paras 28, 29]

As regards the argument that provisions of sections 65(48) and 67(r) and 67(s) are confusing and contrary, the tone of the argument was that the Legislature had picked and chosen chartered accountants or cost accountants and left out other professionals like doctors and lawyers. That argument was incorrect because it is for the Legislature to select any particular service or any particular subject for taxing. The celebrated judgment in Federation of Hotel & Restaurant Association of India v. Union of India [1989] 178 ITR 97/46 Taxman 47 (SC) aptly covers the subject. [Paras 32, 33]

Therefore, there would be no question of finding any fault with the Legislature for picking up chartered accountants or cost accountants or architects also for taxing their services. [Para 34]

A practical difficulty was pointed out that chartered accountants normally issue a composite bill for multifarious services offered by them and such bill cannot be split up with regard to the services offered by them. From that it was suggested that the concerned provisions suffer from the 'vagueness' and are confusing and as such, can be labelled as 'arbitrary provisions'. In that regard, it was to be pointed out that it is only the services offered by chartered accountants in their 'professional capacity' which are made taxable and the services other than of auditing and accounting provided by practising chartered accountants are exempted from this tax. Therefore, it could not be said that there is any confusion regarding the taxable services. The notification issued under section 93 of the Finance Act, 1994 specifying that other services excepting the one for accounting and auditing is a complete answer to the said argument. It specifically provides the services which are made taxable and the other services which are not taxable. This is besides the fact that there is a complete machinery available in the Act itself to decide the nature of the services. There is also a provision for appeal within the machinery of the Act and, therefore, it cannot be said that there can be confusion about the services offered by chartered accountants or cost accountants. [Paras 34, 35]

It was, therefore, to be held that the impugned provisions did not offend article 14 of the Constitution and that all the petitions had to be dismissed. [Para 35]

[The Court refused to grant leave to appeal to the Supreme Court].

established that the charging of interest @ 6.5% was a revenue neutral exercise. This could be only ascertained after all entries were examined by the special auditor. On the question of commercial expediency, it has been observed in the impugned order that it would come into play when the actual picture was ascertained i.e. extending of loan to the subsidiary and charging of interest was thoroughly examined. [Para 20]

Profit from SEZ and non-SEZ units With regard to the profit from SEZ and non-SEZ projects it was noted that profit of Rs.1,78,63.73 lacs has been declared on SEZ income/turnover of Rs.2,38,31.36 lacs and profit of Rs.6,57,01.92 lacs has been declared on non-SEZ income/turnover of Rs.24,19,20.81 lacs. The order records that the assessee was required to submit comparative detail with regard to expenditure in SEZ and non-SEZ income projects but this was not filed. The affairs of the company, therefore, were not transparent and required audit. [Para 21]

SEZ and non-SEZ income figures mentioned by the Assessing Officer were contested in the reply. Discrepancies were alleged. Reference was made to the earlier reports of the statutory auditor and the fact that in the special audit reports no adverse inference was drawn in respect of deduction under section 80-IAB. Further provisions of section 142(2A) were not invoked for the assessment year 2009-10 in regard to SEZ accounts. [Para 22]

Related party transacton

There was no merit in the contention raised by the assessee that related party transactions or reasonableness of interest paid to the assessee on loans and advances by its subsidiary was an issue which was never raised in the show cause notice and therefore, there was violation of principles of natural justice. This question was specifically raised in the show cause notice and answer or reply was called for. Thus it is accepted and admitted position that detailed queries in writing and orally were raised. This shows due application of mind and focus on the issues and aspects that arose for consideration. The said facts are indicative of the Assessing Officer's conduct in trying to understand the accounts and whether true and correct income had been disclosed. The aforesaid submissions of the assessee, therefore, do not appeal. [Para 24]

Assessing Officer had applied his mind to various aspects like nature of accounts, method of maintaining accounts, entries recorded etc. and reached the conclusion that the accounts were complex and it was in the interest of the revenue that special audit under section 142 (2A), should be directed. No doubt in the past also special audit was directed but the Assessing Officer has not directed special audit in the present assessment year without examining the accounts for the year in question, the entries made, peculiarity involved etc. Special audit has not been directed for getting over the limitation or in routine. [Para 25]

Scope of powers under section 142(2A)

Powers under section 142(2A) have to be exercised in terms of the legislative provisions. The object and purpose behind the legislation is to facilitate investigation and proper determination of the tax liability. The importance and relevancy of the legislation cannot be underestimated and it is a power available with the Assessing Officer to aid and assist him. Accounts should be accurate and provide real time record of the financial transactions of the assessee. Preparation of accounts is the work of the accountant on the payrolls or employed by the assessee. In order to ensure reliability and accuracy, enterprises resort to internal audit and an external audit which can be a statutory audit. Internal audits are normally conducted inhouse generally by acquainted or qualified accountants. Statutory audit is compulsory under the Companies Act, 1956 or when stipulated by the Act and accounts have to be audited by a qualified Chartered Accountant. Chartered Accountants are not ordinary accountants but specialists who have successfully undergone academic study and have extensive practical experience and trained for the said work. Curriculum requires articleship under a mentor who is himself a Chartered Accountant with some years of experience. As opposed to an ordinary accountant, a Chartered Accountant with his experience and academic background is in a better position to investigate, examine and scrutinize entries and records of financial transactions. Calibre and competence of Chartered Accountants is of a high degree and should not and cannot be equated with the capability of an ordinary accountant or a normal person having knowledge or acquainted with accounts. Off late there has been demand for increased public scrutiny of accounts, inspite of statutory audit. Enron and other cases abroad and Satyam's case in India have highlighted the need and necessity to have controls and system of checks, perhaps even beyond scope of traditional audit. Financial statements and accounts are being increasingly exiguously examined to rule out possibility of wrong doings, cover up or evasion of taxes. Financial statements and accounts are coming under increasing scrutiny and investigation. A Chartered Accountant is a financial investigator and prober, is required to be curious, tenacious and well conversant to identify and unearth frauds, misreporting and wrong claims in the accounts. [Para 26]

HEADNOTE: Section 21 of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 - Misconduct - Procedure in inquiries relating to misconduct of members of Institute - Joint Director of Industries, made a complaint against respondent, a C.A. stating that respondent had issued certificates for consumption of raw material and production in respect of units showing value of imported raw materials at CIF value without taking into consideration customs duty payable on said imported goods and average price of raw materials as certified by respondent could not be low as shown in certificates and also units had no record of past consumption and therefore certificates issued were not correct - Disciplinary Committee held that respondent was guilty of professional misconduct and submitted its report to Council - Council concurred with said report and forwarded case to High Court under section 21(5) with a recommendation that name of respondent be removed from register of members for a period of three months - Whether since there was no evidence on record to show that raw materials were imported by units, question of paying any customs duty by said units did not arise at all - Held, yes - Whether without establishing that apart from price shown in purchase bills, units had paid any other amount 
 towards price of raw materials either by way of customs duty or otherwise, it could not be said that certificates issued by respondent were erroneous - Held, yes - Whether since there was no evidence on record to show that units did not maintain books of account, it could be said that complaint had no merit - Held, yes - Whether since charges levelled against respondent could not be proved, findings given by Disciplinary Committee and concurred by Council that respondent was guilty of professional misconduct could not be sustained - Held, yes

FACT: The Joint Director of Industries, Aurangabad made a complaint against the respondent, a C.A. stating that the respondent had issued the certificates for consumption of raw material and production in respect of the three units; that the consumption certificates showed the value of imported raw material as CIF value; that the respondent issued certificates without seeking records, since imported value of the raw material should have been shown as value of the raw material and not CIF value; that the units had no record for past consumption; that based only on the CIF value, production value had been worked out and customs duty, etc., were not taken into account while working out production figures, and that it showed that the figures were manipulated and certificates issued were not correct. On being prima facie satisfied that the respondent was guilty of professional and/or other misconduct, the Council of Institute of the Chartered Accountants of India (Council) referred the above complaint to the Disciplinary Committee.

The Disciplinary Committee after recording evidence and after hearing the respondent submitted its report to the Council holding that the respondent was guilty of professional misconduct within the meaning of clauses (7) & (8) of Part I of the Second Schedule, read with sections 21 & 22. The Council concurred with the report of the Disciplinary Committee and after recording its findings to that effect under section 21(3), forwarded the case to the High Court under section 21(5) with a recommendation that the name of the respondent be removed from the register of members for a period of 3 months.

HELD: As regards the charge levelled against the respondent that he had issued consumption certificate showing the value of the imported raw materials at CIF value without taking into consideration the customs duty payable on the said imported goods, first of all, there was no evidence on record to show that the raw materials were imported by the units and, therefore, the question of paying any customs duty by the said units did not arise at all. The case put forth by the respondent was that the raw materials were purchased by his clients locally. Where the goods are purchased locally, the question of paying customs duty on the said goods does not arise at all. Thus, neither there was any material on record to show that the raw materials in question attracted customs duty nor there was any material to show that any customs duty had been paid by the units on those raw materials. In the said circumstances, non-inclusion of the customs duty amount in the value of the raw materials could not be said to be faulty. [Para 9]

Secondly, the charge that the average price of the raw materials as certified by the respondent could not be as low as shown in the certificates was also without any merit. The valuation of the raw materials is to be determined on the basis of the actual cost incurred and not on the basis of average cost. In any event, without establishing that apart from the price shown in the purchase bills, the units had paid any other amount towards the price of the raw materials either by way of customs duty or otherwise, it could not be said that the certificates issued by the respondent were erroneous. [Para 10]

HEADNOTE: Section 61 of the Maharashtra Value Added Tax Act, 2002 read with articles 14, 19 and 265 of the constitution of India - Accounts to be audited in certain cases - Whether section 61 of Maharashtra Value Added Tax Act which requires accounts of certain dealers to be audited by Chartered Accountants is constitutionally valid and it does not infringe article 14 - Held, yes Words and phrases : ‘audit’ as judicially defined

FACT: The petitioners, Sales Tax Practitioners Association of Maharashtra; Small Scale Industries Association; and others, challenged the constitutional validity of section 61(1) and Explanation thereto of the Maharashtra Value Added Tax Act which requires accounts to be audited by the Chartered Accountants on ground that it infringes the equality clause as enshrined in article 14, the right to carry on profession under article 19(1)(g) as also under section 254 as the provisions for ‘audit’ would not fall within the competence of the State Legislature under Entry No. 54 of the List II of the VIIth Schedule to the Constitution. In the alternative the petitioners contended to read down or interpret section 61 so as to empower Advocates and Sales Tax Practitioners to audit and give report in Form No. 704. The petitioners contended that section 61 has confined the function of audit only to a Chartered Accountants and excluded other professionals and authorized persons like the Sales Tax Practitioners and Advocates. The petitioners, further, contended that the impugned provision sought to keep out a class of Advocates and Sales Tax Practitioners from their legitimate field of practice; and since audit is in fact a statutory return of the dealer for the purpose of enabling the sales tax officer to complete the assessment and, therefore, involved minor skills which can be better performed by the Advocates and as such exclusion of Advocates and Sales Tax Practitioners from performing audit or carrying on audit clearly discriminatory, arbitrary and unreasonable. It was also contended that under section 61, the dealer will also have to engage a Chartered Accountant apart from engaging Advocate or Sales Tax Practitioner and their financial liability would increase and by such an increase in their financial liability, the same would affect their trade by cutting into their profits and that it is in fact in pith and substance nothing but compulsory levy amounting to tax and in contravention of article 265 of the constitution.

HELD: Section 82 permits the Sales Tax Practitioners and others set out therein, the right of appearance before any authority in proceedings under the Act. The right of appearance, therefore, has not been taken away. The right to appear subsists. [Para 9]

Before proceeding further, one may look into the meaning of the words ‘audit’ and ‘auditor’. In P. Ramanatha Aiyar’s Advanced Law Lexicon, 3rd Edition the ‘audit’ has been explained as a verb : to draw up or present an account; to make an official investigation and examination of accounts and vouchers; and as a noun : an examination of accounts in general; a formal or official examination and authentication of accounts, setting of accounts; the process of auditing accounts; the hearing and investigation had before an auditor."In President, Councillors and Ratepayers of the Shire of Frankston and Hastings v. Cohen, 102 CLR 607, before the High Court of Australia the expression ‘Audit’ came up for consideration and it was explained that the word, ‘audit’ is a well known English word, and the general nature of what constitutes an audit seems plain enough. The Oxford English Dictionary defines the noun ‘audit’ as ‘an official examination of accounts with verification by reference to witnesses and vouchers’. Mr. R.A. Irish in his book ‘Practical Auditing’ (p.1) says that ‘an audit may be said to be a skilled examination of such books, accounts and vouchers as will enable the auditor to verify the balance sheet’. The main objects of any audit are : (a) to certify to the correctness of the financial position as to shown in the balance sheet, and the accompanying revenue statements, (b ) the detection of errors, (c) the detection of fraud- the detection of fraud is generally regarded as being of primary importance." [Para 10]

Thus the word ‘audit’ has a specific connotation in the matter of examination, investigation and auditing of accounts, where detection of fraud is of primary importance. [Para 10]

The challenge in a nutshell is to the exclusion of Advocates and Sales Tax Practitioners from doing the work of audit under section 61. [Para 11]

HEADNOTE: Section 40(a)(i), read with section 194J, of the Income-tax Act, 1961, and articles 7, 13 and 15 of the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement between India and UK - Business disallowance - Interest, etc., payable outside India - Assessment years 1994-95 to 1997-98 - 'N' Ltd., UK (non-resident company) was authorized to issue ISO certification - Assessee-company entered into MoU with 'N' Ltd. and was accredited to provide ISO certification to business and other organizations in India and abroad on behalf of 'N' Ltd. - For said purpose, assessee had to pay certain fees to 'N' Ltd. - Apart from that, assessee also paid some amount to one 'P' (non-resident) for rendering his auditing services in the matter - Assessee claimed aforesaid payments as deduction while computing its taxable income - Assessing Officer held that since no tax had been deducted or paid in respect of payments made outside India to non-residents, claim for deduction for those payments was to be disallowed in view of provisions of section 40(a)(i) - On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) held that payments in question were in nature of royalty and fees for technical services rendered and taxable in India as per Indo-UK DTAA - Accordingly, he confirmed disallowance made by Assessing Officer - On appeal, it was, however, seen that services rendered in instant case did not result in making available any technical knowledge, experience, skills, know-how or process to assessee - Whether since nature of work carried out by non-resident ('N' Ltd.) involved making surveillance for purpose of ISO Certification, said service could not fall within ambit of fees for technical services as defined in article 13(4) of Indo-UK Treaty - Held, yes - Whether, moreover, since non-resident ('N' Ltd.) did not have permanent establishment in India, its business profits could not be taxed in India in view of provisions of article 7 of Indo-UK DTAA - Held, yes - Whether when amounts paid by assessee to 'N' Ltd. were not chargeable to tax in India, there was no obligation on part of assessee to deduct tax at source - Held, yes - Whether, consequently, provisions of section 40(a)(i) were not attracted - Held, yes - Whether as regards amounts paid to 'P', since fee paid was for rendering professional services, same could be taxed in India only if person rendering service stayed in India for a period aggregating 90 days during relevant fiscal year or had a fixed base regularly available to him in India for performing such activities - Held, yes - Whether when it was not case of revenue that 'P' was present in India for a period aggregating 90 days or had fixed base in India, fee paid to 'P' was not taxable in India - Held, yes - Whether in view of aforesaid, authorities below were unjustified in refusing to allow deduction by taking recourse to provisions of section 40(a)(i) - Held, yes

FACT: 'N' Ltd., UK, was authorized to issue ISO certification. The assessee-company entered into MoU with 'N' Ltd. and was accredited to provide ISO certification to business and other organizations in India and abroad on behalf of 'N' Ltd. The assessee had to pay certain fees to 'N' Ltd. for that purpose. The assessee also paid some amounts to one 'P' for auditing services rendered by him in that matter. However, while remitting the payments, the assessee did not deduct tax at source since the recipients thereof were non-residents. The assessee claimed the aforesaid payments as deduction while computing its income. It was the case of the assessee that the payments in question were not chargeable to tax in India in the hands of the recipient because the same were 'taxable profits' within the meaning of the DTAA between UK and India; that, consequently, the same were taxable in UK only, and, thus, there was no violation of section 40(a)(i ). The Assessing Officer was of the view that since admittedly no tax had been deducted or paid in respect of the payments made outside India to non-residents, the claim for deduction of those payments as expenditure was to be disallowed in view of the provisions of section 40(a)( i).

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the payments in question were in the nature of royalty and fees for technical services rendered and taxable in India even as per the Indo-UK DTAA. Accordingly, the Commissioner (Appeals) affirmed the disallowance.

On appeal :

HEADNOTE: Section 21, read with section 22, of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 - Misconduct - Procedure in inquiries relating to misconduct of members of Institute - Whether once statutory obligation is cast on a person and such obligation provides for a period of limitation within which a particular document is required to be submitted, failure to do so within prescribed period is by itself liable to be visited with penalty, unless explained by a reasonable cause - Held, yes - Commissioner of Income-tax found that respondent-chartered accountant had issued a back-dated audit report to assessee-concern and also that he prepared tax audit report without examination and verification of books of account - On complaint, petitioner-Council recommended in terms of section 21(5) that respondent be removed from register of members for a period of six months as he was guilty of professional misconduct - Whether since respondent had no reasonable cause to plead except that he wanted to oblige his friend, there was no infirmity in finding recorded by Disciplinary Committee and Council in relation to charge of giving back-dated certificate - Held, yes - Whether since concurrent finding recorded by Disciplinary Committee and Council that books of account had, in fact, not been audited was a finding recorded after appreciation of evidence on record, there was no reason to interfere with finding recorded by Disciplinary Committee and Council - Held, yes

FACT: The respondent-Chartered Accountant had issued a tax audit certificate in favour of the assessee-concern under section 44AB of the Income-tax Act. The Commissioner of Income-tax, during the course of survey proceedings at the premises of the assessee, found certain discrepancy and recorded a statement of the respondent in which the respondent had accepted that he had issued a back-dated certificate showing the completion of audit of the assessee on behest of and to oblige his friend who was the tax consultant of the assessee. The Commissioner further averred that the respondent had prepared the tax audit report without examination and verification of the books of account. On complaint, the Disciplinary Committee of the petitioner-Council concluded that the respondent was guilty of both charges and was, thus, guilty of professional misconduct under sections 21 and 22. The petitioner-Council accepting the aforesaid conclusion recommended in terms of section 21(5) that the respondent be removed from the register of members for a period of six months.

On reference :

HELD: The respondent had admittedly issued a back-dated certificate. The contention that back-dating of the tax audit report had not occasioned any loss of revenue nor had it benefited anyone did not merit acceptance. Though in financial terms the respondent may be correct in stating that there was no loss of revenue, the said contention was bereft of any substance when the underlying idea of obtaining tax audit report was considered. [Para 8]

Once statutory obligation is cast on a person and such statutory obligation provides for a period of limitation within which a particular document is required to be submitted, failure to do so within the prescribed period of limitation, is by itself liable to be visited with penalty, unless explained by a reasonable cause. In the instant case, the respondent had no reasonable cause to plead, the only defence being that the respondent wanted to oblige his friend. In the circumstances, there was no infirmity in the finding recorded by the Disciplinary Committee and the Council in relation to the first charge. [Para 9]

Insofar as the second charge was concerned, it was apparent from the record that both the Disciplinary Committee and the Council had recorded concurrent finding that books of account had in fact not been audited. The finding per se was a finding recorded after appreciation of evidence on record and there was no submission that there was any violation of the principles of natural justice. In the circumstances, even the second charge stood proved and there was no reason to interfere with the finding recorded by the Disciplinary Committee and the Council. [Para 10]

Therefore, no ground was made out calling for any interference with the recommendation made by the petitioner-Council and the same was accepted in toto. [Para 11]

The reference was, accordingly, disposed of.

Inc. USA in bank account owned by GIA Inc. USA and, thus, assessee was entitled to the benefit of DTAA between India and USA. The Commissioner (Appeals) noted that the diamond certification was issued by GIA Inc. USA and copy of grading certificate was also issued by GIA USA, but due to clerical mistake the beneficiary of the remittance was erroneously specified as GIA Hong Kong Laboratory and held that payment was not tax deductible at source.

On appeal : HELD: The Assessing Officer treated the assessee in default under section 201(1) on the basis of details on the Form15CA/15CB about the remittance by taking view that testing related work has been carried out at GIA Laboratory at Hong Kong set up under the company GIA Hong Kong. The testing services were rendered by Hong Kong Laboratory. The payments were made in bank account located in Hong Kong as per condition of payment, since there exist no branch of GIA, Inc in Hong Kong; it is incontrovertible that the testing and certification related services are rendered by GIA Hong Kong. The payments were merely made to GIA Inc., America even though all services were rendered by GIA Hong Kong Laboratory at Hong Kong, thus, GIA Hong Kong Laboratory is the rightful owner of such payment which merely routed through GIA, Inc, America. The state of source is not obliged to give up the taxing rights over the passive income in the nature of Fees for Technical Services (FTS) merely because the income was paid direct to recipient of a state with which the state of source had concluded/executed DTAA. As recorded above that before the Commissioner (Appeals) the assessee contended that the entry on Form15CA/15CB were wrongly filled up and that the payment of certification charges were infact made to GIA Inc USA and furnished certificate of HSBC Bank that the bank account wherein the remittance were made owned by GIA Inc USA. The Commissioner (Appeals) on appreciation of facts held that there is no dispute about the services rendered by GIA to assessee. Further the diamonds certification is issued by GIA Inc USA. Certification issued by GIA USA is considered as standard benchmark by the trade as well as by the customers and all intellectual property rights in the certification belongs to GIA Inc USA. The assessee had agreement with GIA Inc USA, on perusal of which it can be seen that the term of agreement clearly describes the status of GIA Laboratory in Hong Kong. It is clear from the contents of agreement that Hong Kong, Dubai and Israel are the 'take in window' where articles are delivered. However, the services agreement is between the assessee and GIA USA. Copy of grading certificate is also issued by GIA USA, but due to clerical mistake the beneficiary of the remittance was erroneously specified as GIA Hong Kong Laboratory. [Para 15]

The Commissioner (Appeals) further held that the assessee-firm has furnished confirmation letter from HSBC Bank, confirming that the payments were made by assessee to GIA Inc USA in Bank Account owned by GIA Inc USA. The Assessing Officer tried to establish that the nature of services rendered by the non-resident is 'fee for technical services', however, the services rendered are not disputed by the assessee. The Commissioner (Appeals) pin point the dispute and held that the dispute is whether the services rendered by GIA are 'fee for technical services' under tax treaty by virtue of 'make available clause' under article 12 of India USA-DTAA. The benefit of treaty can be availed only by the residents of either country and tax resident certificate is an important document to avail the benefit of treaty in respect of payment made to non-resident as per section 90(4). Further requirement is of furnishing Form 10F. The assessee had furnished copy of Tax Residency Certificate (TRC) from USA authority in Form 10F as required under section 90(4) and 90(5). As per the TRC and Form 10F of non-resident company, GIA Inc USA for the relevant year under consideration, the assessee is entitled to the benefits of DTAA between India and USA. [Para 16]

On the specific submission made by the assessee that activity of grading of certification is merely the application of knowledge and experience the Commissioner (Appeals) held that there is no parting of information concerning industrial, commercial or scientific experience by GIA when it issues the grading certificate. GIA Inc USA has the experience of grading and report certificate and there is no imparting of its experience in favour of assessee. The assessee only receive report of certification. This activity of issuing certificate cannot be said to be imparting of information by the person who possesses such information. On considering the definition of 'fee for included services' under article 12, it was observed that there is no parting of rendering of technical services either of military, technical consultancy services or industrial commercial or scientific experience. The grading report are not make available' for the reasons that assessee, who is utilising the services will not be able to make use of technical knowledge, by itself in its business without recourse to GIA Inc. USA in future. The technical knowledge, experience skill, etc., will not remain with the assessee after rendering the services. [Para 17]

9-10-2002 [(2002) 177 CTR (St) 41], it is not necessary for an assessee to obtain prior determination of tax withholding liability. The assessee could, under the new scheme, approach any independent chartered accountant for determining his withholding tax liability from a remittance, and make a remittance on the basis of this certification, as long as the assessee tax deductor gave an undertaking to the Assessing Officer. [Para 7] So far as TDS under the revised procedure of making remittances to non-residents is concerned, the position is now like this. In case a person has to make a remittance to a non-resident, and he is of the view that the no TDS is warranted or tax is required to be deducted at a certain rate, he can approach an independent chartered accountant for certifying, in the prescribed format, the rate at which tax is to be deducted or that tax is not to be deducted, and make the remittance on the basis of such a certificate. Even this remittance on the basis of the chartered accountant's certificate is at assessee's own risk of consequences which follow the short deduction or non-deduction of tax at source. The assessee has to give an undertaking to that effect. However, as long as the assessee's stand is at least supported by a chartered accountant's certificate, the assessee is at least allowed to make the remittance on that basis. Contrast this with the old procedure of prior certification of withholding tax requirement by the Assessing Officer, in which, the assessee has to first pay the tax and then make the remittance. Under the revised scheme, the assessee can, subject to the support of a chartered accountant's certificate and furnishing of an undertaking extracted earlier in this order, first make the remittance and the finalization of withholding tax liability follows. All it does is that the real time control mechanism to ensure revenue collections from foreign remittance at the point of remittance, which was in the nature of steering control, is given up, though naturally with the right to take suitable remedial measures when any loss of revenue is caused by the tax-deductors. Nothing more than this paradigm shift in approach needs to be read into this scheme of things. It is not abandonment of the institution of the Assessing Officer (TDS) in favour of the professionals in accountancy practice. It is also important to take note of a clarification issued by the CBDT. As clarified by the CBDT, vide Circular No. 767, dated 22-5-1998 [(1998) 147 CTR (St) 1] to the effect that 'if an order under section 195(2) has been obtained by the person responsible for deducting tax, the new procedure of filing an undertaking along with the certificate prescribed in Circular No. 759 would not be applicable.' It is thus clear that the new scheme of remittances being allowed on the basis of chartered accountant's certificate is not in substitution of the scheme of things envisaged under section 195(2) but merely to supplement the same. However, the Commissioner (Appeals) appears to have proceeded on the basis that as long as chartered accountant's certificate is on record, it is not necessary for the Assessing Officer to examine the matter any further, so far as disallowance under section 40(a )(i) is concerned. By implication, thus, the chartered accountant's certificate is treated as conclusive to finalize the status of taxability, in the hands of the recipient of payment, in India. [Para 8]

The certificate issued by the chartered accountant, on the question of taxability of payment to non-resident in India, has no decisive impact on determination of taxability of income in the hands of the recipient non-resident; it is only a prima facie evidence about the taxability status and its acceptability by the revenue authorities is confined to permitting the remittance on the basis of taxability status certified by the chartered accountant. It cannot substitute for adjudication on taxability in the hands of non-resident by the Assessing Officer, nor can it be used as a shield by the assessee to thwart any probe on that aspect of the matter by the tax authorities. As a matter of fact, as assessee tax deductor's mandatory undertaking accompanying this certificate shows, the question of taxability in the hands of the recipient remains open and the assessee continues to have obligation to file all the relevant details, enabling determination of such liability, before the revenue authorities. In this view of the matter, the Commissioner (Appeals) was clearly in error in accepting the chartered accountants' certificates, on the basis of which foreign remittances were made, as decisive of the question that the assessee did not indeed have any obligation to deduct taxes at source from these payments. The Commissioner (Appeals) ought to have directed the assessee to furnish complete details about each of the foreign remittance, and examine these details to determine whether or not tax was indeed deductible under section 195(1) from each of these payments - particularly as admittedly assessee did not furnish these details before the Assessing Officer, and the Assessing Officer had no occasion to decide the matter on merits. To that extent, relief granted by the Commissioner (Appeals) cannot be sustained. [Para 9]

HEADNOTE: Section 9 , read with sections 44D, 44BB and 90, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and article 12 of the India-USA Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (FTS) - Assessment year 2009-10 - ONGC had made payment to non-resident assessee, for auditing/third party certification of oil reserves - Work was carried out by non-resident assessee at its work place in Dallas, USA - Assessing officer treated payment as fees for technical services on ground that assessee was not rendering any services relating to construction, assembly, mining or like project as mentioned in exclusion clause of Explanation 2 to section 9(1)(vii) and, thus, all receipts emanating from contract under consideration were to be taxed in India as a 'FTS' - ONGC had not been enabled to apply technology in future on its own without recourse to assessee and knowledge required to carry out similar work had not been made available to ONGC - Whether payment made was in connection with prospecting for extraction or production of mineral oil and, therefore, revenue received for auditing/third party certification of oil reserves would be charged to tax under section 44BB, read with Para 4(b) of article 12 of Indo-USA DTAA - Held, yes - Whether payment made by ONGC to assessee could not be taxed as 'fees for technical services' under section 44D - Held, yes [Para 10] [In favour of assessee]IT/ILT : Where non-resident assessee was providing auditing/third party certification service in respect of oil reserves of ONGC and ONGC had not been provided with relevant technology and knowledge required to carry out similar work in future, payment made by ONGC to assessee could not be taxed as 'fees for technical services' under section 44D; revenue received would be charged to tax under section 44BB, read with Para 4(b) of article 12 of Indo-USA DTAA as it was in connection with prospecting for extraction or production of mineral oil

FACT: During the relevant previous year, ONGC had made payment of certain amount to non-resident assessee against tax protected contract. The assessee was required by the Assessing Officer to show cause as to why the revenues received by it may not be treated as fees for technical services. The assessee was engaged by ONGC for auditing/third-party certification of in-place and reserves of 56 fields of ONGC and additional 12 fields. The work was carried out by the assessee at its work place Dallas, USA. Also the assessee did not have any office in India. It was submitted by the assessee before the Assessing Officer that:-

-

It was the Indian Government's view that the fact that the provision of service may require technical input by the person providing the service does not, per se, mean thattechnical knowledge, skills etc. were made available to the person purchasing the service, within the meaning of paragraph 4(b) of India USA Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement.

-

In the course of rendering of services to the ONGC, the non-resident itself may have used its technical knowledge skills etc. However, since ONGC had not been enabled to apply the technology in future on its own without recourse to the non-resident and the knowledge required to carry out similar work had not been made available to the ONGC, the payments made by ONGC to the non-resident could not be taxed as 'Fees for Included Services' under India USA Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement.

-

The receipts for the services rendered by the non-resident were not chargeable to income tax in India.

However, the Assessing Officer was of the opinion that the scope of work mentioned in the contract made it clear that the assessee was not rendering any service relating to the construction, assembly, mining or like project as mentioned in the exclusion clause of Explanation 2 to section 9 (1) (vii). The Assessing Officer proceeded to hold that the assessee's activities were covered under 'Fees for Technical Services' and all the receipts emanating from the contract under consideration were to be taxed in India.

The appeal of assessee was dismissed by the Commissioner (Appeals) following the decision of Tribunal, Delhi Bench rendered in the case of CGG Veritas Services, SA. v. Addl. DIT, International Taxation in [2012] 50 SOT 335/18 taxmann.com 13

On assessee's appeal :

HEADNOTE: I. Section 9, read with sections 40(a)(i) and 195, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and article 12 of India-USA DTAA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalty/FTS - Certification charges) - Assessment years 2005-06 and 2008-09 - During year, assessee-company made payment to an organization, namely, IFANCA for obtaining certification of product exported by assessee to USA as 'halal' so as to enable said product access to Islamic market in USA - Revenue was of view that services rendered by said organization to assessee qualified as 'included services' as it involved making available technical know-how to assessee and, thus, same was taxable in terms of article 12(4) of DTAA with USA and TDS was to be deducted on same - It was noted that procedure which IFANCA followed for halal certification did not mention what technical know-how was made available to assessee - In fact entire procedure adopted by IFANCA ensured that proper sanitation and cleanliness procedures were followed by assessee while manufacturing its product and product was not contaminated so as to qualify as halal - Whether, on facts, such payment made by assessee for halal certification did not qualify as 'included services' in terms of article 12(4) of India-USA DTAA and, thus, no TDS was to be deducted on such payment - Held, yes - Whether accordingly, impugned disallowance of certificate charges paid by assessee under section 40(a)(i) for non-deduction of TDS was unwarranted - Held, yes [Paras 17 and 18] [In favour of assessee]INTERNATIONAL TAXATION : Where assessee made payment to an organization of USA for obtaining certification of product exported by it to USA as 'halal' so as to enable access of said product to Islamic market in USA, since said certification ensured that proper sanitation procedures were followed by assessee while manufacturing its product and product was not contaminated so as to qualify as halal, such payment of certification charges did not qualify as 'included services' in terms of article 12(4) of India-USA DTAA and did not qualify for withholding of tax   INCOME TAX : Where a reopening notice was issued upon assessee on ground that no TDS was deducted on payment made by it towards legal and professional charges and carriage outward expenses, thus, same was to be disallowed, since said issue was not discussed during original assessment and no opinion was formed on it, validity of reassessment could not be challenged on account of change of opinion and thus, impugned reopening was justified

FACT: The assessee company made payment to an organisation, namely, IFANCA for obtaining certification of product exported by it to USA as 'halal' so as to enable said product access to islamic market in USA. The Assessing Officer disallowed said payment towards certification fee for non-deduction of tax at source on same under section 40(a)(i).

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) went through the supervision procedure adopted by the IFANCA, and after going through the same he came to the conclusion that entire process of supervision and certification involved making available to the assessee specific methods to be adopted in the manufacturing process so as to ensure the products manufactured being halal, and therefore, it involved making available technical knowledge to the assessee so as to be treated as "included services" as per article 14(2) of the DTAA with USA for the purpose of holding taxes on the same.

On appeal :

HELD: The term "halal" is an Arabic term/word that means "permissible" in English. In regard to the food, halal is set of standards for determining whether or not a product meets Islamic dietary restrictions. There are varying standards of halal and different understanding of halal law by the Islamic scholars, and that is why, there are multiple halal certifications. But there are three main requirements to consider halal viz. (i) the person performing action must have belief in God, (ii) the person performing action should attend to the act with proper intention and (iii) action should not harm anyone else. In a sense, halal means "permitted and allowed" by law Giver Allah. Islamic law places high importance on the life of animals. In order for food to qualify as halal, end of animals life must be taken only in the name of God. Thus, in a sense, halal certification means "permitted" under the Sharia or Islamic Law, which in sum and substance, implies slaughtering to be done for good intention and in the name of "God". [Para 16]

HEADNOTE: Section 61 of the Maharashtra Value Added Tax Act, 2002 read with articles 14, 19 and 265 of the Constitution of India - Accounts to be audited in certain cases -  Whether section 61 of Maharashtra Value Added Tax Act which requires accounts of certain dealers to be audited by Chartered Accountants is constitutionally valid and it does not infringe article 14 - Held, yes

FACT: The petitioners, Sales Tax Practitioners Association of Maharashtra; Small Scale Industries Association; and others, challenged the constitutional validity of section 61(1) and Explanation thereto of the Maharashtra Value Added Tax Act which requires accounts to be audited by the Chartered Accountants on ground that it infringes the equality clause as enshrined in article 14, the right to carry on profession under article 19(1)(g) as also under article 254 as the provisions for 'audit' would not fall within the competence of the State Legislature under Entry No. 54 of the List II of the VIIth Schedule to the Constitution. In the alternative the petitioners contended to read down or interpret section 61 so as to empower Advocates and Sales Tax Practitioners to audit and give report in Form No. 704. The petitioners contended that section 61 has confined the function of audit only to a Chartered Accountants and excluded other professionals and authorized persons like the Sales Tax Practitioners and Advocates. The petitioners, further, contended that the impugned provision sought to keep out a class of Advocates and Sales Tax Practitioners from their legitimate field of practice; and since audit is in fact a statutory return of the dealer for the purpose of enabling the sales tax officer to complete the assessment and, therefore, involved minor skills which can be better performed by the Advocates and as such exclusion of Advocates and Sales Tax Practitioners from performing audit or carrying on audit clearly discriminatory, arbitrary and unreasonable. It was also contended that under section 61, the dealer will also have to engage a Chartered Accountant apart from engaging Advocate or Sales Tax Practitioner and their financial liability would increase and by such an increase in their financial liability, the same would affect their trade by cutting into their profits and that it is in fact in pith and substance nothing but compulsory levy amounting to tax and in contravention of article 265 of the constitution.

HELD: Section 82 permits the Sales Tax Practitioners and others set out therein, the right of appearance before any authority in proceedings under the Act. The right of appearance, therefore, has not been taken away. The right to appear subsists. [Para 9]

Before proceeding further, one may look into the meaning of the words 'audit' and 'auditor'. In P. Ramanatha Aiyar's Advanced Law Lexicon, 3rd Edition the 'audit' has been explained as a verb : to draw up or present an account; to make an official investigation and examination of accounts and vouchers; and as a noun : an examination of accounts in general; a formal or official examination and authentication of accounts, setting of accounts; the process of auditing accounts; the hearing and investigation had before an auditor."In President, Councillors and Ratepayers of the Shire of Frankston and Hastings v. Cohen, 102 CLR 607, before the High Court of Australia the expression 'Audit' came up for consideration and it was explained that the word, 'audit' is a well known English word, and the general nature of what constitutes an audit seems plain enough. The Oxford English Dictionary defines the noun 'audit' as 'an official examination of accounts with verification by reference to witnesses and vouchers'. Mr. R.A. Irish in his book 'Practical Auditing' (p.1) says that 'an audit may be said to be a skilled examination of such books, accounts and vouchers as will enable the auditor to verify the balance sheet'. The main objects of any audit are : (a) to certify to the correctness of the financial position as to shown in the balance sheet, and the accompanying revenue statements, (b) the detection of errors, (c) the detection of fraud- the detection of fraud is generally regarded as being of primary importance." [Para 10]

Thus the word 'audit' has a specific connotation in the matter of examination, investigation and auditing of accounts, where detection of fraud is of primary importance. [Para 10]

The challenge in a nutshell is to the exclusion of Advocates and Sales Tax Practitioners from doing the work of audit under section 61. [Para 11]

by it to 'C' was not chargeable to tax in India, due to the exception contained in section 9(1)(vii)( b).

HELD: In order to fall within exception of section 9(1)(vii )(b), the technical services, for which, the fees have been paid, ought to have been utilized by a resident in a business outside India or for the purposes of making or earning any income from any source outside India. [Para 16] The KEMA certification obtained by the assessee from 'C' for enabling exports of its products was unassailed. The sole stand of the department was that this service of testing and certification had been applied by the assessee for its manufacturing activity within India. However, neither the Assessing Officer, nor the Commissioner (Appeals) had been able to bring anything on record to buttress such a stand. Thus, the initial onus under section 9(1)(vii)( b) lay squarely on the assessee to prove that the exemption available thereunder was in fact available to it. The assessee had maintained throughout that the testing and certification services provided by 'C' were utilized only for its export activity and that the same were not utilized for its business activities of production in India. Thus, the assessee had discharged the onus, which lay on it under section 9(1)(vii)(b ). Therefore, the impugned payment made by the assessee to 'C' was not chargeable to tax in India. [Para 21]

Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) had erred in confirming the disallowance made by the Assessing Officer. [Para 30]

. The contention of Shri Mehta for revenue that the certificate of the Singapore revenue authorities is opposed to provisions of section 10 of the Singapore Income Tax Act also cannot be accepted. The Revenue does not question genuineness of the certificate. It cannot dispute the contention on the ground that the same are opposed to the statutory provision." [Para 13] ■

The Tribunal has referred to and relied upon the above findings of this Court in relation to applicability of Article 8 of the DTAA. However, the Tribunal has ventured to distinguish the decision of this Court on the question of the veracity of the certificate dated 09.01.2013 on the ground that the genuineness of the said certificate was not questioned by the Revenue before this Court and hence, the Tribunal has thought it fit to restore the matter to the Assessing Officer to verify the contents of the said certificate with a rider that in case the Assessing Officer is not able to obtain any specific material to rebut the contents of the certificate issued by the Singapore Tax Authority, then respectfully following the decision of this Court, relief was to be granted to the appellants. [Para 14]

■

When this Court has already considered the certificate dated 09.01.2013 and during the pendency of the appeal before the Tribunal for the year under consideration, the Revenue has not been able to bring any material on record or has challenged or doubted the certificate issued by the Singapore Tax Authority, as observed by the Tribunal in Para 20 of the impugned order, it has noted that the Departmental Representative has challenged the veracity of the certificate issued by the IRAS during the course of the appellate proceedings before the CIT (A) and thereafter, the Tribunal has referred to the territorial tax system of the Singapore Income Tax Act to hold that the certificate has not given any basis whatsoever as to how the assessee is deriving income from "business carried on in Singapore", when admittedly, the appellants-assessee have been operating in international waters. The Tribunal has also considered the fact that the certificate does not specify the factual basis on which the Singapore Tax Authority has concluded that the income from shipping business have been derived by the assessee from "business carried on in Singapore". Thus, in effect, the Tribunal has overreached the findings arrived at by this Court in case of M.T. Maersk Mikage v. DIT (International Taxation) (supra) in absence of any material brought on record by the Revenue before the Tribunal to show that the certificate issued by the IRAS is not reliable or cannot be considered for the income of ST Shipping to be taxed in Singapore on accrual basis. [Para 15]

■

It is also pertinent to note that from the documents placed in form of paper- book filed before the Tribunal, in fact, the ST Shipping has shown the income arising from the operations as per letter dated 09.10.2012 issued by the Deloitte and Touche LLP, Certified Public Accountants, Singapore stating that the ST Shipping has confirmed that the position adopted in the Year of Assessment 2010 to treat charter income derived by the overseas branches as Singapore sourced income and part of qualifying income under Approved International Shipping Enterprise Incentive remains unchanged in the Year of Assessment 2012. [Para 16]

■

The impugned order of the Tribunal is, therefore, contrary to the decision of this Court as the Tribunal could not have restored the matter back to the Assessing Officer only on mere suspicion and the doubts contrary to the findings arrived at by this Court regarding the same certificate dated 09.01.2013 issued by IRAS. The Tribunal ought not to have analysed the certificate in its order more particularly in Para 22 of the order in absence of any material on record. On perusal of Para 22 of the impugned order it is clear that the Tribunal has made the observation with regard to the language of the certificate more particularly, when this Court has accepted the part of the certificate which certified that the income earned by the ST Shipping from the operations carried out in ports at India was liable to be taxed at Singapore on accrual basis and as per Article 8 of DTAA, when the income accrues in Singapore and was taxed as such, the same would be exempt from tax in India. This Court has further clarified that reference to Article 24 of DTAA in the certificate is nothing but an opinion of the IRAS. [Para 17]

■

Hence, the Tribunal ought not to have further deliberated upon contents of the certificate which is already held to be applicable in the facts of the case in the absence of any other material on record to demonstrate that the veracity of the certificate issued by IRAS is doubtful and merely because the Tribunal is of the opinion that the language of the certificate is not conducive to the opinion of the Tribunal, the matter could not have been restored to the Assessing Officer in face of the observation made by this Court regarding the same certificate dated 09.01.2013 issued by the IRAS. [Para 18]

HEADNOTE: Section 22 of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 - Misconduct - Professional or other misconduct - Petitioner was a partner of a firm - It filed a complaint against respondent-chartered accountant before ICAI alleging various acts of misconduct - According to petitioner, respondent certified balance sheet of firm without carrying out audit and said balance sheet was accepted by Arbitrator while settling dispute between partners regarding settlement of accounts of firm - Council was of prima facie opinion that complaint filed by petitioner was frivolous and that respondent was not guilty of any professional or other misconduct - Whether since arbitrator who was an independent person had accepted balance sheet audited by respondent as correct, there was no reason to interfere with prima facie view of ICAI on complaint filed by petitioner - Held, yes [Para 13]Chartered Accountants Act : Where balance sheet audited by chartered accountant was accepted by arbitrator in arbitration proceedings, ICAI was right in forming prima facie opinion that chartered accountant was not guilty of any professional misconduct

FACT: The petitioner was one of the partners of a firm.

On retirement of the petitioner, dispute arose between the partners regarding the settlement of the accounts of the firm.

According to petitioner, another partner made changes in the accounts of the firm which were detrimental to the interest of petitioner.

According to petitioner, respondent No. 1 who was a chartered accountant certified the accounts of the firm without taking proper care.

According to the petitioner, during the arbitration proceedings filed by that partner against the petitioner and the other partners, the said partner submitted a purported audited accounts of the said firm.

During the pendency of the said arbitration proceedings, the petitioner filed a complaint against the respondent No. 1 before the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI) alleging various acts of misconduct and praying for disciplinary action.

During the pendency of the said complaint, the arbitrator made an award in which he accepted the figures as reflected in the balance sheet which was audited by the respondent No. 1 and was duly signed by the other two partners of the said firm.

Later, the petitioner was informed that Council was prima facie of the opinion that the respondent No. 1 was not guilty of any professional or other misconduct and, therefore, the papers relating to the case had been filed.

The petitioner was further informed that since the Council was of the opinion that the complaint filed by the petitioner was frivolous, deposit of Rs. 100 made by the petitioner had been forfeited.

The petitioner filed instant writ petition for quashing the order passed by the Council holding that the complaint filed by the petitioner against respondent No. 1 was frivolous.

Arguments of petitioner

The appointment of respondent No. 1 as an auditor was not by consent of the petitioner.

Respondent No. 1 had not carried out audit but had certified the purported balance-sheet.

He had mentioned the status of the firm as registered, though he was aware that the firm was not registered.

The procedure followed by the Institute was in violation of principles of natural justice.

Argument of Institute

The rejection of the complaint made by the petitioner could not be faulted with, once the balance sheet audited by respondent No. 1 was accepted as correct.

Issue involved

Whether ICAI was right in holding that respondent No. 1 was not guilty of any professional or other misconduct?

HELD: From the perusal of the arbitration award, it is clear that one of the partners had examined the witness to prove the contents of the balance sheet audited by respondent No. 1 which was signed by the other two partners.

The arbitrator had given a finding of fact that though repeated opportunities were given to the petitioner to cross-examine the witness examined by the one of the partners, no cross-examination was conducted by the petitioner and as a result thereof, the statement made by the said witness remained unchallenged. The arbitrator accepted the balance sheet of the firm based on the books of the account maintained in the regular course duly audited by respondent No. 1 and accepted the figures as reflected in the said balance-sheet. [Para 12]

Considering the fact that the dispute between the partners in respect of the accounts of the said firm was referred to the arbitrator who was an independent person and the said arbitrator looking to the entire evidence has accepted the balance sheet audited by respondent No. 1 as correct, there is no reason to interfere with the prima facie view of the Institute on the complaint filed by the petitioner.

HEADNOTE: Section 21 of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 - Disciplinary Directorate -  Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (Institute) received a complaint from complainant-Central Bank of India alleging that respondent-Chartered Accountant had assisted various companies in availing credit facilities of huge amounts from various banks by issuing false documents certifying valuation of work undertaken and completed by accused companies - Bank also alleged that respondent had also certified sales registers and list of supply bills of accused companies without verifying facts and figures to facilitate loans being sanctioned to said companies - Institute prima facie, found respondent guilty of professional misconduct and accordingly, referred case to Disciplinary Committee - Committee also held respondent guilty of misconduct - Accordingly, Institute decided to recommend to High Court that respondent be reprimanded - It appeared from report of committee that working papers of respondent revealed nothing of substance pertaining to basis of material on which certificates were issued by him - Certificates simply stated that they were issued on specific request of firm - On being asked to produce vouchers for purchase and machinery documents regarding statements of expenditure incurred by accused firms, invoices/vouchers for purchase of plant and machinery for civil work and land development etc, respondent was unable to produce any document - Committee also enquired from respondent as to how he had satisfied himself about existence and valuation of assets as mentioned in certificates issued by him, but apart from his working papers which also did not contain any basis for arriving at any satisfaction, respondent failed to establish any cogent justification for same - Respondent thus, failed to perform due diligence before issuing certificates - Further, respondent was completely aware that accused companies were seeking specific verification and certification to complete documentation required by bank to sanction credit facilities to them and, he was naturally aware that issuing such certificates in absence of proper valuation was a fraud on banks as such public and financial institutions rely upon certificates of professionals as part of its due diligence - Whether in these circumstances, respondent was reprimanded in accordance with section 21(6)(b) - Held, yes [Paras 8, 10 and 15]INCOME TAX/CHARTERED ACCOUNTANT ACT : Where respondent-Chartered Accountant had assisted various companies in availing credit facilities of huge amounts from various banks by issuing false certificates, in view of fact that respondent was naturally aware that issuing such certificates was a fraud on banks as such public and financial institutions rely upon certificates of professionals as part of its due diligence, respondent was thus reprimanded in accordance with section 21(6)(b)
