HEADNOTE: Section 21, read with section 22 and clause (7) of Part I of Second Schedule to the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 - Professional misconduct - Respondent CA certified wrong FOB value of export in terms of Import and Export Policy - Whether failure of CA to exercise skill, care and caution while making wrong verification amounted to gross negligence - Held, yes - Whether having regard to fact that respondent had communicated said mistake to exporter involved but only failed to inform authorities concerned he was acting bona fide and, therefore, word of caution to be more careful would suffice instead of reprimanding him - Held, yes
Words & phrases - ‘negligent’ occurring in clause (7) of Part I of the Second Schedule to the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949

FACT: The respondent Chartered Accountant had certified an application of certain exporter in accordance with the requirements of Import and Export Policy certifying the FOB value of exports at Rs. 4,44,77,996. The figure was found to be wrong and on information in this regard being given to the Institute, the matter was referred to the Disciplinary Committee who found the respondent guilty of professional misconduct within the meaning of section 21, read with section 22, and clauses (6) and (7) of Second Schedule to the Act. When the matter came up before the Council, the benefit of doubt was given in respect of charge under clause (6) but in respect of the charge under clause (7) it was found that the respondent had not exercised due care and skill and, therefore, reprimand to him was recommended.

On reference under section 21(5) :

HELD: The respondent had not been found to have contravened clause (6), but clause (7). The latter clause relates to grossly negligent action in the conduct of professional duties. On the background facts, it had to be seen whether failure of the respondent to notice the mistake would constitute an act of negligence. It depends upon the fact whether the concerned person had applied his mind diligently to the job entrusted to him, and whether due care and caution, as is required to be adopted, was taken. The respondent took the stand that by mistake CIF value was typed out instead of FOB value. When a certificate is given, arithmetical accuracy has to be ensured. That is the minimum requirement to be done by a Chartered Accountant. The test is whether in addition to the failure to do the duty, there was failure to act honestly and reasonably. The word ‘negligence’ is associated in the provision with the word ‘misconduct’ and involves some element of moral culpability. Mere imprudence or want of judgment or grave error in judgment is not enough. Misconduct implies failure to act honestly and reasonably either according to the ordinary and natural standard or according to the standard of a particular profession. But error or mis-interpretation of law and specially one view or another over a debatable construction cannot be a ground for the allegation and finding of professional misconduct against a Chartered Accountant. Negligence is the omission to do something which a reasonable man, guided upon those considerations, which ordinarily regulate the conduct of human affairs, would do, or doing something which a prudent and reasonable man would not do. It is not absolute or intrinsic, but relative to some circumstances of time, place or persons, imposing a duty to take care. In dealing with the matters of professional propriety, one cannot ignore the fact that the profession of Chartered Accountant occupies the place of nobility, pride and honour and is a profession of trust. Expertise in the field of accounting and auditing is the hallmark of Chartered Accountant’s profession. When a Chartered Accountant signs certificates, the minimum that he is expected to do is to verify the accuracy of the figures certified. As part of his professional duty and responsibility, he is required to take reasonable steps to satisfy himself that the figures were correct. Elementary verification would have been sufficient to notice the mistake. Failure to carry-out such elementary verification amounts to gross negligence and carelessness. Skill, care and caution, which a reasonably competent and cautious auditor was expected to exercise, was not exercised. Lack of it had affected veracity of his competence. The intendment and object of the Act is to maintain the standard of the profession at a high level.

It was observed by the Apex Court in the context of an Advocates’ professional misconduct that an act which is done otherwise than with utmost good faith is unprofessional - Pandurang Dattatreya Khandekar v. Bar Council of Maharashtra AIR 1984 SC 110.

HEADNOTE: Section 21 of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 - Preferential or other misconduct - Assessee claimed deduction under section 80HHC - In order to claim said deduction, provisions of section 80HHC required that a certificate be filed in Form 10CCAC which was to be issued by chartered accountant certifying that export had in fact been made - Respondent, a chartered accountant, issued said certificate which was submitted before Assessing Officer - Assessee's claim was found to be false because export amount remained outstanding and was not realized though as per certificate given by respondent, amount had been realized - Whether, on facts, respondent was guilty of professional misconduct falling within meaning of clause (7) of Part-I of second schedule under section 22, read with section 21 and, thus, ends of justice would be subserved by removing name of respondent from register of members for a period of six months - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee had claimed deduction under section 80HHC. In order to claim this deduction, the provisions of section 80HHC required that a certificate be filed in Form 10CCAC which was to be issued by the chartered accountant certifying that the export had in fact been made. This certificate was given by the respondent as chartered accountant which was submitted before the Assessing Officer. The claim of the assessee was found to be false as against the alleged export the amount remained outstanding and was not realized. Though, as per the certificate given by the respondent, the amount had been realized. This would clearly show that certificate furnished by the respondent was wrong and bogus. An inquiry was held by the Council of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India on the allegations contained in a complaint submitted by the Commissioner. The Disciplinary Committee found that the allegations were substantiated and proved. After considering the report, the Council held the respondent guilty of professional misconduct falling within the meaning of clause (7) of Part-I of the second schedule under section 22, read with section 21 of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949. It accordingly recommended to this Court that the name of the respondent be removed from the register of members for a period of three years.

On reference :

HELD: The entire controversy was about the certificate issued by the respondent certifying that the exports were duly made and payments had been received by the assessee against those exports. It has been established on record that no such payment was received. The assessee had also accepted this fact when he was confronted with this aspect during the assessment proceedings whereby the claim of deduction under section 80HHC was rejected. Once it is established that no payment was received against the export, certificate issued by the respondent was false. It is a bogey raised by the respondent that he has verified all the documents and only then issued the certificate. One fails to understand what kinds of documents were shown by the assessee to the respondent on the basis of which the respondent felt satisfied. Thus, there was a clinching evidence to prove the charge. [Para 7]

In the instant case, on the one hand the respondent pleads his sickness, has otherwise unblemished practice of 21 years and that the incident is old which may provide some mitigating factors in his favour, on the other hand, the misconduct is of serious nature. Submitting a false/bogus certificate to the client to enable him to make false claim of deduction under the Income-tax Act, is a serious offence. The deduction to the tune of Rs. 18,32,985 was claimed on the strength of this certificate which would mean the tax saving of almost 6.5 lakhs. The attempt was thus to dupe the tax authorities and help the assessee to avoid the tax to that extent such a conduct has to be taken seriously. [Para 11]

After weighing the aforesaid factors on either side, it is opined that in the present case the respondent cannot be left off merely by giving him reprimand. Some penalty needs to be imposed so that it acts as deterrent and such professional misconduct is not committed. Weighing the circumstances, the ends of justice would be subserved by removing the name of the respondent from the Register of Members for a period of six months. [Para 12]

HEADNOTE: Section 21, read with section 22, of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 and regulation 11 of the Chartered Accountants Regulations, 1964 - Misconduct - Chartered Accountant certified accounts prepared by client as correct without verifying totals in profit and loss account resulting in excess deduction under the Agricultural Income-tax Act - Whether failure to carry out elementary verification amounted to gross negligence and carelessness affecting veracity of his competence and, therefore, respondent was guilty of 
 professional misconduct within meaning of section 21, read with section 22 and clause (7) of Part 1 of the Second Schedule to the Act and penalty of reprimand as recommended by Council was adequate and proper - Held, yes

FACT: The respondent was the Chartered Accountant who audited the accounts of an assessee and certified the same to be correct. Based on it, the Agricultural ITO allowed the entire claim of expenditure of Rs. 3,19,163.55 as shown in the expenditure side of the profit and loss account filed by him. However, on subsequent scrutiny it was found that the total amount on expenditure side of the profit and loss account was really Rs. 2,19,163 which resulted in penal consequence to the assessee. A complaint was made to the ICAI against the respondent which called for the statement of the auditor with respect to charge of professional misconduct under regulation 11(6). After going through the complaint and the written statement of the auditor, the President of the Council called for the copies of the profit and loss account, etc., under regulation 11(8) and after considering the documents the matter was referred by the counsel to the Disciplinary Committee which was of the view that the respondent was guilty of professional misconduct within the meaning of section 21, read with section 22 and clause (7) of Part I of the Second Schedule to the Act. The Council accepted the view of the Committee and recommended the penalty of reprimand.

HELD: The job of a Chartered Accountant is not to make a compilation. When a certificate is given, arithmetical accuracy has to be ensured. That is the minimum requirement to be done by a chartered accountant. The test is whether in addition to the failure to do the duty, there is failure to act honestly and reasonably. The word ‘negligence’ is associated in the provision with the word ‘misconduct’ and involves some element of moral culpability. Mere imprudence or want of judgment or grave error of judgment is not enough. Misconduct implies failure to act honestly and reasonably either according to the ordinary and natural standard or according to the standard of a particular profession. But error or misinterpretation of law and specially one view or another over a debatable construction cannot be a ground for the allegation and finding of professional misconduct against a chartered accountant. Negligence is the omission to do something which a reasonable man, guided by those considerations which ordinarily regulate the conduct of human affairs, would do. It is not absolute or intrinsic, but relative to some circumstances of time, place or persons, imposing a duty to take care. In dealing with matters of professional propriety, one cannot ignore the fact that the profession of chartered accountancy occupies the place of nobility, pride and honour and is a profession of trust. Expertise in the field of accounting and auditing is the hallmark of the chartered accountant’s profession. When a chartered accountant prepares a profit and loss account from the books of account and signs a certificate to that effect, the minimum that he is expected to do is to verify the accuracy of the figures in the profit and loss account with reference to the relevant books of account and he cannot escape the responsibility by pleading that he did not audit it and that verification of accounts was done by the staff. As part of his professional duty and responsibility, he is required to take reasonable steps to satisfy himself that the work is carried out in a proper, fair and efficient manner. The certificate is issued by him and the professional relationship is between him and the client. There could not be any escape by the respondent by taking the plea that an experienced accountant was verifying the totals. Elementary verification of totalling would have been sufficient to notice the mistake. Failure to carry out such elementary verification amounted to gross negligence and carelessness. Skill, care and caution, which a reasonably competent and cautious auditor is expected to exercise, was not done. The lack of it had affected the veracity of his competence. Delegation of duties does not necessarily absolve a principal from the liability arising out of gross negligence. The intendment and object of the Act is to maintain the standard of the profession at a high level.

HEADNOTE: Section  40(a)(i), read with section  143(1), of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Business disallowance -  Interest, etc., paid to a non-resident without deduction of tax at source (Scope of provision) - Assessment year 2020-21 - Assessee-company made payment to a foreign company towards certification fees for products which was necessary to sell products in USA and Canada market - Centralized Processing Centre (CPC) made disallowance under section 40(a)(i) for non-deduction of tax at source on said payment - Assessing Officer in scrutiny proceedings under section 143(3) accepted contentions of assessee and had not made any disallowance under section 40(a)(i) - However, while computing total taxable income Assessing Officer inadvertently took income computed under section 143(1) which inter alia included disallowance under section 40(a)(i) - Whether since issue had been examined in scrutiny proceedings and details in support of same were placed, impugned disallowance made by CPC deserved to be deleted - Held, yes [Paras 8 and 9] [In favour of assessee]INTERNATIONAL TAXATION/INCOME TAX : Where Assessing Officer accepted contentions of assessee that payment made to a foreign company towards certification fees for products was not chargeable to tax in India and had not made any disallowance under section 40(a)(i), however, while computing total taxable income Assessing Officer inadvertently took income computed under section 143(1) which inter alia included disallowance under section 40(a)(i), since issue had been examined in scrutiny proceedings, impugned disallowance made by CPC deserved to be deleted

Section  40(a)(i), read with section  143(1), of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Business disallowance -  Interest, etc., paid to a non-resident without deduction of tax at source (Scope of provision) - Assessment year 2020-21 - Assessee-company made payment to a foreign company towards certification fees for products which was necessary to sell products in USA and Canada market - Centralized Processing Centre (CPC) made disallowance under section 40(a)(i) for non-deduction of tax at source on said payment - Assessing Officer in scrutiny proceedings under section 143(3) accepted contentions of assessee and had not made any disallowance under section 40(a)(i) - However, while computing total taxable income Assessing Officer inadvertently took income computed under section 143(1) which inter alia included disallowance under section 40(a)(i) - Whether since issue had been examined in scrutiny proceedings and details in support of same were placed, impugned disallowance made by CPC deserved to be deleted - Held, yes [Paras 8 and 9] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee-company made payments to a foreign company towards certification fees for products which was necessary to sell the products in USA and Canada market. The return was processed under section 143(1)(a) wherein CPC made prima facie adjustments making disallowance under section 40(a)(i) for non-deduction of tax on the payment.

■

The assessee's case was selected for scrutiny and the same was carried out under section 143(3) read with section 144B and in the course of scrutiny proceedings one of the issue raised in the show cause notice by the Assessing Officer was regarding the alleged addition made under section 40(a)(i). The Assessing Officer accepted the contention of the assessee and it was further stated that no disallowance was required under section 40(a)(i).

■

However, while computing the total taxable income the Assessing Officer inadvertently took income computed under section 143(1)(a) which inter alia included the disallowance under section 40(a)(i).

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) dismissed the ground for statistical purposes.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: ■

following factors should be present in the transaction :

(a)

There should be a consideration for use or transfer of right to use;

(b)

The payment shall be towards grant or share for acquiring, inter alia, information concerning industrial, commercial or scientific experience, including gains derived from the alienation of any such right, property or information;

(c)

Such use or right to use such property or information shall be for the stipulated period in accordance with the terms of the contract. [Para 9] From the impugned order of the authorities, it emerged that GIA, by using its experience, does the work of diamond grading. In other words, parts in favour of the person seeking its specialized knowledge to the particular diamond in the form of grading certificate. It was on account of that activity that in the impugned order, it was set out that there was a transfer of commercial experience in the shape of diamond grading report. It is true that GIA may have the experience of grading. However, there is no imparting of its experience in favour of the client. What the client receives is the report where the GIA uses its commercial or technical knowledge to give a report to the client. Illustrative example would be a lawyer giving advise to his client; a doctor giving his medical opinion; a laboratory submitting blood analysis report and the like. These cannot be said to be imparting of information by the person who possesses such information. What such person does is to use of his experience and technical know-how for a consideration without parting with that information. Therefore, considering the definition of royalty under article 12, there was no parting or rendering of technical services either of managerial, technical or consultancy nature or industrial, commercial or scientific experience. Once the consideration/fees received did not fall within the expression 'royalty', the action of the respondents in refusing the certificate under section 195 was clearly without jurisdiction and, consequently, the impugned order was to be set aside with a further direction to the Deputy Director to issue the certificate as applied for by the assessee. [Para 11]

]

In the entirety of facts and circumstances of the case, the matter is to be set aside to the file of the Assessing officer for verification of declarations so filed by the assessee in Form 27C and examination of claim of the assessee under section 206C(1A) afresh in accordance with law. [Para 48]

Issue of alleged relief on basis of additional evidence without calling for remand report under Rule 46A and enquiry under section 250(4) The certificates in Form 27BA from the Chartered accountant and related declarations from the buyers were filed before the Assessing officer during the course of assessment proceedings and the same have been taken on record and examined by the Assessing officer. It was observed by the Assessing Officer that he has gone through the documentation so submitted by the assessee firm and on perusal thereof, he noticed that complete information in the Form/certificate have not been given by the accountant/party as required by the legislature and most of the columns are either not filled up as required or simply mentioned as per details/enclosure. Moreover, the accountant has signed the forms with conditional remarks "As certified by the buyer" whereas the forms should have been filled up and certified by the accountant itself on the basis of records. Further, some of the parties have not filed return on or before due dates prescribed under section 139. Further, on appeal, it is founed that these certificates in Form 27BA from the Chartered accountant and related declarations from the buyers have again been considered and examined by the Commissioner (Appeals) and the observations of the Assessing Officer regarding these certificates were not found tenable by the Commissioner (Appeals) and on basis his independent review and examination, the relief has been provided to the assessee firm as per his findings of his order. The Revenue has not pointed out what further evidence by way of additional evidence has been filed by the assessee during the appellate proceedings before the Commissioner (Appeals). Therefore, the ground so taken by the Revenue is to be dismissed. [Para 54]

The limited issue under consideration is whether at the time of submitting the certificates in Form 27BA as required under proviso to section 206C(6A), the assessee is required to deposit interest and give details of such interest deposit in such certificates. Firstly, on reading of provisions of proviso to section 206C(6A), it may be found that there is no requirement as such which has been specified in the statute. All it requires is that the accountant should certify as to whether the buyer has furnished his return of income, has taken into account such amount for computing income in such return of income and has paid taxes due on the income declared by him in such return of income or not. Further, on perusal of Form 27BA, it is found that besides such certification, it contains a statement whether the assessee has to specify whether it has paid any interest under section 206C(7) or not for non-collection or short collection of taxes. Thus, there is no mandatory requirement to pay any interest under section 206C(7) as part of certification in Form 27BA and where the assessee has already paid, he has to specify that he has paid and where he has not paid, he has to specify accordingly. It is only an information seeking requirement and not a requirement in absence thereof which will make the certification in Form 27BA invalid where there is substantial compliance as to the mandatory requirements of certification. In the result, the ground so taken by the Revenue is dismissed. [Para 58]

The Commissioner (Appeals) has clearly held and directed the Assessing Officer to allow the benefit to the assessee in light of Supreme Court decision in case of Hindustan Coca Cola Beverage (P.) Ltd. (supra) which he has discussed at length in the earlier part of the order and held that ratio of the said decision clearly applies in the instant case as there is no substantive difference in provisions relating to TDS and TCS. However, such direction was subject to verification by the Assessing Officer as to the filing of the return of income by the respective buyers and where it was found by the Assessing Officer that return of income has been filed, relief was directed to be allowed to the assessee and where such return of income has not been filed, no relief was directed to be allowed. Such direction by the Commissioner (Appeals) is well within his powers and jurisdiction under section 250(1) and doesn't result in setting aside the matter to the file of the Assessing Officer for making a fresh assessment and adjudication afresh. In the result, the ground of appeal so taken by the Revenue is dismissed. [Para 63]

The Revenue has challenged the findings of the Commissioner (Appeals) where he had held that there is no material difference in the provisions of tax deduction at source (TDS) under Chapter-XVIIB and tax collection at Source (TCS) under Chapter-XVIIBB of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and the facts and the judgment held in assessment proceedings under section 201(1)/201(1A) for default in the case of Hindustan Coca Cola Beverage (P.) Ltd. (supra) are squarely applicable in the case of the assessee for assessment proceedings under section 206C(6)/206C(7) for TCS defaults. [Para 64]

]

FACT: One MA opened a bank account in the name of some persons induding entity, BK in Indian Bank, and presented some import documents to the Branch Manager, requesting him to transfer foreign exchange to certain entities abroad. The Branch Manager sent said import documents to the Principal Commissioner of Customs for verification. The Principal Commissioner of Customs verified those import documents, including the documents of BK and found that most of them were forged ones immediately, the Principal Commissioner of Customs informed the Enforcement Directorate about this transaction. The Enforcement Directorate initiated investigation and found that BK was started in the name of one K, and, current accounts were opened in the name of BK in seven banks, but, in all the applications submitted to the bank, the photograph of K was not affixed. After completion of investigation against BK a complaint was filed under PMLA with allegation to the effect that these persons have opened fictitious bank accounts, submitted forged bills of entry, parked huge amounts in those bank accounts and had them transferred to various parties abroad through the bank, in order to make it a licit transaction for the alleged purpose of import.

During investigation, the Enforcement Directorate stumbled upon some Form 15CB that were issued by petitioner auditor. During interrogation, petitioner revealed facts that one of his clients KM had approached him for issuance of Form 15CB under rule 37-BB of the Income-tax Rules, 1962, and submitted documents in support of his request; accordingly, petitioner perused those documents and issued certificates to the effect that it is not necessary to issue Form 15CB in respect of overseas payment of imports. The five numbers of Form 15CB relating to BK were also uploaded in the website portal of Income-tax Department and were presented to the Branch Manager, State Bank of Travancore, for transferring a sum to various entities in Honk Kong. After completing this part of the investigation, the ED filed a supplementary complaint under PMLA by virtue of which, petitioner KM and AH were arrayed.

In instant petition, the petitioner-auditor had requested for quashing of prosecution.

HELD: As regards the requirements for submission of Form 15CB, it is found from the records that only the State Bank of Travancore had insisted upon the said certificates and not the other six banks through which, foreign remittances were made by KM and AH. The complaint and the accompanying background show that AH had operated the bank accounts and KM had facilitated the opening of the bank account and preparation of various documents by availing the services of various persons including petitioner - auditor, for the limited purpose of obtaining Form 15CB for transferring monies from State Bank of Travancore. A reading of the impugned complaint, shows that petitioner had issued five numbers of Form 15CB in favour of entity BK, which were handed over by him to his client KM for which, a sum of Rs. 1,000 per certificate was given to him as remuneration. [Para 10]

Even on a demurrer, on a perusal of Form 15CB, it is found that a CA is required to only examine the nature of the remittance and nothing more. The Chartered Accountant is not required to go into the genuineness or otherwise of the documents submitted by his clients. This could be compared with the legal opinion that are normally given by panel lawyers of banks, after scrutinizing title documents without going into their genuinity. A Panel Advocate, who has no means to go into the genuinity of title deeds and who gives an opinion based on such title deeds, cannot be prosecuted along with the principal offender. Applying the same anomaly, the prosecution of petitioner, in the facts and circumstances of the case at hand, cannot be sustained. [Para 11]

In the result, this Criminal Revision is allowed and the order passed on the file of XII Additional Special Court for CBI cases at Chennai, is set aside and the petitioner is discharged from the prosecution. [Para 12]

Section 65(35) of the Finance Act, 1994 - Custom house agent - Period 2000-04 - Whether activities relating to freight forwarding cannot be brought under category of services of ‘Customs house agents’ (CHA) - Held, yes - Whether activity of CHA relates only to entry or departure of conveyances or import or export of goods at any customs station and, therefore, activities of CHA are limited to customs station and they cannot extend beyond it; and where assessee collected air freight for export from consignee, activity being related to transportation service rendered by airline company, such freight forwarding could not be said to be a part of activities of CHA - Held, yes - Whether where, from nature of various charges collected by assessee, it was found that those were not includible in computation of service tax towards CHA services; however, Commissioner held that those charges were related to CHA services though he himself had repeatedly pointed out that assessee had not produced a chartered accountant’s certificate with regard to deductions claimed by it, matter was to be remanded to original authority for re-adjudication - Held, yes [Para 6]

Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm's length price (Comparables and adjustments/Adjustments - General) - Assessment year 2002-03 - During relevant year assessee paid legal and professional charges to its AE - In transfer pricing proceedings, TPO held that assessee had not furnished any details to establish that services were infact rendered and, further, there was no material to establish that AE was involved in any manner in obtaining export orders for assessee - TPO thus disallowed payments made to AE - Tribunal, however, found that services rendered by AE were supported by an invoice - Further, Tribunal accepted assessee's contention that it was able to achieve export turnover of Rs. 29 crores which demonstrated prima facie that services were infact rendered by AE - Tribunal thus deleted disallowance made by TPO - High Court by impugned order held that since view taken by Tribunal was a possible view, it did not require any interference - Whether Special Leave Petition filed against impugned order was to be granted - Held, yes [Paras 24 and 25] [In favour of revenue]IT/ILT : SLP granted against High Court's ruling that where services rendered were supported by invoices and assessee had achieved huge export turnover which demonstrated prima facie that services were infact rendered by AE in obtaining exports order for assessee, TPO was not justified in determining value of said services at nil

Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Comparables and adjustments/Adjustments - Allocation of expenses) - Assessment years 2012-13 and 2013-14 - Assessee had paid cost allocation charges pertaining to intra group services received from its AEs - During assessment proceedings, based on request of TPO details about nature of services provided by AE, cost allocation methodology adopted as well as evidence of receipt of services by assessee were submitted to TPO - However, TPO rejected ALP of cost allocated to assessee by stating that assessee failed to produce supporting documents/evidence to substantiate that services were rendered by AE and charge reflected value/benefit of service received - Further, TPO applied CUP method to benchmark said transaction and made additions - However, it was found that necessary evidence had been brought on record by assessee which had not been examined by authorities - It was found assessee's allocation of expenses was based upon a global agreement between AEs in this regard - Various allocation keys, i.e., asset, revenue, number of employee, depending upon nature had been used and methodology adopted had mandate of guiding of OECD - Further, allocation was supported by a CPA certificate which had been duly authenticated - Whether thus, action of authorities below in rejecting CPA certificate was not sustainable and accordingly order of authorities was to be set aside - Held, yes [Paras 27 to 29] [In favour of assessee]IT/ILT: Where TPO rejected ALP of cost allocated to assessee and made additions by stating that assessee failed to produce supporting documents/evidence to substantiate that services were rendered by AE, however, it was found that assessee's allocation of expenses was based upon a global agreement between AEs and was supported by CPA certificate, additions so made were to be set aside

I. Section 9, read with sections 40(a)(i) and 195, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and article 12 of India-USA DTAA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalty/FTS - Certification charges) - Assessment years 2005-06 and 2008-09 - During year, assessee-company made payment to an organization, namely, IFANCA for obtaining certification of product exported by assessee to USA as 'halal' so as to enable said product access to Islamic market in USA - Revenue was of view that services rendered by said organization to assessee qualified as 'included services' as it involved making available technical know-how to assessee and, thus, same was taxable in terms of article 12(4) of DTAA with USA and TDS was to be deducted on same - It was noted that procedure which IFANCA followed for halal certification did not mention what technical know-how was made available to assessee - In fact entire procedure adopted by IFANCA ensured that proper sanitation and cleanliness procedures were followed by assessee while manufacturing its product and product was not contaminated so as to qualify as halal - Whether, on facts, such payment made by assessee for halal certification did not qualify as 'included services' in terms of article 12(4) of India-USA DTAA and, thus, no TDS was to be deducted on such payment - Held, yes - Whether accordingly, impugned disallowance of certificate charges paid by assessee under section 40(a)(i) for non-deduction of TDS was unwarranted - Held, yes [Paras 17 and 18] [In favour of assessee]INTERNATIONAL TAXATION : Where assessee made payment to an organization of USA for obtaining certification of product exported by it to USA as 'halal' so as to enable access of said product to Islamic market in USA, since said certification ensured that proper sanitation procedures were followed by assessee while manufacturing its product and product was not contaminated so as to qualify as halal, such payment of certification charges did not qualify as 'included services' in terms of article 12(4) of India-USA DTAA and did not qualify for withholding of tax   INCOME TAX : Where a reopening notice was issued upon assessee on ground that no TDS was deducted on payment made by it towards legal and professional charges and carriage outward expenses, thus, same was to be disallowed, since said issue was not discussed during original assessment and no opinion was formed on it, validity of reassessment could not be challenged on account of change of opinion and thus, impugned reopening was justified

Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm's length price (Comparables and adjustments/Adjustments - Professional charges) - Assessment year 2002-03 - During relevant year assessee paid legal and professional charges to its AE - In transfer pricing proceedings, TPO held that assessee had not furnished any details to establish that services were infact rendered and, further, there was no material to establish that AE was involved in any manner in obtaining export orders for assessee - TPO thus disallowed payments made to AE - Tribunal, however, found that services rendered by AE were supported by an invoice - Further, Tribunal accepted assessee's contention that it was able to achieve export turnover of Rs. 29 crores which demonstrated prima facie that services were infact rendered by AE - Tribunal thus deleted disallowance made by TPO - Whether since view taken by Tribunal was a possible view, it did not require any interference - Held, yes [Paras 24 and 25] [In favour of assessee]IT/ILT : Where assessee-company paid legal and professional charges to its AE, in view of fact that services rendered were supported by invoices and, moreover, assessee had achieved huge export turnover which demonstrated prima facie that services were infact rendered by AE, TPO was not justified in determining value of said services at nil

Section 65 of the Finance Act, 1994 - Chartered Accountant - Assessees-Chartered Accountants, were awarded contract by MESCOM for purpose of sending ordinary clerks for recording electricity meter reading and ledger maintenance work relating to billing activities on behalf of MESCOM - Original authority demanded service tax from assessees under category of ‘Practising Chartered Accountant’ for above activities - Assessee’s case was that part of contract entered into by MESCOM was not activity of ‘practising chartered accountants’ as present activity was done by non-professional chartered accountants; it was merely clerical work of non-professional employees who were employed on contract basis; and they were covered under various Labour Legislations such as Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition Act, 1970) and Minimum Wages Act - Whether in view of decision of Tribunal in Jaded Siddappa & Co. v. CCE [Final Order Nos. 1146 to 1148 of 2007, dated 26-9-2007] activity of outsourcing of meter reading, billing and ledger maintenance did not come within ambit of professional activity of chartered accountant and, therefore, demand raised was to be set aside - Held, yes [Para 9]

III. Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Adjustments - Benefit from transaction/Allowability of expenditure) - Assessment year 2005-06 - Whether where a sum was claimed to be paid by assessee-company for internal audit services received from its Associated Enterprise and assessee-company submitted that it did not have any internal audit department and, hence, internal audit services were required to be availed in order to have an internal audit system commensurate with its size and nature of business and even benefits received from such internal audit services were explained by assessee, authorities below were not justified in making addition on ground that no tangible benefit was derived by assessee - Held, yes [Para 31] [In favour of assessee]

Section 65 of the Finance Act, 1994 - Chartered Accountant - Assessee, a Chartered Accountant, was carrying on billing of electricity and other related work for ‘M’ - Whether activities carried out by assessee could not be considered to be associated with Chartered Accountant’s service and, therefore, assessee was entitled to waiver of requirement of pre-deposit of service tax demanded under category of ‘Practising Chartered Accountant’ - Held, yes [Para 2]

Section 11B of the Central Excise Act, 1944 - Claim for refund of duty - Period May, 2004 to September, 2004 - Under a contract, assessee was providing survey and mapping services to ‘G’ - It paid service tax in category of ‘Consulting engineer’s services’ - Subsequently, it filed refund claim on ground that said services were not covered under service tax net during relevant period - Though revenue did not dispute about admissibility of refund claim on merits, but rejected said claim on ground that as per contract with its clients, consideration received by assessee was inclusive of all taxes, duties, etc. and, hence, claim was hit by unjust enrichment - Assessee contended that service tax was not recovered from its clients and produced a Chartered Accountant’s certificate in support of said contention - It was found that said certificate was only to effect that in invoices raised, assessee had not charged service tax separately; there was nothing in said certificate to show or establish that such tax paid by assessee had not been collected by it from its clients - Whether in view of this, there was no infirmity in rejection of refund claim - Held, yes [Para 5]

II. Section  92C  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Transfer pricing  -  Computation of arm’s length price  (Comparables - Functional Similarity-Information Technology Enabled Services (ITES)) - Assessment year  2020-21  - Whether a company engaged in accounting, auditing and bookkeeping services could not be considered as a valid comparable for assessee rendering routine ITES/DCM services - Held, yes - Whether further lack of reliable segmental information to carve out margins relating to comparable services would further disqualify said company from being considered as valid comparable - Held, yes [Para 36.1] [In favour of assessee]

Section 92CA of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Reference to TPO - Assessment year 2007-08 - Where payment made by assessee to its AE for services rendered was basically an expenditure incurred for purpose of business, same was to be determined under section 37(1) by Assessing Officer; such payment could not be determined by TPO [In favour of assessee]

Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Methods for determination of - Cost plus method) - Assessment year 2011-12 - During assessment proceedings, Assessing Officer found that assessee entered into international transactions with its AEs worth Rs. 12.54 lakhs - Assessing Officer directed assessee to furnish details of transactions and method adopted for determining Arm's Length Price (ALP) - Assessee stated that it had applied Cost Plus Method (CPM) for determining ALP on basis of agreement entered into with AE.s and basis is adapted as per agreement was mark-up of 23.45 per cent on salary and rent expenses incurred by assessee - Assessing Officer directed assessee to explain as to why mark-up should not be applied to entire cost incurred since assessee was rendering exclusive services to AE.s - On reply, however, Assessing Officer opined that assessee did not file an explanation with regard to proposed mark-up adjustment - Considering available material, Assessing Officer held that assessee had not submitted any documentary evidence like transfer of shares, appointment of new directors to substantiate its claim and certificate of chartered accountant of foreign entity was without any authority - One of directors in company was existing director and shareholder in assessee company is on close of balance sheet date i.e. 31-3-2011 and audit report was filed almost after one and half year from date of entry of shareholders/directors of foreign entities and there was no reason as to why assessee had not disclosed such vital facts of time of filing audit report - Thus, Assessing Officer rejected claim of assessee and held that two entities were AE's of assessee and transactions entered by it with them were squarely covered under definition of IT within meaning of provisions of section 92 - As regards proposed adjustment and working of CPM, Assessing Officer held that assessee had not submitted any explanation as to why other than salary and rent had not been included in invoices raised and mark-up had been charged thereon and assessee was into service sectors and was providing software related services to AE's involving lead restrictive utilities and method followed by assessee was not in accordance with provisions of Act, and entire cost was required to be taken into consideration for applying mark-up under CPM - Since, assessee had failed to do so total amount of expenditure debited to profit  loss account had to be considered as qualifying amount for mark-up on invoices to be raised on AE's as per method applied by it, Assessing Officer made an upward adjustment to total income of assessee under section 92C(4) - On appeal, after considering submission of assessee and assessment order, FAA held that assessee had argued that Star and DTL were not its AE's and it had merely submitted a copy of certificate issued by chartered accountant of AE and certificate was not supported by any documentary evidence like transfer of shares hence, argument was not acceptable - Further FAA held that assessee had not filed an explanation with regard to mark-up rate of 23.45 per cent for expenses other than salary and rent and assessee had not produced any documentary evidence with regard to annual reports of other companies for verification and it had not filed any TP study report during assessment proceedings for appellate proceedings and it had not followed provisions of section 92, thus, assessee had not discharged its primary onus of benchmarking transaction and upheld order of Assessing Officer - Whether since assessee did not file any confirmation or certificate from auditors about incorrectness of audit report especially about existence of AE's therefore, order of FAA does not suffer from any legal infirmity - Held, yes - Whether since assessee had included only two of items of profit and loss account i.e. salary and rent, and had not included other charges for determining ALP then mark-up determined as 23.45 per cent needs further verification on part of Assessing Officer and if assessee had not incurred any expenditure for alleged three items same should not be considered for mark-up purposes - Held, yes [Para 5] [Partly in favour of assessee]

Section 73 of the Finance Act, 1994 - Recovery of service tax not levied or paid or short-levied or short-paid or erroneously refunded - Assessee was registered under category of ‘Security Agency’ and had been paying service tax - However, department proceeded to work out short-levy of service tax in terms of returns filed by assessee with income-tax department - Assessee submitted that amount shown in income-tax return had not been received and same was still due - But as it did not produce chartered accountant’s certificate in support of its plea, Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed demand - However, before Tribunal, assessee produced chartered accountant’s certificate in support of its plea - It also pleaded issue of time bar, which had not been considered by adjudicating authority - Whether, on facts, order of Commissioner (Appeals) was to be set aside and matter was to be remanded to original authority for de novo consideration - Held, yes [Para 3]

Section 65 of the Finance Act, 1994 - Practising chartered accountants - Whether billing activity carried out by ordinary clerks who have not even completed SSLC is not part of chartered accountants’ activity - Held, yes

I. Section 9, read with sections 40(a)(i) and 195, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and article 12 of India-USA DTAA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalty/FTS - Certification charges) - Assessment years 2005-06 and 2008-09 - During year, assessee-company made payment to an organization, namely, IFANCA for obtaining certification of product exported by assessee to USA as 'halal' so as to enable said product access to Islamic market in USA - Revenue was of view that services rendered by said organization to assessee qualified as 'included services' as it involved making available technical know-how to assessee and, thus, same was taxable in terms of article 12(4) of DTAA with USA and TDS was to be deducted on same - It was noted that procedure which IFANCA followed for halal certification did not mention what technical know-how was made available to assessee - In fact entire procedure adopted by IFANCA ensured that proper sanitation and cleanliness procedures were followed by assessee while manufacturing its product and product was not contaminated so as to qualify as halal - Whether, on facts, such payment made by assessee for halal certification did not qualify as 'included services' in terms of article 12(4) of India-USA DTAA and, thus, no TDS was to be deducted on such payment - Held, yes - Whether accordingly, impugned disallowance of certificate charges paid by assessee under section 40(a)(i) for non-deduction of TDS was unwarranted - Held, yes [Paras 17 and 18] [In favour of assessee]  II. Section 40(a)(ia), read with section 148, of the Income-Tax Act, 1961 - Business disallowance - Interest, etc., paid to a resident without deduction of tax at source (Reassessment) - Assessment years 2005-06 and 2008-09 - Regular assessment in case of assessee was framed under section 143(3) - Thereafter, Assessing Officer issued a reopening notice on ground that assessee had not deducted TDS on legal and professional charges and carriage outward expenses paid by it - He further made disallowance on account of these payments - It was noted that Commissioner (Appeals) found that this issue pertaining to disallowance was not discussed during original assessment order and no opinion was formed on it, thus, reopening was to be upheld - Whether since assessee was unable to controvert findings of Commissioner (Appeals) that this issue was not discussed during original assessment, validity of reassessment framed under section 147 could not be challenged on account of change of opinion and impugned reopening was unjustified- Held, yes [Para 10] [In favour of revenue]

II. Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm's length price (Adjustments - Reimbursement of expenses) - Assessment year 2008-09 - Assessee had claimed deduction for payments made by assessee to its AEs contending same to be reimbursement of out of pocket expenses incurred by AEs on behalf of assessee - Since assessee could only furnish bills for part of amount, TPO determined ALP of balance out of pocket expenses to be 'Nil' and proposed transfer pricing adjustment - Whether since auditors in audit report had certified financial statements to be true after carrying out verification on test check basis and TPO had not pointed out any discrepancy in supporting documents furnished by assessee which constituted 78 per cent of expenses reimbursed by assessee to its AE, no adjustment on account of such expenses would be permitted - Held, yes [Para 18] [In favour of assessee]

Section 11B of the Central Excise Act, 1944 - Claim for refund of duty - Assessee, a receiver of services of goods transport agencies, discharged service tax liability - However, it having noticed that it had paid service tax in excess without claiming any abatement as per Notification No. 1/2006-ST, dated 1-3-2006, filed refund claim by furnishing Chartered Accountant’s certificate certifying that incidence of tax had not been passed on to customers -Revenue, however, rejected refund claim - Whether in view of Chartered Accountant’s certificate, assessee was entitled to refund - Held, yes [Para 7]
Section 65(83) of the Finance Act, 1994 - Practising Chartered accountants service

I. Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm's length price (Adjustments - Reimbursement of expenses) - Assessment year 2011-12 - Assessee-company had claimed deduction for payments made by it to its AEs contending same to be reimbursement of out of pocket expenses incurred by AEs on behalf of assessee and submitted third-party invoices for part of expenses - TPO proposed transfer pricing adjustment by taking ALP of out-of-pocket expenses as 'Nil' - Auditors in audit report had certified financial statements to be true and correct after carrying out verification on test check basis and TPO had not pointed out any defect/discrepancy in bills/supporting documents furnished by assessee which constituted 78 per cent of out of pocket expenses reimbursed by it to its AE - Whether TPO was not justified in making additions - Held, yes [Para 11] [In favour of assessee]TRANSFER PRICING : No transfer pricing addition should be made in relation to reimbursement of out-of-pocket expenses to AE, where auditors in audit report had certified financial statements to be true and correct after carrying out verification on test check basis and TPO had not pointed out any defect/discrepancy in bills/supporting documents furnished by assessee which constituted 78 per cent of out of pocket expenses reimbursed by assessee to its AE  TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee had made payment to it's AE claiming same to be reimbursement of software maintenance expenses incurred by AE in form of connectivity charges which were in addition to Software Maintenance Expenses and project closure report of AEs and monthly intra-group account statements showed that same were being reimbursed at cost, TPO was not justified in making addition for reimbursement of software maintenance expenses and IT connectivity charges

Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and article 13 of India-UK DTAA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties/Fees for technical services - Make available) - Assessment years 2018-19 and 2019-20 - Assessee, a UK based company, entered into intragroup agreement with its Indian AE and provided services pertaining to human resources, finance, legal and compliance and conducting of internal audit assurance work - Assessee received certain amount with respect to said services which was not offered to tax while filing return - Assessing Officer held that such receipts were for services in nature of FTS under article 13 and would be taxable in India - It was noted from service agreement that services rendered by assessee were in nature of advisory services and assessee's role was to assist AEs in making correct decision on aspects specifically referred to in agreement - Whether since such rendition of services did not result in transfer of technical knowledge, know-how, skill etc. to Indian AE, 'make available' condition provided under article 13(4)(c) remained non-compliant and thus, receipts would not fall within definition of FTS as provided under article 13(4) of India - UK DTAA - Held, yes [Para 12] [In favour of assessee]INTERNATIONAL TAXATION : Where assessee, a UK based company, received certain sum for providing services to its Indian AE pertaining to human resources, finance, legal and compliance and conducting of internal audit assurance work, since said services were merely for enabling and assisting Indian AE in making correct decisions on certain aspects and did not result in transfer of technical knowledge, know-how, skill etc., 'make available' condition provided under article 13(4)(c) remained non-compliant and, thus, receipts would not fall within definition of FTS as provided under article 13(4) of India - UK DTAA

Section 65 of the Finance Act, 1994 - Consulting Engineer - Period April 2000 to June 2003 - Assessee claimed that test inspection and certification done by it was not consulting engineer’s service and it was not taxable service prior to 1-7-2003 - However, agreement with some heavy industrial companies showed that assessee’s mechanical engineers had to inspect customers’ machines and to certify those as fit for use - In case, machinery required modification of design or other changes, engineers would render requisite advice - Whether prima facie nature of service rendered by assessees looked like consulting engineer’s service - Held, yes - Whether further since assessee could not show that copies of agreements together with relevant invoices had been produced before departmental authorities, assessee could not said to have been able to establish that there was no suppression on its part and plea of limitation could not be held genuine - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, stay on requirement of pre-deposit could not be granted - Held, yes [Paras 2 & 3]

Section 92CA, read with section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Reference to TPO (Section 37(1) v. section 92CA) - Whether jurisdiction of Assessing Officer under section 37 and TPO under section 92CA is distinct and, therefore, a referral made by Assessing Officer to TPO for limited purpose of determining ALP does not take away power of Assessing Officer to determine as to whether payment made by assessee to its AE for services rendered was basically an expenditure incurred for purpose of business so as to allow same under section 37(1) - Held, yes [In favour of revenue]IT/ILT : Jurisdiction of Assessing Officer under section 37(1) and TPO under section 92CA is distinct and, therefore, a referral made by Assessing Officer to TPO for limited purpose of determining ALP does not take away power of Assessing Officer to determine as to whether payment made by assessee to its AE for services rendered was basically an expenditure incurred for purpose of business so as to allow same under section 37(1)  IT/ILT : Authority of TPO is to conduct a transfer pricing analysis to determine ALP and not to determine whether there is a service or not from which assessee benefits; therefore, TPO cannot determine ALP of payments made by assessee to its AE at nil taking a view that assessee did not derive any benefit from services rendered by AE

Section 271B of the Income-tax Act
Where assessee had accepted that books of account were handed over to his auditor in July 1992 for tax audit and this fact had also been accepted by auditor, but subsequently audit reports signed by some other Chartered Accountants were filed along with income-tax returns on 29-11-1992, it could be taken as proved that books of account were not at all audited and in such a case of levy of penalty on assessee would be justified
C. Ramaswamy v. ITO [1999] 63 TTJ (Mad.) 647
Where the assessee had accepted that the books of account were handed over to his auditor in July 1992 for tax audit and this fact had also been accepted by the auditor, but subsequently the audit reports signed by some other Chartered Accountants were filed along with the income-tax returns on 29-12-1992, it could be taken as proved that books of account were not at all audited and in such a case of levy of penalty on the assessee was justified.

Section 9  of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 13 of the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement between India and United Kingdom (FTS) - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India - Assessment years 2010-11 and 2014-15 - Whether where assessee a UK based company rendered inspection and testing services to Indian customers in respect of imported/exported cargo and certifying in relation to quality and price, without making available any technical knowledge, experience, skill, know-how or processes to recipient of service so as to enable recipients to use those services independently, payment made for services in question could not be termed as 'fee for technical services' - Held, yes [Para 6][In favour of assessee]IT/ILT: Where inspection and testing services rendered by assessee a UK based company to Indian customers but no technical knowledge, etc. were made available so as to enable recipients to use those services independently, payments received could not be termed as 'fee for technical services'

Held, that when a chartered accountant prepares a profit and loss account from the books of account and signs a certificate to that effect, the minimum that he is expected to do is to verify the accuracy of the figures in the profit and loss account with reference to the relevant books of account. He cannot escape responsibility pleading that he did not audit it and that verification of accounts was done by the staff As part of his professional duty and responsibility, he was required to take reasonable steps to satisfy himself that the work was carried out in a proper, fair and efficient manner. Failure to carry out such elementary verification amounted to gross negligence and carelessness. Skill, care and caution, which a reasonably competent and cautious auditor was expected to exercise, was not done. The Council was justified in its conclusion that the respondent was guilty of professional misconduct within the meaning of section 21 read with section 22 and clause 7 of Part I of the Second Schedule to the Act. Penalty of reprimand, as recommended by the Council, was adequate and proper.

Section 65 (31) of the Finance Act, 1994 - Consulting engineer - Period prior to 1-7-2003 - Revenue on finding that assessee was providing technical inspection and certification service during relevant period, confirmed demand under category of ‘Consulting engineer’ - Commissioner (Appeals) held that prior to 1-7-2003 assessee was not held to be providing any technical inspection and certification service as same came under scope of service tax only with effect from 1-7-2003 - Whether there was no infirmity in impugned order of Commissioner (Appeals) - Held, yes [Para 4]

Section 92CA of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Reference to TPO (General principles) - Whether authority of TPO is to conduct a transfer pricing analysis to determine ALP and not to determine whether there is a service or not from which assessee benefits - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, TPO cannot determine ALP of payments made by assessee to its AE at nil taking a view that assessee did not derive any benefit from services rendered by AE - Held, yes [Para 34] [Matter remanded]

Section  92C,  read with section  92CA,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Transfer Pricing  -  Computation of Arm’s length price  (Adjustments - Segmentation) - Assessment year  2018-19  - Assessee, engaged in testing, inspection and certification (TIC) services to third-party customers in India and to AEs, also provided ITES support and shared services to AEs - For transfer pricing, it prepared segmental accounts showing AE margins of about 15% in ITES, shared services and certification segments, a 4% margin in non-AE certification services, an overall margin of about 6%, and ITES revenue of about Rs. 4.53 crores out of total revenue of about Rs. 124.81 crores (non-AE certification about Rs. 97.40 crores; AE certification about Rs. 15.09 crores; shared services about Rs. 7.79 crores) - In its TPSR, it benchmarked ITES transactions of about Rs. 4.5 crores under TNMM using OP/OC with a margin of 15% - On reference, TPO grouped TIC, shared services and ITES together as ITES, rejected assessee's segmental results stating that HR, finance, operations, legal and admin costs were not allocated to AEs, computed a consolidated margin of 4.44%, rejected TPSR and proposed a TP adjustment of about Rs. 26.18 crores - Whether since for earlier AYs TIC and ITES services were benchmarked separately, as TIC services and ITES services did not share same FAR, and TP Order did not explain why TIC and ITES services were being grouped together, combining TIC and ITES services for benchmarking was not justified - Held, yes [Para 24] [In favour of assessee]

Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Reference to TPO - Assessment year 2011-12 - Whether when Assessing Officer makes reference to TPO for determining ALP of international transaction of services availed by assessee from its AE, job of TPO is to consider actual transaction of rendition of service and find out its ALP, however, TPO has no jurisdiction to examine whether service was needed or is duplicate in nature or stewardship or shareholder service because such an exercise falls in exclusive domain of Assessing Officer, thus, if undertaken by TPO, it would thwart determination of ALP - Held, yes [Para 26] [In favour of assessee]

I. Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Comparables - Functional similarity - Business support services) - Assessment year 2010-11 - Assessee was engaged in provision of business support services to its AE - Whether a company engaged in provision of highly technical consultancy services in nature of project report preparation, technical and economic studies, feasibility studies, micro enterprise development, skill development, project management consulting, industrial cluster development, environmental management consulting, energy management consulting, market and social research and asset reconstruction management services would not be comparable to assessee - Held, yes [Paras 1.5 and 1.6] [In favour of assessee]TRANSFER PRICING : Company engaged in provision of highly technical consultancy services would not be comparable to company engaged in provision of business support services to its AE  TRANSFER PRICING : Company engaged in providing support services for execution of various projects and, thus, primarily engaged in back-office support services would be functionally similar to assessee engaged in provision of business support services to its AE  TRANSFER PRICING : Payroll processing support services are comparable to activities in nature of processing of accounting data for AEs  TRANSFER PRICING : Company engaged in provision of business support services to its AE would be comparable to company engaged in services of valuation of assets of third parties and assisting in their disposal by way of auction  TRANSFER PRICING : Company engaged in rendering services, namely, registrar and transfer agent activity, records management activity and payroll  trust fund activity, which had majority of income from registry and share transfer business would not be comparable to company engaged in provision of business support services to its AE

II. Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Comparables and adjustments - Professional services) - Assessment year 2008-09 - In transfer pricing proceedings, TPO took a view that ALP of professional fee paid by assessee was to be taken at nil as assessee failed to furnish evidence showing that services were actually rendered - Accordingly certain adjustment was made to assessee's ALP - In appellate proceedings, assessee brought on record an agreement entered into with AE in terms of which CEO of said AE himself provided consultancy/managerial service - Assessee also produced invoice raised by AE for said fee and tax paid thereon - Whether in view of above, impugned adjustment was to be set aside - Held, yes [Para 10][In favour of assessee]

Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Comparables, functional similarity - Consultancy service providers) - Assessment year 2014-15 - Whether where assessee was captive service provider rendering routine marketing support services to AE, a company engaged in providing consulting and liasioning services relating to foreign trade, customs, excise, GST etc., to independent clients/agencies could not be accepted as comparable - Held, yes [Para 6] [In favour of assessee]TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee was rendering marketing support services to AE, a company engaged in providing consulting and liasioning services relating to foreign trade, customs, excise, GST etc., could not be accepted as comparable

Limitation - Section 11-A - price approved by the Assistant Collector on the basis of Chartered Accountant's certificate given without verifying the books - suppression established proviso to section 11-A rightly invoked

Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Comparables and adjustments/Comparables - Illustrations) - Assessment year 2011-12 - Whether in case of assessee rendering marketing support services to AE, a company engaged in procurement related advisory services and financial audit for projects in India and abroad, could not be accepted as comparable - Held, yes [Para 30] [In favour of assessee]

IX. Section  92C , read with sections  92  and  92CA , of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section 165, read with sections 161 and 166 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 – Transfer Pricing - Computation of Arm’s length price (TP Adjustments -  Illustrations  - Support Services Fee) - Assessee paid its US AE for marketing, regulatory liaison and customer support services, reimbursed on cost plus 20 per cent basis, and benchmarked transactions under entity-level TNMM showing higher margins than comparables - TPO held entity-level TNMM inappropriate, proposed to treat AE as tested party, questioned necessity/benefit and documentation, and determined ALP of service charge/markup at Nil - CIT(A) recorded that assessee had substantial US exports and multiple ANDA filings, that services were actually rendered and costs were certified by an independent CPA, and that TPO had not brought comparables or disproved rendition; disallowance of mark-up was deleted - Whether ALP cannot be determined at Nil in absence of contrary evidence; services accepted and TNMM sustained; adjustment deleted - Held, yes [Paras 19.21 to 19.28] [In favour of assessee]

III Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Comparables, functional similarity - Consultancy service providers) - Assessment year 2011-12 - Whether where assessee was engaged in providing consultancy and advisory services including project construction and execution thereof in field of water management industry, a BPO company whose business products were payroll and employees trust fund administration and management, Registry and Transfer for shares, debentures and FD, category I registrar by SEBI, records management, transaction/ document processing for securitization, loans etc, could not be accepted as comparable - Held, yes [Para 36] [In favour of assessee]

VI. Section  92C  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Transfer Pricing  -  Computation of Arm’s length price  (Comparables - Factors to determine - Data in Public Domain) - Assessment year  2014-15  - Whether a company engaged in accounting, audit support, tax and consultancy services, being professional and consultancy-oriented in nature and lacking adequate public domain financial data, was functionally not comparable with assessee providing routine IT enabled services and, therefore, was to be excluded from final set of comparables - Held, yes [Para 64] [In favour of assessee]

facts.text:
The assessee was a practising chartered accountant. The revenue levied tax on certification service holding that it was an auditing service and, therefore, not entitled to exemption in terms of Notification No. 59/89-ST, dated 16-10-1998.

On appeal :

The assessee was operating as licenced registrar under the office of AQA, USA. As per the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between the parties, the assessee was to represent AQA for the purpose of assisting clients in achievement of ISO 9000, ISO 14000 and QS 9000 certificates. It used to receive Company Information Sheet (CIS) from prospective clients, review the CIS, prepare quotation and send same to prospective clients, provide information connected with Quality Management System (QMS) certification, conduct audit/assessment of the quality system at client’s place with reference to ISO standard and after successful completion of the assessment process, send such assessment to AQA, which issues above certificates. For doing the audit work, the assessee charged certain fee as audit fee from the prospective customers. The revenue treated the service of the assessee as that of ‘technical inspection and certification agency’ and demanded service tax. The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the demand.

On appeal :

The assessee company made payment to an organisation, namely, IFANCA for obtaining certification of product exported by it to USA as 'halal' so as to enable said product access to islamic market in USA. The Assessing Officer disallowed said payment towards certification fee for non-deduction of tax at source on same under section 40(a)(i).

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) went through the supervision procedure adopted by the IFANCA, and after going through the same he came to the conclusion that entire process of supervision and certification involved making available to the assessee specific methods to be adopted in the manufacturing process so as to ensure the products manufactured being halal, and therefore, it involved making available technical knowledge to the assessee so as to be treated as "included services" as per article 14(2) of the DTAA with USA for the purpose of holding taxes on the same.

On appeal :

The assessee dealing in LPG sent LPG through tank trucks to various LPG bottling plants of oil distribution companies.

Whenever LPG tank truck required any repair or mandatory testing of safety valves, the tank truck was cleaned and completely degassed. During this activity, water was filled in tank mounted on the truck and discharged. Water was displaced by LPG vapors. For this activity, the assessee collected cost of water and the labour charges from the truck owner.

The Adjudicating Authority held that the said activities undertaken by the assessee would fall under the category of 'technical inspection and certification service' and raised tax demand upon it.

The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the impugned order.

On second appeal:

The assessee, a company incorporated at Germany, had a branch in India. The Indian branch was engaged in the business of audit and procedure of norms for ISO 9000 certification. The services offered by Indian branch were ISO 9000 quality system certification where in quality system auditor of assessee company would visit the company opting for ISO certification, carry out a pre-assessment audit and then a certification audit and submit report to the assessee. After verification of report by the assessee, ISO 9000 certification was granted. The assessee treated its income as business income. The Assessing Officer opined that such services should be taxed as 'fees for technical services' under article 12 of Indo German DTAA. The assessee submitted that these services did not come under FTS within meaning of article 12 and, thus, it was business income which was to be computed in view of article 7(1) as business was carried out through PE. However, the Assessing Officer held that said services came within purview of FTS and, hence, provisions of section 44D had to be applied, and, accordingly, he assessed the income after applying tax rate of FTS; i.e., at rate 20 per cent of entire gross receipts. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the findings of Assessing Officer.

On appeal to the Tribunal:

The applicant, a tax resident of Hong Kong, belongs to X group of companies. The group entities are engaged in the business of inspection, verification, testing and certification (IVTC) services to various customers. The X trademark is owned by ABC (Parent Company), who had entered into a trademark license and Support Services Agreement (Support Services Agreement) with all its group entities, separately, including the applicant. The support service agreement is stated to bring uniform standards, procedures and policies described therein to IVTC services. It is stated that the inspection services are generally performed either at the load port or discharge port of a product or activity and are based on scientific and internationally accepted techniques and as per the clients' requirements. Verification services are used to evaluate whether the product services are system complaint with given regulation, specifications or condition. Testing services are used to determine the quality of the product or services as per the customer's requirements and are carried out in laboratories owned by respective X entities which are accredited to international bodies. Certification services refers to the confirmation of regulations, standards or contractual specifications of a product or organization or training. The applicant provided IVTC services to Indian Customers either directly or through X India. The applicant states that the IVTC Services are provided to the Indian Customer outside India if there is a direct arrangement between the customer and the applicant and the payment is made on the invoice raised by the applicant. But when the arrangement is not direct and is through the X India, then the invoice is raised either on X India or the Indian customer. Explaining it by an example, the applicant states that where a customer approaches X India to have its goods inspected in India and outside India, then X India sub-contracts the inspection to its applicant and the applicant raises invoice on X India for services provided by it and a consolidated invoice is raised on the customer. The applicant sought advance ruling on the question as to (i) whether the payments received/receivable the applicant in connection with transactions under taken/proposed to be undertaken in relation to the (a) inspection and verification services (b) testing/analysis services; and (c) certification services are chargeable to tax in India as 'fees for technical services' (FTS) under section 9(1)(vii)( b) and (ii ) whether payments received/receivable in connection with procurement of goods/services and reimbursement of other expenses proposed to be incurred for and on behalf of X India are chargeable to tax in India. The applicant also raised issue relation to withholding of taxes under section 195 and filing of return under section 139.

The respondent-Chartered Accountant had issued a tax audit certificate in favour of the assessee-concern under section 44AB of the Income-tax Act. The Commissioner of Income-tax, during the course of survey proceedings at the premises of the assessee, found certain discrepancy and recorded a statement of the respondent in which the respondent had accepted that he had issued a back-dated certificate showing the completion of audit of the assessee on behest of and to oblige his friend who was the tax consultant of the assessee. The Commissioner further averred that the respondent had prepared the tax audit report without examination and verification of the books of account. On complaint, the Disciplinary Committee of the petitioner-Council concluded that the respondent was guilty of both charges and was, thus, guilty of professional misconduct under sections 21 and 22. The petitioner-Council accepting the aforesaid conclusion recommended in terms of section 21(5) that the respondent be removed from the register of members for a period of six months.

On reference :

The assessee-firm was engaged in the business of import of rough diamond, cutting and polishing and sale thereof. It paid a certain sum to a Belgian company (HRD) towards grading and certification of diamonds.
