The assessee contended that the service of certification was carried out by HRD entirely outside India, i.e., in Belgium and the gradation certificate/report given by HRD was only an analysis of the quality of each piece of diamond and it did not constitute transfer of any technology, commercial interest, skill or technical knowledge in favour of the assessee and, therefore, such services could not be regarded as 'technical services'.

The Assessing Officer noted that HRD was having a specialized knowledge in diamond grading and certification, which was technical in nature, and therefore, he held that the impugned payment fell in the category of 'fees paid for technical services' and the assessee was liable to deduct tax at source therefrom.

The Commissioner (Appeals) noted that in providing grading or certification services of diamonds to the assessee, HRD had not parted with any technical knowledge or made available any technical expertise to the assessee so as to classify the impugned payment to HRD as 'fees for technical services' in view of MFN clause in India-Belgium DTAA. Accordingly, he deleted the disallowance made by the Assessing Officer by invoking section 40(a)(i).

On appeal:

A firm of chartered accountants under the CBDT Circular No. 759, dated 18-11-1997 issued a certificate certifying certain rates as the rates at which taxes were required to be deducted at source from the remittances made by the assessee-tax deductor. The assessee filed an appeal under section 248 before the Commissioner (Appeals) challenging the correctness of certificate. The Commissioner (Appeals) dismissed the assessee’s appeal on merit.

On second appeal :

Company ‘S’ had furnished to the Joint CCI & E a statement of export of leather goods including those of other manufacturers for the years 1976-77 and 1977-78, duly certified by the respondent - Chartered Ac-countant, and on that basis, the Export House Certificate was issued. The respondent had certified that he had checked and verified the particulars of export from the books/documents of the company and found them to be correct. On demand by the Jt. CCI & E, the company replied that it had not purchased any finished leather/leather goods from any other party and denied having exported finished goods manufactured by other units. The Jt. CCI & E made a complaint to the Institute that the respondent had issued the certificate without verifying the books of account inasmuch as he did not have any contact with that company. The respondent, in his reply, asserted his certificate to be correct and complete, based on the documents produced by the concerned parties. He further submitted that he was retained by the consultants of the company to verify the export statements from the records produced by it and he certified the facts accordingly. The Disciplinary Committee held that the then existing export policy required that 20 per cent of the total exports goods should be manufactured by others to get Export House benefits and since the only dispute was that the figures were not correct, the respondent was guilty of professional misconduct under section 21, read with section 22, and under clauses 5, 6 and 7 of the Part I of the Second Schedule. The Council, after considering representations, found him grossly negligent and thus guilty under clause 7 of Part I of the Second Schedule. It accordingly recommended that the respondent be reprimanded.

On a reference under section 21(5) :

■

The assessee, an Indian company, was engaged in the business of development of software product and providing IT Solutions. It had paid product certification expenses to non-resident entities from the USA, UK, Korea, and China.

■

The Assessing Officer disallowed said expenses on account of non-deduction of withholding tax under section 195 and non-genuineness of expenditure.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the disallowance made under section 40(a)(i) holding that providing certificates could not be compared to providing technical services as per section 9(1)(vii) and therefore the assessee was not in default.

■

On the revenue’s appeal to the Tribunal:

Pursuant to a search conducted in the assessee’s premises, it was found that the books of account and documents seized from the premises of the assessee did not give a true and correct picture of the assessee’s income. Therefore, a Chartered Accountant was appointed under section 142(2A) as a special auditor to examine the matters. The Chartered Accountant, after completing the exercise, submitted a bill of certain amount including service tax. The Commissioner, after careful consideration of all the relevant aspects and the work done by the auditors, reduced the amount by the impugned order under section 142 (2D).

On writs :

During the relevant previous year, ONGC had made payment of certain amount to non-resident assessee against tax protected contract. The assessee was required by the Assessing Officer to show cause as to why the revenues received by it may not be treated as fees for technical services. The assessee was engaged by ONGC for auditing/third-party certification of in-place and reserves of 56 fields of ONGC and additional 12 fields. The work was carried out by the assessee at its work place Dallas, USA. Also the assessee did not have any office in India. It was submitted by the assessee before the Assessing Officer that:-

-

It was the Indian Government's view that the fact that the provision of service may require technical input by the person providing the service does not, per se, mean thattechnical knowledge, skills etc. were made available to the person purchasing the service, within the meaning of paragraph 4(b) of India USA Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement.

-

In the course of rendering of services to the ONGC, the non-resident itself may have used its technical knowledge skills etc. However, since ONGC had not been enabled to apply the technology in future on its own without recourse to the non-resident and the knowledge required to carry out similar work had not been made available to the ONGC, the payments made by ONGC to the non-resident could not be taxed as 'Fees for Included Services' under India USA Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement.

-

The receipts for the services rendered by the non-resident were not chargeable to income tax in India.

However, the Assessing Officer was of the opinion that the scope of work mentioned in the contract made it clear that the assessee was not rendering any service relating to the construction, assembly, mining or like project as mentioned in the exclusion clause of Explanation 2 to section 9 (1) (vii). The Assessing Officer proceeded to hold that the assessee's activities were covered under 'Fees for Technical Services' and all the receipts emanating from the contract under consideration were to be taxed in India.

The appeal of assessee was dismissed by the Commissioner (Appeals) following the decision of Tribunal, Delhi Bench rendered in the case of CGG Veritas Services, SA. v. Addl. DIT, International Taxation in [2012] 50 SOT 335/18 taxmann.com 13

On assessee's appeal :

The assessee-company availed managerial services from AACL (an Israel company). Before making the payments to AACL, the assessee approached a firm of chartered accountants for certification under section 195 and the said firm confirmed that the assessee was not required to withhold any taxes. Yet, the assessee had made the payment of taxes, apparently as a measure of abundant caution, and proceeded to file an appeal before the Commissioner (Appeals).

The assessee sought declaration from the Commissioner (Appeals) under section 248 that no tax was deductible in respect of the payment made to AACL, Israel in respect of rendering of managerial services as the said managerial services did not make available technical knowledge, experience, skill, know-how or processes or consist of the development and the make available provisions, which find place in Indo Portuguese tax treaty, must be read into the Indo Israel tax treaty as well in the light of the MFN clause set out in the Indo-Israel tax treaty.

On appeal:

The appellant was sanctioned a refund by the adjudicating authority on basis of the factual situation prevailing and certificate given by the Chartered Accountant. However, the Commissioner reviewed the order of adjudicating authority and demanded the refund amount back on the ground that the certificate of the Chartered Accountant only stated that amount had been debited to expenses account in profit and loss statement. In appeal, the appellant contended that the amount had been paid as service tax which was not payable by the appellants and since they had not recovered the said amount from their customers. Therefore, the question of doctrine of unjust enrichment did not arise.

■

The assessee, a company based in UK, was engaged in the business of providing corporate and management services. The assessee entered into an agreement with its Indian AE, AIPL. As per the agreement, assessee provided management and governance support functions in the area of legal, tax, treasury, finance, information technology, human resources, enterprise risk management, etc

■

The assessee filed application under section 197 seeking 'Nil' withholding tax certificate. The assessee claimed that costs cross charges were reimbursement of costs on cost-to-cost basis and the same were not FTS within the meaning of section 9(1)(vii) of the Act or under Article 13 of the India-UK DTAA.

■

The Assessing Officer rejected said application on ground that the services rendered by the assessee were highly technical, managerial as well as consultancy in nature which required special skills and technical qualifications. He, thus, concluded that services rendered by the assessee to its AE were technical services and the charges paid were taxable as FTS.

■

The Assessing Officer further, held that the assessee centrally procured software/tools for joint use by its AE and thus, cross charges would be reimbursement of actual cost of such software/tools and would be taxed as royalty.

■

On writ :

OMIC, the parent body of the assessee-company had entered into a contract for cotecna inspection in respect of various countries. For the purpose of rendering services in India, the assessee was appointed by the OMIC. The assessee was required to make inspection and survey of cargo either exported from India or imported to India and certify in relation to quality, quantity and price of exported item. Further, the relevant tariff code of the commodity was to be certified for the purpose of ascertaining the correct import duty by the concerned authority of the importing countries to ensure that there was no excess foreign exchange payments being made at the time of import. The assessee was doing the job on behalf of OMIC and had been receiving payment in convertible foreign exchange. The assessee's claim for deduction under section 80-O was disallowed by the Assessing Officer by holding that services were being rendered in India. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the finding of the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal :

The assessee-company was an Indian company engaged in the business of project and construction management. It entered into a Management Service Agreement [MSA] with one of its group concerns, namely, ‘L’, a company based in Singapore. Under the said agreement ‘L’ agreed to provide services to the assessee-company in relation to day-to-day business operations consisting of administrative, legal, finance and accounting matters. In consideration of rendering of services, ‘L’ agreed to recover only the costs incurred by it for providing the above services to the assessee-company. According to the agreement, the cost recovery was based on the time spent in rendering of services to the assessee-company. The recovery did not include any profit mark up. The auditors report also certified that the amounts charged to the assessee-company did not include any profit mark up. An application was made under section 197(1) by ‘L’ for receiving the payments under the MSA without deduction of tax at source. A copy of the auditors report certifying that the payments under the MSA did not include any profit element was also enclosed along with the said application. The Assessing Officer, after considering the application issued certificate under section 197 to the assessee-company for making payments to ‘L’ without deduction of tax at source. The certificates issued under section 197 on various dates were neither revoked nor cancelled thereafter. Subsequently, notices were issued under section 201 by the Assessing Officer to show cause as to why the payer should not be treated as an assessee-in-default under section 201(1A) and also why interest should not be levied under section 201(1A). Detailed written submissions were made rebutting the Assessing Officer’s claim. Rejecting the submissions of the assessee-company, the Assessing Officer went ahead and passed the impugned orders, wherein it was held that the payments represented fees for technical services under the Act as well all the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement (Treaty) between India and Singapore and that the certificates issued were not in accordance with law. The Assessing Officer further held that since the payments made to ‘L’ represented Fees for Technical Services [FTS] the assessee was required to deduct tax at source under section 195(1). As the assessee failed to deduct tax, it was to be treated as an assessee-in-default in terms of provisions of section 201(1) and, therefore, it was liable to pay tax along with interest under section 201(1A). On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal:

■

The assessee was a company incorporated in the United States of America and was also a tax resident of that country. The assessee had entered into an agreement with its Associate Enterprises (AE) - AECOM India Private Limited (AIPL) and AECOM India Global Services Private Limited (AIGSPL). The assessee was engaged in the business of design and consultancy services, construction management and infrastructure development.

■

In terms of the agreements with the AEs, the assessee provided management and governance supports functions in the area of legal, tax, treasury, finance, information technology, human resources, enterprise risk management, etc. The assessee filed the application under section 197 seeking the ‘nil’ withholding tax certificate.

■

The assessee stated that costs cross charges were reimbursement of costs on cost-to-cost basis and contended the same were not chargeable to tax under the Act.The assessee also set out in detail its explanation as to why cost cross charged in terms of the aforesaid agreements were not fees for technical services (FTS) within the meaning of section 9(1)(vii) of the Act or ‘fees for included services’ (FIS) under Article 12(4) of the India USA Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement (India-US DTAA).

■

The Assessing Officer rejected the aforesaid application by the impugned order. The Assessing Officer noted the services rendered by the assessee as well as the submissions made by the assessee and observed 'services are highly technical, managerial as well as consultancy in nature which require special skills and technical qualifications'. The Assessing Officer also concluded that 'the services rendered by the assessee do make available knowledge, experience, know-how to the recipient and this is clearly visible when one examines the nature of the services rendered and the consequential benefits obtained by the recipient'.

■

On the aforesaid basis, the Assessing Officer concluded that the charges paid to the assessee by its AEs were taxable as FTS and FIS.

■

On writ:

The assessee-firm was carrying on profession of chartered accountancy. It had rendered computerized data processing for billing and accounts management service, under an agreement with APCPDCL. The revenue, by invoking the extended period of limitation, issued a show-cause notice to the assessee alleging that the services rendered by the assessee to APCPDCL would fall under the category of ‘Business auxiliary service’. The assessee replied that the service rendered by it was only information technology service which was outside the purview of ‘Business auxiliary service’ till 1-5-2006 and, therefore, it was not liable to pay tax during period of dispute; that activities of spot billing and account management would not fall under sub-clause (i) or (vii) or (iii ) or (vi) of the definition of ‘Business auxiliary service’; and that it was rendering service to APCPDCL and not on behalf of APCPDCL. The original authority confirmed the demand and imposed penalties under sections 75A, 76, 77 and 78. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the adjudication order on the grounds; that the service provided by the assessee was in the nature of service rendered in connection with promotion of business activities of APCPDCL, that computerized data processing to qualify the exemption under ‘Information technology service’ would have to be in relation to operation of computer systems and, therefore, spot billing could not be considered as a service rendered to APCPDCL but was a service rendered on behalf of APCPDCL; and that service rendered was not covered under ‘Business support services’ as it was covered under other general existing entries.

On appeal :

On application by the assessee under section 256(2), the High Court directed the Tribunal to send up reference to the High Court. On the question as to whether and if so how far a chartered accountant is entitled to bind his client by statements made in the course of assessment proceedings. The revenue brought to the notice of the High Court that no certificate as provided by the rule 191 had accompanied the application made under section 256(2).

The assessee-company was engaged in the business of arranging travel for domestic customers by facilitating services entailing booking of air tickets, accommodation, cab, conference rooms, catering services, management of corporate events, public relation services etc. It had entered into a master transition services agreement (TSA) with its AE and undertook various international transactions in respect of availing of transitional support services.

The TPO was of view that the assessee had not received benefits from said services and that only a facade was created to give an impression that some vital benefit had been passed on to the taxpayer, which was not the case in reality. Accordingly, he made TP adjustments on account of such service charges, taking it to be NIL by applying CUP as the most appropriate method.

The DRP noted the fact that the issue involved was squarely covered by the decision of the Tribunal in the assessee's own case. The Tribunal held that since documentary evidences in form of e-mails and invoices were vis-a-vis TSA Agreement clearly showed rendition of services by AE to assessee-company and TPO himself had accepted fees received by assessee from rendering these services no additions were to be made. He, accordingly directed the Assessing Officer to verify from the record if no appeal has been preferred by the department before the High Court against the order of the Tribunal for assessment year 2015-16, then no addition should be made.

On the assessee's appeal to the Tribunal :

■

The assessee-company made payments to a foreign company towards certification fees for products which was necessary to sell the products in USA and Canada market. The return was processed under section 143(1)(a) wherein CPC made prima facie adjustments making disallowance under section 40(a)(i) for non-deduction of tax on the payment.

■

The assessee's case was selected for scrutiny and the same was carried out under section 143(3) read with section 144B and in the course of scrutiny proceedings one of the issue raised in the show cause notice by the Assessing Officer was regarding the alleged addition made under section 40(a)(i). The Assessing Officer accepted the contention of the assessee and it was further stated that no disallowance was required under section 40(a)(i).

■

However, while computing the total taxable income the Assessing Officer inadvertently took income computed under section 143(1)(a) which inter alia included the disallowance under section 40(a)(i).

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) dismissed the ground for statistical purposes.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

The assessee was a firm of chartered accountants. The original authority confirmed demand of service tax on the assessee for the period 16-10-1998 to 31-7-2002 under the heads ‘Practising chartered accountant’, ‘Manpower recruitment service’, ‘Management consultant’ and ‘Business auxiliary service’. Modifying the findings of the original authority, the Commissioner (Appeals) found that the assessee was not liable to pay service tax under the head ‘Business auxiliary service’. He affirmed the demand on the assessee in respect of other categories of services. In the instant appeal, the assessee contended that it had rendered services as management consultant and man-power recruitment agent which were exempt in terms of Notification No. 59/1998-ST, dated 16-10-1998. The assessee also contended that Commissioner (Appeals) had wrongly held that the Notification No. 15/2002, dated 1-8-2002 which inserted an Explanation to Notification No. 59/1998-ST, dated 16-10-1998, had come into effect from 16-10-1998.

■

The assessee was a part of TDK EPCOS Group and primarily engaged in the manufacturing and sale of electronic components such as materialized plastic film capacitors and soft ferrite components. The assessee had aviled intra group services from its AE. During the year, the assessee had also filed an audit report in Form 3CEB for international transactions.

■

The case of the assessee was referred by the Assessing Officer to TPO for determination of transfer pricing adjustment in respect of intra group service by the AEs. The TPO passed an order under section 92CA(3) and determined the adjustment holding that the nature of services rendered by AE were in the nature of stewardship activity or shareholder activity and that no charges ought to have been paid by the assessee.

■

On appeal, the DRP after hearing the assessee passed an order under section 144C(5) restricting the adjustment.. Accordingly, the final order was passed by the Assessing Officer making the said addition.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

The respondent Chartered Accountant had certified an application of certain exporter in accordance with the requirements of Import and Export Policy certifying the FOB value of exports at Rs. 4,44,77,996. The figure was found to be wrong and on information in this regard being given to the Institute, the matter was referred to the Disciplinary Committee who found the respondent guilty of professional misconduct within the meaning of section 21, read with section 22, and clauses (6) and (7) of Second Schedule to the Act. When the matter came up before the Council, the benefit of doubt was given in respect of charge under clause (6) but in respect of the charge under clause (7) it was found that the respondent had not exercised due care and skill and, therefore, reprimand to him was recommended.

On reference under section 21(5) :

The Income-tax authority had engaged the petitioner Chartered Accountant's service to conduct special audit under section 142(2A). The petitioner completed the task and submitted its report above six years back and submitted the bills.

Despite of repeated reminders, the authority did not fix the remuneration and pay the fee.

The respondent submitted that petitioner's fee was fixed and cheque of Rs. 12,96,541 was made over.

The petitioner contended that fixation of fee was not as per norms prescribed by ICAI in term of section 142(2D) and that they were substantially underpaid.

The assessee had claimed deduction under section 80HHC. In order to claim this deduction, the provisions of section 80HHC required that a certificate be filed in Form 10CCAC which was to be issued by the chartered accountant certifying that the export had in fact been made. This certificate was given by the respondent as chartered accountant which was submitted before the Assessing Officer. The claim of the assessee was found to be false as against the alleged export the amount remained outstanding and was not realized. Though, as per the certificate given by the respondent, the amount had been realized. This would clearly show that certificate furnished by the respondent was wrong and bogus. An inquiry was held by the Council of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India on the allegations contained in a complaint submitted by the Commissioner. The Disciplinary Committee found that the allegations were substantiated and proved. After considering the report, the Council held the respondent guilty of professional misconduct falling within the meaning of clause (7) of Part-I of the second schedule under section 22, read with section 21 of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949. It accordingly recommended to this Court that the name of the respondent be removed from the register of members for a period of three years.

On reference :

■

The assessee, company incorporated in Singapore, provided credit rating and annual surveillance services to clients including Indian entities. It claimed that the receipts were not taxable in India as it had no PE in India and the services did not involve transfer of any technical knowledge or know-how.

■

The Assessing Officer held that the credit rating reports constituted commercial information and that the annual surveillance services were ancillary thereto, and accordingly treated the receipts as FTS taxable in India under section 9(1)(vii) of the Act and Article 12 of the India–Singapore DTAA.

■

The assessee filed objections before the DRP, which were rejected, and a final assessment order under section 143(3) read with section 144C(13) was passed assessing Rs. 73.22 crores to be taxed as FTS at 10 per cent.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal :

'N' Ltd., UK, was authorized to issue ISO certification. The assessee-company entered into MoU with 'N' Ltd. and was accredited to provide ISO certification to business and other organizations in India and abroad on behalf of 'N' Ltd. The assessee had to pay certain fees to 'N' Ltd. for that purpose. The assessee also paid some amounts to one 'P' for auditing services rendered by him in that matter. However, while remitting the payments, the assessee did not deduct tax at source since the recipients thereof were non-residents. The assessee claimed the aforesaid payments as deduction while computing its income. It was the case of the assessee that the payments in question were not chargeable to tax in India in the hands of the recipient because the same were 'taxable profits' within the meaning of the DTAA between UK and India; that, consequently, the same were taxable in UK only, and, thus, there was no violation of section 40(a)(i ). The Assessing Officer was of the view that since admittedly no tax had been deducted or paid in respect of the payments made outside India to non-residents, the claim for deduction of those payments as expenditure was to be disallowed in view of the provisions of section 40(a)( i).

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the payments in question were in the nature of royalty and fees for technical services rendered and taxable in India even as per the Indo-UK DTAA. Accordingly, the Commissioner (Appeals) affirmed the disallowance.

On appeal :

The respondent, a Chartered Accountant, was appointed as a Statutory Auditor of the company.

During the course of investigation, SEBI found that the respondent, as the statutory auditor of the company, had given a certificate dated 9-6-1995 certifying that the entire promoters contribution had been received by the company.

It was noticed by the SEBI that promoters contribution, only to the extent of Rs. 35 lakhs, was received by the company and not Rs. 225 lakhs as certified by the Auditor. The cheques issued against the balance amount had bounced. However, shares worth Rs. 225 lakhs were allotted to the promoters by the company.

SEBI concluded that the respondent/Auditors, without actually verifying the bank statements regarding realisation of the cheques, had given a false certificate regarding receipt of promoters contribution, in full, by Company. The respondent was held guilty of professional misconduct, and to have abetted the promoters in the fraudulent activity by issuing a false certificate, as he could have issued the certificate with the remark that subject to realisation of the Cheques deposited. Instead of doing so, the respondent had issued certificate as if the entire contribution of the promoters was received.

On receipt of the said letter from SEBI, the Institute addressed letter dated 28-07-2005 to the respondent alleging that the amount received towards contribution was only Rs. 35 lakhs, but the respondent had certified that Rs. 225 lakhs was received by the company towards promoters contribution, and the cheques issued against the balance amount had bounced. However, shares for Rs. 225 lakhs were allotted to the promoters by the company. The respondent was called upon to disclose the name(s) of the member (s), answerable to the charge of misconduct, as per Regulation 12(6) of the Chartered Accountants Regulations, 1988.

In response to the letter dated 28-07-2005 of the Institute, the respondent submitted his reply dated 05-08-2005 admitting that he, as the Proprietor of 'G' had issued the certificate dated 09-06-1995 stating that the promoters contribution of Rs. 225 lakhs was received as per the books of account maintained by the Company. The certificate was issued, after verifying the Share Application Account maintained in the General Ledger of the Company, the bank book showing receipt of the payments (in the form of cheques deposited) into State Bank of Mysore, and the bank deposit slip counterfoils duly bearing the bank acknowledgements of the cheques deposited. The certificate was issued, on the basis of the documentary evidence produced before him on the date of issue of the certificate, in the belief that the cheques deposited would not bounce, keeping in view the past track record of the promoters. The respondent, however, admitted that he should have issued the certificate with the remark subject to realisation of the cheques deposited, and stated that, while it was an omission on his part, it was not done with any mala fide intention, and he did not receive any financial benefit in this connection.

Being dissatisfied with the explanation submitted by the respondent, the Institute initiated disciplinary proceedings. The disciplinary committee framed charges and, after following the procedure prescribed under the Act and the Regulations, found the respondent guilty of misconduct under clause (7) of Part I of the Second Schedule read with sections 21 and 22.

Recommended that the Court impose the punishment of removal of his name from the Register of Members, for a period of 3 years, on the respondent.

On reference:

Assessee PWH was an independent firm of Chartered Accountants managed and controlled by its partners who were individuals and residents of India.

It had entered into an agreement with Price Water HouseCoopers International Limited (PwCIL) a company incorporated in the United Kingdom to become member of PwCIL. The member firms of PwCIL were collectively known as PwC Network.

PWH had become a member firm of PwC Network, at the same time it was a separate independent legal entity whose affairs were managed and controlled only by its partners.

Price Water HouseCoopers Services BV, Netherlands(Services BV) was the central services entity of the PwC Network and operated exclusively for mutual benefit of all PwC Network member firms. Neither PWH nor any of its partners was a shareholder of Services BV. Services BV had not conferred on PWH any right regarding use of any brand name as Services BV itself did not own any brand name.

During relevant year PwC received a non-refundable loan to strengthen PWH's audit practices in India. Such loan was received under contractual arrangement existing between Services BV and PWH and PWH had shown it as business income in its return.

On scrutiny assessment, the Assistant Commissioner of Income-tax (R-3) issued notice requiring PWH to file its computation of income and tax for year, audit profit and loss account and balance sheet, tax and audit report issued under section 44AB. PWH filed all the necessary documents

Thereafter R-3 issued a letter to PWH informing it that a reference had been made to the TPO and called upon PWH to file details requested for in earlier notices.

PWH contended that TPO regulations did not apply to PWH as it did not have a relationship of being AE with any overseas network entity. It further contended that it had never entered into any international transaction envisaged under section 92B, and hence, it was unable to comprehend the reasons for which reference had been made under section 92CA(1) to the TPO. Further the fact that the transactions between PWH and Services BV were not international transactions had been accepted in the previous assessment year and hence there was no justification for R-3 to take a different view on same set of facts and law.

The assessee was engaged in testing and inspection of materials, machinery, designs, etc., under agreement with its clients. It was registered under the ‘Technical inspection and certification service’ since 1-7-2003. The revenue found that the assessee rendered service of consulting engineer and not of ‘Technical inspection and certification service’ and, accordingly, demanded service tax in category of ‘consulting engineer’ during the period April, 2000 to June, 2003. The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld that order.

On appeal :

The assessee was engaged in providing taxable service under the category of ‘Technical inspection and certification service’ and was also liable to pay service tax on goods transport service received by it. It availed benefit of abatement under Notification No. 32/2004-ST, dated 3-12-2004 with respect to goods transport service received. The revenue issued show-cause notice to the assessee denying benefit of said notification on ground that in view of relevant Boards’ circular in the consignment notes issued to the assessee by goods transport agencies, there was no declaration to the effect that no credit on input or capital goods used for providing services had been taken nor the benefit of Notification No. 12/2003-ST, dated 20-6-2003 was availed. However, the Commissioner taking into consideration the Chartered Accountant’s certificate to the effect that the transporters had neither availed CENVAT credit nor the benefit of Notification No. 12/2003-ST, dated 20-6-2003, dropped the demand against the assessee.

On appeals :

The assessee undertook to do job work on the materials sent by the Space Research Stations. The adjudicating authority levied service tax on it on the ground that it was rendering technical inspection and certification services. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the assessee was not rendering any technical inspection and certification service and, therefore, it was not liable to pay service tax.

On appeal :

Facts

Assessee was a Government of India Undertaking under the Ministry of Defence and was engaged in shipbuilding, ship repair and engineering for the Indian Navy & Coast Guard.

They placed a purchase Order on M/s. Maritime, Netherlands for the Model Testing of 90M OPV. The activities covered were preparation of ship model including all appendages as per the technical data and design provided by assessee and verification of the correctness of technical data.

The above referred service was to be received by assessee in Netherlands. No part of the service was performed by M/s. Maritime, Netherlands in India.

The Department demanded service tax under reverse charge relying on section 66A and classified under Consulting Engineer service and not under 'technical testing and analysis service' or 'technical inspection and certification service'.

Assessee's Arguments

Since the said service was wholly received in Netherlands they were not liable to service tax under the reverse mechanism.

Consulting Engineer : Service received was not covered under the category of 'consulting engineer'. The word 'technical assistance' is preceded by the words 'advice and consultancy', the term should be read ejusdem generic with the preceding word viz 'advice' and 'consultancy'. Both 'advice' and 'consultancy' does not involve any physical work. Hence, 'technical assistance' could not include any physical work such as repair/maintenance/servicing etc. Therefore, physical work such as development of the model could not be covered. Further, service provider Maritime Research Institute, Netherlands, was a non-profit institute and did not come within the definition of 'consulting engineer'.

Technical testing & analysis service : Service received by the assessee can be classified under the category of 'technical testing & analysis service'. No specified qualification has been prescribed for technical testing and analysis agency. Such agency may or may not be approved under any statutory provisions for rendering the said service. Service of 'Technical testing and analysis service' are covered under clause (ii) of Rule 3 of the Taxation of Services (Provided from Outside India and Received in India) Rules, 2006. As per clause (ii) of Rule 3 of the Taxation of Services (Provided from Outside India and Received in India) Rules, 2006 at the relevant time the service to be taxable under this category must be performed in India. Since no part of service was performed in India, it was not liable to tax.

Technical inspection & certification services : Service received by the assessee can, alternatively, be classified under the category of 'technical inspection & certification services'. The word 'process' in definition of said service simply means the activities performed for the purpose of achieving the desired objectives. Therefore, under the said definition all types of examination or inspection will be covered. No particular form of certification has been stated. Therefore certification in any form will be covered under the definition. It may further be noted that the taxability of certification under this category is not restricted to advice, consultancy or technical assistance but includes any work done in connection with the inspection or examination of the items specified therein. Manufacture of the vessel is a complex and costly affair and service provider gives certification as regards to the standard of the developed model. In view of the above, service is to be classified under the category of 'Technical inspection and certification service'. Since the said service is covered under clause (ii) of Rule 3 of the Taxation of Services (Provided from Outside India and Received in India) Rules, 2006, the service to be taxable under this category must be performed in India. Since no part of it was performed in India, no service tax could be charged.

Limitation & Penalty : The audit was conducted and all details were supplied to Department in February and March, 2008. Since all the facts were to the knowledge of the department, issuance of notice on 31-3-2011 was barred by limitation as there was no suppression. Even otherwise, merely wrong claim of classification by itself does not amount to suppression or mis-declaration. Even mere non-declaration is not sufficient to invoke larger period but some positive act is required. Further, assessee was Government of India Undertaking under the Ministry of Defense, and it is inconceivable that they would try to evade tax. Further, payment under reverse charge would have neutral effect, as tax paid would be eligible as credit. The entire demand is barred by limitation. Similarly, penalty was not leviable.

Calculation incorrect : Value of services should be = Value of Purchase Contract (net of discount) - Cost of manufactured goods (net of discount).

Revenue's Arguments

The assessee was engaged in providing services to promote, coordinate, guide, implement and maintain an accreditation system for laboratories, suitable for the country in accordance with the relevant national and international standard and guides and also to ensure that all measurements either during calibration or testing by accredited laboratories were related to appropriate national/international standards. It appeared to the department that these services were covered under 'Technical inspection and certification services' and were being provided to commercial and other laboratories on commercial terms without charging and paying service tax on the services rendered under section 65(105)( zzi). The Commissioner, accordingly, confirmed service tax demand on the assessee under category of 'Technical inspection and certification service', along with interest and penalty. In the instant application, the assessee contended that the Commissioner had wrongly invoked the extended period when no evidence was available to the effect that it had wilfully suppressed the facts by not filing the returns with intent to evade tax. The assessee further submitted that the show-cause notice which was answerable to the Commissioner had been issued by Additional Director General of Central Excise Intelligence. The Commissioner had failed to appreciate that law does not envisage that one authority would initiate the proceedings and other would pass the adjudication order.

The assessee, a UK based company, entered into intragroup services agreement with the Indian AE. According to the agreement assessee provided services pertaining to human resources, finance, legal and compliance and conducting of internal audit assurance work. The cost incurred for performing said services was allocated to the group companies on the basis of time spent, activity level or head count and cost incurred was cross charged to the group companies on cost plus 5 per cent basis. The assessee filed return of income for relevant assessment years.

The Assessing Officer opined that services provided by the assessee were in nature of technical or consultancy services. He, thus, held that receipts for said services would be in nature of FTS under article 13 of India-UK DTAA and brought receipts to tax at rate of 10 per cent.

The DRP upheld the order of the Assessing Officer.

On appeal to the Tribunal.

The assessee, engaged in the business of project and construction management, entered into an agreement with a Singapore Company, under which the Singapore Company was to provide certain services to the assessee in relation to day-to-day business operations consisting of administrative, legal finance and accounting matters. In consideration of rendering of services, the Singapore Company agreed to receive the costs incurred by it. The cost recovery, according to the agreement, was based on the time spent for rendering the services. The Chartered Accountant's report certified that the amounts charged to the assessee did not include any profit margin.

An application under section 197(1) was made by the Singapore Company for receiving the payments under the agreements without deduction of tax at source. The assessee was authorized to make payments to the Singapore Company without deduction of tax at source. Notices were issued to show-cause as to why the payer should not be regarded as an assessee-in-default under section 201(1). Detailed submissions were made in response to this notice. Rejecting the submissions of the assessee-company, the Assessing Officer passed orders under section 201 wherein it was held that the payment represented fees for technical services under section 9(1)(vii) as well as the DTAA between India and Singapore. It was held that the certificates issued permitting payments without deduction of tax at source were not in accordance with law.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the action of the Assessing Officer. On further appeal, the Tribunal allowed the appeal of the company. It was concluded that the assessee cannot be treated as an assessee-in-default under section 201(1) and no interest is leviable under section 201(1A).

On rectification petition :

The assessee, a charitable trust, was granted exemption from levy of tax under section 11 up to the assessment year 1983-84. For the assessment year 1984-85, however, the IAC denied exemption under section 11 on the ground that while the accounts of the assessee were audited by a firm of chartered accountants, namely, L, the certificate required under clause (b) of section 12A was given by another firm of chartered accountants, namely, K, which did not satisfy the requirements of section 12A(b). on appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the disallowance of exemption claimed and added that the assessee in obtaining the prescribed particulars from an accountant who had not audited the accounts failed to satisfy the requirements of section 12A.

On second appeal:

■

The assessee–company, incorporated in Singapore and engaged in the practice of law, provided legal services including advisory services in relation to mergers, acquisitions, restructuring, financing, taxation and allied matters to its client Barclays Bank Plc, U.K., in relation to client of Barclays bank (REC Ltd). The assessee filed a return declaring nil income. The invoice for these services was raised on Barclays, with payment arranged by REC Ltd., and the assessee asserted there was no contractual relationship with REC Ltd.

■

During reassessment, the AO proposed taxability under section 9(1), including section 9(1)(vii), and Article 12(4)(b) of the India–Singapore DTAA; the assessee contended the services were rendered from Singapore to Barclays and not taxable in India. The Assessing Officer held that technical knowledge, experience and skill were made available through the legal advice and treated the receipts as Fees for Technical Services; a draft order proposed an addition of about Rs. 1.01 crores.

■

The DRP, after considering the assessee’s submissions, upheld the AO’s action.

■

On the assessee’s appeal to the Tribunal.

Facts

The assessees had provided chartered accountant's services prior to 1-4-2012 and raised the bills therefor prior to that date, levying service tax at the rate of 10 per cent.

Up to 1-4-2012, Chartered Accountants services were governed by rule 7 of the Point of Taxation Rules, 2011 wherein point of taxation was determined based on date of receipt of payment.

With effect from 1-4-2012, rate of service tax was increased to 12 per cent and services of chartered accountants were excluded from Rule 7 ibid.

Circular No. 158/9/2012-ST dated 8-05-2012 and Circular No.154/5/2012-ST dated 28-03-2012 had provided that since, prior to 1-4-2012, services of Chartered Accountants were covered by rule 7 of the Point of Taxation Rules, 2011, hence, point of taxation of services provided prior to that date will continue to be governed by said Rule 7, as it stood before that date. Accordingly, in case of services provided and invoices raised before 1-4-2012, the point of taxation would be date of payment and if payment was received on or after 1-4-2012, revised rate of service tax viz. 12 per cent would apply.

The assessees argued that point of taxation, in their case, was determinable as per Rule 4 of the Point of Taxation Rules, 2011.

Therefore, the assessees challenged the said circulars as ultra vires the Constitution and the provisions of the Finance Act, 1994 and rules.

Issue Involved

Whether Circular was ultra vires the Act ?

The assessee, a public sector undertaking, was engaged in the business of refining of crude oil and marketing of petroleum products. During the previous year, the assessee had engaged one ‘P’ of Singapore for carrying out market study for updating its assessment of the out look for domestic refining capacity throughout India. The assessee applied for issue of no-objection certificate (NOC) for making the payment to ‘P’ based on the proposal agreed upon by the assessee. In the application for NOC, the assessee contended that the scope of services rendered by ‘P’ fell outside the ambit of article 12 of the DTAA between India and Singapore. The Assessing Officer passed an order under section 195 authorising the assessee to make the payment to ‘P’ after deduction of income-tax at source. The Assessing Officer treated the amount payable for the services rendered by ‘P’ as fees for technical service. The assessee, therefore, made the payment to ‘P’ after deducting tax at source and deposited the TDS with the department.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the impugned order. He held that the consultancy fees paid by the assessee to ‘P’ was chargeable to tax in India as per the provision of article 12.

On second appeal :

For the assessment year in question, the assessee claimed deduction under section 80-I in respect of a sheller as supported by the requisite certificate of the chartered accountants. The Assessing Officer found that the sheller was installed in the accounting year 1983-84 and the first year of the business was shown as 1985-86 and the assessee having already availed of deduction for eight years it was not eligible for deduction under section 80-I for the assessment year in question. The Assessing Officer, therefore, referred the matter to the assessee’s chartered accountant who apparently sent a letter stating that they were neither competent to certify nor had certified that the assessee was eligible for deduction under section 80-I. In view of the said submissions of the chartered accountants, the Assessing Officer disallowed the claim for deduction and also imposed penalty on the assessee under section 271(1)(c) for furnishing inaccurate particulars of the income. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) dismissed the same. On further appeal, the Tribunal accepted the assessee’s contention that it had claimed the deduction in a bona fide manner on the basis of the certificate issued by the chartered accountant and, therefore, cancelled the penalty.

On appeal :

■

During the year under consideration, the assessee incurred expenses towards customisation existing systems to comply with the GST regulations implemented in India. The assessee recharged the said costs to its Indian AE and the same was reimbursed.

■

The Assessing Officer treated the said customisation receipts as FTS. The DRP held that these receipts are not independent service and very much part of BSS, thereby, holding that these services being akin to / part of BSS fall within purview of make available and is taxable as FTS.

■

On appeal to Tribunal:

uploading the final typesetting.

• Once assessee was given format and specification and also technical instructions, it was possible for the assessee to use such technical knowledge for its other assignments also, giving an enduring benefit to it.

• The advisory services also involved special technical knowledge and hence, it was nothing but technical service.

• The inspection, testing and certification services are in the nature of technical services.

• Further, there was no requirement for a business connection or territorial nexus to levy tax.

Issues involved • Whether the US company, which incidentally was a subsidiary of the assessee, was rendering any technical services, which warranted a deduction of tax at source, in accordance with section 195?

■

The assessee— a management consultancy company focused on Human Resource Management services—filed its return under section 139(1) declaring income of about Rs. 2.56 crores for AY 2022-23. The case was selected for scrutiny under CASS due to large value of international transactions and low profitability risk parameters. The assessee entered into international transactions with AEs in Hong Kong and Japan; its entire revenue was from export of services to AEs. For benchmarking, it adopted TNMM as the most appropriate method and operated on a cost-plus model with about 5% markup as per the service agreement, supporting this with a FAR-based set of comparables.

■

A reference under section 92CA(1) was made. The TPO rejected the assessee’s comparables, selected a fresh set of comparables, noted the assessee’s OP/OC at about 3.51% as below the stipulated 5% markup under the agreement, held the assessee’s benchmarking unreliable, and proposed a TP adjustment of about Rs. 6.99 crores under section 92CA(3). Consequent draft assessment under section 143(3) read with section 144C(1) proposed to assess total income at about Rs. 9.56 crores.

■

On objections, the DRP confirmed the TPO’s action, treated the services under the broader head of management consultancy, accepted the TPO’s comparables, held that the service agreement primarily governed pricing and did not materially affect comparability, and rejected objections on export filter, turnover disparity and functional dissimilarity. The AO thereafter passed the final assessment under section 143(3) read with section 144C(13) in line with the DRP’s directions.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal.

An agreement was entered into between an Indian company and the assessee, a non-resident company, whereunder the assessee agreed to render technical assistance and consultancy services to the Indian company in erecting its plant and in putting it on stream. The agreement provided, inter alia, (i) that the assessee would train Indian personnel abroad, (ii) that during the construction of the plant, the assessee would render consultancy services relating to the problems of construction, etc., by deputing a group of designing experts to India, (iii) that the consultancy activity would consist of granting of expert technical advice, opinions, and/or recommendations in basic technical matters by the assessee's experts to the corresponding experts of the Indian company, and (iv) that the total fee for the consulting activities of the assessee for the designing works and for introducing production would be a specified amount worked out on the basis of man-months calculated in direct proportion to the number and duration of stay in India of the assessee's specialists. The assessee claimed that the consultancy fees paid by the Indian company to it was not on account of any activity carried on by it in India but on account of something done by it in the foreign territory itself and, therefore, the said amount was not taxable. The ITO rejected the assessee's claim and held that part of the total turnover of the Indian company should be treated as income arising on account of the assessee's activity in India. On appeal, the Tribunal held that the consultancy fees paid to the assessee must be held to have arisen on account of its activity carried on in India, but observed that what part of it should be attributed to the consultancy service in India and what part to its activity/if any, carried on in the foreign country would have to be determined. Accordingly, it remitted the matter to the ITO with a direction to recompute the profit attributable to the consultancy service in India in accordance with the law and on the basis of a certificate to be produced by the assessee from a qualified chartered accountant in the foreign country.

On reference :

The applicant is a tax resident of Australia. It provides accreditation to CABs (Conformity Assessment Bodies) in several countries including India. It accredits organizations which provide third party certification and/or inspection services. Its main function is to accredit, following the successful assessment, those bodies which are considered competent and impartial to provide an effective service in various spheres. The accreditation vouchsafes the independence of a CAB in performing the certification and such accreditation further assists the CAB in the fields of certification and inspection. Post accreditation, regular surveillance visits are carried out by the applicant’s auditors to ensure that CAB maintains and operates its procedures in accordance with the requirements of the accreditation criteria. In consideration of the accreditation work done by the applicant, it receives fees from CABs in the form of application fee, programme fee, certification fees and fee for conducting surveillance audit, witnessing audit and reassessment visits. On these facts, the applicant has sought advance ruling, inter alia, on the questions whether consideration received by it from an Indian CAB would fall within ambit of ‘royalties’ as defined under article 12 of the DTAA; and whether the visits of the personnel of the applicant for conducting the on-site assessment and witness audit constitutes/deems existence of applicant’s permanent establishment (‘PE’) in India in accordance with the provisions of article 5 of the DTAA.

The certification relating to computation of income from international transactions is in accordance with the provisions of section 92E of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and rule 10E of Income-tax Rules. [Para 2]

The certification follows transfer pricing audit. Therefore, the certification in question would clearly fall under ‘Audit/certification services’ even as per the clarification, dated 7-10-1998, issued by the Ministry of Finance. The verification of the books of account precedes issue of a certificate and such verification will fall within the scope of ‘Accounting & auditing’ function. Therefore, it could not be said that what the assessee was rendering was not ‘auditing service’ liable to service tax. Accordingly, the impugned order was to be upheld and the appeal was to be rejected. [Para 3]

S. Ramachandran for the Appellant. Ms. Indira Sisupal for the Respondent.

Management consultant’s service was a taxable service under section 65(48) during the relevant time and, therefore, the appellants were entitled to exemption under Notification No. 2/99-ST. As regards non-repatriation of foreign exchange, chartered accountant’s certificate had since been produced before the Tribunal, and since the same was not available before the adjudicating authority, the matter was to be remanded back to the adjudicating authority to look into the chartered accountant’s certificate and if nothing contrary was found the exemption should be extended to them. [Para 6(3)]

It could be noticed from the certificate of the chartered accountant that the chartered accountant before issuing certificate had verified the entire books of account and had come to a categorical conclusion that neither the assessee had passed on burden of service tax to the customers nor had it recovered the amount from the transporters. The certificate also categorically stated that the assessee had borne the incidence of service tax. The Commissioner (Appeals) after checking the records was satisfied with the evidences produced before him as regards the non-passing of the incidence of service tax by the assessee to its customers. The revenue in its appeal had not produced any contrary evidence to the said findings nor there was any challenge to the chartered accountants Certificate. [Para 2]

Accordingly, in the facts and circumstances of the case, the impugned order was correct and legal and did not require any interference. The appeal filed by the revenue was to be dismissed. [Para 3]

The Chartered Accountant’s Certificate was a detailed certificate which had been considered in depth by the adjudicating authority. The appellant was engaged in the manufacture and selling of casting on specific rate of contract. The amount of service tax paid by the appellant was on the goods transport operator. That had not vitiated the contract price in any way. Further, the certificate issued by the professional, generally should not be challenged without having contradictory certificate from another professional. The Commissioner in his order had not relied on any contradictory certificate of another professional. In the absence of which, it was to be held that the appellant had made out a prima facie case for waiver of pre-deposit of amount of service tax. [Para 5]

K.K. Banerjee for the Appellant. A. Hore for the Respondent.

Entry 54. The Act requires that the dealer has to maintain books and the books have to be audited and required to be certified by a Chartered Accountant. That will not result in the legislation falling outside the competence of the State Legislature. The Legislation in pith and substance is relatable to imposition of sales tax which is within the competence of the State Legislature. The Courts examine and ascertain the pith and substance on scrutiny of the true character of the enactment. [Para 24] It also cannot be said that in such a case audit by a Chartered Accountant would amount to outsourcing the statutory power to the third party. The Legislature can always delegate its powers as long as such delegation does not amount to abdication of its essential legislative functions. In the instant case, there is no abdication of the essential legislative functions. All that the section requires is that the accountant has to audit the accounts and to issue certificate that the dealer has maintained the books as required to be maintained under the Act and rules. The dealer has to file his accounts audited with the certificate. This neither amounts to abdication nor excessive delegation. Such an exercise also does not amount to conferring on the accountant a power to determine the correct tax liability of the dealer. The power to accept returns is of the Authorities under the Act. Even after the certificate is issued, that the dealer has maintained books, it is always open to the Commissioner under section 20 to ascertain whether the return is correct and complete or order an audit under section 22 to get the accounts audited by the officers of the department. A certificate, therefore, is not determinative but to enable the department to consider that the person having knowledge of audit and subject to the disciplinary control of its parent body has certified that the accounts are properly maintained. This is to aid the officers in discharging their statutory duties. This challenge, therefore, has to be rejected. [Para 25]

Further, it is for the dealer to decide whose services he seeks to obtain for appearance before the Sales Tax Authorities or for getting the accounts audited. Under section 82, there are a class of persons from whom a dealer can obtain services for being represented before the authorities under the Act. Under section 61, he is bound to select one of the class of accountants also. This is for a category of dealers whose turnover is more than 40 lakhs. The amount of fee which has to be paid is the amount to be decided between the dealer and that person, whom he selects from amongst the accountants that are available. This cannot be said to amount of compulsory levy amounting to tax. That being the case, the challenge under article 265 must also fail.

Similarly, the question of article 301 being attracted, does not arise. The challenge on that count also has to be rejected as the right claimed by the petitioners or their members or by the dealer is that Advocate and Sales Tax Practitioner cannot carry out audit in terms of section 61 in the State of Maharashtra. The enactment is pursuant to the power of the State Legislature to make law within its competence. This does not attract article 301. [Para 27]
