Section 72A of Finance Act, 1994 (as inserted w.e.f. 28-5-2012) make provision for special audit by practicing Chartered/Cost Accountant [earlier, section 14AA of Central Excise Act was made applicable to service tax. This section provided only for special audit of Cenvat credit availed].

Special audit can be ordered by Principal Commissioner/Commissioner of Central Excise [Reference to 'Principal Commissioner' has been added w.e.f. 6-8-2014].

Such audit can be ordered if the Principal Commissioner/Commissioner of CE has reason to believe that any person liable to pay service tax—

(i)

has failed to declare or determine the value of a taxable service correctly; or

(ii)

has availed and utilised credit of duty or tax paid - (a) which is not within the normal limits having regard to the nature of taxable service provided, the extent of capital goods used or the type of inputs or input services used, or any other relevant factors as he may deem appropriate; or (b) by means of fraud, collusion, or any wilful misstatement or suppression of facts; or

(iii)

has operations spread out in multiple locations and it is not possible or practicable to obtain a true and complete picture of his accounts from the registered premises falling under the jurisdiction of the Principal Commissioner/Commissioner [section 72A(1) of Finance Act, 1994].

In such cases, the Principal Commissioner/Commissioner may direct such person to get his accounts audited by a chartered accountant or cost accountant nominated by him, to the extent and for the period as may be specified by the Principal Commissioner/Commissioner [section 72A(2) of Finance Act, 1994, inserted w.e.f. 28-5-2012] [Reference to 'Principal Commissioner' has been added w.e.f. 6-8-2014].

The provisions of special audit apply even if audit was conducted under some other law [section 72A(3) of Finance Act, 1994]

The auditee (person liable to pay service tax) shall be given opportunity of hearing in respect of any material gathered on the basis of such special audit and proposed to be utilised in any proceedings against him [section 72A(4) of Finance Act, 1994 inserted w.e.f. 28-5-2012]

Section 14AA of Central Excise Act provides that the audit fees will be paid by Central Government (i.e. service tax department). However, section 72A of Finance Act, 1994 makes no provision of fees of the Chartered/Cost Accountant for such audit.

As per rule 5A(2) of Service Tax Rules (as amended w.e.f. 5-12-2014), assessee is required to produce records maintained by him to cost/chartered accountant nominated under section 72A of Finance Act, 1994.

The idea behind the requirement of a report in the prescribed forms by a qualified chartered accountant is that before a claim is considered, a professional accountant should have checked up the assessee’s accounts and should have satisfied himself that the assessee is maintaining the accounts in such a way that the claim is borne out by the books. That is why this requirement has been dispensed with in the case of the assessees who have to get their accounts statutorily audited. When an assessee who is not statutorily required to get the accounts audited, nevertheless does it, then the assessee is at par with a limited company or a cooperative society. The responsibility of a chartered accountant is the same, whether the accounts should be statutorily audited or not. Therefore, in the instant case, in substance there had been compliance with the requirements of the rules, Thus, the certificate required is only to ensure that the assessee’s accounts are checked by a third party who is professionally qualified for that purpose. When that condition, in substance, has been satisfied, there is no reason why a certificate which is procured validly, though not submitted with the return, should not be accepted. The ITO was, therefore, directed to allow the assessee to produce the certificate before him while giving effect to the order under section 263, and to dispose of the case according to law. There was, however, no question of the assessee being denied the deduction merely on the ground that such certificate was not filed along with the return.

up the work of audit which is in the form of normal audit as also assessment in the same manner as required by the chartered accountant. By denying to the advocates and sales tax practitioners, the right to certify under section 61, it has violated their right to carry on profession.

(g)The mandatory provision of engaging services of chartered accountants is not based on any object of the Act and as such the provision is not within the legislative competence of the respondent State as an ancillary provision. (h)The State Legislature by the impugned provisions has outsourced its statutory powers to assess the tax to a third party. Such delegation of powers is destructive of basic tenet of law and its enforcement. The action is inconsistent with any principles of good governance of any State law. It is also opposed to any procedural law of administration of State Law and is, therefore, impermissible.

(i)The industries also have to engage sales tax practitioners or advocates for their sales tax returns and day-to-day guidance. The audit charges to be paid to CA are perceptively heavy. The industry will have to pay heavy burden by way of audit fees. This is a direct impediment to trade and cuts into their net profit. This additional compliance cost in terms of money and waste of time, is an added impediment. This additional payment to the CA would in pith and substance amount to compulsory levy amounting to tax by the State in contravention of article 265 of the Constitution.

(j)The provisions for punishment to a dealer for not engaging chartered accountants are highly penal and without any cap. The impugned provision does not serve any purpose of revenue under the Maharashtra VAT Act. The provisions are, therefore, unreasonable and a restraint on freedom of trade.

The position of advocates

4. Section 29 of the Advocates Act, 1961 provides that advocates would be the only class of persons to ‘practise the profession of law.’ Section 33 of the Advocates Act bars any other professional to practice in any Court or before any authority, etc. Section 49 of the Advocates Act gives general powers to the Bar Council of India to make such rules. Under this power, the Bar Council of India has framed the rules which prohibit an advocate from engaging in any other profession other than practising the profession of law. The requirement of section 61 is of auditing of the books of account and giving a certificate of his conclusion after verification. This cannot be called as ‘practise the profession of law’. The area under section 61 is practising in the field of accountancy and auditing, which an advocate is not competent to undertake under the Rules framed by the Bar Council of India under section 49 of the Advocates Act. The Parliament of the country has framed the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949. Under section 2(2), the area in which a member of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI) can practice is defined. The practice of accountancy and auditing can be carried out by the chartered accountants who are members of ICAI and are holding a certificate of practice. If the advocates embark on practice in the area of accountancy and auditing work, then it would amount to practise in accounting and auditing and, thus, will violate the provisions of the Advocates Act and, the rules framed thereunder by the Bar Council of India. Therefore, the advocates cannot be allowed to carry out the function of an accountant or of an auditor.

Sales tax practitioners

5. The sales tax practitioners are not governed by any professional Act. Any graduate having acquired a Diploma in Taxation or having passed specified accountancy examination and acquired such qualifications as are prescribed by the Central Board of Revenue or having retired as an officer from the Sales Tax Department can enroll with the Sales Tax Department as a sales tax practitioner. He is not required to be a qualified auditor nor is he governed by the strict discipline and acceptability required under the Chartered Accountants Act, for any acts of omission and commission in the conduct of audit. Hence, a sales tax practitioner cannot be expected to provide the level of assurance and creditability of the audit of the accounts of a VAT payer expected by the revenue. Hence, while a sales tax practitioner is qualified to appear in proceedings, he cannot conduct audit under section 61.

6. Reasons for rejection of the challenge based on article 14

(i)The chartered accountants by reason of their training have special aptitude in the matter of audit. An income-tax practitioner does not have the same expertise as the chartered accountants in the matter of accounts. The argument, therefore, that the effect of such a provision will be to exclude all other categories of authorized representatives except the chartered accountants from carrying on their profession is liable to be rejected, as they constitute two distinct classes having a nexus with the object of the provisions, which is evasion of tax dues.

(ii)The contention that such a provision brings in an oppressive restriction is also liable to be rejected as auditing of accounts is a specialized job. It may be true that some income-tax practitioners may also acquire that skill by sheer practice without passing the necessary examination. But that does not preclude the Parliament from prescribing special qualifications with reference to the auditing of accounts.

FAQs on Transfer Pricing Audit

SRINIVASAN ANAND G.

CA

Who is primarily responsible to furnish information in Form No. 3CEB - Taxpayer or the auditor?

The Explanatory Memorandum to the Finance Bill,2012 clarifies that "If the assessee does not report such a transaction in the report furnished under section 92E then the Assessing Officer would normally not be aware of such an International Transaction so as to make a reference to the Transfer Pricing Officer." Thus, from the Explanatory Memorandum, it is clear that it is the primary responsibility of an asssessee to furnish correct and complete details of all international transactions/SDTs undertaken by him during the year.

Who can be appointed for conduct the audit envisaged under section 92E

Who is eligible to be the auditor u/s 92E?

According to section 92E, the report should be an 'accountant'. Section 92F(i) defines 'accountant' has having the same meaning as in Explanation below section 288(2). According to the above mentioned explanation, it covers a CA and Restricted State auditor.

According to ICAI's 'Guidance Note on Report on International Transactions under section 92E of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (Transfer Pricing)' hereinafter referred to as "Guidance Note on Transfer Pricing" :

♦ Section 92E refers to "an accountant" which means a Chartered Accountant as defined in Chartered Accountants Act, 1949.

♦ However, audit under section 92E can be done by a firm of Chartered Accountants also.

Extending the above logic of the Guidance Note further, a view can be taken that w.e.f. 1-3-2011 [date on which Chartered Accountants (Amendment) Act, 2011 came into force] LLPs of CAs in practice/CAs in practice with other prescribed professionals can be appointed for transfer pricing audit u/s 92E. CBDT/ICAI needs to clarify this.

Can audit under section 92E be conducted by an employee of assessee-client?

In Sahara India (Firm) v. CIT [2008] 169 Taxman 328 (SC), the Supreme Court held that "An auditor is a professional person". He has to function independently. He is not an employee of the assessee.

Is it necessary that tax audit under section 92E shall be a CA in full-time practice?

Yes. At its 242nd meeting, the Council of ICAI has decided that any member in part-time practice (i.e. a member who is holding certificate of practice and also engaged in any other business/occupation) shall not be entitled to perform attest functions. Therefore, a CA in part-time practice cannot be appointed as auditor under section 92E.

In case of companies, is it necessary that audit u/s 92E be conducted by statutory auditor?

No. In case of companies, it can be done by the statutory auditor of the company appointed under section 224 of the Companies Act, 1956 or by any other CA in practice or firm of CAs. This is because section 92E does not require that only the statutory auditor should perform the audit under section 92E.

Whether a CA or firm of CAs appointed as tax consultants can conduct audit u/s 92E?

A CA/firm of CAs who are appointed as tax consultants may be appointed as auditor under section 92E. [ICAI's Guidance Note on Transfer Pricing]

Can a CA or CA firm who is internal auditor of assessee can also be auditor u/s 92E?

No. Internal auditor cannot give audit report u/s 92E. [ICAI's Code of Ethics]

Is there any limit on the number of audits under section 92E which a CA/CA firm can accept?

No. There is no limit on number of audits u/s 92E which CA/CA firm can accept.

Is there any minimum fee to be charged by CA firms for Tax audits?

No. Chapter XII of the Council General Guidelines has been omitted with effect from 7-6-2011. Hence, no minimum fee stipulated for audits at the moment.

Scope of audit under section 92E

What are the matters covered by scope of the audit u/s 92E?

It covers the following:

♦ Examination of only those accounts and records of the assessee which relate to international transactions/SDTs entered into by him during the previous year under audit.

♦ Ascertaining and reporting whether the assessee has maintained proper information and documentations prescribed in respect of international transactions entered into by him.

Issue Involved

Whether services were liable to service tax ?

HELD: Services were not liable to service tax :

Assessee is a testing agency. The contract of service was with the overseas purchaser of goods. Thus, the privity of contract of the assessee is with the buyers of the goods who are located or situated outside India. This is a contract based tax. The contract is of services. Further, there is no contract and no privity between the assessee and the exporter of the goods who is stated to be based in India. The service was complete when the report was delivered to the foreign client. Definition of Term Taxable service is inclusive. It also includes technical testing and analysis (see section 65 (106) (zzh)). In such circumstances, when technical inspection and certification is also a service and goods in question have been inspected or tested, but the services were of the nature noted above, the payment was also made in terms aforesaid, then, the benefit of exemption/Circular was available. That was on the footing that the services rendered were exempt from whole of the liability to pay service tax. [Para 21]

Circular dated 25th April 2003 referred to Notifications dated 1st March 2003 and 9th April 1999. The 9th April 1999 is a notification of exemption. The April 2003 circular clarifies that service tax would be levied on all taxable services consumed or rendered in India, irrespective whether the payment thereof is received in foreign exchange or not. It has been clarified that the question of taxability of secondary services which are used by primary service provider for the export of services. Hence, the services provided by the assessee were not taxable. This aspect once becomes more clear if one peruses the notification no.21/03ST, dated 20th November, 2003. [Para 22]

The services rendered in the present case are fully covered by the clarification given and even by the principle laid down in the decision of the Supreme Court of India in All India Federation of Tax Practitioners v. Union of India [2007] 10 STT 166. Service tax is a tax on each activity. When it comes to a service tax on professions, the services rendered are of advise and hence, the Supreme Court with regard to the nature of the tax concluded that it is rendered by a Chartered Accountant, for example when he advises his client or audits his account. Similarly, a cost accountant charges his client for advise as well as doing his work of costing. For each transaction or contract, Chartered Accountant/Cost Accountant renders professional based services. all over the country and perhaps this also is the practice prevalent over the rest of the world that a Chartered Accountant can always rely upon the certificate given by another Chartered Accountant. This is done day in and day out in day to day practice. In the cases of large companies, public sector undertakings, nationalised ‘banks the statutory auditors always rely upon the certificate given by other Chartered Accountants appointed to audit the accounts of various other transactions or: branches or other aspects . While reliance upon the’ audit report of, another Chartered Accountant is permissible under the auditing procedures, it is for the auditors, who rely upon such a report, to establish, if necessity arises, that there was no negligence on his part in performing his duties and if as a consequence of such a reliance, negligence results and that negligence causes a loss or injury to the users of those statements certified by him, then again he will be liable for defending himself against negligence and if unable to prove, for misconduct and disciplinary proceedings under the Chartered Accountant Regulation Act of 1949 would ensue. Thus the Chartered Accountant, who relies upon the certificate given by another Chartered Accountant, -takes the risk of exposing himself to a charge of negligence in the performance of his duties. But that does not mean that the certificate given by him is not a valid certificate unless the contrary is proved. Therefore the expression "such accountant" merely describes the Chartered Accountant, who is to furnish the certificate and it does not suggest that, the statutory auditor alone is entitled to give the certificate required under clause (b) and no one else. It is open to a trust or to an institution to have its accounts audited for the purpose of the management or to satisfy the requirements of other enactment by one Chartered Accountant and to have the accounts audited for the purposes of clause (b) by another Chartered Accountant. The only requirement is that the Chartered Accountant, who is appointed to furnish a certificate under clause (b) of section 12A must audit the accounts in the same manner as the statutory auditor must have conducted the audit because the certificate that the statutory auditor is required to give appears to be more or less the same as the certificate required to be furnished by the Chartered Accountant conducting the audit under clause (b) of section 12A. From the mere similarity of the language it cannot be inferred that the Legislature intended that the statutory auditor must alone give the certificate under clause (b) also. It is a matter of convenience and greatly facilitate the work if the same statutory auditor gives the certificate also but there is no prohibition as such that could be inferred from the language of clause (b) of section 12A. We are therefore of the opinion that the certificate given by M/s Khare Associates is a valid certificate and when he had certified that he has audited the accounts and when he has furnished the required certificate in the prescribed form, that certificate has to be acted upon and the only occasion when that certificate could. be discarded is when it is proved to be false. That not being the case of the department in this case, we hold that the certificate given by M/s Khare Associates cannot be discarded as invalid. This view of the department cannot there fore be accepted as being borne out from the language of clause (b) of section, 12A.

Section 65(105)(zm ) - Banking and other financial services - Lending money to borrowers v. Hire Purchase Service

6.4 The assessee was engaged in lending finances to various persons for purchase of automobiles and collecting interest from the borrowers. Revenue proceeded against the assessee by way of issue of show-cause notice demanding service tax under category of ‘banking and other financial services’. On adjudication, the Assistant Commissioner dropped the proceedings against the assessee. However, the Commissioner reviewed the said order and held the assessee to be liable to pay service tax under the said category. He also levied interest and imposed penalties on the assessee.

The Tribunal held that the assessee was simply lending money as per the records available and receiving interest. The lending during the relevant period was not a taxable service. Even if it was held that the assessee was giving money under the ‘Hire purchase scheme’, it was clearly seen that the Tribunal in Bajaj Auto Finance Ltd. v. CCE [2007] 9 STT 569 (Mum. - CESTAT) had clearly drawn a distinction between ‘Hire Purchase Service’ which is taxable and ‘Hire Purchase Finance Service’ which is not a taxable service. In any case, it was clear that the assessee had not rendered the services of hire purchase. It only lent money to the borrowers. Therefore, it could not be brought under the category of taxable services under banking and financial services. In view of the above, the Tribunal does not find any merit in the impugned order and, consequently, the assessee was held not liable to pay the tax demanded and penalties.

Section 65(105)(zn ) - Taxable service - Port services - Stevedoring activities

6.5 Assessee was paying service tax under category of ‘steamer agent’s’ service. Subsequently, assessee contended that after obtaining stevedoring licence from NMPT it was carrying out stevedoring operations, viz., loading and unloading of cargo within port premises and said service would amount to cargo handling service. Assessee further contended that it would not come within ambit of taxation, because in respect of ‘Cargo Handling Services’, cargo in relation to exports are excluded from purview and since it was only handling export cargo, it would not be liable to pay service tax even under category of ‘Cargo Handling Services’. Revenue, however, held that assessee was carrying out services within port and it had been authorized by port to render such services in view of licence given to it and, therefore, services rendered by assessee would fall within ambit of ‘Port Services’ and rejected assessee’s claim of refund.

The Tribunal on similar facts in previous case of Konkan Marine Agencies v. CCE, Mangalore [2008] 12 STT 82 (Bang. - CESTAT) had held that, on facts, services rendered by assessee would not amount to ‘Port Services’ and since in respect of ‘Cargo Handling Services’, cargo in relation to exports are excluded from purview of service tax, assessee would not come within ambit of taxation. Following this decision, the Tribunal held that in view of this decision, activity of assessee did not come within ambit of ‘Port Services’ and, therefore, assessee was held entitled to refund claim.

HEADNOTE: †Section 44D of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with articles 12 and 7 of DTAA between India and Germany (Royalty/FTS) - Royalties in case of foreign companies - Assessment Years 1998-99 and 2000-01 - Assessee, a company incorporated at Germany, had a branch office in India - Indian branch was engaged in business of audit and procedure of norms for ISO 9000 certification - Assessee treated said income as its business income - However, Assessing Officer opined that said services came within purview of technical service under article 12 DTAA with Germany - Accordingly, by applying section 44D he assessed income at rate of 20 per cent of entire gross receipts - Whether services rendered by assessee were mostly in nature of audit work and, thus, services could not be termed as technical, managerial or consultancy services - Held, yes - Whether, entire nature of services and activities of assessee came within realm of 'professional services' and not within meaning of FTS as provided in article 12 and, thus, assessee's income could not be determined under section 44D but had to be computed as per provisions of sections 28 to 43 in view of article 7(1) - Held, yes [In favour of assessee]

FACT: The assessee, a company incorporated at Germany, had a branch in India. The Indian branch was engaged in the business of audit and procedure of norms for ISO 9000 certification. The services offered by Indian branch were ISO 9000 quality system certification where in quality system auditor of assessee company would visit the company opting for ISO certification, carry out a pre-assessment audit and then a certification audit and submit report to the assessee. After verification of report by the assessee, ISO 9000 certification was granted. The assessee treated its income as business income. The Assessing Officer opined that such services should be taxed as 'fees for technical services' under article 12 of Indo German DTAA. The assessee submitted that these services did not come under FTS within meaning of article 12 and, thus, it was business income which was to be computed in view of article 7(1) as business was carried out through PE. However, the Assessing Officer held that said services came within purview of FTS and, hence, provisions of section 44D had to be applied, and, accordingly, he assessed the income after applying tax rate of FTS; i.e., at rate 20 per cent of entire gross receipts. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the findings of Assessing Officer.

On appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: After examining the value of services and activities carried out by the assessee in the light of definition of terms 'royalty' and 'fees for technical service', it is found out that the assessee's case does not in any manner come within the meaning of 'royalties', as there is no right to use of any other items described therein. One is concerned with the meaning of term 'fees for technical services' as given in para 4 of Article 12. FTS has been defined as the payment of any amount in consideration of service for 'managerial' or 'technical' or 'consultancy' in nature, which is quite similar to definition given in Explanation 2 to section 9(1)(vii). Looking to the nature of services provided by the assessee as has been described above, it is simply evident that it is mostly in the nature of 'audit work' wherein the auditors of the assessee visit the sites of the client's and evaluate the clients' quality system as prescribed in International Standard for ISO 9001/2, ISO 14001, QS 9000 etc. Based on this audit work, a report is prepared which is sent to certification body the assessee company in Munich, Germany, which provides a certificate for a certain period, after reviewing the report and several stages of audit work which has been carried out for this purpose. Nowhere from such services, it can be inferred that the assessee has been providing technical, managerial or consultancy. Technical services require expertise in technology and providing the client such technical expertise. In this case no technology is transferred. 'Managerial services' is used in the context of running and management of the business of the client while here in this case, there is no management of client's business, but evaluation of standards as per international guidelines. Consultancy is to be understood as advisory services wherein necessary advice and consultation is given to its clients for the purpose of client's business. In an audit work there may be some incidence of advice at the time of evaluation but certainly it cannot be termed as pure consultancy services as in the audit work the auditor has to only evaluate the quality system and environmental system. [Para 10.2]

HEADNOTE: Section 21, read with section 22, of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 - Professional misconduct - On basis of report of Disciplinary Committee and after taking into consideration representations made, respondent was held guilty of gross negligence, for having signed and certified a statement of export of leather goods including those of other manufacturers, without verifying facts from relevant books/documents of company concerned - Whether, on facts, respondent had been rightly found to be guilty of gross negligence, and recommendation of reprimand was reasonable and had to be accepted - Held, yes

FACT: Company ‘S’ had furnished to the Joint CCI & E a statement of export of leather goods including those of other manufacturers for the years 1976-77 and 1977-78, duly certified by the respondent - Chartered Ac-countant, and on that basis, the Export House Certificate was issued. The respondent had certified that he had checked and verified the particulars of export from the books/documents of the company and found them to be correct. On demand by the Jt. CCI & E, the company replied that it had not purchased any finished leather/leather goods from any other party and denied having exported finished goods manufactured by other units. The Jt. CCI & E made a complaint to the Institute that the respondent had issued the certificate without verifying the books of account inasmuch as he did not have any contact with that company. The respondent, in his reply, asserted his certificate to be correct and complete, based on the documents produced by the concerned parties. He further submitted that he was retained by the consultants of the company to verify the export statements from the records produced by it and he certified the facts accordingly. The Disciplinary Committee held that the then existing export policy required that 20 per cent of the total exports goods should be manufactured by others to get Export House benefits and since the only dispute was that the figures were not correct, the respondent was guilty of professional misconduct under section 21, read with section 22, and under clauses 5, 6 and 7 of the Part I of the Second Schedule. That leaves us with the additional submission made in Writ Petition No. 1777 of 2007. The issue of competence of the State Legislature. The Petitioner does not dispute that in the matter of enacting the law pertaining to recovery of sales tax, the same clearly falls within entry 54 of the State List. If in the process of making legislation, the Legislature in its wisdom provides for the procedure in the manner in which tax has to be levied, maintenance of books, procedure for checking correctness or verification of books, we fail to see as to how the same amounts to ancillary Legislation or procedure not falling within the competence of the State Legislature under Entry 54. The Act requires that the dealer has to maintain books and the books have to be audited and required to be certified by a Chartered Accountant. That will not result in the legislation falling outside the competence of the State Legislature. The legislation in pith and substance is relatable to imposition of Sales Tax which is within the competence of the State Legislature. The courts examine and ascertain the pith and substance on scrutiny of the true character of the enactment. See E.V. Chinnaiah v. State of A.P. [2005] 1 SCC 394. It is so in the instant case. The burden where such a challenge is raised is always on the Petitioner who attacks the competency of the State Legislature. The normal presumption is that the State Legislature does not exceed its jurisdiction. See Welfare Association A.R.P. Maharashtra v. Ranjit P. Gohil [2003] 9 SCC 358.

25. We also fail to understand how in such a case audit by a Chartered Accountant will amount to outsourcing the statutory power as is sought to be contended by the Petitioners to the third party. The Legislature can always delegate its powers as long as such delegation does not amount to abdication of its essential legislative functions. In the instant case, there is no abdication of the essential legislative functions. All that the section requires is that the Accountant has to audit the accounts and to issue certificate that the dealer has maintained the books as required to be maintained under the Act and rules. The dealer has to file his accounts then audited with the certificate. This neither amounts to abdication nor excessive delegation. Such an exercise also does not amount to conferring on the Accountant a power to determine the correct tax liability of the dealer. The power to accept returns is of the Authorities under the Act. Even after the certificate is issued, that the dealer has maintained books, it is always open to the Commissioner under section 20 to ascertain whether the return is correct and complete or order an audit under section 22 to get the accounts audited by the Officers of the Department. A certificate therefore, is not determinative but to enable the department to consider that the person having knowledge of audit and subject to the disciplinary control of its parent body has certified that the accounts are properly maintained. This is to aid the officers in discharging their statutory duties. This challenge therefore, has to be rejected.

We are unable to see merit in this argument. It is for the dealer to decide whose services the dealer seeks to obtain for appearance before Sales Tax Authorities or getting the accounts audited. Under section 82, there are a class of persons from whom a dealer can obtain services for being represented before the authorities under the Act. Under section 61, he is bound to select one of the class of accountants also. This is for a category of dealers whose turn over is more than 40 lakhs. The amount of fee which has to be paid is the amount to be decided between the dealer and that person, whom he selects from amongst the accountants that are available. This cannot be said to amount of compulsory levy amounting to tax. That being the case, the challenge under Article 265 must also fail.

CORPORATE LITERATURE/SERVICE TAX

SERVICE TAX LEVY ON CHARTERED ACCOUNTANTS - UNCONSTITUTIONAL, ILLEGAL, INVALID AND UNWARRANTED

N. Vijia Kumar*

‘Service tax’ was first introduced in India by the Finance Act, 1994, on a few services and subsequently extended to several other services by the relevant Finance Acts. The Finance Act, 1998 brought the services rendered by a chartered accountant within the purview of service tax. In this article, the author attacks the levy of service tax at its very root by arguing that under the Constitution of India, the Parliament has no power to enact service tax legislation and, hence, the levy in question is lacking in constitutional validity. The author also specifically questions the extension of the levy to the profession of chartered accountancy, inter alia, on the ground that the exercise of profession by a chartered accountant does not amount to rendering of ‘service’ - EDITOR

Introduction

1. The Finance Minister in his Budget Speech for the year 1998-99 has observed in para 169 as hereunder:

"169. In the last budget, a number of services were added in the tax net. These included the service rendered on transportation of goods by road. The House is aware that it led to widespread resistance and protests. As a result, this service tax was virtually kept in abeyance and rightly so. I have decided to abolish the service tax on transportation of goods by road. I have also decided to abolish the service tax payable by outdoor caterers and pandal contractors. However, I have proposed service tax on some new services. These are services provided by: Architects, Interior decorators, Management Consultants, Chartered Accountants, Cost Accountants, Company Secretaries, Private security services, Real estate agents and real estate consultants, Market research agencies, Credit rating agencies, Underwriting agencies, Slaughter houses using mechanised means for the large animals.

We will examine how in respect of certain segments liable to Service Tax, the manner and mode of payment could be further simplified to improve compliance. These new service taxes will yield Rs. 220 crore in a full year."

With a view to effecting the aforesaid policy decision, the Finance Bill (No. 2) of 1998 by Chapter VI thereof and clause 129 has effected several ancillary and consequential amendments in the Finance Act, 1994, section 65, etc.

Section 116 of the Finance Act, 1998 has provided for a levy of service tax at 5 per cent on services rendered by practising chartered accountants, cost accountants and company secretaries. The said ‘service tax’ has been brought into effect with effect from October 16, 1998. A further notification issued by the Revenue Department provides that the taxable services rendered to a client by a practising Chartered Accountant or a company secretary or cost accountant which will attract service tax include: accounting and auditing or cost accounting or secretarial auditing or verification of declarations in prescribed forms under section 149 of the Companies Act, 1956 or signing of annual return of listed companies under section 161 of the Companies Act or certification requirements of Schedule XIII to the Companies Act, or certification of documents to be filed with Registrar of Companies or certification in Form No. 1 under the Companies Unpaid Dividend Rules, 1978 or certification of documents under Export and Import Policy (1997-2002) or Certification for exchange control purposes under FERA 1973 or certification in respect of valuation of instruments or assets as per rule 8A(7) of the Wealth-tax Rules, 1957. Vide GSR 597E, Notification Nos. 53, 54, 57 of 1998 Service Tax, issued by the Ministry of Finance (Department of Revenue) vide F. No. B11/3/93 TRU dated October 7, 1998.

Service Tax - Finance Act, 1994 - Chapter V - Salient and relevant provisions

2. In India we are familiar with direct taxes like income-tax, and indirect taxes like customs and central excise duties. For the first time in India, ‘service tax’ was introduced in 1994 by the Finance Act, 1994 (32 of 1994) Chapter V-sections 64 to 96. It was introduced consequent to the acceptance of the Chelliah Committee on Taxation. Service tax is charged on something intangible, i.e., a service, and is administered by the Central Excise Department of the Government of India. The scope of the services covered was extended by the Finance Acts of 1996, 1997 and 1999.

12. The challenge to the vires of the section may now be summarized :— (a)The impugned provision is for certification of the veracity of statutory claims by the dealers under the Act and to certify that the Sales and Purchases are correctly accounted by the dealers and their claims are legally valid. The caption ‘Accounts to be audited in certain cases’ is nothing but the same judicial process of deciding the legality or otherwise of the claims of the dealers under the Act, in case of dealers having turn over exceeding rupees forty lakh in any year, which includes turn over of capital goods. This certificate has to be given by the Accountant to the exclusion of the Sales Tax practitioner or Advocates though the said class of persons are specialized in sales tax laws and practice. Under section 61, what is to be done is not mathematical correctness but judicial authenticity, legality or authenticity of the various claims under the Sales Tax Laws for which verification and certification is required to be done by the Chartered Accountant. This is over and above verification done under the returns by respective dealer while filing the return. This certificate can only be given by the Chartered Accountant. Since, 1946, apart from Chartered Accountants, it was open to all categories of persons described in section 82, having sufficient expertise and qualifications to do the accounts as also audit. The impugned section 61, has resulted in divisive exclusion of advocates and Sales Tax Practitioners, as the traders would not like to engage services of Sales Tax Practitioners or advocates for certification. The result is that a large section of Practitioners in mofusil area and small towns will be rendered out of the practice and consequently adversely affecting their livelihood. As there is no reasonable basis for the exclusion, the provision is arbitrary being violative of Article 14.

(b)The practice of Sales Tax Accounts was open to all including Chartered Accountants, advocates and tax practitioners. The Chartered Accountants who happens to pass the examination and has no expertise to adjudicate upon the legality or otherwise of the assessee’s claims of sales tax law can issue certificate.

Similarly Chartered Accountants however, senior they may be, who have not practiced sales tax law and who could not gather experience can issue certificate. There is no relation with object of the enactment for such arbitrary selection of class without relation to their authority, efficiency or otherwise. The sole object and purpose of section 61(1) is that every dealer who is covered by sub-sections (a) and (b) should get their returns verified and get their tax liability assessed by a Professional so as to enable them to provide the information required to furnish a report under Rule 65 and to fill out Form 704. There is no other purpose behind section 61. This purpose and object completely exhausts the scope of section 61. If this being so, the requirement of CA alone for the certification in Form 704 is wholly irrelevant and arbitrary. In any case, all information contained in Form 704 is for assessment of tax liability by the expert professionals who on the basis of same information are authorised to fill all types of returns in Forms 221 to 225 and no purpose is served by CA’s certification of correctness under the garb of audit of books of account. For the reasons already discussed, we find that the challenge to the Constitutional validity of the legislation under Articles 14 and 19 at the instance of the Bar Council will also have to be rejected. 24. That leaves us with the additional submission made in Writ Petition No. 1777 of 2007. The issue of competence of the State Legislature. The Petitioner does not dispute that in the matter of enacting the law pertaining to recovery of sales tax, the same clearly falls within entry 54 of the State List. If in the process of making legislation, the Legislature in its wisdom provides for the procedure in the manner in which tax has to be levied, maintenance of books, procedure for checking correctness or verification of books, we fail to see as to how the same amounts to ancillary Legislation or procedure not falling within the competence of the State Legislature under Entry 54. The Act requires that the dealer has to maintain books and the books have to be audited and required to be certified by a Chartered Accountant. That will not result in the legislation falling outside the competence of the State Legislature. The legislation in pith and substance is relatable to imposition of Sales Tax which is within the competence of the State Legislature. The courts examine and ascertain the pith and substance on scrutiny of the true character of the enactment. See—E.V. Chinnaiah v. State of A.P. [2005] 1 SCC 394. It is so in the instant case. The burden where such a challenge is raised is always on the Petitioner who attacks the competency of the State Legislature. The normal presumption is that the State Legislature does not exceed its jurisdiction. See—Welfare Association A.R.P. Maharashtra v. Ranjit P. Gohil [2003] 9 SCC 358.

25. We also fail to understand how in such a case audit by a Chartered Accountant will amount to outsourcing the statutory power as is sought to be contended by the Petitioners to the third party. The Legislature can always delegate its powers as long as such delegation does not amount to abdication of its essential legislative functions. In the instant case, there is no abdication of the essential legislative functions. All that the section requires is that the Accountant has to audit the accounts and to issue certificate that the dealer has maintained the books as required to be maintained under the Act and rules. The dealer has to file his accounts then audited with the certificate. This neither amounts to abdication nor excessive delegation. Such an exercise also does not amount to conferring on the Accountant a power to determine the correct tax liability of the dealer. The power to accept returns is of the Authorities under the Act. Even after the certificate is issued, that the dealer has maintained books, it is always open to the Commissioner under section 20 to ascertain whether the return is correct and complete or order an audit under section 22 to get the accounts audited by the Officers of the Department. A certificate therefore, is not determinative but to enable the department to consider that the person having knowledge of audit and subject to the disciplinary control of its parent body has certified that the accounts are properly maintained. This is to aid the officers in discharging their statutory duties. This challenge therefore, has to be rejected.

26. The last challenge is that under section 61, the dealer will also have to engage a Chartered Accountant apart from engaging Advocate or Sales Tax Practitioner and their financial liability would increase and by such increase in their financial liability, the same will affect their trade by cutting into their profits and that it is in fact in pith and substance compulsory levy amounting to tax and in contravention of Article 265 of the Constitution. We are unable to see merit in this argument. It is for the dealer to decide whose services the dealer seeks to obtain for appearance before Sales Tax Authorities or getting the accounts audited. Under section 82, there are a class of persons from whom a dealer can obtain services for being represented before the authorities under the Act. Under section 61, he is bound to select one of the class of accountants also. This is for a category of dealers whose turn over is more than 40 lakhs. The amount of fee which has to be paid is the amount to be decided between the dealer and that person, whom he selects from amongst the accountants that are available. This cannot be said to amount of compulsory levy amounting to tax. That being the case, the challenge under Article 265 must also fail.

27. Similarly, the question of Article 301 being attracted, does not arise. The challenge on that count also has to be rejected as the right claimed by the Petitioner or their members or by the dealer is that Advocate and Sales Tax Practitioner cannot carry out audit in terms of section 61 in the State of Maharashtra. The enactment is pursuant to the power of the State Legislation to make law within its competence. This does not attract Article 301.

The Commissioner proceeded against the assessee for short payment of service tax under the category of CHA and also in respect of services provided as CFA. The Tribunal remanded the matter for de novo decision. Subsequently, the Commissioner concluded that the amounts, viz., charge collect fees, break bulk fees, profit share from margin, unallocated income, currency adjustment factor, air/sea freight rebate, commission/brokerage, air freight incentive and expenses reimbursement billing were liable to be taxed under CHA services. Similarly, certain other charges such as rental income, distribution charges, warehousing charges and transportation charges had been held to be forming a part of the value of the CFA services rendered by the assessee. The assessee opposed the said order.

On appeal :

HELD: The activities relating to freight forwarding could not be brought under CHA. The assessee had clearly explained the nature of the charges collected such as charge collect fees, break bulk fees, profit share from margin, unallocated income, currency adjustment factor, air/sea freight rebate, commission/brokerage, air freight incentive, expenses reimbursement billing, etc. Such charges would not be includible in the computation of service tax towards CHA services. However, the Commissioner in the impugned order even while holding that those charges were related to CHA services, had also repeatedly pointed out that the assessee had not produced a chartered accountant’s certificate with regard to the various deductions claimed by it. Hence, while holding that the above charges could not be included in the value of CHA services, the matter was to be remanded to the Commissioner to re-examine the issue after giving an opportunity to the assessee to produce the chartered accountant’s certificate in respect of the various deductions claimed by it including the reimbursement.

On appeal to Tribunal: HELD: There is no dispute between the parties that the sum so received is chargeable to tax according to the provisions of domestic tax laws. Therefore, only issue to be examined is whether the above sum can be taxed in India as per the articles of Indo-UK Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement. The claim of the assessee is that above sum is chargeable to tax as fees for technical services as per article 13(4)(c) of DTAA if the assessee makes available technical, knowledge, experience, skill etc to the Indian entities. The Assessing Officer has agreed that the services provided by the assessee are technical in nature. According to him as the assessee is also carrying analysis, testing and inspection, hence, it is providing the consultancy services also. He therefore, held that on close scrutiny of nature of services the service recipient get equipped to carry on that business model or service model on their own without reference to the service provider. Therefore, according to him such services fall within the ambit of making available technical knowledge under the tax treaty. The Dispute Resolution Panel also agreed with the order of the Assessing Officer and accordingly, sum received of Rs. 187.7 lakhs was considered as fees for technical services. Now coming to the nature of services rendered by the assessee to the various entities, the assessee has provided services to Hindalco Ltd. and the nature of services is umpire instruction based on which a certificate of Umpire Analysis was given. For the certification, different methods such as F25, G18, I18, i20 and I23 were employed. It also certified the state of material and element of such certification. The other service rendered to Hindalco Industries Ltd. is with respect to weighing, sampling the moisture determination services. After providing these services a certificate of inspection was also provided. The service provided to Grifith India also involved chemical analysis of different products and then providing a certificate thereof. The services of Indian Oil Corporation is inspection of the vessel on arrival. The services provided to Dell International is also with respect to data security audit and auditing. The services provided to Nirma was also with respect to the certificate of analysis of various parameters of spent pacol catalyst. The services provided to Vedanta Ltd. is also pertaining to chemical certification of material. Undoubtedly all the above services provided by the assessee are in the nature of technical analysis and unless the assessee is able to perform those services independently without the help of the service provider then only it can be said that services have been made available by the service provider to the service recipient. According to article 13 of Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement the fees for technical services can be chargeable to tax in India only such services are made available to the recipient of such services. However, the assessee has not at all made available any such services to the Indian entity but has merely provided the services in the ordinary course of its business. The revenue has not brought on any material to show that subsequently the recipient of those services have performed these services on their own without the help of the assessee or any other similar service provider. Inspection and survey of imported/exported cargo and certifying in relation to the quality and price, provision of such services does not make available technical knowledge, experience, skill, know-how or processes to the recipient of the service. Hence, the fees for technical services earned by the assessee is not chargeable to tax in India according to article 13(4)(c) of the DTAA as these services are not made available to the Indian parties. Accordingly, it is held that Rs. 187.72 lakhs received by the assessee is not chargeable to tax in India. [Para 6]

The word professional capacity is very confusing and may be very controversial. If this word was not there in this definition, than all the services provided by these practising professionals would have been taxable except the exemption which is now provided. But due to this word there will going to be dispute. There can be two aspects to deal with this situation : u First, whatever can be provided only by these practising professionals can be called as provided in professional capacity and all other services are not covered under these services. For example, certain statutory audit referred under point No. 9 of the table, can be done only by these professionals, so the same is covered under these services [except the new exemption which is provided now]. But accounting work and other work mentioned under point Nos. 1 to 8 can also be done by other, so the same is not covered under these services. This interpretation also seems to be in accordance with this definition otherwise the word professional capacity has not been used. Also otherwise the same may be hit by article 14 of the constitution as discussed above, because the same can also be provided by the Advocates.

u Second, whatever is provided by these practising professionals can be called as provided in professional capacity and the same is covered under these services [except the new exemption which is provided now]. But this interpretation seems to be not in accordance with this definition as the words ‘professional capacity’ will become otiose in this case.

But if we adopt the first interpretation, than the next question is that, whether the accounting and other services, which can be called as non professional, can be covered under other category of services under the service tax? Certainly in that case the same will have to be taxable under other category if the same is not covered under these categories as is also clarified previously under Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated 16-10-1998. Now the mode of classification of taxable services has been provided under section 65A of the Finance Act, 1994, which was inserted by the Finance Act, 2003, w.e.f. 14-5-2003. As per this section, classification of taxable services shall be determined according to the terms of the sub-clauses of clause (105) of section 65 as below :

(1)For the purposes of this Chapter, classification of taxable services shall be determined according to the terms of the sub-clauses of clause (105) of section 65

(2)When for any reason, a taxable service is, prima facie, classifiable under two or more sub-clauses of clause (105) of section 65, classification shall be effected as follows:—

(a )the sub-clause which provides the most specific description shall be preferred to sub-clauses providing a more general description;

(b )composite services consisting of a combination of different services which cannot be classified in the manner specified in clause (a), shall be classified as if they consisted of a service which gives them their essential character, insofar as this criterion is applicable;

(c )when a service cannot be classified in the manner specified in clause (a) or clause (b), it shall be classified under the sub-clause which occurs first among the sub-clauses which equally merit consideration.

So as per clause (a) of sub-section (2), the sub-clause which provides the most specific description shall be preferred to sub-clauses providing a more general description. Previously there can be dispute regarding the classification of services provided by these professional because there was exemption. Now also there are certain exemptions which are provided now. If the same is covered under this category than the same may be covered under this exemption but this type of exemption is not provided under other services. So now there can be dispute that the particular services are covered under this category and the same is exempt being more specific description as per section 65A of the Finance Act, 1994. But it is now utmost necessity to clarify the scope of these services to avoid any future dispute.

CASE STUDY/BUSINESS AUXILIARY SERVICES

HARIOM JINDAL*

Case Study - Implication of decision in Dr. Lal Path Lab’s Case

Services relating to technical inspection and certification have been brought within the purview of service tax net by the Finance Act, 2003 with effect from July 1, 2003, but the Legislature has excluded ‘testing or analysis of human beings or animal’ from the scope of levy. In this article, the author has analyzed the decision of the New Delhi - CESTAT in the case of Dr. Lal Path Lab (P.) Ltd. v. CCE [2006] 5 STT 172. In this case services rendered by the pathological sample collection centres were being subjected to tax by the department on the plea that those services were separate from the testing and analysis service and were taxable as business auxiliary service. However, the CESTAT concluded that such centres are not liable to service tax.

Introduction

1. Services relating to technical inspection and certification have been brought within the purview of service tax net by the Finance Act, 2003 with effect from July 1, 2003. [Notification No. 7/2003-ST, dated 20-6-2003] Prior to July 1, 2003, there were some doubts as to levy of service tax on third party inspections and certifications carried out by certifying agencies in respect of marine as well as non-marine equipments under the category of consulting engineer service. The Government, through Circular F.No. 177/5/2001-CX.4, dated 26-2-2002, has clarified that certificates given under authority of any statute/international protocol/code/convention, cannot be considered to be a consultancy job and, hence, the activity of certification will not fall under the category of advice. It has been further stated that to issue certificates under the authority of any statute, it will obviously be necessary for the certifying agency to conduct some survey/inspection. Thus, the survey/inspection by an agency for the purpose of issuing certificates under the authority of law, will also not amount to consultancy advice or technical assistance. If, however, the shipping company gets the ship surveyed or inspected by another agency before taking it for certification by an authorised agency, only then can it be said that the first agency is providing some technical assistance or advice. Hence, prior to July 1, 2003, the third party inspection and certification was not covered as the taxable service.

Tax on technical testing and analysis services was introduced with effect from July 1, 2003. As per section 65(105)( zzh), at the relevant time, any service provided to any person, by a technical testing and analysis agency, in relation to technical testing and analysis, is a ‘taxable service’. ‘Technical testing and analysis service’ means any service in relation to physical, chemical, biological or any other scientific testing or analysis of goods or material or any immovable property, but does not include any testing or analysis service provided in relation to human beings or animals [section 65(106) at the relevant time]. Thus, medical testing and diagnosis has been excluded from service tax. Technical testing and analysis agency is liable to pay service tax.

Technical testing and analysis agency means any agency or person engaged in providing service in relation to technical testing and analysis [section 65(107) at the relevant time].

The Legislature has excluded ‘testing or analysis of human beings or animal’ from the scope of levy under the category ‘technical testing and analysis’. The definition clearly states the legislative intention that no tax is to be imposed on technical testing and analysis service provided in relation to human beings or animals. If the Legislature had any intention to tax the testing or analysis in relation to human beings or animal at a rate different from technical test and analysis service, the Legislature would have separately specified the levy. Clearly the intention of the Legislature was not to impose any levy at all on testing or analysis of human beings or animals.

2. Before proceeding further, one may look into the meaning of the words ‘audit’ and ‘auditor’. In P. Ramanatha Aiyar’s Advanced Law Lexicon, 3rd Edition the ‘audit’ has been explained as a verb: to draw up or present an account; to make an official investigation and examination of accounts and vouchers; and as a noun: an examination of accounts in general; a formal or official examination and authentication of accounts, setting of accounts; the process of auditing accounts; the hearing and investigation before an auditor.

3. "In President, Councillors and Ratepayers of the Shire of Frankston and Hastings v. Cohen, 102 CLR 607, before the High Court of Australia the expression ‘audit’ came up for consideration and it was explained that the word, ‘audit’ is a well known English word, and the general nature of what constitutes an audit seems plain enough. The Oxford English Dictionary defines the noun ‘audit’ as ‘an official examination of accounts with verification by reference to witnesses and vouchers’. Mr. R.A. Irish in his book ‘Practical Auditing’ (p.1) says that ‘an audit may be said to be a skilled examination of such books, accounts and vouchers as will enable the auditor to verify the balance sheet’. The main objects of any audit are : (a) to certify to the correctness of the financial position as to shown in the balance-sheet, and the accompanying revenue statements; (b) the detection of errors; (c) the detection of fraud - the detection of fraud is generally regarded as being of primary importance." Thus, the word ‘audit’ has a specific connotation in the matter of examination, investigation and auditing of accounts, where detection of fraud is of primary importance.

The assessee contended that the service of certification was carried out by HRD entirely outside India, i.e., in Belgium and the gradation certificate/report given by HRD was only an analysis of the quality of each piece of diamond and it did not constitute transfer of any technology, commercial interest, skill or technical knowledge in favour of the assessee and, therefore, such services could not be regarded as 'technical services'.

The Commissioner (Appeals) noted that in providing grading or certification services of diamonds to the assessee, HRD had not parted with any technical knowledge or made available any technical expertise to the assessee so as to classify the impugned payment to HRD as 'fees for technical services' in view of MFN clause in India-Belgium DTAA. There is no dispute between the parties that the sum so received is chargeable to tax according to the provisions of domestic tax laws. Therefore, only issue to be examined is whether the above sum can be taxed in India as per the articles of Indo-UK Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement. The claim of the assessee is that above sum is chargeable to tax as fees for technical services as per article 13(4)(c) of DTAA if the assessee makes available technical, knowledge, experience, skill etc to the Indian entities. The Assessing Officer has agreed that the services provided by the assessee are technical in nature. According to him as the assessee is also carrying analysis, testing and inspection, hence, it is providing the consultancy services also. He therefore, held that on close scrutiny of nature of services the service recipient get equipped to carry on that business model or service model on their own without reference to the service provider. Therefore, according to him such services fall within the ambit of making available technical knowledge under the tax treaty. The Dispute Resolution Panel also agreed with the order of the Assessing Officer and accordingly, sum received of Rs. 187.7 lakhs was considered as fees for technical services. Now coming to the nature of services rendered by the assessee to the various entities, the assessee has provided services to Hindalco Ltd. and the nature of services is umpire instruction based on which a certificate of Umpire Analysis was given. For the certification, different methods such as F25, G18, I18, i20 and I23 were employed. It also certified the state of material and element of such certification. The other service rendered to Hindalco Industries Ltd. is with respect to weighing, sampling the moisture determination services. After providing these services a certificate of inspection was also provided. The service provided to Grifith India also involved chemical analysis of different products and then providing a certificate thereof. The services of Indian Oil Corporation is inspection of the vessel on arrival. The services provided to Dell International is also with respect to data security audit and auditing. The services provided to Nirma was also with respect to the certificate of analysis of various parameters of spent pacol catalyst. The services provided to Vedanta Ltd. is also pertaining to chemical certification of material. Undoubtedly all the above services provided by the assessee are in the nature of technical analysis and unless the assessee is able to perform those services independently without the help of the service provider then only it can be said that services have been made available by the service provider to the service recipient. According to article 13 of Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement the fees for technical services can be chargeable to tax in India only such services are made available to the recipient of such services. However, the assessee has not at all made available any such services to the Indian entity but has merely provided the services in the ordinary course of its business. The revenue has not brought on any material to show that subsequently the recipient of those services have performed these services on their own without the help of the assessee or any other similar service provider. Inspection and survey of imported/exported cargo and certifying in relation to the quality and price, provision of such services does not make available technical knowledge, experience, skill, know-how or processes to the recipient of the service. Hence, the fees for technical services earned by the assessee is not chargeable to tax in India according to article 13(4)(c) of the DTAA as these services are not made available to the Indian parties. Accordingly, it is held that Rs. 187.72 lakhs received by the assessee is not chargeable to tax in India. [Para 6]

Essential services - Complete exemption is desirable 9. Accounting, auditing and attestation services are essential services required for meeting legal requirements and also for running businesses. The requirement of statutory audit in case of companies, co-operative societies, audit under section 44AB of Income-tax Act, certification of various reports, documents, and declarations under various enactments are statutory requirements, which a businessman is forced to comply with. For example, a small company having little income may not desire to get his accounts audited in view of the nature and size of the business. However, being a company it is its statutory obligation to get the accounts audited. Therefore, audit of such account is a statutory obligation and is an essential service. Even where audit is voluntarily carried out, it helps the Government authorities in getting information in systematic, organized and standard manner duly checked by a competent and responsible professional. This helps Government authorities to easily make assessments, etc. Therefore, these services can also be considered as essential services. Therefore, such important and essential services should not be burdened with higher rate of tax of 12.24 per cent.

Similarly, a cost accountant charges his client for advise as well as doing his work of costing. For each transaction or contract, Chartered Accountant/Cost Accountant renders professional based services. If the taxable event is the provision of services, then, the place where the services have been rendered is of significance. The services will be taxable only if they are provided within India. Service tax is a destination based consumption tax and therefore, it is not applicable on export of services. [Para 23] Assessee rendered services, but they were consumed abroad. The clients of the assessees used the services of the assessee in inspection/test analysis of the goods which the clients located abroad intended to import from India. In other words, the clients abroad were desirous of confirming the fact as to whether the goods imported complied with requisite specifications and standards. Thus, client of the assessee located abroad engaged the services of the assessee for inspection and testing the goods. The goods were tested by the assessees in India. The goods were available or their samples were drawn for such testing and analysis in India. However, the report of such tests and analysis was sent abroad. The clients of the assessee were foreign clients, paid the assessee for such services rendered, in foreign convertible currency. It is in that sense that benefit of the services accrued to the foreign clients outside India. This is termed as 'export of service'. In these circumstances, if services were rendered to such foreign clients located abroad, then, the act can be termed as 'export of service'. Such an act does not invite a service tax liability. Once the Supreme Court has taken the view that service tax is a value added tax which in turn is destination based consumption tax in the sense that it taxes non-commercial activities and is not a charge on the business, but on the consumer, then, it is leviable only on services provided within the country. [Para 24]

Any larger or wider controversy and based on the submissions of assessee need not be decided in this case. Suffice it to hold that the view taken by the Tribunal does not raise any substantial question of law. [Para 26]

It may be noted that the Appeal under section 260A could be admitted only on the High Court being satisfied that the case involves a substantial question of law. The Supreme Court in the case of M. Janardhana Rao versus Joint Commissioner of Income-tax reported in (2005) 2 SCC 324, while dealing with the scope of Section 260A of the Income-tax Act, 1961, observed as under : -

"14.

Without insisting on the statement of substantial question of law in the memorandum of appeal and formulating the same at the time of admission, the High Court is not empowered to generally decide the appeal under Section 260A without adhering to the procedure prescribed under section 260A. Further, the High Court must make every effort to distinguish between a question of law and a substantial question of law. In exercise of powers under section 260A, the findings of fact of the Tribunal cannot be disturbed. It has to be kept in mind that the right of appeal is neither a natural nor an inherent right attached to the litigation. Being a substantive statutory right, it has to be regulated in accordance with law in force at the relevant time. The conditions mentioned in Section 260A must be strictly fulfilled before an appeal can be maintained under section 260A. Such appeal cannot be decided on merely equitable grounds.

15.

An appeal under section 260A can be only in respect of a 'substantial question of law'. The expression 'substantial question of law' has not been defined anywhere in the statute. But it has acquired a definite connotation through various judicial pronouncements. In Sir Chunilal V. Mehta & Sons Ltd. v. Century Spinning & Mfg. Co. Ltd., AIR (1962) SC 1314, this court laid down the following tests to determine whether a substantial question of law is involved. The tests are: (1) whether directly or indirectly it affects substantial rights of the parties, or (2) the question is of general public importance, or (3) whether it is an open question in the sense that issue is not settled by pronouncement of this Court or Privy Council or by the Federal Court, or (4) the issue is not free from difficulty, and (5) it calls for a discussion for alternative view. There is no scope for interference by the High Court with a finding recorded when such finding could be treated to be a finding of fact.

BUDGET 2006-07

Service tax on CA/CS/CWA- Round the World in Eight Years

The service tax was, for the first time, imposed by the Finance Act, 1994. Since then the scope of this tax has been widened almost in every Budget. Service tax on CA/CS/CWA Services was introduced with effect from October 16, 1998. But due to protest against the levy by these professionals, the levy was restricted by Notification No. 57/98-ST, dated October 7, 1998 only to auditing and accounting services. But later on the scope of these services was widened in a phased manner by Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated October 16, 1998. But now by Notification No. 2/2006-Service Tax, dated March 1, 2006, Notification No. 59/98-Service Tax, dated October 16, 1998 [G.S.R. 624(E), dated October 16, 1998] has been withdrawn. So, now all the services provided by these professionals are liable for service tax. Simply, there is no specific exemption notification available to these professionals, except general exemptions which are available in case of all services. It could be presumed that within eight years the scope of these services has rounded off the whole world.

HARIOM JINDAL*

History of service tax on CA/CS/CWA

1. A brief legislative history is that service tax was, for the first time, imposed by the Finance Act, 1994. This tax was levied on three types of services. Since then, the scope of this tax has been widened almost in every Budget. Service tax on practising chartered accountant, a practising company secretary or a practising cost accountants’ services [CA/CS/CWA] was introduced with effect from October 16, 1998. But due to protest against the levy by these professionals, the levy was restricted by Notification No. 57/98-ST, dated October 7, 1998 only to auditing and accounting services. One of the main causes of protest was that, while the service tax was levied on chartered accountants’ services, the same was not levied on the similar services provided by an advocate. So, the Government restricted the same only to auditing and accounting services which are specific to these professionals. So, the services provided by CAs and advocates, which can be of similar nature, remain out of purview of service tax. But the later developments are of crucial nature and patently of discriminatory nature. Perhaps in democracy, you can get no better example of favouritism. Our beloved Finance Minister, who himself is an advocate by profession, can do no better than to spare their fraternity from the ambit of this tax. The position now is that, while the services of lawyers are still out of service tax net, all the services provided by chartered accountants are now under the net of service tax. Notification No. 57/98-ST, dated October 7, 1998, was superseded by Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated October 16, 1998. As per Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated October 16, 1998, service tax is payable only on following services provided by CA/CS/CWA -

(i)accounting and auditing; or

(ii)cost accounting and cost auditing; or

(iii)secretarial auditing; or

(iv)verification of declarations in prescribed forms of compliances for obtaining a certificate of commencement of business or commencement of other business under section 149 of the Companies Act, 1956 (1 of 1956); or

(v)signing of the annual return of listed companies under section 161 of the Companies Act, 1956 (1 of 1956); or
