a limit to the profession tax clause (2) of article 276 itself suggests that income from the profession is irrelevant in the matter of tax on profession. It is only with that idea that clause (2) creates a limit. The creation of the limit itself gives a distinct character to the tax on profession and, therefore, a tax which is not fettered by a limit like one created by article 276(2) and which relates to the professional income cannot be viewed as a profession tax. A tax which the professional had to pay because he has had the privilege to carry on the profession or because he was carrying on the profession in a particular State is totally distinct and separate from the tax which he has to pay on services and which tax he would be able to pass on the customer who has had the advantage of his professional services. A professional tax covered under Entry 60 cannot be transferred in sharp contradistinction with the service tax, which is capable of being transferred to the customer who has the advantage of enjoying the services. Again, professional tax has to be paid whether a professional actually has given the professional service or not, whereas the service tax will not be payable if a professional like a chartered accountant or a cost accountant has in reality not rendered any professional services to a customer. These aspects are distinct aspects and, therefore, an aspect which entirely depends upon the services offered by the professional though may have a nexus with the profession, yet the service becomes a distinct aspect in itself and can be legitimately taxed by the Parliament under Entry 97 of List I as had been done in the instant case.

The petitioners also argued that the provisions of section 65(48 ) and section 67(r) and (s ) were confusing and arbitrary. The contention in short was that the services which the chartered accountants give is a bundle of service. It is akin to the services rendered by any professional including a medical practitioner and a lawyer and the relationship between a chartered accountant and his clients is like that of a lawyer and his client and it cannot be merely construed as a ‘service’ under the Finance Act 32 of 1990. The tone of the argument was that the Legislature has picked and chosen the chartered accountants or the cost accountants and left out the other professionals like doctors and lawyers.

This argument was obviously incorrect because it is for the Legislature to select any particular service or any particular subject for taxing. The tests of the vice of discrimination in a taxing law are less rigorous. In examining the allegations of a hostile discriminatory treatment what is looked into is not its phraseology, but the real effect of its provisions. Therefore, there would be no question of finding any fault with the Legislature for picking up the chartered accountants or the cost accountants or the architects also for taxing their services.

It was argued that the chartered accountant provides various kinds of services including the maintenance of accounts, auditing of the accounts, drawing up of balance-sheets, preparing annual reports, representing their clients before the tax authorities like representing the case before the higher authorities under section 144A of the Income-tax Act or appearing before the Commissioner, representing before the officers of the valuation cell of the Income-tax Department. He has to do multifarious jobs as drafting the appeal petitions, filing the same before the Commissioner or filing petitions under section 263 before the Commissioner and at times, a chartered accountant has to brief a lawyer when an appeal is filed before the Tribunal or in the higher courts. It was then pointed out that there are no guidelines in the impugned legislation to suggest, as to which precisely is the service which is a taxable service out of the multifarious services offered by the chartered accountants.

A practical difficulty was pointed out that the chartered accountants normally issue a composite bill for all these services and such bill cannot be split up with regard to the multifarious services offered by the chartered accountants. From this it was suggested that the concerned provisions suffered from the ‘vagueness’ and were confusing and as such, could be labelled as ‘arbitrary provisions’.

It is only the service offered by the chartered accountant in its ‘professional capacity’ which is made taxable and the services other than of auditing and accounting provided by the practising chartered accountant are exempted from service tax. Therefore, it cannot be said that there is any confusion regarding the taxable services. The notification issued under section 93 specifying that other services excepting the one for accounting and auditing is a complete answer to the argument. It specifically provides the services which are made taxable and the other services which are not taxable. This is besides the fact that there is a complete machinery available in the Act itself to decide the nature of the services. There is also a provision of appeal within the machinery of the Act and, therefore, it cannot be said that there can be confusion about the services offered by the chartered accountants or the cost accountants.

On a busy day in a CA firm, the most dangerous document left in the office is often not the audit report. It's the hurriedly signed one-page "certificate":

A turnover certificate rushed out for a tender.

A net worth certificate as per the requirements of various authorities.

An end-use certificate and a no-dues certificate are demanded "urgently" by bankers/lenders.

A GST compliance certificate as per the requirements of the indirect tax law

Many such certificates are drafted by staff, signed late in the evening, and forgotten the next morning. There is no engagement letter, no checklist, no management representation letter and sometimes no clear understanding of whether we are giving reasonable or limited assurance. A year later, if the bidder is blacklisted, the loan goes bad, or a regulator investigates misuse of funds, that one-page certificate becomes the central document. Behind it, there is often no work paper trail at all.

This is exactly the risk that Institute of Chartered Accountant of India ('ICAI') has tried to address through the "Guidance Note on Reports and Certificates for Special Purposes (Revised 2016) ('Guidance Note')" and the "Handbook on Certificates by Chartered Accountants – Comprehensive Checklist & Formats" issued in October 2025 by the Centre for Audit Quality ('Handbook'). The Guidance Note treats certificates as assurance engagements, not casual attestations, and the Handbook converts that principle into checklists, illustrative formats and tools that firms can actually use. Together with the UDIN framework and peer review expectations, they are reshaping what it means to "just sign a certificate".

This article attempts to convert that framework into a practical playbook for practitioners.

1. Certificates as "instruments of trust"

The Foreword to the Handbook describes certificates issued by Chartered Accountants as "instruments of trust" guiding the decisions of regulators, financial institutions, investors and other stakeholders. They are no longer seen merely as attestations of factual accuracy or compliance; they directly influence important economic and regulatory decisions.

The Handbook notes that Chartered Accountants are increasingly approached to issue certificates for a wide array of purposes, ranging from compliance with statutory regulations to supporting submissions to banks, government authorities and other stakeholders. Examples include net worth certificates, turnover certificates, fund utilisation certificates, working capital certificates, income/earnings certificates, stock or inventory valuation certificates and no statutory dues certificates. These certificates play a critical role in regulatory filings, tender submissions, banking processes and governmental clearances and are often tailored to the specific needs of the intended user and purpose.

The Preface emphasises that each certificate, regardless of its complexity, demands a high standard of professional judgment, independence and ethical responsibility, and that the act of issuing a certificate should never be seen as a routine clerical task.

2. The four pillar framework around certificates

From a practitioner's perspective, the current regulatory and professional framework around certificates essentially rests on four pillars:

2.1. Guidance Note on Reports and Certificates for Special Purposes (Revised 2016)

This provides the conceptual framework for engagements that require members to issue reports or certificates other than those issued in audits or reviews of historical financial information.

2.2. Handbook on Certificates by Chartered Accountants – Comprehensive Checklist & Formats (October 2025)

This Handbook explicitly "draws upon the principles laid down" in the Guidance Note and offers a structured checklist, FAQs and illustrative certificate formats to guide members in identifying, preparing and issuing certificates with due professional care.

2.3. ICAI checklist utility (Annexure I)

This is an Excel based tool and Annexure which contains an Index of certificates divided into three sections. Section A on applicability of various standards and guidance, Section B with a procedural checklist, and Section C with a completion checklist and documentation list.

2.4. UDIN framework and FAQs (Annexure II)

The UDIN system, mandated since February 2019 for all certificates where financial information is certified as true and fair / true and correct, provides traceability and authenticity and is supported by detailed FAQs..

Taken together, these four elements redefine certificate engagements as structured assurance assignments that are expected to withstand regulatory scrutiny and peer review.

3. What is a "certificate" for ICAI purposes?

Chapter 1 of the Handbook defines a certificate as a formal written document that affirms the truth, accuracy or authenticity of a specific fact, condition or status, based on verification or evidence. Typical examples include net worth certificates, turnover certificates and similar attestations.

The Handbook notes that Chartered Accountants are increasingly called upon to issue certificates that serve as formal confirmations of financial data, compliance with statutory requirements and fulfilment of specific conditions laid down by various authorities. These certificates often play a critical role in regulatory filings, tenders, banking and governmental processes, and unlike audit reports, they are frequently tailored to the unique needs of the user and purpose.

Whether the bundle of service, namely, finance assisting and negotiations, purchase of new materials and samples, etc., is a management consultancy services? No same would not fall under ‘Management consultancy services’. Maini Industrial Consultants v. CCE, Bangalore [2006] 4 STT 56 (Bang. - CESTAT). In the instant case, the appellant entered into the agreement to render bundle of services, namely, finance assisting and negotiations, purchase of new materials and samples, finding new markets, marketing strategies, efficient way of production by upgrading technology and human resource development. The department demanded service tax for the above activity under the category of ‘Management consultancy service’. Whether meter reading, billing & ledger posting fall under category of ‘Practising chartered accountant services’?

No. In Jaded Siddappa & Co. v. CST [2008] 12 STT 49 (Bang. - CESTAT), the question before the Tribunal was whether the activities carried out by Chartered Accountant such as opening ledger accounts, preparation of monthly bills, preparation of skeleton bills, recording of demand and recoveries, maintenance of daily abstract and tallying, preparation and issue of disconnection lists to field staff and preparation of Union MIS Statements and consolidated DCB statements would come within the ambit of ‘professional activity of practising Chartered Accountant’ or under any other alternative classification proposed subsequently? In the instant case, the service provider being a Chartered Accountant, obtained the outsourcing work from Mescom, Kptcl and KEB. The Tribunal held that the activity of outsourcing of meter reading, billing and ledger posting which was an activity to be done by the respective companies does not come within the ambit of the ‘professional activity of Chartered Accountant’ and, therefore, held that it is not subject to service tax.

Whether actual construction falls under ‘Real estate agent’s services’?

No. The Government in its Circular F. No. B-11/3/98-TRU, dated October 7, 1998 has clarified that activity of actual construction of any building, carried out by builders/developers does not attract service tax as it is not a service within the meaning of the term ‘Real estate agent’ or ‘Real estate consultant’. Further, the Government in its Circular No. 80/10/2004, dated September 17, 2004 has clarified that estate builders who construct buildings/civil structures for themselves are not taxable service providers.

Whether hiring of locker in a bank falls under the category of ‘Security agency services’?

Yes. In the case of Oriental Bank of Commerce v. State of U.P. [2009] 20 STT 529 (All.), the issue was whether banks providing lockers to their customers on rent are subject to VAT, and can it be termed as a transfer of right to use any goods. The High Court held that locker is part of safe deposit vault embedded to earth in the strong room of the bank, and is therefore, an immovable property, and, hence, it cannot be said to be goods or movable property. Therefore, hiring of locker in a bank falls under the category of ‘Security agency service’.

The challenge in a nutshell is to the exclusion of Advocates and Sales Tax Practitioners from doing the work of audit under section 61. [Para 11]

To consider the challenge under articles 14 and 19(1)(g) one may refer to section 44AB of the Income tax Act, 1961. This provision as in the instant case provides for audit of persons whose total sales or turnover or gross receipts exceed forty lakhs per year. This provision was challenged before the various High Courts. The Supreme Court in an appeal before it, has upheld the legality of the section. Once the Supreme Court in T.D. Venkata Rao v. Union of India AIR 1999 SC 2242 has upheld the legality of section 44AB of the Income-tax Act, 1961 where the same terminology was used and which was also a provision pertaining to audit, and considering the object of both the provisions which is prevention of evasion of tax dues, the challenge by the petitioners on the ground of infraction of articles 14 and 19 of the Constitution will have to be similarly rejected. There are practically no distinguishing features. The only distinction, if any, is that, whereas section 44AB of 1961 Act is for the purpose of ascertaining "total income", section 61 is for certification whether VAT has been correctly assessed, collected and paid. [Para 16]

The challenge based on article 14 is to be rejected on the following grounds :

(i)Chartered Accountants by reason of their training have special aptitude in the matter of audit. An Income Tax Practitioner does not have the same expertise as the Chartered Accountants in the matter of accounts. The argument, therefore, that the effect of such a provision will be to exclude all other categories of authorized representatives except the Chartered Accountants from carrying on their profession is liable to be rejected, as they constitute two distinct classes having a nexus with the object of the provisions, which is evasion of tax dues.

(ii)The contention that such a provision brings in an oppressive restriction is also liable to be rejected as auditing accounts is a specialized job. It may be true that some Income Tax Practitioners may also acquire that skill by sheer practice without passing the necessary examination. But that does not preclude Parliament from prescribing special qualification with reference to the auditing of accounts.

The classification, in the instant case, is reasonable and has a nexus with the object which is to direct a class of dealers getting their accounts audited by a specialized agency so that there is no tax evasion. What is relevant is to consider the object of the Act and in selecting the class of professionals whether the legislature has acted unreasonably or has imposed unreasonable restrictions on the right of the assessee and or Income Tax Practitioners to carry on their occupation or profession. The settled law on the subject is that as long as the twin tests of reasonableness of the classification and nexus with the object are satisfied, wisdom of legislation cannot be substituted. The State Legislature is free to decide in its wisdom as to how best to safeguard the State revenue the different States may adopt different standards and policy of one legislature may not be adopted by another Legislature as the matter lies in the domain of policy making. Because some States have permitted Sales Tax Practitioners to carry on audit need not necessarily mean that as the Legislature of the State of Maharashtra has not so provided, that would be arbitrary or that the classification considering the nexus of the object is arbitrary. It is for the State Legislature to decide how to protect its revenue and this is more true with regard to economic legislation. [Para 20]

The Act was enacted pursuant to a decision to introduce VAT system in the country. An empowered committee of Finance Ministers was appointed. Eligibility of small service provider

1. A Firm of chartered accountants has the gross billing for the year ending on 31-3-2006 as under:— Since the service provided by the firm with respect to audit was only 2.30 Lakh hence the firm is not collecting and paying service tax in the year 2006-07 on the assumption that it is eligible for the benefit of exemption available to the small service providers as per Notification No.6/2005-ST, dated 1-3-2005 (F.No.334/1/2005-TRU) up to the value of 4 Lakh of collection. Please advise properly.

The total taxable service rendered by this firm of Rs.4.30 Lakhs in the previous year ended on 31-3-2006 hence the firm is not eligible for the exemption scheme available to this firm.

For this purpose there is clear provision in the Notification No.6/2005-ST, dated 1-3-2005 (F.No.334/1/2005-TRU) in the form of conditions mentioned in clause 2 of the scheme. The exact wording of clause 2(viii) is as under:—

"(viii)The aggregate value of taxable services rendered by a provider of taxable service from one or more premises, does not exceed rupees four lakhs in the preceding financial year."

Here, to be eligible for exemption scheme available to small service providers, the aggregate value of taxable service should not be more than Rupees 4 Lakh in the preceding financial year and both the Audit services and taxation services were part of taxable service though the tax was exempt on the taxation services. Let us see the exact wordings of the Exemption Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated 16-10-1998 in this respect:—

In exercise of the powers conferred by section 93 of the Finance Act, 1994(32 of 1994); and in suppression of the notification of the Government of India in the Ministry of Finance (Department of Revenue) No. 57/98 Service tax, dated 7-10-1998, the Central Government, being satisfied that it is necessary in the Public interest so to do, hereby exempts the taxable service provided by a practising chartered accountant, in his professional capacity to a client, other than the taxable service related to—

(i)Accounting and auditing; or

(ii)to (xi) Various services Like certification etc. mentioned,

from whole of the service tax leviable thereon.

Here that the service is taxable but this taxable service is exempt from paying the whole of tax. The point here is that the taxable service is exempt from paying the tax and in that case its structure of taxable service remained intact but the tax payable on it is exempt.

Hence the value of taxable service provided by the firm of Chartered Accountant is Rs. 4.30 Lakhs and as per provisions of clause 2(viii) of the exemption notification, the service provider having turnover of taxable service over Rs.4 Lakhs is not eligible for exemption scheme provided to the small service provider.

Though while claiming exemption under this notification "the aggregate value not exceeding Rupees 4 Lakhs" means excluding the taxable service on which no service tax is payable and this has been provided in Explanation (B) the said notification and the "the aggregate value not exceeding Rupees 4 Lakhs" is applicable for the claiming the exemption but to ascertain the status "Small service provider" and the eligibility of the assessee to claim the exemption which is based on "the aggregate value of taxable service rendered" of the previous year, no such explanation is issued and in absence of any clarification from the Government in this respect,the opinion mentioned above is given.

The term "accountant" has been defined in clause (i) of section 92F as under:

"accountant" shall have the same meaning as in the Explanation below subsection (2) of section 288.

The above-mentioned Explanation reads as under:

"accountant" means a chartered accountant as defined in clause (b) of subsection (1) of section 2 of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 (38 of 1949) who holds a valid certificate of practice under sub-section (1) of section 6 of that Act, but does not include [except for the purposes of representing the Assessee under sub-section (1)]

Therefore, the meaning of "accountant" now applies for the definition of an "Authorized Representative" under section 288(2). As a result, in order to be appointed as an Authorized Representative for an Assessee for any proceedings under the Act, a Chartered Accountant must have a certificate of practice. However, a Chartered Accountant having any other qualification specified in section 288 may be appointed as an Authorized Representative.

Therefore, after this amendment, a Chartered Accountant who does not satisfy both the following conditions cannot be appointed as an Authorized Representative for an Assessee:

He/she does not have a certificate of practice; and

He/she does not have any other specified qualification.

Section 92E does not stipulate that only the statutory auditor appointed under the Companies Act or other similar statute should perform the examination. The examination can, therefore, be conducted either by the statutory auditor or by any other chartered accountant in practice having certificate of practice.

The accountant should obtain from the Assessee a letter of appointment for conducting the examination as mentioned in section 92E. It is advisable that such an appointment letter should be signed by the person competent to sign/verify the return of income in terms of the provisions of section 140 or by any person who has been authorized by the company to make such an appointment. The accountant should get the statement of particulars, as required in the annexure to the report, authenticated by the Assessee before he proceeds to verify the same. The accountant is required to submit his report to the person appointing him viz. the Assessee.

The Act prohibits a relative or an employee of the Assessee being appointed as an accountant under section 92E. Also, as per a decision of the Council (reported in the Code of Ethics under clause (4) of Part I of Second Schedule), a chartered accountant who is in employment of a concern or in any other concern under the same management cannot be appointed as an auditor of that concern. Therefore, an employee of an Assessee or an employee of a concern under the same management cannot examine the accounts and records of an Assessee under section 92E.

An accountant responsible for writing or the maintenance of the books of account of the Assessee should not examine such accounts. This principle will apply to the partner of such an accountant as well as to the firm in which he is a partner. In view of this, an accountant who is responsible for writing or the maintenance of the books of account, his partner or the firm in which he is a partner should not accept the examination assignment under section 92E in the case of such an Assessee.

Similarly, an internal auditor of the Assessee cannot conduct the examination if he is an employee of the Assessee. However, an accountant or a firm of accountants appointed as tax consultants of the Assessee can conduct the examination under section 92E.

In the case of an examination, the accountant is required to express his opinion as to whether the Assessee has maintained the proper information and documents, as prescribed, in respect of the international transactions entered into by him. As regards the statement of particulars to be annexed to the report, he is required to give his opinion as to whether the particulars are true and correct. In giving his report the accountant will have to use his professional skill and expertise and apply such tests as the circumstances of the case may require, considering the contents of the report.

The report by the accountant given under section 92E sets forth such particulars as have been prescribed in Form 3CEB. In order that the accountant may be in a position to explain any question which may arise later on, it is necessary that he should keep detailed notes about the evidence on which he has relied upon while conducting the examination and also maintain all his working papers. Such working papers should include his notes on the following, amongst other matters:

work done while conducting the examination and by whom;

explanations and information given to him during the course of the examination and by whom;

decision on the various points taken;

the judicial pronouncements relied upon by him while making the report;

certificates issued by the client

Section 92E requires certification by way of a report from a chartered accountant in the prescribed Form 3CEB. It is understood that chartered accountant is not responsible for the choice of the method but only for the working on the basis of which the choice is made by the assessee. In the result, the choice is left to the assessee with no requirement on the part of the chartered accountant to certify that the method chosen is the MAP. This is a glaring defect, since the assessee is not likely to have the necessary expertise. Again, column 13 of the Form requires certification of the arm’s length price as computed by the assessee on the single method chosen by him and does not provide for arithmetical means of more than one method, so as to require certification of application of two methods, where more than one arm’s length price is available with option of the assessee to vary the same by 5 per cent. The result is that, the Assessing Officer, it can be said, does not get all the assistance that may be expected from such a certificate.

Not surprisingly, the choice of the method is a disputed issue in almost every case. 2 SECTION 65(105)(s ) - CHARTERED ACCOUNTANT SERVICES - CONSTITUTIONALITY

History of service tax on chartered accountants

2.1 A brief legislative history is that service tax was, for the first time, imposed by the Finance Act, 1994. This tax was levied on three types of services. Later on the scope of this tax has been widened almost in every Budget. Service tax on practising chartered accountants was introduced with effect from 16-10-1998 by the Notification No. 53/98-Service Tax, dated 7-10-1998. But there were protests against this levy by the CA community all over India. One of the main causes of protest was that, while the service tax was levied on Chartered Accountants’ services, but the same was not levied on the similar services provided by an advocate. Also in case of Jodhpur Chartered Accountants Society v. CCE [1998] STT 33/(105) ELT 290 (Raj.) [dated 24th November, 1998], the operation and implementation of Notification No. 53/98-Service Tax, dated 7-10-1998, was stayed and kept in abeyance so far as its application was concerned to the practising chartered accountants practising in the State of Rajasthan. Also, in many of the other cases, the stay was granted. Thus, due to protest against the levy by chartered accountants and certain Court decisions, the levy was restricted by Notification No. 57/98-ST, dated 7-10-1998 only on auditing and accounting services. So, the services provided by CAs and Advocates, which can be of similar nature, remain out of service tax. But the later developments are of crucial and patently of discriminatory nature.

Notification No. 57/98-ST, dated 7-10-1998, was superseded by Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated 16-10-1998. From this notification, the nature of services was made more explicit as compared to Notification No. 57/98-ST, dated 7-10-1998. But this is not all which happens to these professionals. Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated 16-10-1998 was amended by Notification No. 15/2002-ST, dated 1-8-2002 w.e.f. 1-8-2002 by inserting an Explanation under this notification. This Explanation provides that, "Nothing contained in this notification shall apply to the services provided by a practising chartered accountant, a practising company secretary or a practising cost accountant which may fall in any other taxable services as defined in clause (105) of section 65 of the said Act". Also, the same was clarified by the following illustration:

"The service provided by a practising chartered accountant, a practising company secretary or a practising cost accountant in connection with the management of any organisation in any manner or recruitment of manpower in any manner shall be deemed to be the taxable service provided under the category of management consultant or manpower recruitment agency, as the case may be. Therefore, no exemption under this notification shall be applicable to such practising chartered accountant, a practising company secretary or a practising cost accountant."

Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Methods for determination of - Cost plus method) - Assessment year 2011-12 - During assessment proceedings, Assessing Officer found that assessee entered into international transactions with its AEs worth Rs. 12.54 lakhs - Assessing Officer directed assessee to furnish details of transactions and method adopted for determining Arm's Length Price (ALP) - Assessee stated that it had applied Cost Plus Method (CPM) for determining ALP on basis of agreement entered into with AE.s and basis is adapted as per agreement was mark-up of 23.45 per cent on salary and rent expenses incurred by assessee - Assessing Officer directed assessee to explain as to why mark-up should not be applied to entire cost incurred since assessee was rendering exclusive services to AE.s - On reply, however, Assessing Officer opined that assessee did not file an explanation with regard to proposed mark-up adjustment - Considering available material, Assessing Officer held that assessee had not submitted any documentary evidence like transfer of shares, appointment of new directors to substantiate its claim and certificate of chartered accountant of foreign entity was without any authority - One of directors in company was existing director and shareholder in assessee company is on close of balance sheet date i.e. 31-3-2011 and audit report was filed almost after one and half year from date of entry of shareholders/directors of foreign entities and there was no reason as to why assessee had not disclosed such vital facts of time of filing audit report - Thus, Assessing Officer rejected claim of assessee and held that two entities were AE's of assessee and transactions entered by it with them were squarely covered under definition of IT within meaning of provisions of section 92 - As regards proposed adjustment and working of CPM, Assessing Officer held that assessee had not submitted any explanation as to why other than salary and rent had not been included in invoices raised and mark-up had been charged thereon and assessee was into service sectors and was providing software related services to AE's involving lead restrictive utilities and method followed by assessee was not in accordance with provisions of Act, and entire cost was required to be taken into consideration for applying mark-up under CPM - Since, assessee had failed to do so total amount of expenditure debited to profit  loss account had to be considered as qualifying amount for mark-up on invoices to be raised on AE's as per method applied by it, Assessing Officer made an upward adjustment to total income of assessee under section 92C(4) - On appeal, after considering submission of assessee and assessment order, FAA held that assessee had argued that Star and DTL were not its AE's and it had merely submitted a copy of certificate issued by chartered accountant of AE and certificate was not supported by any documentary evidence like transfer of shares hence, argument was not acceptable - Further FAA held that assessee had not filed an explanation with regard to mark-up rate of 23.45 per cent for expenses other than salary and rent and assessee had not produced any documentary evidence with regard to annual reports of other companies for verification and it had not filed any TP study report during assessment proceedings for appellate proceedings and it had not followed provisions of section 92, thus, assessee had not discharged its primary onus of benchmarking transaction and upheld order of Assessing Officer - Whether since assessee did not file any confirmation or certificate from auditors about incorrectness of audit report especially about existence of AE's therefore, order of FAA does not suffer from any legal infirmity - Held, yes - Whether since assessee had included only two of items of profit and loss account i.e. salary and rent, and had not included other charges for determining ALP then mark-up determined as 23.45 per cent needs further verification on part of Assessing Officer and if assessee had not incurred any expenditure for alleged three items same should not be considered for mark-up purposes - Held, yes [Para 5] [Partly in favour of assessee]

Crux of the provisions relating to audit 2. Section 61 of the Maharashtra VAT Act requires that in certain cases the dealer shall get his accounts audited by an accountant within the prescribed period and furnish within the prescribed period the report of such audit in prescribed form. The form should be duly signed and verified by such accountant. For the purposes of this section ‘accountant’ has been defined to mean a chartered accountant within the meaning of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949. Section 61 was amended by the Amendment Act No. 25 of 2007 to include within the meaning of the term ‘accountant’, a cost accountant also and, thus, cost accountants have also been authorised to conduct such VAT audit. Failure to comply with the provisions of the section attracts penalty. Section 82 of the Act vests in sales tax practitioners and others set out therein, the right of appearance before any authority in proceedings under the Act.

Grounds of challenge

3. The question before the Court was whether under section 61, the exercise of getting the accounts audited, can be said to be part of the right to appear and plead before the Courts or judicial forums and/or getting the accounts audited is part of the right conferred by section 82 or in the alternative excluding categories other than chartered accountants and cost accountants is arbitrary or violative of the rights of those excluded categories to carry on their trade or profession. The challenges to the vires of section 61 were mainly as under :

(a)Since, 1946, apart from chartered accountants, it was open to all categories of persons described in section 82, having sufficient expertise and qualifications, to do the accounts as also audit work. Section 61 has resulted in divisive exclusion of advocates and sales tax practitioners, as the traders would not like to engage services of sales tax practitioners or advocates for certification. The result is that a large section of practitioners in mofusil area and small towns will be rendered out of the practice and, consequently, adversely affecting their livelihood. As there is no reasonable basis for the exclusion, the provision is arbitrary being violative of article 14 of the Constitution.

(b)The sole object and purpose of section 61(1) is that every dealer who is covered by clauses (a) and ( b) should get his returns verified and get his tax liability assessed by a professional so as to enable them to provide the information required to furnish a report under rule 65 of the Maharashtra VAT Rules, 2005 and to fill out prescribed Form. This purpose and object completely exhausts the scope of section 61. If this being so, the requirement of chartered accountants alone for the certification is wholly irrelevant and arbitrary.

(c)Once the provisions of section 82 have brought all practitioners in one class, creating a minimum classification by the Explanation to section 61, which does not appear to have any distinguishing marks for subserving the object sought to be achieved, causes equals to be treated unequally. This violates the equality right under article 14.

(d)Section 22 also provides for audit. There is no indication of any requirement of audit before filing of returns and as such section 61 is directly in conflict with section 22 and is ultra vires the scope of section 22. Section 22(3) permits the audit to be conducted by an officer who may not be a chartered accountant. Section 61 which requires an audit only by a chartered accountant is, therefore, discriminatory. There is no reason why section 61 audit cannot also be conducted by a person who is not a chartered accountant.

(e)Section 61 also suffers from arbitrariness as it violates article 14 by being classificatory. Section 61(1)(a) and (b) create two classes. If the object of section 61 is to create a class of taxpayers who would be liable to pay tax, then the classification with reference to turnover exceeding Rs. 40 lakhs is understandable. However, the creation of another class under section 61(1)(b), namely, dealers in liquor, irrespective of their turn over is an arbitrary classification, having no nexus with the object of section 61, viz., to tax traders whose turnover exceeds Rs. 40 lakhs.

(f)The legal compliances under the law are administered by the Sales Tax Officers who are not chartered accountants and yet they are entitled to check up the work of audit which is in the form of normal audit as also assessment in the same manner as required by the chartered accountant. By denying to the advocates and sales tax practitioners, the right to certify under section 61, it has violated their right to carry on profession.

(g)The mandatory provision of engaging services of chartered accountants is not based on any object of the Act and as such the provision is not within the legislative competence of the respondent State as an ancillary provision.

EXCISE/ST/VAT : Certificates issued by qualified professionals like Cost Accountants, Chartered Accountants, Chartered Engineers should not be brushed aside merely because corroborative evidence not produced

TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee company was engaged in export of customers electronic data to its AEs, a comparable company, earning revenue from operation which mainly included activities of certification, recertification, safety audit, HSE management system for offshore and onshore oil and gas facilities, third-party inspection of equipment and installation in hydrocarbon and other sectors, could not be accepted as valid comparable

is liable to be rejected, as they constitute two distinct classes having a nexus with the object of the provisions, which is evasion of tax dues.

(ii)The contention that such a provision brings in an oppressive restriction is also liable to be rejected as auditing accounts is a specialized job. It may be true that some Income Tax Practitioners may also acquire that skill by sheer practice without passing the necessary examination. But that does not preclude Parliament from prescribing special qualification with reference to the auditing of accounts. (iii)Legal Practitioners and Chartered Accountants are equal for the purpose of representation of assessee before Assessing Authority but they are not equals for the purpose of compulsory audit. The preferential treatment given to the Chartered Accountants for the purpose of compulsory audit does not militate against the rule of equality under article 14 of the Constitution. The terms "audit", "auditing" and the "functions of auditor" clearly bring about the difference between the Chartered Accountants and others. The object and purpose in providing compulsory audit is to facilitate the prevention of evasion of taxes, administrative convenience in quick and proper completion of assessments etc. In the light of this object, Chartered Accountants and others cannot be said to be similarly situate. The qualifications and eligibility to be enrolled as Income Tax Practitioners are entirely different from that of Chartered Accountants from the point of view of auditing.

(iv)Merely because apart from dealers whose turnover is more than 40 lakhs, dealers dealing in liquor trade have also to get their accounts audited does not make the provision arbitrary. Such dealers are a class by themselves as they are carrying on a trade which is res extra commercium. They constitute a class by themselves and if the Legislature in its wisdom has provided that their accounts should be audited, it is neither unreasonable nor treating them as a class arbitrary.

The classification, in the instant case, is reasonable and has a nexus with the object which is to direct a class of dealers getting their accounts audited by a specialized agency so that there is no tax evasion. [Para 19]

On behalf of petitioners, a distinction was sought to be made in certification under Income-tax Act and under the VAT Act. The legality of the provisions or its non-arbitrariness is not dependent on the manner in which the form has to be filled, the contents thereof and the procedure. What is relevant is to consider the object of the Act and in selecting the class of professionals whether the legislature has acted unreasonably or has imposed unreasonable restrictions on the right of the assessee and or Income Tax Practitioners to carry on their occupation or profession. It must be noted that the Chartered Accountant cannot certify the correctness and completeness of the sales tax returns unless they audit the accounts of the dealer as maintained in the first part of section 61. After audit Chartered Accountant has to certify the various items in Part I of Form No. 704. These items are subject to audited Chartered Accountant’s observations and comments about the non-compliance, shortcomings, deficiencies, in the return filed by the dealer. There are various other requirements. Suffice it to say that it is a specialized job which can only be undertaken by the person professionally competent and trained to audit. Advocates are not qualified. The other sales tax practitioner and retired employees definitely not. [Para 19]

The settled law on the subject is that as long as the twin tests of reasonableness of the classification and nexus with the object are satisfied, wisdom of legislation cannot be substituted. The State Legislature is free to decide in its wisdom as to how best to safeguard the State revenue the different States may adopt different standards and policy of one legislature may not be adopted by another Legislature as the matter lies in the domain of policy making. Because some States have permitted Sales Tax Practitioners to carry on audit need not necessarily mean that as the Legislature of the State of Maharashtra has not so provided, that would be arbitrary or that the classification considering the nexus of the object is arbitrary. It is for the State Legislature to decide how to protect its revenue and this is more true with regard to economic legislation. [Para 20]

Section 65(105)(j) - Clearing and Forwarding Agent’s Services - Whether service receiver can deduct amount of service tax from service provider’s bill

6.2 Facts The respondent, a transport contractor, entered into a contract with the appellant for handling of its materials. During the pendency of the said contract, section 65 was substituted by section 88 whereby 5 per cent service tax was introduced on various services including ‘clearing and forwarding (C&F) agent’. The appellant, consequently, deducted 5 per cent service tax from the respondent’s bills on the assumption that the respondent was a C&F agent from 31-10-1997 in spite of respondent’s objections. On reference, the sole arbitrator dismissed the respondent’s objection. On petition filed by the respondent, the Single Judge of the High Court allowed the same by setting aside the impugned award.

Decision of Bombay High Court:

u The High Court held that the constitutional validity with regard to the extension of service tax in view of the amendment to the Finance Act, 2000, section 116(a) and section 65(6) to treat the recipients of the services as an assessee in case of services rendered by goods transport operators and clearing and forwarding agents, was upheld by the Supreme Court in Gujarat Ambuja Cements Ltd. v. Union of India [2005] 1 STT 41.

u The High Court further held that Single Judge had set aside the award passed by the arbitrator by which the arbitrator held that the appellant was entitled to deduct the service tax amount from the amount payable to the respondent. Admittedly, the appellant was recipient of the service of the respondents as per the agreement-in-question. The appellant, pursuant to the provisions of service tax was registered and recognized as an ‘assessee’ and had also filed returns as contemplated accordingly. The appellant, therefore, was liable to pay the service tax being the recipient of the services from the respondent. Admittedly, there was no specific agreement with regard to payment of service tax-in-question by the respondent to the extent the appellant would be entitled to deduct the amount so paid or payable under the service tax, though the respondent was not an assessee and/or not liable to pay service tax under the law. There was no specific clause that such service tax liability would be deductible from the amount payable by the appellant to the respondent pursuant to the contract-in-question. The deduction as claimed and as directed by the award in absence of any agreement or clause, therefore, was not correct. The department, on application filed by the applicant, already rejected the specific claim of refund of that amount.

u The High Court further observed that there was nothing to show even from the plain reading of the agreement and the clauses thereof that, payment of service tax, though payable by the ‘assessee’, yet it would be the respondent, the service provider, to re-pay the same to the appellant and, therefore, the appellant was entitled to deduct service tax from the bills of the respondent in terms of the clauses of the agreement. The Single Judge, therefore, was right in reversing the award passed by the arbitrator. The agreement nowhere entitled the appellant to deduct and/or to recover such service tax from the respondent. Therefore, the High Court held, as rightly held by the Single Judge, that the award was, on the face of it, illegal and erroneous.

[Rastriya Ispat Nigam Ltd. v. Dewan Chand Ram Saran [2008] 14 STT 328 (Bom.)]

Thus the word 'audit' has a specific connotation in the matter of examination, investigation and auditing of accounts, where detection of fraud is of primary importance. [Para 10]

The challenge in a nutshell is to the exclusion of Advocates and Sales Tax Practitioners from doing the work of audit under section 61. [Para 11] To consider the challenge under articles 14 and 19(1)(g) one may refer to section 44AB of the Income tax Act, 1961. This provision as in the instant case provides for audit of persons whose total sales or turnover or gross receipts exceed forty lakhs per year. This provision was challenged before the various High Courts. The Supreme Court in an appeal before it, has upheld the legality of the section. Once the Supreme Court in T.D. Venkata Rao v. Union of India AIR 1999 SC 2242 has upheld the legality of section 44AB of the Income-tax Act, 1961 where the same terminology was used and which was also a provision pertaining to audit, and considering the object of both the provisions which is prevention of evasion of tax dues, the challenge by the petitioners on the ground of infraction of articles 14 and 19 of the Constitution will have to be similarly rejected. There are practically no distinguishing features. The only distinction, if any, is that, whereas section 44AB of 1961 Act is for the purpose of ascertaining "total income", section 61 is for certification whether VAT has been correctly assessed, collected and paid. [Para 16]

The challenge based on article 14 is to be rejected on the following grounds:

(i )

Chartered Accountants by reason of their training have special aptitude in the matter of audit. An Income Tax Practitioner does not have the same expertise as the Chartered Accountants in the matter of accounts. The argument, therefore, that the effect of such a provision will be to exclude all other categories of authorized representatives except the Chartered Accountants from carrying on their profession is liable to be rejected, as they constitute two distinct classes having a nexus with the object of the provisions, which is evasion of tax dues.

(ii )

The contention that such a provision brings in an oppressive restriction is also liable to be rejected as auditing accounts is a specialized job. It may be true that some Income Tax Practitioners may also acquire that skill by sheer practice without passing the necessary examination. But that does not preclude Parliament from prescribing special qualification with reference to the auditing of accounts.

(iii )

Legal Practitioners and Chartered Accountants are equal for the purpose of representation of assessee before Assessing Authority but they are not equals for the purpose of compulsory audit. The preferential treatment given to the Chartered Accountants for the purpose of compulsory audit does not militate against the rule of equality under article 14 of the Constitution. The terms "audit", "auditing" and the "functions of auditor" clearly bring about the difference between the Chartered Accountants and others. The object and purpose in providing compulsory audit is to facilitate the prevention of evasion of taxes, administrative convenience in quick and proper completion of assessments etc. In the light of this object, Chartered Accountants and others cannot be said to be similarly situate. The qualifications and eligibility to be enrolled as Income Tax Practitioners are entirely different from that of Chartered Accountants from the point of view of auditing.

(iv )

Merely because apart from dealers whose turnover is more than 40 lakhs, dealers dealing in liquor trade have also to get their accounts audited does not make the provision arbitrary. Such dealers are a class by themselves as they are carrying on a trade which is res extra commercium. They constitute a class by themselves and if the Legislature in its wisdom has provided that their accounts should be audited, it is neither unreasonable nor treating them as a class arbitrary.

The classification, in the instant case, is reasonable and has a nexus with the object which is to direct a class of dealers getting their accounts audited by a specialized agency so that there is no tax evasion. [Para 19]

FACT: The assessee dealing in LPG sent LPG through tank trucks to various LPG bottling plants of oil distribution companies.

Whenever LPG tank truck required any repair or mandatory testing of safety valves, the tank truck was cleaned and completely degassed. During this activity, water was filled in tank mounted on the truck and discharged. Water was displaced by LPG vapors. For this activity, the assessee collected cost of water and the labour charges from the truck owner.

The Adjudicating Authority held that the said activities undertaken by the assessee would fall under the category of 'technical inspection and certification service' and raised tax demand upon it.

The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the impugned order.

On second appeal:

HELD: The assessee though is performing certain activities in relation to maintenance and safety of the tank trucks and is issuing a certificate to the effect that the tank trucks are purged/degassed, same cannot be considered to be a service within scope of 'technical inspection and certification service'. It is to be understood that the assessee is not basically an agency involved with the testing and certification. In fact, it is abundantly clear that it is performing certain activities which make the tank truck fit to be filled with LPG for further transportation. This is to be construed only as an activity related to the safety and maintenance of the tank truck. The assessee has not fulfilled the conditions so as to impart the activity of purging and degassing tank truck as 'technical inspection and certification service'. [Para 5]

HEADNOTE: Section 65(108) of the Finance Act, 1994 - Technical inspection and certification service - Period 1-7-2003 to 31-3-2004 - Assessee was operating as licensed registrar under office of AQA, USA - It represented AQA for purpose of assisting clients in achievement of ISO 9000, ISO 14000 and QS 9000 certifications - It received Company Information Sheet (CIS) from prospective clients, reviewed CIS, prepared quotation and sent same to clients, provided information connected with quality management system certification, conducted audit/assessment of quality system at clients’ place with reference to ISO standard and after successful completion of assessment process, sent such assessment report to AQA - It charged audit fee for doing audit work from clients - Revenue treated said service of assessee as that of ‘Technical inspection and certification agency’ and demanded service tax - Whether word ‘process’ mentioned in definition of ‘Technical inspection and certification’ can relate only to physical and chemical processes and it cannot be transported to province of management relating to human beings - Held, yes - Whether therefore, activities carried out by assessee for certification of quality management system practised by clients, would not come within purview of ‘Technical inspection and certification service’ - Held, yes [Para 5.2] Words & Phrases : Word ‘process’ as occurring in section 65(108) of the Finance Act, 1994 Interpretation of statutes : Principles of Ejusdem Generis

FACT: The assessee was operating as licenced registrar under the office of AQA, USA. As per the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between the parties, the assessee was to represent AQA for the purpose of assisting clients in achievement of ISO 9000, ISO 14000 and QS 9000 certificates. It used to receive Company Information Sheet (CIS) from prospective clients, review the CIS, prepare quotation and send same to prospective clients, provide information connected with Quality Management System (QMS) certification, conduct audit/assessment of the quality system at client’s place with reference to ISO standard and after successful completion of the assessment process, send such assessment to AQA, which issues above certificates. For doing the audit work, the assessee charged certain fee as audit fee from the prospective customers. The revenue treated the service of the assessee as that of ‘technical inspection and certification agency’ and demanded service tax. The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the demand.

On appeal :

HELD: The assessee received certain consideration for the services rendered by it. Without going into the nitty-gritty, it could be safely concluded that the activities of the assessee were pre-requisites for any client in India to obtain ISO certification. However, the certification relates only to management system or management processes. The principles of ejusdem generis are clearly applicable in the interpretation of the word ‘process’ which is found in the definition of ‘technical inspection and certification service’. No doubt, the said word keeps company with the other words ‘goods or material or immovable property’. These inspections relate only to activities connected with matter. In other words, the ‘process’ mentioned in the definition can relate only to physical and chemical processes. It cannot be transported to the province of management relating to human beings. In other words, the activities carried out by the assessee for certification of quality management system practised by clients would not come within the purview of ‘Technical inspection and certification service’. Further, the assessee had carried out the audit of quality of various schools and organizations. Obviously, these processes would not relate to matter or immovable property. [Para 5.2]

The assessee had stated that on its, own it had approached the Department as early as on 18-8-2003 with regard to the taxability of its services. However, the show-cause notice, dated 7-1-2005, had invoked the longer period, which is invoked for only suppression of facts, mis-statement or fraud with an intent to evade tax. In the instant case, the ingredients for invocation of longer period were not present. Hence, invocation of the longer period was not sustainable. In view of the above, there was no merit in the impugned order and the same was to be set aside. [Para 5.3]

The assessee was giving inspection related services. Another undisputed fact was that the assessee was contracted for inspecting and reporting on the work done by another party on the construction site. CBEC Circular No. 59/8/03-ST, dated 20-6-2003, clarified that the new service ‘Technical inspection and certification service’ will cover certification of all types including that of immovable property. If that be so, there was no reason to interfere with the order of the learned Commissioner (Appeals) who had held so. [Para 4]

The services provided by the assessee would get covered under ‘Technical inspection and certification services’ with effect from the date it had been notified in the statute ,and the said services cannot be covered under ‘Consulting engineer’s services’. In view of this, the revenue’s appeal was devoid of merits and the impugned order was liable to be upheld. [Para 5]

Legislature to select any particular service or any particular subject for taxing. The tests of the vice of discrimination in a taxing law are less rigorous. In examining the allegations of a hostile discriminatory treatment what is looked into is not its phraseology, but the real effect of its provisions. Therefore, there would be no question of finding any fault with the Legislature for picking up the chartered accountants or the cost accountants or the architects also for taxing their services. [Paras 37 & 38] It was argued that the chartered accountant provides various kinds of services, including the maintenance of accounts, auditing of the accounts, drawing up of balance sheets, preparing annual reports, representing their clients before the tax authorities-like representing the case before the higher authorities under section 144A of the Income-tax Act or appearing before the Commissioner, representing before the officers of the valuation cell of the Income-tax Department. He has to do multifarious jobs, such as drafting the appeal petitions, filing the same before the Commissioner or filing petitions under section 263 before the Commissioner and, at times, a chartered accountant has to brief a lawyer when an appeal is filed before the Tribunal or in the Higher Courts. It was then pointed out that there are no guidelines in the impugned legislation to suggest as to which precisely is the service which is a taxable service out of the multifarious services offered by the chartered accountants. [Para 39]

A practical difficulty was pointed out that the chartered accountants normally issue a composite bill for all these services and such bill cannot be split up with regard to the multifarious services offered by the chartered accountants. From this, it could be said that the concerned provisions suffered from the ‘vagueness’ and were confusing and, as such, could be labelled as ‘arbitrary provisions’. [Para 40]

It is only the service offered by the chartered accountant in its ‘professional capacity’ which is made taxable and the services other than of auditing and accounting provided by the practising chartered accountant are exempted from service tax. Therefore, it cannot be said that there is any confusion regarding the taxable services. The notification issued under section 93, specifying that other services, excepting the one for accounting and auditing, is a complete answer to the argument. It specifically describes the services which are made taxable and the other services which are not taxable. This is besides the fact that there is a complete machinery available in the Act itself to decide the nature of the services. There is also a provision of appeal within the machinery of the Act and, therefore, it cannot be said that there can be confusion about the services offered by the chartered accountants or the cost accountants. [Para 41]

The impugned provisions did not in any manner offend article 14 of the Constitution. The petition had no merit and was liable to be dismissed. [Para 41]

TC services relate to commodities, the scope includes acid value, moisture and impurities, beta carotene, AOCS, PFA, physical parameters of the grains. The inspection of the ship tank done by the surveyor involves testing of steam heating coils. The moisture content analysis is carried out by Toulene Distillation method. Samples are kept. The remittance information narration in the bank's document shows nature of the remittance as 'Quality Analysis Fee'. [Para 8.2] The IVTC services specific to certification with reference to a factory assessment services extends to production capability, quality system, health and safety measures and is carried out as per ISO9001 standards. Findings on factory strengths/weaknesses and recommendations for improvements/development is also stated. [Para 8.3]

With the description of services it is not difficult to come to the conclusion that the services which the applicant is rendering for a fee is a technical service rendered by carrying out tests and certifying that the goods imported/exported confirmed to certain specifications. Inspection and survey of imported/exported cargo and certifying in relation to quality and price; laboratory testing; certification services for assuring quality; testing of samples; rendering technical assistance in preparation of project reports are held to be 'technical services'. The reports are produced by experienced surveyors, coordinators, chemists and inspectors. The reports are highly technical in nature and help the customers to protect their immediate and long term financial interests during cargo loading/unloading and storage, transport custody and other business activities. The purpose for which the report is prepared is not diluted or perish soon after evaluating the quality and quantity of the cargo/product, but is useful to evaluate contracts to secure maximum commercial value for each deal, post deal reconciliation, demurrage calculation and negotiations. The reports are cargo/activity specific for which fee for IVTC Services is arrived at/calculated after negotiations. These are admittedly customized services and not routine commercial services. Thus, the technical services provided to the customers/X India for which a fee is charged is covered under the term "fee for technical services" under section 9(1)(vii ).

The expenses incurred, whether in the form of reimbursement or sharing administrative cost, are in connection with the provision of IVTC services. For example, the invoice issued by X Thailand to PQR India Pvt. Ltd. for certification/inspection fee for "Injection Mould for foldable crate base" includes expenditure incurred on travelling, hard copy of the certificate and for additional copy of the report/certificate provided to the customer. The issue is not whether any amount over and above the expenditure incurred is charged. The crux of the issue is whether the expenditure is in connection with the IVTC services. When it is applicants own admission that it is in connection with the provision of IVTC services, then it makes no difference whether such expenditure is included in the fee or charged separately. The employees are seconded to render services. The expenditure is wholly and exclusively laid out to perform the IVTC services. Hence, the expenditure incurred even when it does not involve any element of profit, bear the same character as fee for technical services and chargeable to tax under section 9(1)(vii ).

Thus it is ruled as under :

(i) the payment received/receivable by the applicant in connection with IVTC services are taxable as FTS under section 9(1)(vii). The exception provided under section 9(1)(vii)(b ) is not available to the applicant.

(ii) The payments received/receivable in connection with the cost incurred and recovery of administrative cost for and on behalf of X India are chargeable to tax as FTS under section 9(1)(vii).

(iii) As the applicant has tax presence in India, X India/Indian customers are required to withhold taxes under section 195 at the rate in force mentioned in the Finance Act for the relevant year on the payment made/proposed to be made to the applicant.

(iv) As the applicant has taxable income in India, it is required to file tax return under the provision of section 139. [Para 9]
